Narrated by the Tiantai Śramaṇa Shi Yunkan.

The great compendia compiled by Nanshan number three in total: the *Shanbu Chao* (Excerpts Revised and Supplemented), the *Jieben Shu* (Commentary on the Precept Text), and this present commentary (*Shu*).
His various other writings likewise supplement these three works and assist in promoting the ultimate transformation [of sentient beings].

Once, during the intervals between lectures, I explored the depths of numerous scriptures and compiled records such as those for the *Shishi Chao*. One day, my disciples ascended the hall and prostrated themselves before me.
[The requester] said: "Regarding the single school of the Southern Mountain (Nanshan), the various records are already complete; however, the *Yeshu* alone has not yet been extensively expounded.

I wish for you to compose a record of it. I accordingly agreed and told him: "Now, *śīla* (precepts) is the sublime gateway to cessation (*śamatha*), while *karmavācanā* (ritual procedures) is the pure model for action (*pravṛtti*).
That the Compassionate One established these two is like the two wheels of a chariot. Formerly, I..."
The Patriarch practiced this before him and further composed a preface to broaden its path; yet, those who have driven forth its exposition in later times have been few.

It is a pity that the purport of this literature is profound and its principles subtle, its composition extensive and its meanings rich; were it not for one who draws it out and extends it, [the truth would remain hidden].
"Then I have failed the instructions of my ancestors; this is my fault. Among you, there may be one who inspires me, like Bo Shang (Yanzi) of the Confucian school.
The disciples performed the rites and withdrew behind the wall. Thereupon, [the Master] sat silently with his hand resting on his armrest, took up his brush, and composed this work.
He then reflected that the *Karmavācanā* was the distant source through which Tan-di first transmitted the lineage to Fa-zheng. Thus, it passed...

The record was completed the following year, and thus "The True Source" (Zhengyuan) was adopted as its title. May future masters of the great brush not reproach this work for the skills of a mere mouse.
Written on the third day of the first month of the third year of the Huangyou era of the Great Song (the Xinmao year), at the White Lotus Pond of Jingzhu Temple in Qiantang.

The three characters "Sifenlü" (Four-Part Vinaya) are the general title of this specific school; the following eight characters are deleted as they constitute a specific designation in this commentary.

Furthermore, while the [specific] Vinaya appeared only after one hundred years, it ought to have been placed later; however, the [general] Vinaya existed from the time of the Enlightenment and ought to have been titled first. Now, I say:

without the distinction of "one hundred years," there would be no means to differentiate it from the general category of the five schools; therefore, "Sifen" is designated first, followed by the subsequent [title].
This is the Vinaya. As for the phonetic meanings of the Sanskrit and Chinese terms, they are as explained in the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts).

Furthermore, the six characters at the bottom have been deleted, as they constitute the dharmas expounded within the four divisions [of the Vinaya]. These deletions and supplements were made according to the needs of the occasion; this is the practical application of Nanshan’s writings.

Where the text was redundant, it was excised; where there were omissions, they were supplemented. Now, taking what is essential, practitioners may draw upon it and extend its meaning. That which is not essential is simply...

It is merely a designation of names; therefore, it is said to be "according to capacity" (*yathā-vaineya*). *Karma* (羯磨) is translated as "action" (*karman*) in the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā-ṭīkā*;
that which is performed is action, and it is also translated as "that which is done. The *Śata-śāstra* calls it a "matter.

If one seeks its meaning, it is translated as "accomplishing a matter," meaning that when one performs and establishes a ritual according to the Dharma, there must be the merit of successful completion. A *ṭīkā* (疏) is a term for explaining the underlying intent; it is a detailed exposition.
It is also "decisive" (*jue*). It means to be clear, thorough, decisive, and expansive regarding the meanings of the text. Furthermore, the *Wenxin diaolong* states:

"A 'commentary' (*shu*) arranges the endpoints of the subject matter and captures the proximate meaning of the title. Regarding "preface" (*xu*), the *Shi guo* says: "The walls on the east and west are called *xu*. Guo Pu’s commentary notes:
"It is for the purpose of ordering and distinguishing between the interior and exterior. Moreover, "preface" (*xu*) also means "to narrate" (*xu*).
This describes the essential tenets of this sutra and the reasons for composing this commentary (*śāstra*). The *Erya* states: "To unfold, to perform, to follow, and to sequence are 'xu' (緒).

The commentary notes: "The four [aspects] also constitute the beginning or thread. Renfeng Gu stated: "The characters 'xu' (序) and 'xu' (緒) have the same meaning. As for 'xu,' it refers to the thread of a cocoon.
Whenever a cocoon is unwound to produce silk, one first takes its thread; only when the thread is exhausted does the [silk] become visible.
The threads are like the sequence of a classic; when the sequence ends, the classic is revealed. The Great Tang:
Hedang and Jinyang were the ancient fiefs of the dynasties of Tang and Yu.
When Shendao entered the Sui dynasty and received the abdication of Emperor Gong, he first proclaimed the state of Tang. Jingzhao is the name of the commandery of Chang’an. "Jing" means great.
"Zhao" (兆) refers to a number; since ten billion is called a zhao, the place where a billion or ten billion people reside is also called the "Jingshi" (京師).
"Shi" (師) means "multitude"; the capital where the Son of Heaven resides must be designated by its vast population. As for "Shamen" (沙門), it is sometimes called "Shamonana" (沙門那) or "Sangmen" (桑門);
in the language of Tang, it means "diligent cessation," signifying diligent cultivation of wholesome qualities and the cessation and extinction of all evils. Treasure.

The *Jijing* (Sūtra on Accumulation) states: "A śramaṇa is so called because he is tranquil and extinguished; because he is disciplined and subdued; because he receives the teachings; because his aggregate of precepts (*śīlaskandha*) is pure;
because he accords with reality as it is; because he has attained liberation; because he is free from the eight worldly dharmas; because his firm mind is immovable like the earth;
because he protects the minds of both others and himself; and because he is unstained by any external forms, being unimpeded like a hand moving through space."
Because he has accomplished such manifold dharmas, he is named a śramaṇa. Regarding the Great Master’s name and style: his name was Xuandao and his style was Fabian.

However, in poetry and books there is no avoidance of names, and when dealing with formal texts there is no avoidance of names; since the lecturer recites them in full, there is no fault. Furthermore, in the Western Regions (India), it is considered honorable to call someone by their name;
for instance, the names of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are invoked so that people may obtain merit by calling upon them. [This applies to] all karmic activities.

This is fully detailed in the *Xingzhuang* (Biographical Account) composed by Li Yong, as well as in the original stele inscription and the accounts within the *Sengzhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks).
Regarding Zhongnan Mountain, the *Fudi ji* (Record of Blessed Lands) states: "Zhongnan Taiyi Mountain lies fifty li southwest of Chang'an;
within forty li to its left and right, the entire area is a blessed land. As for Fengde Temple, according to the annotated text of the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts), it says:

At the end of Zhongnan Mountain, within the Feng Valley of Taiyi Mountain, Taiping was established as Fengde Temple. If the temple’s name is derived from the valley, how could it also possess "virtue" (de)?
Furthermore, one should know that both the *Jie* and *Ye* commentaries were composed there.

Moreover, these two commentaries, in their extensive and abbreviated versions, underwent a total of two revisions. The colophon states: "In the fourth year of the Zhenguan era, [the author] looked afar at the manifestation of transformation in the north."
He traveled through Bingzhou and Jinzhou, reaching as far east as the territory of Wei. There was the Vinaya Master Li, who was like a towering peak among his contemporaries.
[Daoxuan] relied upon him from afar to study the texts, but after only one month, Li passed away. The pain of my heart at this is beyond words.

He then returned to the mountains of Bishan County, where he produced another three fascicles of commentary for Vinaya Master Ze, further refining and polishing the previous draft so that its structural logic was complete.

He produced the *Xiangtong* (this is mentioned in the *Shichao*), as well as one fascicle of the *Shanbu Jie-mo*, two fascicles of its commentary, and one fascicle of the *Jieben* with its sub-commentary and three fascicles of its commentary (all of which were his initial compositions).
Later, when he went to Nanshan, those who delighted in the precepts requested that he expand upon the text;

consequently, he produced four fascicles of the *Jie-mo* along with its commentary. At the beginning of the Yonghui era, he further produced four fascicles of the *Jieben* with its sub-commentary and its commentary.
(These are all later revised editions). The edition currently being explained is the latter revised edition. As for "temple" (*si*), in Sanskrit it is called *saṃghārāma*, or *saṃgharāma*;
this is translated as "Garden of the Community. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that King Bimbisāra’s gift of the Gṛdhrakūṭa forest grove was the beginning [of such places].
"Garden" (*yuan*) carries the meaning of growth and cultivation; the sons of the Buddha dwell therein and are able to cultivate and grow the sprouts of the Path.

"Guo" (fruit) is its original meaning. Some call it *vihāra*, which here means "a place for wandering and staying. The current term "si" (temple) is a Chinese word. The *Shiming* (Explanations of Names) states:
"Si means succession (*sì*)," referring to those who manage affairs who succeed one another within it. There were nine such institutions in the state.
This was because in the tenth year of the Yongping era of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty, the year Dingmao, the Buddha-dharma first arrived; at that time, there was Kāśyapa Mātanga...
Zhu Falan arrived in Luoyang with scriptures and images transported on white horses. By imperial decree, he was received with honor at the Court of State Ceremonial (Honglu Si).
In the eleventh year, the Wuchen year, an edict was issued to construct a separate monastery outside the Yong Gate, named after the white horse.

This was the very beginning of Buddhist temples in the land of Han. Furthermore, during the Chiku era of Sun Quan, the Ruler of Wu, following the conversion by Kang Senghui, the Jianchu Monastery was established in Jiangnan as the first.
From this point on, monasteries (gārala) began to adopt specific names.
The term "zhuàn" (撰) means to narrate and to establish; it refers to the act of explaining the meaning of the texts to provide a definitive standard. Moreover, the *Book of Rites* says:
One who transmits is called "enlightened" (*ming*); one who creates is called "sage" (*sheng*). Confucius said, "I transmit but do not create"—this is precisely what is meant here.
The term "to observe" (*guan*) means to look upon; it serves as an introductory phrase and is also a word used to point toward a specific matter.
"The Sage" refers to Śākyamuni, the Great Sage. The *Liezi* quotes Confucius as saying: "In the West, there is a sage."
Thus, without governing, there is no disorder; without speaking, they have confidence in him; without transforming them, they act spontaneously.

Vast and expansive, the people are unable to give it a name. Regarding "it is advantageous to be seen": in the *Book of Changes*, the fifth line of the ninth hexagram reads, "The flying dragon is in the heavens;

it is advantageous to see the great man. Wang Bi said: "When the virtue of the dragon is in the heavens, it is the station of the Great Man. For position arises through virtue, and virtue [is manifested] through..."
Regarding the sequence of ranks: it is only fitting that one of supreme virtue should occupy the highest position, for all things to behold him is indeed appropriate.
Furthermore, Zhongni said, "When the Sage arises, all things behold him. Now it is said that when a Great Sage appears in the world, he is seen for the benefit of all sentient beings.

[The character] "miao" (wondrous) follows; by means of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world, we may infer that his benefit is wondrously profound, residing in the clarification of the Three [Baskets].
The afflictions and karma that bind one to the realms are extinguished, and the deluded attachments and calculations of self and person are eradicated.

Thereafter, great compassion is fully manifested and true wisdom is expanded; the boundless response is opened and the supramundane teaching is proclaimed—this is the fundamental intent of our Buddha’s transformation of the world.

"Hence" (*gù*) means "because"; it is a term used to introduce the subsequent explanation. "To open" (*zhāng*) means to expand. Regarding the Three Studies: *śīla* (precepts) is that which "seizes," corresponding to the study elucidated by the Vinaya;

*samādhi* (concentration) is that which "binds," corresponding to the study elucidated by the Sūtras; and *prajñā* (wisdom) is that which "slays," corresponding to the study elucidated by the Śāstras. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:
"Precepts are like seizing the thief, concentration is binding him, and wisdom is slaying him. These are the three practices.
They are mutually dependent. They provide immediate relief and support. As for the source, it is the origin of the stream. Regarding the Eightfold Noble Path (*aṣṭāṅgamārga*):
first is Right View (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), which means cultivating the sixteen aspects of the untainted (*anāsrava*) mind, thereby seeing the Four Truths with clarity.

Second is Right Thought (*samyaksaṃkalpa*), which means that at the time of seeing the Four Truths, thought associated with the untainted mind arises and is activated, causing awakening and knowledge to increase so as to lead one into *nirvāṇa*. Third is Right Speech (*samyagvāc*). By means of...

Through untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), one eliminates the four types of wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*) that comprise verbal action, because one abides in all forms of right verbal action (*samyagvāk-karmānta*).
Through untainted wisdom, one eliminates all bodily wrong actions, because one abides in pure right bodily action (*samyakkāya-karmānta*).

This constitutes the fifth [member], right livelihood (*samyagājīva*), through which untainted wisdom universally eliminates the five types of wrong livelihood within the three types of action, as one abides in...
Sixth is right effort (*samyag-vyāyāma*), because it consists of diligent and energetic cultivation of the path to *nirvāṇa* in conjunction with untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
Seventh is right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*), because it consists of the path of right mindfulness and its auxiliary factors in conjunction with untainted wisdom.

Eighth is right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*), because it consists of the eight concentrations (*samādhi*) in conjunction with untainted wisdom. These eight are collectively termed [the Eightfold Path].

Regarding the "Right Path" (*samyag-mārga*): "Right" (*samyak*) takes the meaning of distinguishing from what is deviant. Now, these eight factors do not proceed by relying on partiality or deviation;
thus they are all called "right. Because they can lead one through to *nirvāṇa*, they are called the "Path. Regarding the "four assemblies":

this refers to the four groups of followers—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—or alternatively, devas, nāgas, humans, and spirits. Regarding the "five groups": [these are] the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās...

The śrāmaṇeras and śrāmaṇerīs are also included. Furthermore, one should know that the Threefold Training and the Eightfold Path pertain to the teaching as the capacity to transform (the *nengbei* dharma), while the four groups and five assemblies refer to the sentient beings as the objects of transformation (*suobei* ji).

Moreover, pure instructions and excellent regulations also belong to the category of the Dharma. Regarding "crossing by wading" (*hengli*): the *Lunyu* states, "If it is deep, one wades across" (*shen ze li*).
Bao Shu explains: "To cross water wearing one's clothes is called 'wading' (*li*). Regarding "heavy gates" (*zhongguan*): Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states: "Gates..."
This is the "Gate on the Realm. It means that the sentient beings bound by the afflictions of the three realms are firm and dense; thus, it is like a heavy barrier.

[The Buddha] causes them to traverse the realms of the five destinies crosswise by means of the Dharma of the Three Learnings and the Eightfold Path, so that they may stride with lofty steps and soar through the heights of existence.
Thus one sees that the Great Sage’s dissemination of pure instructions and establishment of excellent regulations were not established in vain.

"Many positions. This refers to the aforementioned Dharma of the Three Learnings and the Eightfold Path. Regarding the fact that the precepts take precedence, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states:

"The practitioner must first apply themselves to studying the precepts to restrain and rectify transgressions; when the three karmas are pure, right concentration and right wisdom will naturally be established."
"Is it not so? This means that all wholesome dharmas take precepts as their foundation. "Vast and great. Regarding "relying on," the *Śālistambha Sūtra* (Yijiao jing) says:
"By relying on these precepts, one attains various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and the wisdom that extinguishes suffering.
If there is no pure precept, none of the various wholesome merits can arise."

There are two paths: transformation through practice (*xiànhuà*) and transformation through teaching (*jiàohuà*). The latter refers to the sūtras and śāstras, which are teachings that open, transform, and guide.

They encompass all seven assemblies of both humans and devas; hence they are called "the monastic and the lay. Now, in order to distinguish the heterodox from the orthodox and to give rise to faith and understanding, the *Shìshì cāo biéxù* states:

"The teachings of transformation apply universally to both the monastic and the laity; they generally clarify cause and effect and bring about the realization and mastery of what is heterodox and what is orthodox. Thus it is categorized.

Karmic actions are profound and subtle, difficult to discern; yet their resulting retributions are manifest and clear, easy to describe. Furthermore, the *Jie shu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states:

"The transformation [of beings] extends to both monastics and laity, and its names and principles do not conflict. Its intent prioritizes the stilling of inversions and the detachment from attachments. The essence of the teaching is to transform people."

Now, this opening of wisdom and understanding was not originally intended as a statement established in opposition to past views. Regarding the "Teaching on Practice" (*xingjiao*), it urges the fivefold assembly to guard their observance of the precepts.
The Separate Preface states: "The Teaching on Practice is restricted solely to the internal assembly;

it determines what is to be adopted or rejected, establishes its systematic framework, clarifies the nature of upholding and violating the precepts, and resolves doubts and obstructions. It further states: "Internal mental states of contrariness or compliance rely upon principle as their basis."

The fundamental principle follows the teachings of transformation (*parivarta-śāsana*). In outward conduct, one must necessarily guard body and speech by relying on the teachings of practice (*pratipatti-śāsana*).

Thus, while those who violate the teachings of transformation merely receive the retribution of a single path of karma (*karmapatha*), those who contravene the teachings of practice incur the additional gravity of offenses against the sacred regulations (*ārya-vinaya*).

Therefore, it should be understood that although the two teachings are distinguished, they are integrated within the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*) without confusion. As for the "three wheels," these refer to the miraculous powers (*ṛddhi-pāda*) and the preaching of the Dharma (*dharma-deśanā*).
This refers to mindfulness (*smṛti*). The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "The Tathāgata’s transformative activity necessarily relies upon the three wheels.

When first opening the path of practice, one must first employ the supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*) for those who lack faith. Once they have faith that he is a sage, although their bodies submit, there is no way for their wisdom to open;

therefore, he changes the sequence of his teaching to address those lacking understanding. Only when spiritual insight becomes clear can the fetters of affliction and delusion be severed; this cannot be accomplished through mere verbal instruction."
It can be cleared away. Since the meaning must rely on practice to achieve realization, one must maintain mindfulness lest it remain unverified.

Now, this training in the precepts (*śīla-śikṣā*) is subsumed under the "final wheel" (*paścima-cakra*); therefore, it is said that the three wheels are encompassed within mindfulness. Regarding the four collections (*catvāraḥ piṭakāḥ*):

in addition to the three collections, a fourth, the *Kṣudraka-piṭaka* (the Miscellaneous Collection, which comprises the twelve divisions of the scriptures), is added. The present teaching and practice correspond to the *Vinaya* among these four.

This constitutes one *piṭaka*. Regarding the phrase "in terms of meaning" (*yì xià*), the *Jièshū* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "The arising of practice and teaching must be due to transgressions; restrictions are established in accordance with these transgressions.

As for the terminology, it concerns only 'observance' and 'violation,' while the matters encompass both 'cessation' and 'action. Therefore, what is established by the teaching is not intended merely to still delusions, but rather to categorize conduct.

Thus, the single school of Vinaya is confined to this teaching. Regarding the phrase "following the text," in terms of the expressive text itself, it is subsumed within the collection of dharmas (*dharmaskandha*).

Regarding "Dharma-aggregate" (*dharmaskandha*): in Sanskrit it is *khandhaka*, which is translated here as "Dharma-aggregate. Since the original Vinaya contains twenty *khandhakas* and so forth, it is said that "following the text, one returns to and relies upon the Dharma-aggregate.
Regarding "the two types of wholesome conduct—cessation and performance": these refer to the observance of cessation (*nivṛtti-dhāraṇa*) and the observance of performance (*pravṛtti-dhāraṇa*).

Because these two modes of practice accord with the essential nature [of the precepts], and since that nature is not evil, they are termed "wholesome. As stated in the "Chapter on Observance and Transgression": "One guards [the precepts] through skillful means and right mindfulness..."

That which one originally undertakes—restraining the body and speech so as not to commit various evils—is called "cessation" (*shi*). Diligently exerting the three karmas to cultivate virtuous conduct and maintain protection against non-virtue is called "action" (*zuo*). "Name" (*ming*) is the guest of "reality" (*shi*); reality is itself practice. "That which accords with the occasion" (*ji*) refers to the present occasion; it means that the two virtues of cessation and action are termed the correspondence of practice. Because it distinguishes between the fundamental practices of cessation and activity based on the root of the Path, it governs and subsumes the essential principles of the Buddha-dharma.

"Later generations" refers to those who come after. "Exhortation" means to provide a formal encouragement. "Sublime" means that the essential subtlety lies solely in the two dharmas of the *Prātimokṣa* (the root precepts) and the *Karmavācanā* (ritual procedures).
"The Sun of Wisdom sets in the West" refers to the Tathāgata’s period of transformative activity nearing its end, as he manifested his entry into *nirvāṇa* at the Śāla trees. Thus, at the Śāla...

It can be known that all sentient beings suffer in the distress of darkness. Furthermore, the Dharma-water flowing eastward is intended to wash away the defilements of the minds of sentient beings.
The Buddha-dharma flowed from the West to the East; hence it is called "flowing eastward. Regarding the Semblance and True Dharma: the Buddha-dharma has three periods.

The True Dharma lasts for one thousand years, the Semblance Dharma for one thousand years, and the Final Dharma for ten thousand years. It was during the Final Dharma period that [the Master] appeared in the South Mountains.

It was already during the Age of Semblance (xiàngjì). Thus, the Preface to the *Chao* states: "By the time of the Age of Semblance, [the teaching] had become increasingly diluted and corrupt. It further says: "I was born and live in the final period of the Age of Semblance.
Regarding the terms "pure" (chún) and "thin" (bó): "pure" refers to correctness and integrity, while "thin" refers to frivolity and shallowness.
The two schools: The *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* states that these are the Sthavira (Elders) school and the Mahāsāṃghika (Great Assembly) school. Nanshan says:
"The Sthaviras and Mahāsāṃghikas were the first to split at the site of the council. The five schools:
The Dharmaguptaka, Sarvāstivāda, Mahīśāsaka, Kāśyapīya, and Vātsīputrīya schools emerged one hundred years after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata.

It is divided into eighteen [schools], which means that from among the twenty schools, the root has been removed and only the branches remain. This occurred approximately four hundred years after [the Buddha’s passing], when the division into twenty schools took place.
For details, see the *Abhidharma-viniścaya-saṃgraha-śāstra* (The Treatise on the Adherence of the Eighteen Schools). Regarding the five hundred schools, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there were five hundred heterodox schools who heard of ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*) and felt as if their hearts were wounded by a blade. At the end of the passage, "branches" refers to the multitude of sharp points.

"Mutually cited. From this point onward, as time passed and capacities declined, each vied with others to follow divergent paths; their number is beyond reckoning. Hence it is said they are "mutually cited.

The phrase "some people" refers to the various masters mentioned above. Beginning from the initial schism and ending with the myriad points of contention raised by each side, it is evident that they all diverged according to their respective conditions.
Nevertheless, they were all intended to assist in propagating the True Dharma and prevent its decline. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"Because of these differing views, factions support one another and engage in mutual disputes; yet through all of this, they will fully awaken to the Way. Furthermore, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* says: [and so forth].

"Ancient and modern" spans from the Cao-Wei period at its beginning to the Tang dynasty at its end.
"Regarding 'increasing and complicating' below: it refers to how Master Guang [of the Vinaya school] added to the wording of the request for alms (*yācanā*).

"Compassionate Proclamation" (*cīhào*). "Proclamation" (*hào*) is also written as "announcement" (*gào*). Liu Xi’s *Shìmíng* states: "When the superior issues an edict to the subordinates, it is called an 'announcement' (*gào*).

Since the Buddha’s words are words of awakening, and he causes the bhikṣus to know his intention, they are thus termed "proclamations" (*hào*). Furthermore, since the Vinaya Piṭaka flows forth from within the gate of Great Compassion, it is said: [as follows].

Having fully examined these matters according to the characteristics of each fascicle, it is clear that without accumulated study, they will remain difficult to comprehend even with sudden effort. Therefore, I now prioritize the general exposition of the single dharma of *karmavācanā*.

Regarding the essentials of this compendium, I feared that they might not yet be fully encompassed; therefore, I have separately set forth this method and compiled its texts to bequeath them to future students.

"Translated as 'activity'" (*ye*) refers to "active duty" (*ye-wu*); because all one hundred and eighty-four dharmas are entirely matters of performance and maintenance (*zuo-chi*).

It is also a matter of ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*). That which is "applied" consists of the Dharma as the agent of application, while matters such as the production of wholesome states and the cessation of unwholesome states constitute that which is applied.

Because of this *karma*, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished or saved. Regarding the term "briefly" (*lue*): "brief" means concise. This means that within the introduction, the general outline has been described in summary; it does not exhaust the Sage’s intent.
As one proceeds to the subsequent chapters, the essential meanings will be extensively expounded to open the path for study. From here on...

It means to eliminate the fetters and delusions. The Vinaya asks: "What is meant by training? It is to cause the three poisons to be exhausted.

Inferring from this, it is evident that ordained monks and nuns are truly a gathering of meritorious and wholesome dharmas; their exalted status above humans and devas is precisely due to this. Furthermore...
The Great Master said: "Now, one who receives the precepts transcends the defiled stream of ordinary and base beings and enters the precious rank of the noble assembly.
'Manifesting the lower' clarifies the virtue of the precepts: above, they serve as the seeds for the causes of the Three Vehicles;

below, they serve as the field of merit for the six realms of existence. The Great Master further said: "The reason they constitute a fertile field for the world is truly due to the essence of the precepts."

The internal and external stages of cultivation consist of the four internal ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and the three external ordinary beings, which belong to the stage of the Seven Sages. Regarding ordinary beings and noble ones (*ārya*):

in the Hīnayāna, those from the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*) upward who have entered the untainted (*anāsrava*) state are called noble ones; all below that are ordinary beings. In the Mahāyāna, according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, there are eight stages:
first, the stage of the five grades of disciples (external ordinary beings); second, the stage of the ten faiths (internal ordinary beings); third, the stage of the ten... [text continues]

The stages of abiding (the first stage of the noble ones): 40 practices (*caryā*), 50 dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), 60 grounds (*bhūmi*), 7th: equal enlightenment (the end of the causal stage), and 8th:

"Upholding" means being fully endowed with both substance and appearance, which is fit for the task of the gate of extinguishing evil. "Violating," however, means the substance is defiled.
"Purity of mutual characteristics" refers to matters that should give rise to the gateway of wholesome qualities (*kuśala*).
"The convergence of emotional sentiments and views" is one of the two aspects of the six harmonies (*ṣaḍ-sāmagrī*): when emotional sentiments are identical, the intention is harmonious;

when views are identical, they accord with a single correct understanding. "Superior goodness" refers to matters such as the arising of wholesome qualities, which are accomplished through harmony; this refers to their successful attainment.

"Subduing evil" refers to the cessation of unwholesome states and so forth; it is through patience (*kṣānti*) that such cessation is attained. Furthermore, harmony necessarily entails patience, and patience likewise encompasses harmony.

Since the cultivation of goodness and the cessation of evil require both harmony and patience, they must be fully prepared; here, however, they are treated specifically in opposition [to one another].

the commentary below concerns the reception of precepts (*upasaṃpadā*), etc.

Quelling heterodoxy is like the methods for dealing with those who are insane or deluded; silencing slander is like the methods for admonishing and banishing those who slander; repentance and eradication are like the methods for training in repentance and the removal of offenses.

"Obtainable by the Saṃgha" means that the Saṃgha may exercise autonomy over it, whether performing a formal act (*karma*) or acting according to circumstances. "Obtaining" above includes what is below;
that is, when there is no one present for a formal act of the assembly, one may perform it as a face-to-face or mental recitation (*manasikāra*). What is below does not supersede what is above;

the methods of mental recitation and face-to-face recitation cannot be administered by the assembly. Therefore, the lower is mentioned to demonstrate the method by which the upper may include the lower. Although [the text] says...

Below. As it is said, the essence of the *śīla* (precepts) is that they are performed by the assembly (*saṃgha*). Now, [this rite] being performed face-to-face (*pratyekam*) seems contrary [to that principle]. However, the manifestation of purification once every half-month is the same.
Furthermore, because this and that are performed in relation to one another, it is said that the dharma of the precepts mutually encompasses both self and other. The remainder follows below.

However, not all dharmas necessarily apply down to the level of the *zuo* (monastic attendants), such as the rites of boundary-establishment (*sīmā-bandha*) and receiving the precepts (*upasampadā*), which by principle must be presided over by the *saṃgha*;
therefore, it is said that these are restricted to their respective positions.

Regarding "coming and going with the mind bound," this refers to minor transgressions committed during the four modes of deportment; for these, the text permits a light confession through mental remorse (*citta-vinodana*) to ensure good fortune. And...
Regarding clothing and food, one should practice contemplation at every thought-moment;

on the occasion of the *Poṣadha* (confession of precepts), one should perform confession and so forth—these are "provisional witnesses," meaning that a single person acts as a witness. Now, because there is no such person, it is called a "deficiency of conditions. Regarding "waiting for a physical form," this means that the physical form has something upon which it depends.
If there is currently no person present, the principle dictates that one should perform mental recollection (*manasikāra*) to sustain the physical life.
Regarding the conditions for the giving of clothing: it is like the method for distributing the light belongings of a deceased person.

When there is no one within the boundary [to receive them], one may accept them through a mental resolve (*cittotpāda*) to alleviate the suffering of the physical form, provided that the mind harbors no other ulterior motives.

Regarding the formal declaration for the accomplishment of purification (*pratideśanā-samudācāra*): it includes, for example, the declaration for receiving the seven-day rule (*saptāha-vidhi*), the declaration for the various practices regarding *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, the declaration for entering a village, and so forth.
One maintains the confession by formally accepting robes and medicine, confessing *pāyattika* offenses, and even confessing grave *duṣkṛta* offenses.

Regarding "confession, relinquishment, and so forth," this refers to the rules for forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya) and other such dharmas; it includes the formal recitation of the precepts (poṣadha), the invitation for criticism (pravāraṇā), receiving offerings obtained by the Saṃgha, and receiving the clothing and belongings of the five groups of monastics who have passed away.

"Not different from the lower [category]. This explains the *pratideśanīya* (confession) performed through mental recollection (*manasikāra*). Originally, this was a rite performed before another person (*pratimukha*), but because there was no one present within the boundary (*sīmā*), it was opened as a mental recollection.

When one finds a person to perform the rite before them, that is its original status. Originally, it was for one person; others need not assemble. Therefore, it is said: "When a person is found, it is distinct from the assembly.

Regarding the mental recollection and the rite before another person performed according to the rules of the assembly (*saṃghadharma*), both take as their object that there is no one present within the original boundary. Next...

When opening the [Vinaya] for the first time, there was one case that was not included; these were all instances of a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*). Therefore, it is said: "In general, they are the same as this.

Because the *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses are the same, the *sthūlātyaya* is established by name within the middle and upper three categories of objects—namely, the great assembly, the small assembly, and the single person.

As for those who receive the precepts: there are differences in the procedure for receiving them. The preceptor calls the candidate into the assembly; they undergo questioning before the assembly, followed by the formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (one motion and three proclamations).
Regarding the relinquishing of the bowl, there is the practice of walking with the bowl. During the formal confession (*poṣadha*), the presiding confessor makes a formal announcement to the assembly.

Regarding the receiving of the *guṇa-cīvara* (merit robe), there is the procedure for appointing the five virtuous ones (*pañca-guṇa*) and the formal announcement (*jñapti*) for the distribution by those five virtuous ones, including the harmonious reception of the merit robe according to the Dharma.

Regarding the property of the deceased, there is the procedure for the distribution of the light goods (*laghu-dravya*) of the deceased according to the Dharma, and the method for appointing the five virtuous ones to perform the distribution.
Regarding the method for rewarding those who tend to the sick: although there are three or four methods starting from the bottom, they ultimately accomplish but one matter;

therefore, it is specifically designated as "one condition" (*ekapratyaya*). As the *Dà cǎo* (Great Commentary) states below the section on the ancients: "The *Śāriputrābhidharma* may also be cited; therein, there are definitely one hundred and one [items], totaling one hundred."
Thirty-fourth: regarding the conditions and categorized by their characteristics, there are in total one hundred and thirty-four *karmas*. To speak briefly, it is as follows;
yet when further expanded, there are thirty-nine *jñapti* (single-announcement), fifty-seven *jñaptidvitīya* (two-part announcement), and thirty-eight *jñapticaturtha* (four-part announcement).
If the fifty distinct rules (*pṛthagdharma*) are included, there are then one hundred and eighty-four rules.

Regarding the differences between monks and nuns: among the monks, there are the procedures for appointing a teacher for nuns, as well as the methods for receiving ordination and the confession of residual offenses (*śeṣa-āpatti*).

Among the nuns, there are the procedures for appointing those who seek instruction, the method for appointing those who go into the assembly of virtuous monks (*bhadanta-saṃgha*) to perform the invitation for self-examination (*pravāraṇā*), the method for dispatching messengers to receive ordination, and the method for appointing envoys.

Furthermore, there are matters such as the rule that nuns do not pay homage to monks; these are shared practices, namely the methods for receiving ordination and the confession of residual offenses. (2)
The "sections" (varga) refer to the monks and nuns.

Regarding the compilation of the various *śuklavāda* (white-clad) texts: for example, the accounts of being dispatched to the royal city to compile the Dharma; the questions posed to Upāli regarding the Dharma and Upāli’s answers regarding the Dharma;

and the questions posed to Ānanda regarding the Dharma and Ānanda’s answers regarding the Dharma. Since these were all composed through collective consensus after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, they are known [as such].
The matter is as stated, and it is also understood through principle.

Thus, below [the text says]: "Because one studies without weariness; being broad, one attains penetration. *Zhan* means "abundant. As the ancients said, "Extensive learning serves to alleviate poverty"—this statement is truly verified.
*Zi* means "to benefit. The *Dàcǎo* (Great Commentary) states: "If one has not yet at all participated in the Dharma, then according to..."

One section of the *Ren* (Ren-ji) serves as a support; following the text, one may reverently put it into practice and take it as a standard. "Comprehensive view" (*tōkan*) means to observe and contemplate.
"Reaching far" (*kyōen*) refers to its enduring legacy throughout boundless time. Because this comprehensive survey provides a basis for verification, it shall be trusted by future generations;
such is the utility of study. The *Daishō* states: "If the *Sifen lü* (Dharmaguptaka Vinaya) were deficient in matters of ritual and dharma..."
Other schools have their own explicit texts; in principle, one must follow them without deviation. Second is the "narrow view":
this refers to adhering to the perspective of a single school, which is like peering at the sky through a tube. The *Zhuangzi* says:
"This is simply using a tube to gaze at the heavens, or using a needle to point at the earth—is it not too small?"

There are three grades: the single motion (*jñapti*), the motion followed by one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*), and the motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*). Furthermore, the procedures for mental recitation (*cittānuvartana*) and face-to-face address (*saṃmukha*) are all consistent with the Vinaya.
"Seeking permission" (*yācanā*) refers to seeking the consent of the Saṃgha; this corresponds to what is stated below regarding the announcement of the matter to open the hearing.

It is also termed the "intermediate *karman*. The *Daochao* states: "Regarding the receiving of [extra] days, the various schools differ. In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there are two types: first, seven days..."
It is the same as in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. Once the subsequent matter is concluded, one then employs the intermediate distinct method (*madhyama-bheda-dharma*).

This is because there are no differing categories; it is also the same as in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* regarding the three categories of *karmavācanā*. As clarified here, an intermediate *karmavācanā* is not established separately; rather, the ten citations below serve as proof.
Since the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* does not set forth the names or characteristics of distinct methods among the collective rules (*saṃghadharma*), all distinct methods are collectively termed *karman*.
"Mò" (grinding/polishing). If the ancient masters say that "fifty" refers to distinct dharmas, this is not the fault of a lack of extensive knowledge.
"Suǒzuò" (that which is made) is viewed as the object for the Sangha to act upon. Regarding "Tángfàn" (Chinese-Sanskrit): "Fàn" (Sanskrit) should be treated as a transliterated character;

"qià" (pronounced kǔjiá) means "correct" or "precise," and thus it is so. However, the *Śata-śāstra* translates it as "matter" (*vastu*); since "matter" is precisely what is produced by action, it is so designated.
This is correct. The commentary explains that this refers to matters established by the *Satyasiddhi* school, or matters such as the establishment of regulations within the Saṃgha.
The question below explains the meaning of *karmavācanā* (formal act): because the Saṃgha listens with patience and does not obstruct it, the action performed is called *karma*.
This is also termed the "direct announcement method" (*jibai-hō*). Striking the wooden gavel refers to the present-day method of using the ritual mallet (*bai-chui-hō*).

Regarding the "one-part proclamation" (*jñapti-ekadeśa*): as stated in the ritual for the formal announcement (*jñapti-dharma*): "Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This bhikṣu, [Name], is observing the rains retreat here.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent; there is no need for a formal announcement. This is the first part. Furthermore, it says:

"This bhikṣu, [Name], shall go out of the boundary for the sake of the Saṃgha’s affairs or the Stūpa’s affairs, and will return to this place to observe the rains retreat. May the Saṃgha grant its consent..."
Because of silence, this matter is thus maintained. This is called one part of the *karmavācanā*.
The latter two refer to the *jñapti-dvitīya* and *jñapti-caturtha* [procedures], while the former three refer to the *kṛta-jñapti* (the single announcement) used in the interim.

According to what follows, it appears to be interrogative wording; "now" and below is the explanation. Regarding the modification of the phrasing: for example, when there are only three [monks], one simply changes the address to "Venerable Sirs. This principle applies universally.
There is no error. The treatise itself clarifies the treatise. That [text] states that the intermediate [form] is direct and plain; these three *karmas* may be performed by three persons or more.
The remaining two must necessarily involve four or more persons.

The nine kinds of dharmas refer to the three [categories] within each of the aforementioned three stages. The ten conditions refer to weighing the preceding matters up to the tenth, which is answering the dharma that has been accomplished.
Regarding the "establishment of the meaning" (*yǐngì*), this refers to encouraging those who will lecture and explain later on by citing the subsequent text to clarify what is presented here.
The following text provides an internal explanation among the seven types of "non-[proper] cases.

Third, regarding the "conjunction of animate and inanimate objects": it is said that animate and inanimate objects are conjoined. Here, the robe belongs to the inanimate category, while old age and illness belong to the animate category.

Building a house belongs to the category of non-sentient things (*asattva*). Regarding the giving of a bowl: one should simply pass it down through the succession of monks, taking it from below and handing the bowl to him.
To hold onto it now as a non-sentient thing is incorrect; for a person is a sentient being (*sattva*).

Regarding the mutual existence of "is" and "is not," these do not transcend the three categories of person (*pudgala*), phenomenon (*dharma*), and principle (*li*); all arise based upon one of these factors.

What is not established is termed a "fallacy" (*doṣa*), while the opposite is termed a "proof" (*siddhi*). This is analogous to the concept of "perception" (*saṃjñā*). Below, taking the act of receiving the precepts as the primary subject, if a person has no obstacles or impediments (*antarāya*), it is termed "real."
To falsely claim otherwise is termed "falsehood. Regarding those who break the precepts: if the *upādhyāya* commits an offense of *thullaccaya*, the other monks incur an offense of *dukkaṭa*.

This is self-affliction; to cause others to receive such affliction in vain is to afflict them. Furthermore, on the day of the invitation (*pravāraṇā*), to leave the boundary grounds in vain incurs public censure and obstructs the Path—all these are included.
Those with wisdom should apply these principles according to the circumstances; they cannot be exhaustively discussed.
"Generating wholesome [roots]" means generating mundane wholesome states of mind. "The field for supramundane [attainment]" refers to being a fertile field for supramundane results.

"Fruit and fruition directed toward the laity" means that among the laity there are those who have realized the fruits and those who are candidates for them. As for the bestowal [of precepts], it must necessarily be performed by one who has left the household life;
it requires the fivefold assembly to bestow them upon such a person.
"Comparing with the multitude" means comparing it to a multitude; this translates the name *saṃgha*. By adding the term "harmony," it becomes the "harmonious multitude.

Regarding the "Dharma, Buddha, and Saṃgha": here, the "multitude" is precisely the *saṃgha*. It is not established unless there are four [monks]. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that using the metaphor of four trees forming a forest does not clarify the meaning of the *saṃgha*.
Other sūtras do not mention *karmavācanā* (formal ritual acts) or the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*); this constitutes the meaning of harmony within the *saṃgha*.
Therefore, we follow the majority of translations.

Fearing that [the term] might be confused with "a group of two or three people," we use the single term "group" (zhòng) for the former, while adding the term "pair" (liǎng) for the latter. Nevertheless, even "pair" is fundamentally based upon a "group."
Now, regarding the following: if one relies on Confucianism, three people constitute a group; thus, the "Table of Meritorious Ministers" in the *Hanshu* states, "Three people form a multitude.
Here, "lǎn jiǎ" (seizing the provisional) refers to seizing the provisional function of form (*rūpa*). Now, four monks constitute the basis, seizing the function of harmony as the Sangha.
Therefore, it is said that their meanings are analogous.
Ordinary and Holy: "Ordinary" refers to those from the stage of the inner ordinary person downward; "Holy" refers to those from the Path of Seeing upward. Rite and Jewel:
"Rite" takes external form, referring to the maintenance [of the Dharma]; "Jewel" relies on the realization of truth, referring to the Jewel of Principle.

Function and Virtue: this refers to the power and application of merit. "Principle" is spoken of in terms of penetration and realization; "Affairs" is designated in terms of the six harmonies being without distinction. Capacity and Teaching: these are now...

Regarding the principle that the capacity for teaching is like water and milk being non-dual, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "It is like milk mixing with milk, or water mixing with water;

one cannot say 'milk mixes with water,' because their combination is merely of appearance (*lakṣaṇa*) and not of essence (*svabhāva*), as the goose is able to distinguish them. This applies to the [remaining] three types of persons; thus, it is said that for these three types of persons as well...

This is called a "group" (gaṇa). Furthermore, because a group of four is constituted by relying upon the three lower [numbers], it must likewise encompass all four to constitute the essence of the Saṃgha.

This is like gathering the fingers to constitute the lifting of the entire body. Since the conditions for its formation are present, even one, two, or three persons fully possess the conditions for the four;
therefore, it is said below that these [lower numbers] share the meaning of being a "group."

The *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā* treatises [state that] the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are the real dharmas, such as form (*rūpa*), which distinguish them from provisional, conventional forms, such as the form of a single karmic retribution (*ekabhavika-rūpa*).
Their distinct functions are like the way a single person simultaneously employs various mental states as distinct functional dharmas. These are not obscured (*anivṛta*).

This refers to the direct perception of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). They are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), because one form and three minds have not yet flowed into the mind of formation (*saṃskāra-citta*); all belong to the indeterminate.

Regarding the maintenance or violation [of precepts], it is said that they must flow into the mind of formation to constitute a distinct cause. This clearly indicates that the five aggregates as substantial dharmas (*dravya-dharma*) serve as the essence.
As for the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), it is subsumed under the wholesome aggregate of formations.
The "person" (*pudgala*) is provisional; it takes as its essence the provisional application of skillful means arising upon real dharmas.
Because real dharmas belong to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and do not extend to the wholesome or unwholesome, they are said to be "without function. The "aggregates" (*skandha*) are fundamental;

that is, provisional [designations] arise upon the real, and since the provisional still relies upon the real, it is like the example given below. The movement of body and speech is provisional; the matter and sound obtained through retribution are real.
Furthermore, the "retribution-form" (vipākavarṇa) serves as the basis for the aggregates (skandha), while "agitation" (sphuraṇa) is a metaphor for their provisional function.
Now, regarding the section below: this follows the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra) and aligns with the tenets of the *Dharmaguptaka* school; both belong to the Emptiness school (Śūnyavāda).

However, although it is stated below that the Vinaya and the *Tattvasiddhi* share the same tenets, it does not say that the provisional function constitutes the essence (svabhāva); it merely cites one person's view.
This continues up to the assembly of twenty; as it differs from what precedes, I have not cited it at length.

Nevertheless, since none of the five preceding sections provide a definitive resolution, I shall now evaluate and infer based on their underlying meaning. By way of numerical convention and provisional application, the internal and external elements mutually require one another, and their essential flavor remains the same;
this is what I take as my position (reflect upon this).
There are three roots: seeing, hearing, and suspecting. Regarding "holding and explaining," this refers to holding [the robe] and explaining [the medicine].
If one does not meet the required number for the Saṃgha, nor even the number for an individual, then "equal" refers to taking twenty monks.
Regarding the section on Legal Affairs (*dharmakārya*): this is discussed solely in terms of the number of people actually assembled for the specific legal procedure at hand.

As for "both the agent and the object being the substance" (*tattva*), this means that both the speaker and the listener together constitute the substance [of the ritual]. For example, in the *Poṣadha* ceremony with four monks, one acts as the speaker (*vaktṛ*) and three act as the listeners (*śrotṛ*).

Excluding those who are the objects of the action—such as those who have received a formal authorization (*anujñāta*) to attend—they do not belong to the substance of the monastic community (*saṃgha*) that performs the rite.

Regarding "neither collectively nor individually": the Sangha-dharma is not distinguished by individual [dharma], and the individual dharma is not distinguished by the Sangha. Therefore, the *Dai-shō* states: "The Sangha merely possesses the dharma for governing the assembly;
apart from this, regarding the *pratimokṣa* (confession before another) and *manasikāra* (mental recitation) dharmas and their respective matters, one must certainly not perform them as a collective.

To do so would constitute an individual dharma, which likewise is not established. Each category is distinguished according to its own sphere; the communal dharma and the individual dharma each have their own proper domain."

"Examining the lower [section]" correctly clarifies the general discussion of the three conditions within their respective categories: namely, "one person," "many people," and so forth. Regarding "monastic order" (*saṃgha-krama*), it cites scriptural evidence for the case of "one person.

As for "the function being extremely great," it is like eating in a separate group (*pṛthag-jana-bhojana*); if even one person can enter, one avoids the fault of a separate group. Is this not a case where one person benefits the multitude?
"Throughout the boundary" and below refers to the assembly of monks from across the entire boundary; if [the number] is not yet complete...
One who performs the communal rites through mental recollection—once these rites are accomplished—is equal to those who perform the communal rites with hundreds of thousands of people.
To "spread the teaching" means to propagate the true teaching; thus, one is the same as many.

There is a "lower" [section]. This concludes the four preceding meanings. However, by initiating the subsequent [section], the dharma to be explained is established; that is, only when the six harmonies (*ṣaḍ-samaya*) are complete does the meaning of the *saṃgha* (monastic community) arise.
The sutra is the *Avataṃsaka*.
Right Precepts. Because precepts are correct, they can serve as the fundamental basis for pure wisdom. Furthermore, pure precepts are the foundation for all virtues.
"Receiving together" means sharing the same essence of reception; "practicing together" means sharing the same subsequent conduct. There may be deficiencies.
Those who are deficient in the requisite conditions do not constitute the Saṃgha. "Identical vision" (*dṛṣṭi*) refers to the wisdom (*prajñā*) arising from the same correct view;
it does not refer to the false wisdom of the sixty-two views held by heterodox persons. Regarding "identical realm but distinct dharmas":

although they belong to the same realm, each performs their own ritual acts (*karmavācanā*) without transgressing against one another, as they remain distinct. For example, the faction of Devadatta does not enter the Saṃgha of correct vision.
Furthermore, "pure conduct" refers to practicing in harmony with others. One should sustain one's life by remaining free from the four and five types of wrong livelihoods.
"Incompatibility with benefit" means that because of wrong livelihood, the benefits one receives become discordant.
The "three superiors" refer to precepts, views, and livelihood. The "three karmas" refer to the harmony of body, speech, and mind. Harmony of body means dwelling together;

harmony of speech means remaining silent in unison; harmony of mind means sharing mutual forbearance. If the first three [superiors] are identical in substance while the latter three [karmas] are not in harmony, this likewise violates the meaning of the *saṃgha*.

Regarding "virtue" (de) and "function" (yòng): the three natures constitute virtue, while the three harmonies constitute function. Furthermore, within both the natures and the harmonies, there are respectively virtue and function;
therefore, they are spoken of in combination.

The "three positions" refer to matters of great, medium, and small importance. The "three dharmas" refer to the procedures for mental recollection (*cittānuvartana*), face-to-face confession (*pratyakṣa*), and the assembly (*saṃgha*).

The "three types of assemblies" refer to those consisting of one person, many persons, and four or more persons. Regarding the classification of persons according to different rules: where there are four persons, the *Poṣadha* (recitation of the precepts) may be performed;

where there are five persons, one may be dispatched alone to perform the *Pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults) for the five virtuous qualities. In border regions, five persons suffice; in the Central Kingdom, ten are required.

Regarding the reception of the precepts and so forth, it is abbreviated to five or ten people. Among these, the former two groups—four and five people—are designated by the name "Dharma" (the formal procedure) when contrasted with the latter.

Thus, the term refers to the Dharma; it is applied using only four or five members. This is because, in the *Poṣadha* ceremony, since there is no one to perform the recitation or to listen to it, the rite is accomplished by mutual binding through the use of four members.
In the *Pravāraṇā*, however, one person is appointed as the *pañcavarga-guṇa* (one endowed with five virtues), and their name is formally announced.
They enter the Dharma but do not enter the count of the Saṃgha; therefore, five must be present to administer the punishment and receive the confession for the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

This is because the presiding confessor (*sāṃghika-vinayadhara*) performs the formal motion (*jñapti*) alone and does not enter the count. As for "the one who brings forth the evidence," this refers to the person of fivefold virtue who is appointed to bring forth the charge against the offender.

"Certifying and receiving the assembly of monks" means that these individuals serve as witnesses to those who have committed offenses. Furthermore, they receive the confession master to witness his repentance for his transgressions.

Regarding the latter two cases—namely ten people and twenty people—they receive their subsequent titles in contrast to the former. As for "following the circumstances," the Central Kingdom (Madhyadeśa) established the rule of receiving the precepts from ten people;

this was because, as the monastic community there is large, there was concern that the recipient might become negligent. When there are many people present, a sense of earnestness and respect will surely arise. Below...
It is said that this is because their virtuous minds are distracted and impure. Furthermore, twenty people must perform the repentance for the transgression;
since the offender’s state of mind was grave, they must increase the number of those receiving the precepts by one-and-a-half times before they can be saved.

Regarding "central and peripheral regions": in the central lands, one receives [the precepts] with ten persons; in the peripheral regions where the Sangha is scarce, it is permitted to receive them with five persons.

Because one receives the essence [of the precepts] by following the lower [number] in relation to the higher, it is called "following" (*anuvartana*). Regarding "second, single-minded application": being free from transgressions from the outset is termed "single-minded application."

Having committed an offense, to give rise to remorse is called the second [stage]. In the presence of those who are diligent, one may perform the *poṣadha* with four persons; in the presence of those who have given rise to remorse, one may effect the removal of the offense (*āpatti-vyutthāna*) with twenty persons.

Regarding the statement that fewer than four do not constitute [a formal assembly]: it is because the Great Sage knew that for three or fewer persons, their power was not yet sufficient and their task was not yet complete;
therefore, he limited the number to four.

"Receiving [the precepts] in a border region" refers to receiving the precepts in a frontier area. The section beginning with "But below" clarifies the reasons for employing the five [qualities]. When there is no verbal expression, purity is not manifested;

only when the five qualities are present and there is no verbal expression is purity manifested. The above explains that the *pravāraṇā* (self-invitation) requires these five. The section beginning with "Below" explains receiving the precepts in a border region. Regarding the specific inquiry:
one delegates the master of decorum (*viniya*) to descend to the altar to pose the questions and report back, while the master on the upper altar summons the śrāmaṇera to enter.

The assembly is harmonious and pure. When receiving [the precepts] beforehand, one is indeed able to receive them; however, because the scope of the five-member *saṃgha* is limited, there is room for the arising of arrogance toward them.

If the number is increased to ten, the objective field becomes superior and the mind more intense, thus the precepts can be generated. "Floating sentiment" refers to a state where the mental disposition is buoyant and arrogant.
"Receiving in the middle" means receiving in the central region. "The three groups of monks" refers to groups of five, ten, or twenty people.
"Intensity and mildness" means that the latter is intense while the former is mild. "The preceding boundary" refers to the boundary of the three groups of monks.
"Just as" [indicates] that the three grades—namely seven days, half a month, and one month—may be understood by analogy through the principle of doubling.

The same as the five [monks]. In border regions, the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for self-criticism) may be performed by five people; this is the same as the other case. It is reduced by half—that is, reduced by half compared to the Central Kingdom.

According to the formal objection below, the meaning is: "Since the reception [of the precepts] is permitted for five in border regions, should the confession of a *śeṣa* offense also be permitted for ten people?
This refers to the *jīhòu* (the celestial sphere), which corresponds above to the celestial wheel (*cakravāṭa*) without any discrepancy, thereby observing the timing.

Furthermore, we now merely adopt the ritual procedures that deviate from the original intent of the teachings; namely, the reduction of the number of participants for minor offenses due to urgent circumstances.

Therefore, this is not treated as a general opening [of the rule]. Regarding the exclusion of those in the Central Kingdom (*madhyadeśa*): if the Vinaya stated "excluding," it would clearly indicate that the number is opened to ten for those in the border regions (*pratyantajanapada*).

Since there is no such exclusion here, both the Central Kingdom and the border regions require twenty people for the *śeṣa-saṃghāvaśeṣa* (residual saṃghāvaśeṣa) confession. The *Dàshù* (Great Commentary) refers to the *Shǒushù* (Initial Commentary).

"Morning and evening reflections" refers to the six morning recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*), the confession of minor transgressions (*laghu-āpatti*), and so forth. "Various announcements" (*śuddha-vijñapti*) refers to the announcement of entering a village (*grāma-praveśa-vastra*), the declaration of purity regarding medicine (*bhaiṣajya-śuddhi*), and so forth.
"Various bindings and releases" pertains to formal acts consisting of one motion and one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).

Examples include the binding of two [robes] together as three small ones, and by the "etcetera," the rules for constructing dwellings and distributing robes are included. As for those that do not interpenetrate: for instance, the six recollections cannot be performed in response [to such formal acts].
The same applies to the *pratimukha* (face-to-face) procedure for the *śīrṣa* (head) and the *saṃghabhinna* (schism), etc.
It should be understood that these apply downward; there is no higher dharma that can be applied downward.

As for lower dharmas, they cannot be applied upward—this refers to the matters mentioned previously. It is likewise [the case] when one is permitted to perform the *pratimukha* and *manasikāra* (mental recitation) procedures.
Regarding the category of persons (*pudgala-viṣaya*): this applies generally to one, two, three, or four persons. It is divided into three types:

the formal assembly procedure (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*), the procedure for an assembly with a specific interlocutor (*sāṃghika-praṭimokṣa-karman*), and the mental recitation (*cetanā-manasikāra*). Since these three positions have been established, there ought to be differences according to the conditions for their performance;

yet it is not known which is incorrect, nor the relative frequency of each. "Many" refers to cases of four or more persons; "few" refers to only three, two, or one person. This applies to the subsequent sections as well.

There are two types of *pratimukha-manasikāra* (recitation by two facing individuals). Third is the *pṛthag-jana-dharma-pratimukha-manasikāra* (the method for a separate assembly involving recitation by two facing individuals).

The *saṃgha* is restricted to essential formal acts (*karmavācanā*) within a defined boundary (*sīmā*). This applies to both the specific and the general; it pertains exclusively to the establishment of boundaries because the transmission of *chanda* (consent) is not permitted therein.

First, because the ground is weak and cannot support [the ritual]; second, because one must know the limits of the boundary. Regarding other dharmas, some are opened while others are closed; there is no opening [for them].

This refers to the meaning of *chanda* (consent). There are three distinctions. The Vinaya states: "Those who should come must come; those who should give their consent (*chanda*) must give their consent and come;
and those present must not be censured by anyone. This is called *sāmagrī* (concordance). The opposite of these three forms of concordance constitutes a *pṛthag-jana* (a separate assembly).

If one faces the assembly below, this refers to facing a great multitude. Among the three aforementioned distinctions, there is simply an absence of the second type; in both the preceding and following cases, [the same applies].
These two types coexist. If one applies them to a single person, they constitute the "mental recitation" (*manasikāra*) and the "recitation before another" (*sammukhībhūta-manasikāra*);
they differ only in that one is individual (*pratyeka*). In the text, the character "against" (*duì*) merely carries the sense of "in relation to" or "facing toward."
For half a month: one should immediately perform the *mānatva* penance for half a month. Regarding the "one announcement and inquiry," this refers to the time when one asks before the assembly.

Each performs their respective communal rites; that is, each performs the formal act within their own assembly and dispatches a messenger. This is like requesting instruction: it is the nuns who dispatch a messenger to the monks.
One endowed with the necessary virtues should provide the instruction; this refers to the monks being dispatched to the nuns. Upon reaching the respective communities...

The two assemblies of monks and nuns: "assembly" (bu) here refers to a group or category. "Facing one another" means performing the ritual in person; it does not mean performing the ritual while facing away from them.

The first three [cases] refer to receiving the precepts, the half-monthly confession, and the expiation of offenses. The section beginning with "a group of twenty" cites specific instances as evidence.

Regarding the "one aspect," the text mentions monks being addressed by nuns but does not explicitly state nuns being addressed by monks; these shall be clarified according to their respective sections. The passage beginning with "the Vinaya says" explains this point.
These are methods not common to others. Upon receiving and reciting [the precepts], if a nun does not understand them, she is permitted to receive and recite them within the assembly of monks;
having returned to her temple, she should then perform them according to her own section.
"Receiving the precepts," etc.—the "etc. includes the two methods of expiating offenses every half-month. "Not bowing":
not bowing upon seeing the Saṃgha, not speaking, and not showing respect—these three methods must not be performed face-to-face; they may only be administered at a distance.

Furthermore, according to the following passage, this one method likewise is not face-to-face, but is performed for a nun at a distance because it violates the rules regarding the relinquishing of instruction by the Saṃgha.

There are three [methods]: namely, face-to-face confession (*pratimukha*), confession before an assembly (*sāṃghika*), and mental recollection (*manasikāra*). Furthermore, there are these three types of procedures for an assembly. Regarding two or three people, this refers to confession within a small group.

As for a single person, one may only confess minor offenses of the *duṣkṛta* (light) grade; if it is an offense of the medium grade, one must employ the procedure of confession before a single person.

Thus, there would be no authoritative teachings to rely upon, were it not for three dharmas: namely, the reception of the precepts (*upasaṃpadā*), the invitation to criticism (*pravāraṇā*), and the removal of offenses (*āpattivyutthāna*).
There are four types of *saṃgha*: that consisting of four persons, five persons, ten persons, and twenty persons.

Regarding the identity of form and dharma: it is identical in form to shaving the hair and mounting a white horse; it is identical in dharma to the white [robes] received upon leaving the household life and receiving the ten precepts.
Among the offenses of causing provocation, because of the prior act of frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*), one subsequently commits bodily frivolity, thereby gravely provoking the Saṃgha.
The various regulations include: the formal announcement regarding the acceptance of the *kaṭhina* robe during times of difficulty, the abbreviated *pravāraṇā*, and so forth;

the appointment of individuals, such as the appointment of those to announce grave offenses (*sthūlātyaya*) or the appointment for the distribution of bedding and furniture; and the application of circumstances, such as the rules concerning the returning of robes or being separated from one's robes.

The procedures for assigning dwellings, the method of instructing the construction of rooms, and so forth—all these employ the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation).

The "seven methods" refer to the seven *karman*s, namely: reprimand (*tarjanīya*), banishment (*pravāsanīya*), dependence (*niśraya*), prohibition from entering the homes of laypeople (*apravāsanīya*), and so on.

"Admonition and proof" refers to the four types of admonitions, such as the exclusion of those who violate [the rules], and the proofs—namely, the formal means of correct knowledge through recollection (*smṛti*), the state of being non-deluded (*amūḍha*), and the locus of the offense (*sthāna*). The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes...

This refers to the remaining methods for undertaking the *śikṣamāṇā* training, the method for receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), and the various methods for repentance. All of these are performed by means of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations).

Thus, although the rules are numerous, they are comprised within thirty-nine *jñapti-eka-karman* (formal acts consisting of a single motion), fifty-seven *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (formal acts consisting of one motion and one proclamation), and thirty-eight *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.
Those subsumed under the latter two do not exceed the two types: the same recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) and the same formal act (*karman*).

This refers to the inclusion of the Saṃgha. Regarding the "four or fewer": since four persons collectively administer all dharmas, it is only because of the magnitude of the matter that the number is increased to five, ten, or twenty persons.

The "first saṃgha" refers to the four-member saṃgha. Excluding the three formal procedures (karmas)—namely, the five-member, ten-member, and twenty-member procedures—the "doubling of the three" refers to the five, ten, and twenty members, each being a double increment of persons. This excludes the three types of single-announcement (jñapti) procedures.

Excluding the *pravāraṇā*, the fivefold virtuous qualities for harmonizing the Saṃgha, and the two types of *jñapti* (the invitation and the two *jñaptis*), these are all subsumed under the category of the five persons (namely, the harmonization and the two *jñaptis*).

Among the two *jñaptis*, the four [karmas] include the *jñapti-caturtha* for the removal of offenses (*āpatti-vyutthāna*). Regarding "the three dharmas that are universally applicable," this refers specifically to the universal application of the three aforementioned single *jñaptis* (*jñapti-ekakarma*);
the others are not so applicable. The section "Based on the Matter" (*vastu*) correctly elucidates the meaning of the three single *jñaptis* and the two *jñapti-caturthas*. The three *jñaptis*.

The *śikṣādattaka* (one undergoing instruction) makes one formal motion (*jñapti*). The instructor makes one formal motion to summon him. He undergoes one formal motion for the interrogation before the assembly.

Only after these formal motions of reconciliation is he considered a master of the five virtues; having completed the formal motion of reconciliation, he returns to the count and shares the same status as the other monks.
The four-member saṃgha is established because the instructor is not counted among the number; thus, it is accomplished by only four persons.

As for the five-member [saṃgha], the novice being summoned to receive instruction is included in the count, and furthermore, the *karmavācanā* master who joins the saṃgha to pose questions is also included in the count;

therefore, it is said to be subsumed under the five-member saṃgha. If one relies on the formal reception [of precepts], it should be accomplished by four persons; this matter must be asked separately.
Therefore, five persons are employed.

The Preceptor (śikṣācārya) is the Karmavācanā-preceptor who confers the precepts; his status is not "inferior," which clarifies that he does not fall within the counted number [of the five], yet he alone presides over those who are inferior.

It must be clarified that the meaning of "entering the number" (of the quorum) is as follows: because the preceptor performs the formal motion (*jñapti*) to harmonize the Saṃgha on behalf of the Saṃgha, he does not constitute a separate entity [within the count].
Once the invitation is completed, the formal motion is made to invite harmony and to state any dissent;
since both [the motion and the response] occur within the Saṃgha, the preceptor together with the other four persons constitute the group of five.
Regarding the receiving of the robe: one who receives the *guṇa-cīvara* (robe of merit) does not receive the benefits; that is, they do not receive the five privileges.

As for "one who acts as the presiding monk from beginning to end": this means that from the initial stage of being able to preside over the *saṃgha*, until the conclusion, one is still termed a presiding monk.
