This may be termed "inclusion by the Saṃgha. If the preceding and succeeding [members] mutually enter [the quorum], then five persons must be present to fulfill the function of the Saṃgha;

this is precisely what is intended. Observing the intention of the ancients, it seems that the inclusion of four persons refers to the previous category. The Master’s current point of clarification can be understood as follows:
when a formal announcement (*jñapti*) is made for the sake of another, there must necessarily be four other monks outside of one's own person.

It is not necessarily required that they sit together, as the long robe (saṃghāṭī) is used to separate them during the overnight stay. Regarding the entry into the assembly with dignified deportment, this refers specifically to the *śikṣādāyaka* (instructor);

it is entirely distinct from the role of the *pratideśanācārya* (confession master), whose formal announcement (*jñapti*) and consultation with the Saṃgha are not required here. This inquiry appears to accord with the ancient tradition regarding the confession of transgressions.

Since no one is capable of presiding over the two rites of the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) and the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*), it is permitted for one who is undergoing penance (*śikṣādattaka*) to preside;
however, such a person does not count toward the required quorum. This may be taken as a precedent.

Regarding "receiving [precepts] at the borders": in border regions, one must have five persons to receive the precepts; for the thirty *naiḥsargika* offenses involving forfeiture and confession, five persons are likewise required.

Thus it is said, "all *naiḥsargika* [offenses]. This is not the same as the case below, because those who establish the boundary by proclaiming its characteristics and those who recite the *Poṣadha* act on behalf of the *saṃgha*;
they are not subject to measurement by others. "When four are complete, one may proceed" means that once the number of four is reached, one may then carry out the action.
Because both self and others follow this same rule, it is necessary for practical matters;
"necessary" means that it must be employed. Why is it not listed? Within the context of the fourfold assembly, it simply states that three things are excluded:

namely, the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, receiving ordination in a border region, and the removal of offenses (*āpatti-vyutthāna*). Why does it not say that the establishment of a boundary (*sīmā-bandha*) is also excluded? Because...
Because there is a person who proclaims the boundaries (*sīmā*) within the consecrated area, it should be understood that five people are required based on this.

Regarding the phrase "some people say" (*yǒurén xià*), this is the first interpretation: it means that the Vinaya text provides a brief enumeration, not implying that others are excluded from the list.

He then said, "It is not permitted. He selected and reduced the number by half, leaving five people. Those who are single-mindedly diligent and do not commit offenses constitute the second [category].

As for those who have committed an offense, they must perform repentance; only after the second *śukla-dharma* (pure dharma) arises can they proceed. Thus the text says: "There are two kinds of wise people: first, those who are single-mindedly diligent and do not commit offenses;
second, those who, having committed an offense, are able to repent. This refers to the person in whom the second *śukla-dharma* has arisen.

Furthermore, regarding the *sīmā-bandha* (delimitation of boundaries): although there is a person who proclaims the boundary marks (*cihna*) during the delimitation, and there is a person who receives the *kaṭhina* robe during the *kaṭhina-utsarga*, both act on behalf of the *saṃgha* and are thus included within the fivefold *saṃgha*.
However, those who are not the primary persons for whom the rite is performed are all included within the fourfold *saṃgha*.
The "four assemblies" (*catur-nikāya*) refers precisely to these four groups of persons. This is because the *poṣadha* has no primary person for whom it is performed; therefore, [all] are...

Regarding "the person being saluted": as for the phrase "insulting the person being saluted," the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* cited within the section on the precepts concerning administrators (*karmadāna*) states this.
The *Zhiguī* (Pointing Back) says: "The term 'saluting' takes its name entirely from the act of receiving the command. It is included among the four persons because it is for the sake of the Saṃgha;

it does not belong to those whose actions involve mutual entanglement with the Saṃgha. When the formal proclamation is made above, it is a distinct proclamation similar [to others]. Once one has entered the state of the Saṃgha, there is entanglement."
Below the section on the five hundred [monks]: He asked, "If three or four persons practice the path, may they establish a boundary (sīmā) while staying in the homes of laypeople?
The answer was: "They may not. Five or more persons may establish one. This is a critical examination;
it does not adopt the theory of the five hundred [monks]. As for "entering the teaching," this refers to the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedure).
"Four monks" refers to a *saṃgha* of four persons. As for "three persons," this includes the single person, the group of many, and the four persons.

Regarding the "three methods"—namely, the mind-only (*cittamātra*), the face-to-face (*pratyakṣa*), and the communal (*sāṃghika*) procedures—they all encompass the *saṃgha* because the four-person assembly is capable of performing all *karmavācanās*.

If that is so, why are the latter three [categories] necessary? This is explained as being from five persons downward. The "eight persons" mentioned by ancient masters is an erroneous interpolation; it refers to the confession [of offenses].
The middle-grade *pārājika* offense involves a small group; the upper-grade *pārājika* must be confessed by doubling the number of four people.

The preparatory stage (*upakrama*) for a *pārājika* is itself the preparatory stage of the *pārājika*. According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Ten Recitations), it states that for the upper-grade *pārājika*, one confesses before the entire Saṃgha assembled within the boundary (*sīmā*).
For the middle-grade, one confesses with a small group outside the boundary. For the lower-grade, one confesses alone. Originally, there were not eight people [required].

The *mù* (sections/categories) are fourfold: the assemblies consist of four people up to twenty people. There are only three types of formal procedures (*jñapti*): the single-announcement (*ekajñapti*), the two-announcement (*dvijñapti*), and the four-announcement (*caturjñapti*).

The first assembly is that of four monks; the remaining three refer to groups of five and so forth. "Pure and turbid" refers to thickness and thinness [of the assembly]. When the mind is light but the offense is heavy, it depends upon the objective condition (*ālambana*).

Because it is superior, it causes that mind to become strong. Because it relies upon many conditions, it uproots those heavy offenses. Regarding "matters" (*kāraṇa*): in relation to the Saṃgha, they are called matters. The word "and" (*ca*) is a connective particle;
however, when one simply says "the matter of the *Poṣadha* recitation," it is certainly not necessary to go so far as to mention both.

"Various assignments" (*karmika-viniyoga*) refers to the assignment of bedding and furniture, the assignment of receiving the *Pravāraṇā*, and so forth. "Various formal acts" (*saṃghakarma*) refers to the formal acts for establishing the boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*) and so on.

Regarding the *dhātu*, the *sīmā*, and the *kṣudrasīmā*, as well as the methods for settling disputes—namely, *tarjanīya* (reprimand) and *pravāsanīya* (expulsion)—and the methods for admonishing, namely the four types of admonitions for transgressions:

the meaning of the question below is that within the legal acts (*dharma*) being performed, one does not discuss the essential nature (*svabhāva*) but focuses on the specific matter (*vastu*); whereas within the Saṃgha performing the act, it is necessary to state the essential nature.
Since you have already granted that the "essence" (tattva) is being discussed, why limit it to only four people? Could not five people also be said to constitute the essence?
For they are the basis of the Saṃgha, and the "basis" (mūla) is precisely the essential nature (svabhāva).

Regarding the formal act (*karmavācanā*): just as the presiding master (*karmadāna*) performs a single announcement (*jñapti*) on behalf of others, for this reason he is not counted among the number of the *saṃgha*.

There are three types of *saṃghas*: namely, those of five, ten, and twenty members. Because the former four constitute the basis, it is like branches and leaves which, though lush, must rely upon a root;
therefore, the former receives the name "the basis" (*mūla*). This refers to the actual substance of the announcement itself; each case should be treated as a single announcement (*jñapti*).

The second [category] takes itself as its own substance (*ātman*). Because it exists in dependence upon the object (*vastu*), it possesses magnitude; thus, in successive order, that which increases is none other than the substance itself.

This [substance] is the object for the purpose of being appointed (*niyoga*) and for the purpose of being summoned together. Beyond these four persons, only they are designated by the term "the substance of the Saṃgha" (*saṃgha-ātman*).

If this is so, why is it necessary to appoint someone to inquire? This is explained below. Regarding the phrase "the Dharma itself is the substance," the following section further clarifies the substance of the Dharma. It says: "It should..."
Whiteness is its own essence; it is not that whiteness is added again as an essence by depending on something external to whiteness.
This is because each of the three dharmas has its own root, and each respective function is established.

Regarding the fourfold assembly: after the names of the individuals have been called out before the multitude, they are subsequently reduced. For instance, if one person is removed, the formal announcement (*jñapti*) for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) becomes invalid.

As for those cases where both [the number and the procedure] exceed the limit and are thus improper, the Vinaya states: "As with a formal announcement, perform it as a formal announcement; as with a formal motion (*karmavācanā*), perform it as a formal motion.

One must not increase a single announcement (*ekajñapti*) into a formal motion consisting of two announcements (*dvijñapti*), nor reduce a formal motion consisting of two announcements into a single announcement. I do not yet understand this.
For what reason can there be no increase or decrease?
Regarding the arising of faults due to separation: if one assumes a fixed number, it is possible that [the conditions] do not assemble. Regarding those who are not afflicted by mental distress:
dharmas are insentient; they are fundamentally incapable of being distressed. This is not like the case where a separate group, through discord, gives rise to affliction.
The "sacred teaching" refers to the *jñapti* (motion) and the *karmavācanā* (formal act). If these are deficient, the purpose is not accomplished;

whether there is a deficiency or a surplus, the preceding matter is not successfully executed. The number of monks is fixed by regulation: four persons may perform the *poṣadha* (recitation of the precepts), five persons may perform the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism), and so forth;

this number is fixed and cannot be reduced. To reduce it beyond the prescribed limit constitutes a transgression of the legal rules. Conversely, exceeding the number—such as having four or more perform the *poṣadha*—is permitted.
If one exceeds this time now, it would be even better; there is no other expedient. If the assembly is easily gathered, it must be done for the entire boundary;

if it is difficult to gather, it is logically necessary to go outside [the boundary] to perform the rite. Apart from these two conditions, there is no other expedient that permits a separate [assembly].
If one follows the lower [text], it uses the Dharma as an analogy for persons; this would only be excessively beneficial and virtuous.

For example, if a *jñapti* (motion) is increased to become a *jñapti-dvitīya* (motion with one proclamation), or a *jñapti-dvitīya* is increased to become a *jñapti-caturtha* (motion with three proclamations), it is even more virtuous. A reduction, however, would not be valid. This is because the schools differ; such is the case in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
Thus, the Dharma must be established with precision; additions or subtractions are not permissible.

Regarding the three types of instruction—the mental recitation (*cittānuvartana*) and the face-to-face (*sammukha*)—these apply to both realms. The three formal procedures (*karmavācanā*), such as the motion (*jñapti*), exclude the ritual for delimiting a boundary (*sīmābandhana*);

these may be performed upon the "natural" realm (*prakṛtisīmā*). All other remaining [procedures] pertain exclusively to the "formal" realm (*kṛtasīmā*). For now, I shall present them in a general manner.

The first [section] is the "lower" [category], which indicates the general scope for undertaking [the practice]. Regarding the conditions that permit making [an item]: in accordance with conditions such as the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*) or the maintenance of robes (*cīvara*), it is permitted to make [them] according to the aforementioned [rules].

"Below 'gathering' (*saṃnipāta*) refers to villages, forest hermitages (*araṇya*), water boundaries, and travel on roads. It permits the formal procedure of establishing a boundary (*sīmā-bandha*) through a motion and second resolution (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).

Because this is the basis for initial establishment, the expression of consent (*chanda*) is not permitted; since the transmission of consent is not allowed during the establishment of a boundary, it is specifically restricted [to those present].

This is the place where the practice occurs, as it permits the performance of the rite on natural ground. Regarding the requirement of five persons, it is because there is the principle of appointing one who possesses the fivefold virtues (*pañca-guṇa*)."
Therefore, one must perform the ritual after having established the boundary (*sīmā*).
It begins with two pairs; this refers to the time when two people face each other to receive the consent (*chanda*), as they have not yet reached the midst of the Saṃgha. This is the reason.

Ultimately, this was transmitted down to later times; it accords with the Dharma of the Saṃgha. Since the Dharma relies upon the demarcation of boundaries (*sīmābandha*), how could desire be permitted to exist spontaneously?
Therefore, the realization of the fruit resides in the Saṃgha.

"If that is so," and so forth. This objection arises because it was previously stated regarding the *mahā-sīmā* (great boundary) and other matters that "the *pratideśanīya* (confession) and *cetanā* (mental resolve) may be performed according to the conditions as permitted.

Since these were originally communal (*saṃgha*) dharmas requiring five persons to perform the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture), the following passage extends [the application] to individuals, as the quorum for a *saṃgha* is not met.

Regarding the opening of the *saṃgha-karma* (formal acts) as *pratimukha-saṃgha* (face-to-face with a group): some do not permit this, yet it is not because it is incompatible with the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) in terms of the boundary (*sīmā*). It is precisely the manifestation of the essential nature of the dharma-characteristics.

This includes the nine grades of rites augmented by the *pratimukha-saṃgha* for small groups, such as when one says, "May the two virtuous ones attend to me with a single mind. Or it may simply remain [as such].

When included within the *pratideśanīya* (confession before another), there are thus eight types of formal procedures (*dharma*). Second, "combination" refers to the combination of sentient and non-sentient factors;

for example, in the case of an old or sick monk being separated from his robe: with respect to the person’s old age or sickness, it is considered sentient; with respect to the weight of the robe, it is considered non-sentient. Only when these conditions are met may the formal procedure be applied.
Those who are collectively designated as "the Saṃgha" range from a single individual up to those comprising twenty-seven positions; all such persons are called the Saṃgha.
Because even a single person is capable of discerning mental states, although there are four—namely, the village, the forest hermitage (*araṇya*), the road, and water—they exist as conditions.

These are the aforementioned four conditions. As for the nine grades, this refers to what was stated above: "extensively categorized into nine positions. Regarding the existence of characteristics, they are the conditions.

Regarding the "perfection of characteristics": it is said that when there is something obtainable for a ritual act, it is called "accomplished" (*siddha*). Conversely, when it is entirely lacking, it is called "non-existent" (*asat*).

When a ritual act is not accomplished, it is called "ruined" (*bhinna*). Thus, that which pertains to both accomplishment and ruin is as follows: it is said that if there is a deficiency in the *saṃgha* for the recitation of the precepts, it is permitted to perform the face-to-face (*pratyakṣa*) or mental (*manasikāra*) procedures, and thus it is accomplished.

If the *saṃgha* is complete but the formal motion (*jñapti*) is not made and the recitation is performed, it is called ruined. "Vigilant effort" (*jing-li*) means to be earnestly diligent and persevering.

"Sun and Moon" refers to the black and white, large and small suns and moons, as well as the presence or absence of the robe and bowl. "Two combined" refers to the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness of the *tàisuì* (the annual terrestrial deity) for that year;
it refers to the person receiving full ordination. "Below the body" means practicing the Way while free from illness; if one has an illness, it should be treated.
Relinquishing an invitation: if one has invitations to eat at two places, one may relinquish one place to a fellow practitioner to avoid the *pāyattika* offense of "turning away from an invitation.

This is done by means of a formal act (*karmavācanā*), as it is a face-to-face procedure (*sammukhavinaya*). Regarding all boundaries, this applies both to those established by formal act and to natural boundaries.

It applies to all three [categories]. It is a combination of both sentient and non-sentient factors. Regarding the two types of "difficulties" that pertain to sentient beings, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "When one wishes to enter the rains retreat (*varṣā*), one should first deliberate on whether there are difficulties or no difficulties.
If there are no difficulties, one should remain. This refers to difficulties from the perspective of personal hindrances, which belong to the category of sentient beings.

In terms of their physical location, they belong to the category of non-sentient things (*asattva*). Regarding medicinal herbs: the medicine itself is non-sentient, while the illness for which it is intended pertains to sentient beings. As for "holding and reciting":

if these were considered from the perspective of persons holding and reciting them, they would also be subsumed under the category of sentient beings; however, here we are defining the limit of non-sentient things from the perspective of the dharmas themselves.

The "sole holding" (*ekapāṇi*) is restricted because there are no other persons present; it is opened up to include the "face-to-face" (*saṃmukha*) and "mental recollection" (*manasikāra*) [procedures].

Regarding the three great boundaries (*mahā-sīmā*): these are the boundaries where both person and dharma coincide, and where dharma and food coincide. A boundary where dharma coincides but food is separate is not permitted for residence, because such a site is not a place where the Saṃgha dwells.
Even if a king were to build a dwelling there, a conscientious bhikṣu would tear it down. The section on the Rains Retreat (*Varṣā*) states: "If one relies upon..."

Regarding the *Poṣadha* (or *Upavasatha*) within the Great Boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), the Precept Platform (*śīla-maṇḍala*), and other minor boundaries (*kṣudra-sīmā*): the formal reception of the day [of observance] is not valid therein, because these are not the primary locations intended by the original resolve.

If there was no prior Great Boundary and one establishes it based on a monastery (*ārāma*), then if two boundaries are subsequently established later, the reception of the day is valid for both boundaries, as neither constitutes a location that deviates from what was required.
This explanation is now given in reference to cases where the platform has already been established; the remaining rules and other counterparts follow accordingly.

The "mental recitation" (*manasikāra*) refers to the method of mental attention. This applies without hindrance to acts such as receiving the three robes (*tricīvara*) or their relinquishment (*utsarga*), because these are natural universal procedures (*sāmānya-karman*).

In terms of the specific object, with respect to the act of reciting the precepts (*poṣadha*), it is non-sentient (*acetana*). When both [the object and the procedure] are combined, with respect to the purity of the recipient (*adhikāra-śuddhi*), it is sentient; with respect to its conformity to the Dharma (*dharma-anurūpa*), it is non-sentient.

This is non-sentient; it is exclusively non-sentient. This is stated from the perspective of the robe itself. From its own measure, it belongs to the sentient; in relation to the robe and so forth, it is non-sentient. Furthermore, this constitutes a "combination of two.

Now, according to the subsequent text, the meaning of this "combination of two" is explained by itself. From the section on *pravāraṇā* (self-exhortation) downward, in relation to the *pravāraṇā* ritual itself, it belongs to the non-sentient;
yet, in terms of the person who should perform the rite, it is called a "combination of two. This is restricted to one. Above, it was established in relation to a single ritual matter.
This refers to the statement:
"It may be performed throughout the boundary. The meaning is that it may be performed if there are no people gathered within the boundary; if there are, it becomes a separate [formal act].

If there are two or more persons, one should change it to a *saṃgha-dharma-pratimukha* (a formal act addressed to the assembly). If there are four or more, change it to a *jñapti-ekavācika* (a formal announcement consisting of a single motion).
Because it concerns the precepts, it is called a "modification of the dharma.
Regarding the three minor boundaries (*kṣudrasīmā*): they are not mutually inclusive. If there are no obstacles, one may not establish the three minor boundaries and perform [the ritual] therein.

However, at the time of establishing the boundary for the precept platform (*śīlāmaṇḍala*), if there is no one at all within the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*), or if there are separate obstacles within the great boundary, one may perform [the ritual] upon the precept platform.
This is not a place for constant activity. [The term] "two combined" (*dvi-samnipāta*) is as follows:

with respect to the medicinal requisites for a seven-day period, the expectation of the illness and its causes belongs to the sentient category (*sattva*), while the expectation of the medicine bowl and its surroundings belongs to the non-sentient category (*asattva*). Regarding the formal announcement (*jñapti*):
with respect to the bhikṣu, it belongs to the sentient category; with respect to the act being performed, it pertains to both the sentient and the non-sentient categories.

One must not face two [confessors], because there is no fault of lacking a formal assembly when it is merely a face-to-face confession (*pratyekamūla*). Even if there are bystanders, they need not be assembled.
For the four persons performing the abandonment of the offense through confession, the presiding confessant (*karmavācaka*) receives the confession; he must question the other three bystanders.

Regarding the "subsequent announcements" (*jñapti*): these include the announcement for the practice of the *dhūtaguṇa* (ascetic practices), the announcement for the various practices regarding *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, the announcement for entering a village, and the announcement for a nun entering a monastery.

In this realm, when performing the ritual of establishing a formal boundary (*karmabhūmi*), it is sufficient to announce it to a single person; in all such cases, the rite is successfully accomplished.

Regarding the mention of the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to admonish) and so forth: the term "and so forth" includes the rules for receiving gifts obtained by the Saṃgha and the rules for receiving the clothing and belongings of deceased members of the five groups of renunciants.

These two combined, when viewed from the perspective of the offense regarding the robe, belong to the category of non-sentient things (*asattva*); when viewed from the perspective of the person capable of repentance, they belong to the category of sentient beings (*sattva*). Thus, the *pravāraṇā* is said to pertain to non-sentient things.

The *Jùwàng* (Local Expectation) explains this in terms of the boundaries of the precepts and offenses. However, if one bases it on those who are subject to the rule and those capable of acting at will, it would again be a combination of two [categories].

This has long been discarded; the statement that "four people may not perform a formal motion (*jñapti*)" is unusable, for according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, five people are correctly determined as being required for relinquishment (*pratyākhyāna*).

Because it follows [the rules], one cannot perform the reconciliation and forbearance oneself. There are five conditions: first, requesting a master of confession (*kṣamāpaka*); second, explaining the name, category, and characteristics of the offense;
third, relinquishing the offense; fourth, the reprimand; and fifth, making a vow. For a small assembly, six conditions are required; the second [condition] is added as "receiving the confession."

Question: For those living on the borders, when there are five or more people, one must further add the initial request to the Saṃgha. The *Dà cǎo* states: "The procedures for three or two people are largely the same.
Since this is entirely distinct [from the standard procedure], the initial relinquishing of the robe says: "O many virtuous ones, please attend to me with a single mind."

Thereafter, one declares for oneself: "I relinquish [this] to the many virtuous ones. Regarding the relinquishment of offenses, if one questions a person at the boundary or addresses a single individual, the general procedure may be understood.

For the relinquishment of property and the returning of robes, it is simply a matter of addressing the person directly. However, as for the removal of the offense itself, there is no requirement to question a person at the boundary;
it is sufficient to possess the five dharmas. Therefore, it is said that these are not fixed, but depend on the circumstances.

The preceding passage states that the object [of the ritual] must be complete in four parts; this refers to the fact that the *karmavācanā* (formal announcement) made by the presiding master (*sāṃghika*) is what is being measured, and thus it could be said that [the offender] does not enter [into the quorum].

However, as for the person performing the confession, they ought to be counted toward the full number. Since the offense has not yet been removed, the person performing the confession is still included within the category of those who have committed the offense, and the removal has not yet taken place.
Even if the confession were completed, they would still belong to the category of those who have committed the offense; ultimately, they are not yet subsumed under the Sangha.

Regarding the "sevenfold pervasion": the three large and two small boundaries, together with the site itself, constitute six realms; the four kinds of natural [boundaries] form one, thus making seven realms.

As for not opening the small boundary for receiving [the precepts], it is because the ritual procedure for a single session is never performed twice; once it is established, it is relinquished by that very act. One immediately confesses the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense and performs the *Poṣadha*.

Within the small boundary, the four-person legal procedure (*caturvarga-karma*) is carried out; for the *Pravāraṇā*, the five-person procedure (*pañcavarga-karma*) is carried out within the small boundary.

Regarding the "human dharma" (pudgala-dharma): if one takes "one" as the subject, it refers merely to three or four types of human dharmas. For now, let us set aside the discussion of subject and object.

"Confessing the *ānantarya*" refers to the medium grade. That which is light is the inferior grade. As for "the matter being a transgression of the emotions," it is, for example, the touching of a woman.

Wearing upper garments on oneself; causing a schism in the Saṃgha through a formal act (karmavācanā); stealing property belonging to the Saṃgha or an individual, valued at three *māṣaka* coins or less—these are subsumed under the middle grade of *sthūlātyaya*.

This applies to the boundary (*sīmā*) as well, encompassing all seven types. As for the five mentioned above, they pertain to the formal procedures (*saṃghadharma*) performed in the presence of others.

Idle talk; making false or evasive speech to vex the Sangha; furthermore, calling someone to come and not coming—these are called bodily vexations. Therefore, they are prohibited by means of a *jñapti* (single announcement). Regarding formalities (*rūpa-dharma*):

being granted the tonsure is identical to the formal act of "shaving the form" (*rūpa-samāna*); being granted the dharma of renunciation is identical to the formal act of "leaving home" (*dharma-samāna*). These are all matters of circumstance (*saṃskāra*).

As for the various monks, when the practice of the Path increases, there is the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to admonish) of increased self-restraint; when disputes increase, there is the *pravāraṇā* of increased [confession of] disputes, and so forth. This concludes the binding.
Regarding the *saṃgīti-dharma* (the dharma of the communal recitation): it is like the procedure for being dispatched to Rājagṛha for the communal recitation;

the questioning of Upāli regarding the dharma and Upāli’s answering of the dharma, and so forth, are considered "non-sentient" (*asaṃskṛta*) from the perspective of the dharma itself. Regarding the "termination" (*nirodha*): this refers to the termination of disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*), the formal announcement (*jñapti*) for an untimely robe (*akāla-cīvara*), and the formal announcement for receiving the *kaṭhina* robe.
From the perspective of the dispute, the untimely robe, and the *kaṭhina* robe, these are termed "non-sentient"; however, from the perspective of the bhikṣu, they are termed "sentient."

Therefore, it is said that these two are combined. Regarding persons: for shaving the hair, four persons are sufficient; for appointing an instructor (*śikṣācārya*), five persons are required. These are divided into two categories.

If there are few people, one performs the *saṃghakarma* (procedures of the community) through face-to-face consultation (*pratyekamukha*). If the number of people is sufficient, one proceeds by self-appointment. As for those who do not belong to this category: although three procedures are performed, having more people is beneficial.

Excellent. For now, let us consider only the thirty-nine dharmas mentioned in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. Since these differ from the procedures for receiving full ordination or the confession of *śeṣa* offenses—which are restricted to groups of ten or twenty—they are termed "inappropriate" (*abhinirhāra*).

Regarding the ritual procedure: because the natural ground is unfit for formal possession (*parigraha*), there are four types—namely, the *kula*, the *ārāma*, the path, and water. As for the seven boundaries (*sīmā*):

these consist of the three types of small boundaries (*kṣudrasīmā*), along with the ritual for binding the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*), the ritual for binding two [boundaries] by the same method, the ritual for binding one [boundary] by the same method, and the seven rituals for binding the *śīlākṣetra* (precept field).
Therefore, the subsequent text states: "The three large and three small [boundaries] are distinguished by name, but their meaning is one; the *śīlākṣetra* is self-contained. Thus it is said.

It must be surrounded by [the assembly]. Regarding the three *jñapti* (formal motions) for the appointment: these are the *jñapti* for appointing the instructor (*śikṣamāṇā-śikṣaka*), the *jñapti* for summoning [the candidates], and the *jñapti* for questioning before the assembly.
These are performed exclusively within the small boundary (*kṣudra-sīmā*) established for receiving the precepts; they do not apply to actions performed upon other boundaries.

Other matters include the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (one motion and one proclamation) for appointing persons for the *pravāraṇā* (invitation ceremony), the *jñapti-pūrvaka-sammata-karman* (proclamation following the appointment of the five virtuous qualities), and the *ekajñapti-karman* (single proclamation) for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*). All of these are restricted specifically to the *pravāraṇā* and the *poṣadha*.

Regarding the two types of small boundaries (*sīmā*), they likewise do not extend to other dharma-boundaries. Furthermore, the three types [of boundaries], when viewed in relation to one another, are also not interconnected.

It is not that there is no lower boundary; rather, one should first ask: "When it is said that an offense is incurred while performing the *pravāraṇā* within a small boundary, does one perform the confession and then the *pravāraṇā* right there upon this small boundary, or does one proceed to a separate boundary? This is resolved by the following text, as stated below:
If one raises a matter without cause, they shall be immediately disciplined and expelled; the matter arises from what occurred later, not from what was done in the present.

Furthermore, once the offense has been confessed, it is permissible to circulate [the bowl] within the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*). This is because there is no rule against bringing a bowl into the kitchen that has not been punished. Regarding the *kaṭhina* robe:
this is because the previous rule established that the robe is awarded to the monk who sat [in the assembly], as the site of labor is not a permanent residence. Form...

Regarding the Dharma: one who has shaved their head and left the household life must announce [their ordination] to the Saṃgha within the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*). The Vinaya text prescribes this because, due to the case of a craftsman’s son being ordained without authorization, the monks did not know [of his status], and thus the rule was established.
If one does not make such an announcement, it is improper; however, if one informs every individual dwelling (*vihāra*), it is permissible. A threshing floor is not a place for formal proceedings.
One may appoint someone to perform tasks, to confess grave offenses (*sthūlātyaya*), or to instruct nuns.

Regarding the various *saṃghāṭī* (robes): this refers to the binding of the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*), the boundary for the precept-platform (*sīmāmaṇḍala*), and the boundary for not losing one's robe (*acīvarāpatti-sīmā*).

Regarding being separated from one's robe: it permits separation due to old age or illness, or when the robe is heavy, provided one performs the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*). Regarding the *vihāra* (monastery/cell): this refers to the assignment of a site for building a dwelling, as well as the legal procedure for entrusting an existing cell to a monastic or layperson for its maintenance.

Regarding the "guardian": this refers to the method of appointing a person to guard the storehouse; it also refers to the method of appointing a person to guard the *kaṭhina* (merit-robe). These are all matters that depend upon other persons.
Regarding "sentient" (*sattva*) and "insentient" (*asattva*): clothing, rooms, and so forth are classified as insentient.
Questioning the section below: among the fifty-seven dharmas of the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, there is the single dharma of appointing [a monk] for the *pravāraṇā*.

Since it was stated above that the *pravāraṇā* requires five persons, why does it now say that regarding the number of people, there are only four and not five, which would constitute a contradiction?

Answer: To raise such an objection is merely a failure of one's own understanding. Now I shall explain it myself: four people constitute those who can preside, while five qualities constitute those who are appointed.
Therefore, it is said that the object [of the action] is not fixed; rather, the person is the condition—that is, the person who has been appointed.
This refers to the formal citation of the candidate within the procedure for appointment. Such a person cannot yet fulfill the requirements of the *saṃgha*’s legal act (*dharmakarma*).
Only when they subsequently personally perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*) and reach consensus do they finally become included in the count. Thus, these five cases follow one another.

As for the remaining appointments—namely, the procedure for appointing a person to distribute the light belongings of a deceased monk, the procedure for appointing someone to distribute bedding and requisites (*śayanāsana*), and so forth—all involve citing the individual’s name into the legal act at the very moment of the formal appointment. It is not [the case that they are cited] otherwise.
They are included in the count of the Saṃgha; once they have been appointed, they are universally admitted. Hence it is said, "to know by analogy.

This does not mean that for groups of one hundred or one thousand people, the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation) is not performed. Furthermore, it is merely prescribed that the *jñapti-ekakarma* (the formal act consisting of a single proclamation) is restricted to five persons, while the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* specifically pertains to four persons.
Those consisting of five or more persons fall outside the limits established by the rule.

"If that were so," and so forth. If it is argued that the recipient does not enter into the count [of the formal act], consider for instance the case of returning a robe within the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules.

Suppose there is a reason for traveling far away, and one returns the robe on the very same day by performing the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) to entrust it to a companion. Now, if it is returned through a series of intermediaries, once that person has received the robe...

It should be entrusted to him in a private place. A *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal act of motion and resolution) for successive entrustment must be performed; the wording is the same as the procedure for light items belonging to a deceased person, with the addition:
"The Saṃgha now holds this robe and gives it to Bhikṣu A so that he may return it to Bhikṣu B.

If this is the case, would it not follow that the person who receives the successive entrustment does not count toward the quorum of the Saṃgha, thereby resulting in only five members? Why, then, do you say that the person for whose sake the act is performed is excluded?

"Is it only with four people? The answer below states, "It is still with four people. The meaning is that those who receive the *kṣepaṇīya* (transference) procedure are the very persons for whom the rite is performed;
they do not count toward the quorum of the Saṃgha. Beyond them, there must be four other individuals, because the names of those being transferred must be included in the formal act (*dharmakarma*).
How can you then harbor further doubt?

The seven *jñapti-dvitīya* (one motion and two proclamations) involve the demarcation of three minor boundaries (*kṣudra-sīmā*) and the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), as well as the *śīla-maṇḍala* (precept arena);

these two share the same legal procedure (*ekadharma*). Once the demarcation is completed, one must not perform it again upon that same site. This is like the "collecting of robes" (*cīvara-saṃharaṇa*): since the collecting of robes arises within the limits of the monastic boundary (*saṃgha-sīmā*), the arena itself is not the place where the formal act is performed.

If one were to perform the formal act there, it would constitute a "remote demarcation. Regarding the "receiving of days" (*divasa-grahaṇa*), one must necessarily rely on the original established boundary.
Because it is a place of residence; a threshing floor (*khal*) is not a site for the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat). Regarding "placing down the bowl":

this refers to the method of subduing within the precept on begging for bowls, which involves passing the bowls around until the very lowest one is collected and held; it carries the sense of penalizing the bowl by consigning it to the kitchen. Since a threshing floor is not a kitchen, [the rule does not apply]. Regarding "dwellings" (*layana*):

this refers to the instruction on the method for constructing dwellings. Since a threshing floor is not a place for construction, these [rules] do not apply to a threshing floor; they pertain only to what is superior to it.
Other procedures, such as the returning of robes and so forth, may be performed in the open air.

Regarding the generation of good and the cessation of evil: for instance, the formal motion and announcement (*jñapti-caturtha*) for receiving the precepts generates good, while methods such as the concealment of offenses (*tirokaraṇa*) cease evil.
The remaining two types of procedures do not apply to non-sentient objects nor to a combination of both sentient and non-sentient entities.
Regarding the four persons: as in the case of the admonition against schism in the Sangha (*saṃghabheda*) and so forth, four persons may serve as the presiding officers;
five persons are not applicable. This does not mean that five persons are generally excluded; rather, it is merely a regulation that five persons alone are restricted to performing separate matters.

It is simply not stated that among the five persons, they are permitted to perform only the single motion for the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) that harmonizes the Sangha. If this is so, why was it previously stated that there are three motions? The answer is: this still follows [the previous principle].

This is the ancient practice. The details are as set forth below. For the *jñapti-caturtha* (motion followed by three proclamations) for receiving the precepts, forty people perform it; for the *jñapti-caturtha* for expiation (*āpatti-vyutthāna*), twenty people perform it.

Regarding the *pravāraṇā* within a small boundary (*kṣudra-sīmā*), because the *poṣadha* consists only of a simple motion (*jñapti-mātra*), whereas the *pravāraṇā* applies both to the simple motion and to the *jñapti-dvitīya* (motion followed by one proclamation), there is no separate motion [required here].

Fourth: matters arise from subsequent occurrences. This refers to what was previously stated: that it is not the case that there is no formal accusation (*codanā*), but rather that there is a public confession (*āviṣkaraṇa*) performed within the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*).
Third, the conditions: this refers to the matter, the Sangha, and the boundary. Fourth, the conditions: this refers to one type of ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*).

There are three [categories]. First, the confession of light offenses (*āpatti*) through the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*) while seated for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*); this is restricted to oneself and does not require a person to be present. Second, the seven dharmas:

namely, the summer retreat (*varṣā*), the declaration of purity (*śuddhi-uddeśana*), receiving medicine, receiving the seven-day permit, receiving the three robes, relinquishing the three robes, and holding and receiving the alms bowl (*pātra*).

These were originally performed as face-to-face procedures (*pratimukha*), but because no other person was available, they were permitted to be performed as mental acts (*manasikāra*). Therefore, it is said that these apply to both face-to-face and mental procedures. Fourth.

The *dharma*, the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*), receiving offerings obtained by the Saṃgha, and receiving the robes and belongings of the five groups of deceased monastics are fundamentally *saṃghakarma* (acts of the community);

therefore, they are said to "apply to the Saṃgha. Since there is no provision for performing them as a mental act (*manasikāra*) in the absence of others, they also "apply to the individual" (*pratyekamukha*). This is found in the text; specifically, it refers to the section on the formal explanation within the text.

There are seven types; that is, from the *upari-varṣā* (summer retreat) up to the receiving of the bowl. There are five types; that is, among the *saṃgha-dharma* (monastic rules), there are five *pratyekamukha* (individual) procedures:

namely, the forfeiture and confession (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*), the acceptance of gifts obtained by the *saṃgha*, and the acceptance of the robes and utensils of the five classes of deceased persons belonging to the *saṃgha*.

These originally belong to the category of *saṃgha-dharma*; however, in the absence of a full assembly, they are permitted to be performed as individual procedures. Therefore, it is said that these apply both to the *saṃgha* and to individuals. Among these, the forfeiture and confession does not apply to the mind alone.

Therefore, the preceding text states: "The four dharmas apply both to the Saṃgha and to individuals. The "remainder" refers to the remaining twenty-two dharmas, which may be performed against a single person.

If one excludes the minor offenses, there are only twenty-one dharmas. The confession of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* is restricted to a small group because it is performed through face-to-face (*pratyekamukha*) confession;
this includes the confession for *sthūlātyaya* (grave offenses), which encompasses the middle grade of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. However, by means of...

The medium-grade small assembly faces [the candidate] directly, and there is likewise only one person. As explained below, this clarifies the meaning of the "general" (*sāmānya*) and "specific" (*pratyeka*) [aspects] regarding the *saṃgha*.

There are three *jñapti* (formal motions): first, the appointment of the instructor (*śikṣamāṇācārya*); second, the *jñapti* for summoning; third, the single *jñapti* by which the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) questions the candidate before the assembly. Regarding the "one *jñapti* and four [motions]" (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*):

at the time of the actual conferral, one *jñapti* and three *karmavācanā* (proclamations) together constitute the "one *jñapti* and four [motions]. This distinguishes the many preceding procedures prior to that.

The initiation of the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*) essence of the precepts has its characteristics. These are as follows: when establishing a boundary (*sīmābandha*), one must proclaim the directional limits;

in maintaining a community, there must be those of virtue. According to the Vinaya, those who have not yet completed five years of seniority (*varṣa*), as well as those who have completed five years but are foolish or dull-witted, are excluded;
"relying on those of virtue" refers to this. One must not add [a boundary] repeatedly; that is, once a boundary has been established, it is not permissible to establish another upon it.

As for "four or more," since four persons are capable of presiding over all *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical acts), there are three [categories].

Thus, there are five, ten, or twenty persons; these three additional positions are added based on the magnitude of the matter. When examining their essential substance (*svabhāva*), they consist of only four persons.
Therefore, it is said that the fundamental principle returns to the initial position. As stated previously, four persons constitute the essence, while adding one more serves a functional purpose.
Consequently, the latter three groups of monks are not termed "fundamental. If the number is reduced, it is reduced from four persons.

Although [the site] is below, the boundaries of the site coincide with the internal boundaries of the *mahā-sīmā*; the empty space below is the intervening space itself.

Western Ward of Qianzhuang, Tuntou Village, Guangxiao-qing, Suqu Township, Huizhai County, Shaoxing Prefecture.
Submitted by the resident lay believer and disciple of the Triple Gem, Jin Yong Fuwei (Lieutenant), Gu You:

I humbly reflect that my late mother, Lady Lou Wuniang, passed away long ago; when I think of her nursing me, I realize how deep was her kindness, and when I consider her pure nature, I realize how heavy was her virtue through her tireless toil.
To offer even a small measure of gratitude, I must rely upon wondrous conditions. Therefore, I respectfully initiate this [act of merit].
With a sincere heart, I offer seventy *kan* of pure wealth and one scroll of the *Kaiki* (Record of Opening).

This is to eternally assist in the transmission and propagation of the glorious majesty of the Triple Gem and to joyfully repay my late mother. Furthermore, I pray that the five hindrances may be eliminated, the six sense-faculties purified, the myriad practices cultivated in unison, and the ten bodies perfected.
Subsequently, I hope for your compassionate regard so that my faculties and objects may be cleansed, and my merit, longevity, and prosperity may increase and extend.
May all beings within the *dharmadhātu*, whether enemies or kin, together ascend to the wondrous fruit.
Written on the first day of the first month of the year Wuchen (1148) of the Shaoxing era.

Chapter One: The Collection on the Conditions for the Formation of Dharmas.

Regarding "the collection of dharmas": this refers to the gathering of one hundred and eighty-four dharmas. Although these dharmas are specifically enumerated, they also encompass all phenomena in general.

The "object" (vastu) is that which is acted upon, while the "dharma" is that which acts. Without the acting agent, there would be no way to encompass the object; therefore, only the dharma is cited to designate it. Regarding "accomplishment through conditions":

whenever any dharma is produced, it necessarily relies upon ten conditions. These range from the initial weighing of the preceding matter to the final response regarding the dharma to be accomplished.

When the conditions are complete, it is called "accomplished"; when the conditions are lacking, it is called "disintegrated. Although "accomplishment" is cited here, the meaning also encompasses "disintegration."

The subsequent text states: "What precedes briefly clarifies the gathering of conditions; what follows distinguishes the formation and destruction of conditions. Regarding the term *piān* (chapter/section), the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) says:
"A place where the meaning of the text is gathered is called a *piān*. The character *piān* is composed of the radicals for 'to act' and 'to gather'; it is thus a name derived from its function."
Prior to the Han dynasty, paper and pens did not exist at all. One used bamboo and wood for writing, supplemented by silk and plain cloth (*wan-su*) to record illustrations and texts.
Later, during the Eastern Han, Cai Lun invented paper, which was more convenient and simple than plain cloth. Consequently, ancient books and scrolls could contain a single chapter.

Because events were compiled and designated as "chapters" (*piān*), it is said that when Confucius read the *Yījīng*, he had to pass through the same passage three times due to the density of the recorded events.

As for the term "number" (*dì*), the *Xiǎoyǎ* states that it means "sequence. Furthermore, the *Biographies of Monks of the Southern Mountains* (*Nánshān Sēngzhuàn*) states that "number" refers to "position," and "one" refers to the "beginning.
Since this [work] occupies the foremost position, it is called "the first" (*dìyī*).

*Zao* (pronounced *chì*) means "to reach. The text refers to the main body of the *Karmavācanā* as it is understood. *Ke* (科) refers to the topical headings. *Tiao* (條) means "explanation" or "interpretation.

*Fenqi* (分齊) means "divisions," referring to the limits of the segmented sections. The three divisions are: the Introduction (*nidāna*), the Main Body (*śarīra*), and the Dissemination (*pariṇāmana*).

In the Western Regions, this began with the Bodhisattva Bandhuprabha; here in this land, it was first initiated by the Dharma Master Dao’an. Thus, the text of the three divisions was established to distinguish the teachings of this school.

This scripture now follows the preceding format and is likewise divided into three parts. "Dharma" refers to the lower [section], because the sacred *karmavācanā* (ritual procedures) never arises in isolation;
it must rely upon conditions that accord with the Dharma to be successfully accomplished. From the lower [section] arises the Main Body (*śarīra-bhāga*).
From the eighth [section] arises the Dissemination (*pariṇāmanā-bhāga*). "Monastic and Private": "Monastic" encompasses the communal laws, while "Private" encompasses the mental [discipline].

Regarding "mindfulness and so forth," as for "calm mindfulness that is free from conditions," the subsequent text states: First, it clarifies that one seeks by taking the body as the object of mindfulness regarding the Dharma;

one should respectfully ensure this is constant, binding the thoughts with single-mindedness to eliminate hindrances. Regarding "assistance," the subsequent text states: The Buddha said there are five kinds of upholders of the Vinaya who achieve establishment through practice:

they recognize the right and wrong paths, are clearly enlightened regarding what is maintained and what is transgressed, and their advancing and halting possess proper decorum; therefore, [they] speak.

It is said that the Vinaya is established; that which is not the Vinaya cannot serve as proof. Conduct arises in accordance with its characteristics; that which is not noble cannot be taken as a model.

This is the principle by which the True Dharma flourishes and once again embraces the distant future—this is the general intent. Regarding the "final age" (*moye*): "final" refers to the world of the final dharma (*mappō*) and the capacities of those to be converted. As the following text states:
"Now, those who wish to illuminate their legacy for future generations and maintain the auspicious fortune of the teaching must rely upon the conduct as their model."
"Only then can it illuminate far and wide" refers to this very point.
As for "the texts being scattered and difficult to seek," this means that the various *karmas* are dispersed throughout the various sections within the twenty *skandhakas*.

"Facing the occasion" (*linji*) means to confront it directly. When the conditions for receiving instruction, settling disputes, or granting indulgences arise, if there are many people present, the proceedings cannot be conducted;

if there are few people, they cannot be distinguished. Those performing the rites do not know whether this belongs to a communal act (*saṃghakarma*) or an individual act (*pṛthagkarma*), resulting in a total confusion.

For this reason, the application of the ritual procedures (*dharmopasaṃhāra*)—whether they are successfully accomplished or not—is vague and obscure, leaving one ignorant of the outcome. "Gang" (綱) means a net.
"Upper rope" refers to the method of touching [the bowl]. "Dilatory deliberation" means being hesitant and full of doubt. "Descending to equality" means descending and returning;

it signifies returning to the state of accomplishment and completion. To cite numbers according to their positions is as follows: for example, saying "a single motion (jñapti) thirty-nine times," or "two motions fifty-seven times," and so forth.
"Following the lower" is as stated in the sub-commentary below: "The procedure for receiving confession and the practice of the bowl."

This refers to the procedures for constructing a Dharma-hall and the methods for distributing bedding. Regarding "open" (*tong*) and "obstructed" (*se*): that which is widely practiced is termed "open," such as the procedure for receiving the *poṣadha* (confession) and so forth;
that which is rarely practiced is termed "obstructed," such as the method for the Council at Rājagṛha.

Furthermore, within the procedures for the assembly, the *pratimukha* (face-to-face), and the *manasikāra* (mental recitation) methods, those that should be taught according to the number of people and can be implemented are termed "open"; the opposite is termed "obstructed. This principle is not uniform. It is still...
Beneath the main frame is the net; beneath the net are the meshes. Beneath the collar is the fur coat; beneath the fur coat are the hairs.

the single announcement (*jñapti*), the motion-and-one-announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*), and the motion-and-three-announcements (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*). The five types that encompass the methods for individuals are: the simple face-to-face (*sammukha-vinaya*) and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "later acts," the *Jieshu* states: "If one acts prior to the announcement, it constitutes an offense; if one acts after the announcement has been made, it constitutes an offense due to violating the established rule (*niyama*). The preceding section on "Lowering" (下) [is explained as follows]: In the Vinaya, because Channa uttered evasive speech (*aññavādaka*) after making a formal motion (*jñapti*), he subsequently troubled the Saṃgha—such as by not coming when summoned and so forth.

The following details clarify the conditions: from shaving the hair to the interrogation before the assembly, it is as described in the section on the "Method of Receiving [the Precepts]"; from the harmony for the recitation of the precepts to the confession by the Saṃgha, it is as described in the section on the "Recitation of the Precepts."

It is called "speaking at the proper time. Whenever a dispute is extinguished on a given day, it is immediately called "harmonious speaking" (*sāmaggī-vāda*).

This is because the Saṃgha possesses the six harmonies—of precepts, views, benefit, body, speech, and mind; if one now differs in view or precept, there is no longer the meaning of "Saṃgha," for the dharma of a harmonious and pure Saṃgha cannot be established.
It is "constant harmony," which refers to the ordinary practice of making announcements and reaching consensus.
"Difficult circumstances" refers to the remaining conditions among the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*). The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:

The stage of patience (*kṣānti*) refers to those who possess the four roots of goodness within the preparatory stage (*prayoga-mārga*: *uṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, *kṣānti*, and *laukikāgradharma*). Regarding the term "patience":
after the root of goodness of the summit (*mūrdhan*), another root of goodness arises, which is called patience. It has two meanings: first, the meaning of confirmation (*saṃpratīcchanā*);

when one confirms the principle of the Four Noble Truths, one realizes that the truth of suffering is truly suffering, and so on, up to the truth of the path being truly the path. Second, the meaning of certainty (*niścaya*).

"Meaning" (*artha*) refers to the fact that these roots of goodness are definitively free from further regression or fluctuation. Regarding those "liberated by waiting for the time" (*samayavimukta*), "liberation" is a designation for the fruit. As the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states:

third, the one intent on guarding (*anurakṣaṇā-dharman*); fourth, the one established in the Dharma (*sthitākampya-dharman*); fifth, the one capable of penetration (*prativedhanādharman*); and sixth, the immovable one.

The first five types are called those of dull faculties (*mṛdv-indriya*). They arise from the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) among those liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*).
They are termed "liberated by time" (*samaya-vimukta*). Thus, a verse states: "The first five arise from those liberated through faith; collectively they are named 'liberated by time'.
This means that these five types of Arhats must wait for a favorable occasion before attaining liberation. According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, there are six kinds of waiting for time.
First, one requires excellent clothing; second, excellent food and drink; third, excellent bedding; fourth, an excellent dwelling place; fifth, an excellent teacher of the Dharma;
and sixth, excellent fellow practitioners. Because liberation is attained only when these six favorable conditions are met, it is called "liberation by time" (samaya-vimukta).
The sixth type is called "sharp-facultied" (tīkṣṇa-indriya), which refers to those who proceed from the stage of the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga).
That which arises from the stage of "attainment through vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta) is termed "sharp-facultied" (tīkṣṇendriya) and "liberation not dependent on time" (asamayavimukta).

This means that one attains liberation without waiting for favorable conditions such as specific times or clothing; thus, it is called "liberation not dependent on time. Because they cause many to be dull-witted, these are subsumed under "liberation dependent on time" (samayavimukta);
