When they gathered to compile the Dharma and Vinaya, [they asked] whether food, drink, bedding, and seating were abundant and not lacking.

They all replied, "In Rājagṛha alone there are many dwellings, food, drink, bedding, and seating; it would be fitting for us to dwell together there. At that time, Kāśyapa made the formal motion (*jñapti*).
If one follows the *Jñānaprasthāna*, it says: at the time of the compilation, those who had attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) all came to the assembly for the purpose of selecting [the canon].
"One thousand. He asked again, "At that time, there were countless Arhats such as these; why was a selection of one thousand made?
He replied, "King Bimbisāra, together with eighty-four thousand officials and attendants, each attained the fruits of the Path.

The king commanded that among his officials, a meal should always be provided for one thousand monks. Kāśyapa thought to himself: 'If we were to constantly beg for alms, it would cause us to neglect our religious duties.'"
"In Rājagṛha, one constantly provides for a thousand people; it would be appropriate to dwell there. One who knows the path of practice must first rely on external resources;
therefore, a formal announcement must be made.
As for the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, it was compiled as the *Mūla* (Basic Section). Later, Kāśyapa made this formal announcement: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha now assemble to discuss the Dharma and the Vinaya. This is the formal announcement (*jñapti*).
If this were omitted—that is, if one did not make this single announcement to inform all—it would be impossible to manifest the purpose of this assembly."
Upāli means "Close Attendant" (Jìnzhí) in this translation; he was the minister who personally attended upon the Buddha when the Buddha was a prince.
The Vinaya is the "life-force of the Dharma," meaning it is the very life-span of the Buddha’s teachings. The *Zhùfǎ túzàn* states:
"Inside the cave, three high seats were established: one for the questioner, one for the respondent, and one for the person transcribing the palm leaves."
The Vinaya states: When Mahākāśyapa was about to convene the council, he made this formal announcement (*jñapti*): "Venerable Saṃgha, listen.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let the Saṃgha now question Upāli regarding the Dharma and the Vinaya. This is the announcement."
[Upāli] answered: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen. If the time for the Saṃgha has come, may the Saṃgha grant its consent.
Let the Elder Mahākāśyapa now question me and I shall answer. Having made this formal motion (*jñapti*), Mahākāśyapa immediately asked:
"Where did the first *pārājika* offense originate? Who was the first to commit it? [He continued] thus through all the *khandhakas*, *vargyas*, and *vinaya* rules.
The *Ekottarika* (Increasing by One) consists of questions and answers provided in response to inquiries, all of which were compiled into the *Vinaya Piṭaka*.
As for Ānanda, his full name is Ānandā; this means "Joyful Celebration. He was born on the night the World-Honored One attained enlightenment.

A deity from the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven came to inform the King, saying, "The Prince has already attained Bodhi. Upon hearing this, the King was filled with joy. Subsequently, the ladies of the inner palace also announced that [King] Śuklodana...

The King’s consort gave birth to a crown prince whose countenance was upright and beautiful. The entire kingdom rejoiced, and thus he was given a name. After entering the religious life, he became foremost in erudition.
For twenty-five years, he served as the Buddha’s attendant. The Vinaya states: "Ānanda was the person who made offerings to the Buddha;
he constantly followed the Buddha’s movements and personally received the teachings from the World-Honored One. Therefore, Kāśyapa [said]...

Kāśyapa held the *jñapti-ekavācika* motion and questioned Ānanda; Ānanda likewise held the *jñapti-ekavācika* motion, and together they completed the formal announcement (*jñapti*) according to the four preceding phrases.
Kāśyapa asked: "Where was the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* preached? Where were the *Saṃgīti-sūtra*, the *Mahānidāna-sūtra*, and the *Śakrapraśna-sūtra* preached?
Ānanda answered each question as it arose, thereby compiling the two Piṭakas. Thus ended the decline of the Buddha-dharma.
These two phrases conclude the preceding Vinaya Piṭaka and extend downward to the present compilation;
that which has been transmitted with its source is the "Thus have I heard" (evam mayā śrutam) uttered at the beginning of all sūtras.
Regarding "seven hundred": this refers to the Council of Seven Hundred. In the *Dharmavinaya*, it is said:

"At that time, one hundred years after the Parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One, the Bhikṣus of the Vajjiputtaka school of Vaiśālī practiced ten matters, claiming them to be pure. What are these ten matters?

First, having finished eating to satiety, they were permitted to eat by picking up food with two fingers without performing the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the ritual for leftover food). Second, having finished eating to satiety... [text continues].
1. Having finished eating, one may eat food obtained between two villages without performing the remaining formal procedures (*dharmas*). 2.

Within a monastery, one may perform a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations) for a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*). 3. Within a boundary (*sīmā*), having performed a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for a separate assembly, it is permitted to assent to it.

4. One may employ the customary formula: "Venerable Elders, this has been done; this is what was previously practiced," without examining the legal codes (*vinaya-dharma*). 5. [The sixth item] is complete.
1. Having finished eating, one may eat ghee, oil, honey, and curd mixed together in one place. 2. Seventh, one may use salt that has been kept overnight, placing it in the food while eating.
3. Eighth, one may drink *śīdhu* liquor. 4. Ninth, one may possess an uncut sitting mat (*niṣīdana*).
5. Tenth, one may accept gold and silver. Regarding "Gana": the Vinaya text states *naśyagana bhikṣu*. This refers to a monk who heard [the news] from the monks of Vaiśālī.
Having performed these actions, he went to the place where Vatsīputra was and declared it to be contrary to the Dharma.
Vatsīputra then convened an assembly and said, "If Udāyin acts as his companion, then this matter can be settled according to the Dharma. First, they went to the banks of the Bahuka River;

subsequently, they sought him throughout three kingdoms, hence the expression "throughout the kingdoms. Later, when people heard of their search, they joined as companions, numbering seven hundred in total.
"Person" refers to the severance of the ten aforementioned matters. Regarding "due to counting," the Vinaya states:
"Seven hundred Arhats of Vaiśālī assembled to discuss the Dharma and Vinaya; therefore, it is called the 'Council of Seven Hundred'."
[The text contains] errors and corruptions regarding the "three measures" (*pramāṇa*): first, authoritative testimony (*āptāgama-pramāṇa*); second, inference (*anumāna-pramāṇa*);

and third, direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*). Regarding "Sarvakāmin": the Vinaya states that there was an elder in Vaiśālī named Sarvakāmin, who was the foremost senior monk (*sthavira*) in Jambudvīpa;
therefore, he is called the "High Seat. At that time, Revata wished to question this senior monk and thus made the formal motion (*jñapti*), saying:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen. The Saṃgha now questions the Elder Sarvakāmin regarding the Vinaya.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Regarding the Elder’s response to this motion, the Vinaya states: "At that time, the Elder Sarvakāmin immediately made a formal motion: 'Venerable Saṃgha...'"

Listen. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen. The Saṃgha now instructs Revata to question me regarding the Dharma and Vinaya concerning the method of answering.
The motion is thus made. Revata asked: "Venerable Sir, is it permissible to take food with two fingers in unequal portions? (and so forth). He concealed his intention;
that is, he transmitted his settled mind [to the assembly].

The calculation follows below. Once the Elder Sarvakāmin has finished answering the questions, he shall distribute voting sticks (*śalākā*) before the assembly to verify the concordant acceptance and thereby manifest the will of the community.
Although this formal motion (*jñapti*) does not appear in the Vinaya, the Great Master [Śīlabhadra], relying on reason, maintains that it ought to be performed first; such is the general meaning.
This is also established by the same four propositions as before.

Regarding the "small hut" (*khuḍḍaka-kuṭī*): it is so named because it is a hut that lacks an owner, has not been formally assigned, and does not exceed the prescribed dimensions. Regarding "many affairs" (*bahukicca*) below, the Vinaya states:
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha. While the virtuous bhikṣus constructed private dwellings, the bhikṣu Āraṇyaka built a large residence.
His begging became so excessive that he troubled the laypeople; as alms were difficult to obtain, he eventually cut down a sacred tree.

Thus it is said that he "troubled both realms. Regarding "not following the measurements": the length did not conform to the Buddha’s twelve spans (*vitasti*), nor was the internal width seven [spans].

"Stretching out the hands" (zhéshǒu) refers to the act of begging for food. "To proceed beyond this" means that once the request has been granted, one should immediately follow the instructions given by the various bhikṣus regarding the designated location;

this is what is meant by being "exclusively independent" and not subject to great regulation. There are, however, two exceptions: the case where one does not beg for leftovers and the case involving obstacles or difficulties.
"Assigning the quarters" refers to the act of directing one to a specific location. The Vinaya states: "At that time, the Sangha shall observe this bhikṣu.

If he is trustworthy, they may allow him to perform the task himself. If he is not trustworthy, the Sangha shall go to inspect it. If the Sangha does not go, they should dispatch someone within the Sangha who is trustworthy to inspect it.
If there are obstacles or difficulties, one should not assign the task [to the untrustworthy person]. This is what is meant.
The distribution of bedding consists of items belonging to the permanent endowment (*sāṃghika-vastu*). Alternatively, it may involve the temporary allocation of rooms;
since this principle applies universally, a formal motion with a subsequent announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) is performed for harmony.

Regarding the section on "Monastics" (*saṃgha*): The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* (*Duolun*) states that one must not speak of their offenses to laypeople for the sake of protecting the Buddha-dharma, lest it cause them to lose faith and reverence for the Buddha-dharma.
As for Devadatta—here translated as "Heavenly Heat"—it refers to the fact that when he was born, the hearts of men and devas were struck with alarm and feverish heat.

According to the Vinaya, speaking [of such matters] is only permitted after the formal authorization of a *saṃghakarma*. For example, when Devadatta first began to cause a schism in the Saṃgha, he convened the three groups including Sunanda and others.

He went from house to house begging for alms. The Buddha ordered that a formal motion (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) be made to appoint Śāriputra to inform the laypeople; this was done. Regarding the royal lineage:
it teaches that King Ajātaśatru killed his father to become a new king, and intended to harm the Buddha to become a new Buddha. This was shown so that people might distinguish between them.
Twenty-seven: This refers to the thirty [rules] with the two [rules on] precious objects, silk, and cotton wool excluded.
As for the subsequent text, it concerns the confession of a *pāyattika* offense regarding the single robe permitted to be separated from the *saṃghāṭī*.
"Constant activity" refers to the practice of the path of the Three Vehicles. Regarding "obstruction due to conditions," the Vinaya states that there was a bhikṣu who suffered from consumption;

his rag-robes were heavy and he was unable to carry them while traveling. The Buddha said: "He should beg three times from the Saṃgha to have new ones made; a formal motion with announcement (jñapti-dvitīya-karman) shall be made to grant them to him."

Regarding the term *kiccha* (difficult/cramped): the Vinaya states that if [the bowls] are of good quality, one should take them away and set them aside; one should then take the lowest-quality, improper ones and give them [to the recipient].
Thereupon, a formal announcement (*jñapti*) is made, and the bowls are exchanged with the elders in successive order. One takes the bowl of the elder and gives it to the next seat;
if one proceeds in this manner toward those bhikṣus, it continues in turn down to the lowest seat.

The ten virtues are: first, being fully endowed with the practice of ethical discipline; second, being widely learned; third, having mastered the recitation of the two sections of the *Prātimokṣa* precepts;

fourth, possessing decisive judgment free from doubt; fifth, being skillful in preaching the Dharma; sixth, having left the household life from a noble family; seventh, possessing a handsome and upright appearance;
eighth, being capable of preaching the Dharma to nuns and exhorting them to joy; and ninth, having gone forth for the sake of the Buddha and wearing the three dharma robes...

Regarding the transgression of the heavy dharmas (*gurutara-dharma*): if one has ten, twenty, or more years of seniority (*vassa*), yet does not possess these ten [qualities], the appointment is not valid.
Concerning those who have attained the vision of the truths (*dṛṣṭisatya*), the Vinaya states: When the Buddha was in Rājagṛha, a householder and his wife both attained the vision of the truths.

Having nothing left to cherish, they even offered their own bodies; having provided such extensive offerings, their clothing and food were completely exhausted. The householder then reproached the bhikṣus for their lack of humility.
Regarding the raising of faults: the Buddha ordered that a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation) be made to prohibit them.

The subsequent details regarding the "future wealth" (*bhaviṣyat-pūrva*) and the "request for the Dharma" (*dharma-yācanā*)—that is, the practice of requesting instruction every half-month—are different [from the monks' rules]. These three dharmas belong exclusively to the bhikṣuṇīs;
the bhikṣus do not have them. This is explained in detail as set forth in the *Bhikṣuṇī-niyama-viniścaya* (The Bhikṣuṇī Manual).
"Various views" refers to the sixty-two views (*dvāṣaṣṭi-dṛṣṭi*). Fearing that [the opponent] might instead raise an objection, one is currently refuting the non-Buddhists (*bāhyaka*).

If one were to accept [their challenge] and turn back upon them, it would become a refutation of our own [Buddhist] school; thus, it would result in refuting both internal and external paths, permanently obstructing the life of renunciation.

Regarding the "four-month trial for non-Buddhists" mentioned in the Vinaya: the *Zhanguoce* states that molding clay is called "pottery" (*táo*), while "metallurgy" (*yě*) refers to casting and smelting.
Zhuangzi said: "It is like a great smith casting gold. The *Shilaozhi* states: "To refine and mold what is coarse and vulgar" (the characters *yao* and *liao* may be pronounced the same).

The "six harmonies" (*liuhe*) refer to the precepts, views, benefits, and so forth. Because there are no six things to be discarded or opposed, they are all called "harmonies. "Sentient beings" refers to those who have first received the precepts;

"there being no subsequent dharma" means that one does not participate in performing subsequent dharma rituals. One should understand this immediately upon sitting [in the assembly]; otherwise, fear arises.
This is because they have lost their way.

Regarding the Uposatha hall, there are generally two types. In the Vinaya, it is stated that because the monks became weary from waiting for one another and exhausted from traveling great distances, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha.
The Buddha said: "From this day forward, wherever you reside, let those who are present, regardless of their number, assemble together."
Regarding the recitation of the *Poṣadha* in a single location: the bhikṣus did not know where they should perform the recitation. The Buddha said:

"I allow you to perform the formal motion (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) for the establishment of a *Poṣadha-śālā*. The motion is as follows: 'Venerable Saṃgha, listen. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent.

We shall establish a *Poṣadha-śālā* at such-and-such a place. The formal motion (*karman*) is to be understood accordingly. Since it says 'at such-and-such a place,' [the boundary] has not yet been proclaimed."

These boundary markers (*sīmā*) are merely indicators of the directions, intended to ensure that the assembly understands them thoroughly. Those who have come from various quarters may become exhausted.

The bhikṣus informed the Buddha of this, and the Buddha said: "From now on, wherever one resides—whether in a village or within its precincts—one may perform the formal ritual of the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for establishing a boundary (*sīmā-bandha*).
When establishing the boundary in this manner, one should proclaim the directional markers of the boundary as follows. [He] spoke thus:

Venerable Sangha, listen. As for the characteristics of the precepts as they have been recited, if the time is right for the Sangha and the Sangha permits, let us perform the formal proclamation (*jñapti*) to establish a single boundary for the recitation of the precepts at this dwelling place.
The *karman* (formal ritual) follows the same pattern. It is necessary to first dissolve and then re-establish [the boundary], for fear that the assembly hall may be moved elsewhere.

The "boundary for not losing one's robe" (*aśithilavastra-sīmā*) is precisely the "boundary for keeping one's robe" (*cīvara-dhāraṇa-sīmā*). This is established upon the boundary of the Saṃgha. If the monastery (*ārāma*) is narrow while the boundary is wide, one may establish it by opening [the space];
however, if the minds [of the monks] do not accord, it is because evil bhikṣus create obstacles, and their views are discordant. The lower path is not manifest.
This is the case because they do not see each other when arriving;
thus, there are mutual deficiencies. For example, the Eastern Temple has the Dharma but no food, while the Western Temple has food but no Dharma; each opens its own fundamental boundary (*sīmā*).
They are combined and bound together as a single boundary so that the two may assist one another.
"One" refers to a single monastery.

To completely deviate from the essence of the Saṃgha means that the benefit is not harmonious. Since the six kinds of harmony are lacking, this constitutes a deviation from the essence of the Saṃgha; it is not a formal act of binding.
The *dhātu*. This is the method of chanting in response. It is not necessary for each person to individually understand the joining and binding.

"The spirit descends when the mind is distracted and ruined" refers to the appearance of madness and delusion. According to what follows, since the Noble Ones permit those with mental illness, there is no offense.

Regarding what follows, whether one recovers memory or returns to normal, it may seem as though one invites worldly suspicion. "Even though" means that even while remaining within the current boundary (*sīmā*), it does not hinder the performance of the ritual act.
Regarding the "obtaining of the begging monk": one must wait for that person to perform the formal procedure of begging (*yācanā-dharma*) before performing the release.

As for "needing the formal procedure," this refers to the need to perform the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) rite. This is because there is a fear that if the Saṃgha disperses, any committed offenses would be difficult to repent.
Furthermore, during the solemn agreement of a single summer retreat, any flaws may be pointed out; if one does not do so now, how could one speak of forming a small boundary for future assemblies?
The method for the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults) within a small boundary (*kṣudrasīma*).

Regarding the distribution of the Sangha’s property and the distribution of the property belonging to the Sangha of the four directions: if there is no legal restriction and eight monks are present, it is difficult to restrict those who arrive later;
therefore, one may distribute the property only when they have heard the sound of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual motion).

Regarding the reward for tending to the sick: one should only distribute the belongings of the deceased as a reward after the caregiver has performed their duties with merit and virtue. This is largely the same as the rule for distributing property belonging to the Saṃgha.

Property belonging to the Saṃgha must be treated with gravity, as it is for the common use of the Saṃgha throughout the four directions; it must not be treated lightly. It is necessary to settle the matter through harmony and principle.
The fingers are bound together at one place; "shāng" (商) means to deliberate whether it is acceptable or not.

"Xiāngyǐ bùshōu" (相倚不收) means that they rely upon one another and refuse to gather them up. Therefore, one person must be specifically appointed as the presiding officer so that there is someone to take charge of the items.
If there is theft or damage, the responsibility falls upon the guardian who was bound by oath. This is what is meant.

It is difficult to live [without it], for it is difficult for the poor to find a means of livelihood. To give away even a small amount of wealth to enter into the merit of this robe is superior to the gift of a great mass of robes as vast as Mount Sumeru.

It is firm; the five benefits do not quickly decay. The *Vyākaraṇa* (Liao-ming-lun) further translates it as "solid and substantial," meaning it can bring about many robes that are free from deterioration.
In ancient translations, it was rendered as "the robe that rewards the good and punishes the evil," rewarding those who come before.
Those who enter the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) early may receive it, but those who enter late in the *varṣā* may not.

It is also called the "robe of merit" (*guṇa-cīvara*), for when the Saṃgha collectively receives this robe, they immediately obtain five kinds of beneficial merits; thus it is said that the merit produced is not small.

Regarding the phrase "one who lacks virtue does not uphold it," the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that the person who guards the robe must possess the five virtues, such as non-attachment, and must have a clear understanding of what constitutes the acquisition, acceptance, and relinquishment of the robe.

It is clear. Furthermore, the *Vyākhyā on the Abhidharmakośa* states: "At the time of first entering the rains retreat (*varṣā*), if one wishes to accept the *kāṭhina* robe, one must inform the Saṃgha:
'I wish to accept the robe. The Saṃgha should then examine this person: does he have many distracting affairs? Is he prone to losing his robes?
Has this person traditionally been free from greed for accumulating wealth? Does he possess a heart of compassion and delight in practicing generosity? If [the Saṃgha]..."

He immediately granted permission. Had it not been so, he would not have granted it. According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, a monk who holds the *kaṭhina* robe must relinquish it if he stays overnight outside the boundary;
therefore, he must remain within for five months and guard it for the sake of the Saṃgha.

Regarding the entrustment of the robe: Once the initial procedure for the appointment has been performed, the person [entrusted] rises from their seat, prostrates at the feet of the Sangha, and kneels with palms joined before the Elder.
The *karmavācanā* (formal act) should then be performed to bestow the robe upon them, as follows: "The Sangha bestows this robe upon the monk so-and-so.
This monk shall take possession of this robe on behalf of the Sangha to serve as a *kaṭhina* robe, and shall remain here [for that purpose]."

"Regarding 'holding the position' (*sthāna-dhāraṇa*) and 'consensus' (*saṃmata*): this refers to when the Saṃgha has previously reached a consensus at the time of the appointment to entrust [the task].

Regarding 'resolving disputes' (*vigraha-vinodana*) below: according to the Vinaya, because the householder Citta had first made offerings to the bhikṣu Sudharma, he later invited Śāriputra to prepare a separate meal of fine flavors.
Sudharma could not bear it and thus sarcastically remarked: 'What you have prepared is indeed excellent; it only lacks sesame dregs.'"

(The householder’s father had the occupation of pressing oil). Upon hearing this, he was displeased. The householder possessed the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), and upon reflecting on wholesome dharmas, he realized that in a former life he had been a young crow.
He then offered this analogy: "Long ago, there were merchants who gathered jewels; they obtained a pair of chickens, a male and a female, and returned to their country.
The male was eaten by a wildcat, but the female remained behind. A crow came and covered her, and she gave birth to chicks. When the chicks made a sound, the father spoke this verse:"
He said: "This child does not belong to me. He was born from the union of a wild father (the wild father being a crow) and a village mother (the village mother being a hen).
He is neither a crow nor a hen. If he wishes to learn his father’s voice, he was born of a hen; if he wishes to learn his mother’s cry, his father is a crow.
He learns the crow to make the hen’s cry, and learns the hen to make the crow’s sound; he possesses the qualities of both crow and hen."
[Regarding] training: both of these are unestablished. Because of this, wholesome dharmas do not proceed. The Buddha ordered that this dharma be enacted to prevent them from departing.
The Vinaya appointed Ānanda, who was endowed with eight qualities, to escort the person undergoing discipline to that place to seek repentance.

If [the offense] had not yet been accepted, he should have placed him in a location where he was visible but out of hearing, and had him seek repentance from afar. He then sent a messenger to personally seek repentance from the lay devotee (gṛhapati). If again...

If they do not accept [the confession], one should have the bhikṣu seek repentance himself. If he still does not accept it, one should have the *pātra-ovadana* (bowl-covering) *karmavācanā* performed, as will be explained clearly below.

As for the eight qualities: first, being widely learned; second, being able to explain well; third, understanding the meaning oneself after explaining; fourth, being able to understand the intentions of others;
fifth, accepting the words of others; sixth, being able to remember and retain them; seventh, being free from errors or omissions; eighth, discerning between good and evil.

As for the statement, "Distribute the voting sticks (*śalākā*)," this refers to the method for settling a dispute involving many people. The Vinaya states that a monk should be appointed to distribute the *śalākās*. There are three ways to distribute them:
first, openly; second, in secret; and third, by whispering into the ear. If there is a senior elder (*sthavira*) who is a leader among those possessed of wisdom...

The Upādhyāya and Ācārya should dwell on the ground of accordance with the Dharma and practice openly. If they dwell in what is contrary to the Dharma, they should perform the two lower forms of conduct.
If those who speak contrary to the Dharma are numerous, they should leave in disorder. Thus, it is said there are three kinds. As for the five kinds:

The Vinaya states: There are five ways of improperly taking voting sticks (*śalākā*): if one does not understand how to settle the matter; if there is no intention to inquire; if there are no virtuous monks present;
if it is contrary to the Dharma; or if the assembly is divided. There are five ways of properly receiving voting sticks (the opposite of the aforementioned cases).
"Regarding 'one of surpassing appearance': this woman’s countenance is so transcendent that she is a treasure capable of overturning a kingdom.
A bandit plotted to seize her on the road; therefore, he opened [the door] and accepted her as a messenger. According to the original rule, she was ordained among the nuns."

Regarding the remote performance of the ritual (*dūre-dharmakriyā*): if a *bhikṣuṇī* performs the ritual from a distance and it is imposed upon [a *bhikṣu*], because there is no principle for a *bhikṣuṇī* to discipline a *bhikṣu*, he feels shame and remorse.
When the *bhikṣu* who was subjected to it later feels shame and remorse in his heart, the *bhikṣuṇī* must then perform the ritual to release him;
he should then retreat and pay respectful obeisance.

Regarding the repair of a dwelling: among the five hundred treatises, it is stated that while dismantling a house is not a violation requiring confession (pāyattika), according to the Vinaya, if there is a layperson capable of repairing a dilapidated house, one should grant them [the materials] through a formal motion and announcement (jñapti-dvitīya-karman).
"Long-standing" means that because it is long-standing, it is ancient. "To place" means to set down. Regarding "to stop":

according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, when a *karmadāna* bhikṣu has completed a dwelling, adorned it with incense, and provided all necessary requisites, he may occupy that room for ninety days. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: [as follows].
Regarding the repair of a dilapidated dwelling, one is granted the right to reside there for six years; regarding the construction of a new dwelling, one resides there for twelve years.

According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if a monastic dwelling was previously ruined and its doors and windows were subsequently rebuilt, the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) is performed to grant the right to reside there for two or three years, depending on the amount of labor expended.
If one does not reside in an empty room, the administrator shall grant permission to stay for a single period.
If the beds, tables, pillows, or mattresses are soiled, greasy, or torn, and are subsequently dyed, washed, or repaired, one may likewise stay for a single period.
The overturning of the bowl (*pātra-nyubja*). The Vinaya states that if a layperson commits eight offenses, one should perform the ritual of overturning the bowl for them:

reviling and slandering bhikṣus; causing harm and providing no benefit; creating a state of instability; inciting strife among bhikṣus; and disparaging the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha in the presence of bhikṣus.
This constitutes the eighth [point].
It informs the household whose bowl has been overturned (*pātra-nyubja*), so that they may know the Saṃgha has performed a *karmavācanā* against them from afar.
Regarding "the aged and the infirm" and below, this explains the principle for carrying a staff. It is like the Confucian rite where those eighty years of age carry a staff at court; now, we...
Regarding those who are young in years and prone to arrogance, it is reasonable that they may not possess the full texts;
thus, the *karmavācanā* texts exist separately. As previously stated, "if one follows specific matters," such matters are infinite;
how could they be limited to the number mentioned before?

Regarding the five heterodox dharmas: Devadatta said to Triśaṇḍha, "I now possess five dharmas which are also superior dharmas of the dhūta practices, for those who have few desires, are content, and delight in renunciation.
They are: begging for food for as long as one lives; wearing rag-robes; sitting in the open air;
not eating ghee or salt; and not eating fish or meat. I now maintain these five dharmas and teach them to the bhikṣus."
This is sufficient to inspire faith and joy. This refers to the five heretics who destroyed the four contentments; thus it is said they "replaced the four right reliances.
The leader was Devadatta, while his companions were the three Śrutadattas and the five hundred who assisted in the schism. The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states:

"When the Saṃgha performed the formal act of admonishing the leader, the four companions acted as shadows and echoes to assist in the schism. The Saṃgha immediately offered further admonitions, but [he] refused them."
They did not accept it; therefore, it is called "assisting in the refutation. "To explain and admonish" (*xiàoyù*) means to provide instruction and counsel together as an exhortation.
Regarding "expelling those who slander": this refers to expelling those who defile the household and slander the Sangha. The Vinaya states:

When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, Aśvajit and others were committing evil deeds and defiling the village of Kāliṅga. The bhikṣus reported their transgressions, and the Buddha ordered Śāriputra and others to go there to formally expel them.
When performing the ritual procedure, one may slander the Saṃgha by saying: "There are others who have committed the same offense, yet they are not expelled;

you are expelling me alone. This shows that the Saṃgha is possessed of anger, fear, and delusion. Regarding the six individuals: the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states that when six people have committed the same offense, two flee and do not appear before the assembly;

since they cannot be subjected to formal disciplinary measures (*pravāsanīya-karman*), they are considered to possess a semblance of fear. The other two meet the path [of the assembly] and repent, submitting themselves; they are without fault.

It can be remedied. Because it resembles affection (*anunaya*), it is said that "coming and going are two contradictions. As for the two persons present who neither flee nor confess, the Saṃgha shall carry out their formal suspension (*pravāsanīya-karman*).
Because it resembles anger (*pratigha*), it is said that "the two persons do not repent," thereby causing them to reverse their previous intent.

It is not that the Saṃgha possesses fear, affection, or anger; rather, they raise the charge and treat the matter according to the Dharma. What ignorance could there be? If one does not offer admonition, there is no way [to proceed].

This is self-evident. Therefore, admonishing others demonstrates that one is without internal flaws; hence it is said, "one proceeds without private interest. Regarding the phrase "those of middle and lower capacity":
conversely, this reveals that those of middle and lower capacities cannot be spoken to using the teachings for those of superior capacity. The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states:

"As for human nature, it is not such that one possesses innate knowledge or can achieve solitary excellence. One must necessarily reflect upon oneself and mutually guide one another; only then can one depart from [delusion]."
Although he had previously cultivated goodness, which was beneficial for the path to liberation, Candana allowed his mind to become deluded and committed transgressions.

When he refused to acknowledge his faults, it was only right that he should have complied when others offered him righteous exhortation according to the Dharma; instead, he relied upon the status of a holy man and, emboldened by his own position, treated others with arrogance.
He then said, "I am the very root of the Buddha’s Dharma. It is precisely I who should instruct the Great Virtuous Ones; why do the Great Virtuous Ones need to instruct me?
Because of this, a formal admonition was established against such evil and heterodox views.
The Vinaya states: While the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, Ariṣṭa gave rise to an evil view and said, "I know what the Buddha has taught."

When a bhikṣu engages in sexual intercourse, claiming it does not obstruct the path, and continues despite being admonished by his fellow monks, he reports this to the Buddha. After the Buddha has questioned him regarding his own statement, he instructs the Saṃgha to admonish him through a formal *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations).

The Admonition and Expulsion of the Two Śrāmaṇeras. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī. The two śrāmaṇeras of Upananda committed unchaste acts together, yet they claimed, "We have heard the Dharma from the Buddha;

practicing sexual desire does not obstruct the path. When the bhikṣus raised this matter as a transgression, the Buddha ordered that a formal motion (jñapti-caturtha-karman) be made to offer them admonition.
If they do not relinquish [the offense], they should be expelled. This refers to admonishing them according to principle; that is, by means of correct reasoning. As stated in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*:
"The World-Honored One, through countless skillful means, has taught that the practice of sexual desire is an obstacle to the Path and so forth. This is what is meant.

Regarding "the bhikṣuṇī who follows the formal act of suspension": The Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya states that while the Buddha was staying at the Gośīrṣa Garden in Kauśāmbī, the bhikṣu Chanda had been subjected by the Saṃgha to a formal act of suspension in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s instructions.

He did not comply and did not repent, and the Saṃgha had not yet granted him permission to co-reside. At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī named Utpalavarṇā (or Wei-ci) who went back and forth to serve him. All...
The nun said, "The Saṃgha has censured Chanda; do not comply with him. Wei-ci replied, "He is my elder brother.

If I do not provide for him now, when shall I wait to do so? After the nun of few desires had rebuked her, she informed the Buddha, who thereupon established a rule: to violate these three [points] constitutes an offense.
If she does not desist despite three admonitions, that bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense.
[Section] Nine. The Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya states: When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, there were two bhikṣuṇīs, one named Soma and the other named Vairaṭī.
They lived together in constant intimacy, engaging in misconduct. Their evil reputation spread abroad, and they concealed their offenses from one another. The other bhikṣuṇīs...

Having rebuked him, he addressed the Buddha. The Buddha permitted the Saṃgha to perform the formal act of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations) for the purpose of reprimanding and advising him, so that he might dwell separately.
One who violates this advice commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
[Section] Ten, Lower Part. The Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya states: When the Buddha was at Śrāvastī, Soma-Pārāyaṇī had been rebuked and advised by the Saṃgha; [this occurred] six times.
The group of nuns instructs them, saying: "You all live together with me; you have also seen other bhikṣuṇīs living together, even to the point of concealing their offenses.
Because the Saṃgha is indignant, they have instructed you to dwell apart. Do not say such things as: 'You should not dwell apart; you must dwell together.
If these bhikṣuṇīs do not relinquish [their position] when admonished, they commit a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. Furthermore, the *Huainanzi* states: "Mo... (The text here appears to be truncated).
Zhai saw dyed silk and was moved to grief because it could be made yellow or black; he said that human nature is likewise. "Crimson" (*zhū*) and "purple" (*zǐ*):
crimson is a metaphor for the good, while purple is a metaphor for the evil. The *Lunyu* says, "I detest how purple usurps crimson. Kong [Qiu] said:
"Crimson is the primary color, while purple is a secondary color that is pleasing. One detests its perverse appeal as it usurps the primary color. If one were to indulge it now..."
If good and evil were to become indistinguishably mixed, it would cause the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox to vanish.
Therefore, admonition is necessary. (11) The Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya states: When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs became angry and displeased over a minor matter and spoke these words:
"I renounce the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. It is not only the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, who exist; there are others as well."
"Regarding those śramaṇas and brahmins who practice the holy life (brahmacarya), we too may practice the holy life among them. ...
[The monks] informed the Buddha, and as a result of this, he established the rule: if one does not desist after three admonitions, it constitutes a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.

Section 12, Part B. The *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya* states: When the Buddha was staying in Kauśāmbī, there was a bhikṣuṇī named Kālī who delighted in quarreling and was unskilled at retaining what she had heard.

Later, out of malice, she spoke thus: "The Saṃgha is possessed of favoritism, hatred, fear, and delusion. Because this bhikṣuṇī, despite being admonished three times, persisted in her refusal to relinquish [this view], she committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Furthermore, within the section on the *pāyattika* (offenses of expiation) in the lower part of the Vinaya, there are instances where the four types of disputes (*caturvivāda*) arise.
Regarding the precepts: one does not transgress them because of a formal admonition. Since this specifically mentions "admonition," it can be understood as encompassing the aforementioned precepts.

In the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*, section thirteen, it says: When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, there was a bhikṣuṇī who associated closely with a layman and lived with him, engaging in conduct that was improper.
Although the other bhikṣuṇīs offered admonitions and rebukes, she would not accept them. Consequently, [the Buddha] established the rule concerning "laymen's sons."

The aforementioned *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states: "If a bhikṣuṇī associates with and dwells together with the son of a layman (*gṛhapati-putra*) and so forth, and does not relinquish this behavior after being admonished three times by the bhikṣuṇīs, she commits a *thullaccaya* offense.
*Śikṣamāṇā* is fully called *śikṣamāṇā*; this means "a woman training in the Dharma. She does not receive the full precepts independently; first, she is established [in the training].

The *Zhì* (Record of the Vinaya) states: "The six dharmas for training the mind serve as the conditions for receiving [the full precepts]. The *Sifen* (Dharmaguptaka-vinaya) states: "An eighteen-year-old maiden should train in the six dharmas for two years. It further says:
"A young woman who has previously been married and is ten years old is granted the six dharmas. The *Sarvāstivāda* states:

"One who attains full ordination at the age of twelve does so because she was compelled by her husband's household to endure various sufferings; having developed a deep weariness with her former circumstances, she recites the six dharmas below."

This is the training of the mind. Observe the conditions for receiving the Great Precepts (*mahāśīla*): the two years [of probation] are the training of the body. One should ascertain whether there was a prior conception in the womb.

One should then establish oneself in a place free from noise and take up a position where one can see [the assembly]. Regarding the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the motion followed by three proclamations) for receiving the precepts:

afterwards, the candidate is summoned and the names of the six rules (*ṣaḍ-dharma*) are recited to them, until they respond, "I am able to uphold them," as is usually stated. As for the "fifteen" regarding the method of receiving the precepts for monks and nuns: "Monk" (*bhikṣu*) refers to the Great [Community].

The term "Saṃgha" refers here to the community of nuns. While the Bhikṣu Saṃgha lacks its own specific *dharmas* (procedures), the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha possesses its own *dharmas*. Consequently, the ancients established the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual acts) for the two divisions [of the order].
However, as the textual characteristics of these procedures are largely identical to those already mentioned, they are not set forth separately here.

Regarding the practice of repentance (*śikṣā-manatta*): the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that if one who has committed an offense weeps and is unwilling to part with the *kāṣāya*, and is one who deeply delights in the Buddha-dharma, one should grant them the formal act of repentance (*śikṣā-manatta-karman*).
"Permanently obstructing one lifetime" means that in this present life, they will be unable to realize the fruits of sainthood (*ārya-phala*).
Therefore, the *Daichao* states: "The metaphor of 'severing one's head' refers precisely to the failure to attain the fruits of sainthood.
Furthermore, the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* says: "In this single lifetime, one shall not transcend birth and death; however, there is an obstruction that prevents entry into hell.

[The text] continues below. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī commits a *pārājika* offense and has no concealment whatsoever, they shall perform repentance according to the Dharma."

Regarding *huì* (repentance): various masters have differing views on what should be discarded or established, each with their own claims of right and wrong. Now, summarizing the principles for guiding and transforming others, there should be no lingering obstructions in the reasoning.

It simply requires that whether one confesses or not, at the time of requesting [the precepts], there must be no concealment whatsoever; one should practice repentance for as long as one lives. Regarding *shù* (forbearance):

"shù" means to measure things through the mind with empathy. Regarding the method for requesting [the precepts]: according to the Vinaya, one should be instructed to say: "Venerable Sangha, please listen. I, bhikṣu So-and-so, have committed the offense of sexual misconduct."
"Pārājika. Without concealment, he now requests the pārājika precepts from the Saṃgha. May the Saṃgha grant me the pārājika precepts out of compassion.
After he has made this request three times, the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is then performed. The Buddha said: "Once the pārājika precepts have been granted..."

One should practice in accordance with this. Thirty-five matters are to be forfeited, which are largely the same as those in the *Senggang* (Monastic Regulations), with the sole addition that one must not recite the Vinaya within the assembly;
however, if there is no one capable of reciting it, such recitation is permitted.

Reproach. In the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*, it is stated that when a bhikṣu is arrogant in mind, disrespectful, and treats others with contempt, the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) is performed for him;

this is merely another name for reproach. Regarding the application of the rule and the explanation of the rule, they are roughly as found in the "Monastic Administration" (*Senggang*) section of the *Daochao*.

Although many types of transgressions are set forth there, I shall now cite four instances of erroneous speech concerning those who break the precepts. That is to say, regarding one who has broken the precepts... [breaks off].
The first three groups refute [wrong] views, namely the sixty-two views. Those that refute [wrong] conduct consist of the latter four groups and so forth.

Those that refute right livelihood refer to seeking through improper means and sustaining life through illicit gain; this includes the five wrongs and the four wrongs. Regarding "internal and external":

"internal" refers to the interior, while "external" refers to the exterior; it is difficult to manifest purity or impurity therein. "Following along" likewise involves the forfeiture of thirty-five matters.
If he complies, the Sangha shall lift the penalty only after he has made three requests for its removal; the wording of these requests is the same as that used for the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses.

Regarding his conduct during this period, his deportment and seating place are to follow the rules for those undergoing the "lower" penance within the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* category. This applies whether there is one person or three persons involved.
They are applied according to their names; they shall not exceed four.

Expulsion: as in the section on the precepts regarding defiling families, evil conduct, and subverting the Buddha-dharma—defiling the virtuous and pure minds of laypeople by taking what is wrong to be right—one must therefore send them out from their original location, subduing and punishing them so that the secular world may take notice.

It is not that they have attained the correct realization; rather, they are still beset by doubt and confusion. Such transgressions are common among many people, and one must rely on strict prohibition to sever them.

As for the methods of governance, the compliance, and the interpretation of the terminology, these are roughly the same as in the aforementioned rules. However, regarding the initial act of banishment, the difference lies in the fact that once their offense has been formally recorded, they must depart from this residence.
This is detailed in the Vinaya-mūla. If they seek compliance and request to be released from the banishment, they must not come back arbitrarily.
One should send a messenger from outside the boundary to invite [the preceptor]; this is difficult to change, for "change" (gé) means to reform or alter.
As for "reliance" (yīzhǐ), the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says it refers to performing the *karmavācanā*; that is, to establish oneself in a place where there are those of virtue. The meaning is the same.
"Sinking" and "floating. Sinking refers to an offense; floating refers to upholding the precepts. The *Dàchāo* states:

"Once you have received formal dependence (*niśraya*), you should associate with those who know the Dharma and Vinaya, study and understand the *vinaya*, and become clear and proficient regarding what constitutes an offense and what constitutes its upholding. Only then should [the teacher] explain it to you."

Regarding "preventing those who have not yet arrived," the *Dàochāo* states: "The Sangha must perform a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) to prohibit their departure, because they were sent to apologize to the layperson (*avadātavasana*).
'Mockery' refers precisely to the words of Subhūti mocking Citta. 'Harmonious joy' means that one has become self-disciplined and gentle, and furthermore, the donor (*dānapati*) is also joyful.
The *Dàochāo* further states: "If a layperson is delighted, then one should release [the restriction]. The above.

There are four types [of persons] who merely impair their conduct but whose minds still possess faith; they fulfill the requirements for the quorum of a *saṃgha* and are eligible for *karmavācanā* rituals, yet they are subject to disciplinary treatment and cannot be subjected to formal censure or suspension.
The phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the two types [of misconduct]: regarding ritual (*vidhi*) and livelihood (*ājīva*). This also represents a reversed exposition of the four matters.

Now, as for the term "source" (*yuan*): it refers to the root source; "mother" (*mu*) signifies that which gives rise [to things]. If one does not believe in the two causes—good and evil—that bring about the two results—suffering and pleasure—then wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) exists in ruin, obstructing the path of training.
This may be due to failing to comprehend the teachings, or knowing them yet deliberately transgressing them. Why did the Saṃgha not ask?

Regarding the case of one who admits having committed an offense but answers "I did not see it" when being formally charged (*ajjhāpanna*): the Saṃgha shall immediately suspend him (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) and impose upon him the disciplinary measure of the "charge of denial.
This is intended to subdue him and lead him toward the Path; for the time being, he is excluded from the community and does not participate in the affairs of the Saṃgha.

Later, if he confesses [his fault], the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states that one who has been subjected to the three types of suspension must practice [the penance] in a place where there are monks. If there are no monks present, it is not permitted.

This is explained as follows: "Sins arise from below" means that sins have no fixed nature; they arise from conditions. Once arisen, they are capable of summoning and accumulating the fruits of future tainted suffering (*sāsrava-duḥkha*).
In principle, they ought to be repented and eliminated so that one may return to original purity. Now, to speak rashly without considering whether one is a vessel of inferior capacity is [an error].
Because the nature of sin and merit is empty, one is unwilling to perform repentance. The Great Master said:

"Nowadays, those who study the Mahāyāna discourse have minds that approach the Way, yet their conduct remains linked to both the Great and Small Vehicles. Their mouths say there is no sin and no repentance;

they claim that lust is the Way, and though their bodies commit evil, they follow their own whims as right and consider anything contrary to them as wrong. All such cases must be treated according to this [rule]. Furthermore, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states... [The text continues with the following: "...being..."

Regarding the third case of one who has been formally charged: if their mind and disposition have become supple and gentle, they should inform the Saṃgha, saying, "My mind is now supple and gentle; I pray that the Saṃgha will grant me release from this legal procedure.

Having made this announcement, they should step back and withdraw. The presiding bhikṣu should then deliberate upon whether the matter is appropriate; only then may he request the lifting of the suspension and allow them to return to the assembly to fulfill the required quorum.

Regarding "one with evil views" (*pāpadṛṣṭi*): The *Dàocháo* states that when one wishes to truly obstruct the Path yet claims it does not obstruct it, and with a perverse mind reaches a definitive conclusion, this is termed a "view.
Because this view-mind rejects the principle, it is designated as "evil. Furthermore, regarding the four dharmas of precepts and views, one explains them erroneously and lacks faith.

Such a person must be formally censured and expelled by the Saṃgha, never to be employed again. Only when they comply without opposition will they be released from this state. These three types of formal acts (*karmavācanā*) are known as... [the name of the specific karmas].
This constitutes three types of formal accusations (*ukkhepanīyakamma*). Their faith and practice are both ruined; they are cast out from the assembly and no longer count as members of the Saṃgha.

Because their transgressions are so grave that they cannot be rehabilitated, this ultimate disciplinary measure was established. The Vinaya treats such individuals as equivalent to those who have committed a grave offense (*pārājika*);

even at the time of death, all their assets shall enter the common property of the monks who performed the formal act of suspension, as a reward for their meritorious service. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that for those who slander the Dharma, this [measure] is applied.
The *karmavācanā* for subduing. Furthermore, it is because it demonstrates that all evil deeds have karmic retribution; [the offender] becomes decayed and cast aside, just like useless timber.

Next is the heavy offense, namely the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. "Knowing and yet" (*jñātvā ca*) means being aware of the characteristics of the transgression and intentionally concealing it. "Subsequently" (*anupūrveṇa*) refers to the beginning...
From one night up to a hundred nights and so forth, the practice of the *parivāsa* (concealment) rite is performed in accordance with the length of time the offense was concealed.

Regarding "half-destroyed," the *Vinayamātṛkā* states: "A *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense requiring suspension from the community) is like a person who has been struck by another; though he is wounded, a throat remains."
Therefore, it is called "residual" (śeṣa). If this is so, then it distinguishes itself from the first category [of offenses], where severing the head is termed "complete destruction.

Regarding the *caraṇīya-dharma* (the practice of penance): when one is performing the *parivāsa* (probation), the *caraṇīya-dharma* is suspended. If the *parivāsa* is completed, then the suspension of the *caraṇīya-dharma* is also completed.

Now, having committed an offense before the period was complete, one must begin the practice again from the first day. For example, if one was performing a *parivāsa* for a hundred nights and has now reached the fiftieth night...
Regarding a repeat offense: the previous fifty nights are forfeited; logically, one must begin again from the first day to complete the full hundred nights.

The same applies to the practice of the *mānatva* for six nights. Therefore, the *Daichao* states: "If one commits a grave offense during either of the two methods, both methods are invalidated by that gravity;
one is granted the *mūlāpatti-śuddhi* (rectification of the root offense). This method should follow after the *mānatva*."

[The text] emerges. Now, regarding the two methods of *paryuṣitaparivāsa* (concealment) and *mūlāpakarṣa* (root-rehabilitation), since neither their presence nor absence is sufficient [to effect purification], they are placed before the six-night penance (*ṣaḍrātra*).

If one is to emerge from the offense through the six-night penance, it must necessarily be practiced; thus the *Chao* says: "Whether there was concealment with the former method or no concealment with the latter method, both are identical in emerging from the offense.
This refers to the joy of mind (*cittaprasāda*), which is also translated as "gladdening the assembly" (*saṃghaprāmodya*), meaning the mind follows and accords with the Saṃgha.
The teaching: all shall harbor joy. "Branches" refers to skillful means (*upāya*) as well as the concealment of offenses. Twenty:
the *Śāstra* says, "If twenty pure bhikṣus expel a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, then my Dharma will not perish; if there are fewer than that, it is not accomplished."

Regarding those who were slandered by the Qingren (Cīna): the Vinaya states that when Trapuṣa Malla served as the administrator (*vaiyāvṛtyakara*) for the Saṃgha, the group known as the Six Companions (Ṣaḍvargika) obtained inferior lodgings and invitations from him.
Becoming angry, they slandered him, saying he was possessed of attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion; they then falsely accused him of sexual misconduct in the midst of the assembly.
The Buddha questioned them about the truth of the matter, and they replied, "From the past until even in my dreams, [I have never done such a thing]."
[How much less so] regarding sexual misconduct? How much less so regarding awakening? When the bhikṣus questioned him on these matters, the group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) said, "Sthavira is pure;
such a thing did not happen. The Buddha said, "Sthavira is one who is free from attachment and does not intentionally violate the precepts.

You should perform the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations) to grant him the *smṛti-dharma* (the rule of mindfulness). Regarding "one who is not insane": the Vinaya says that the bhikṣu Nandika contracted a disease of insanity and wandered about.

He entered [the community] while failing to observe the rules of decorum and frequently committed various offenses. When a bhikṣu questioned him about this, he replied, "I committed these offenses during a period of insanity;

once my illness has cleared, I shall not do so again. The matter was reported to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "A *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) for 'not being insane' should be granted.

This serves as proof that the transgressions were committed during a period of illness and will not be repeated after recovery. The assembly must be pure and sufficient in number. *Huá* (pronounced *hú bā*) means wisdom (*prajñā*)."
