If one knows that another has committed an offense, that person must not be included in the formal procedure, as they are in reality not a bhikṣu.
Furthermore, these ten gates, according to our own Master, generally govern the establishment or abolition of all *karmavācanā* (formal acts).

While the ancient masters sometimes required only nine conditions—as in the case of establishing a boundary (*sīmābandha*), where there is no need for a proxy (*chanda*), or in the case of receiving a day-off or being dispatched, where there is no formal request (*yācanā*)—our school requires that all of these be established.
As stated below: "In the case of establishing a boundary, the condition of having no proxy is established to clarify the requirements; regarding the reception of a dispatch..."

If there is no request, would it not be necessary to inform? To inform is equivalent to the eightfold expression of one's circumstances. Furthermore, regarding the weighing of prior matters, the various schools have abandoned this;
the current Master’s establishment of it is correct.

The balance and the *dou* measure. "Balance" refers to the horizontal beam of the scale. Regarding the *shu* and *lei*: the *Yiqingzhong* states, "The divisions of the balance begin with the *shu*; the *lei* occupies the first place.
As for the origin of measurement, the primary unit for scooping begins with the *shu*. According to the *Sunzi Suanjing*, the origin of weighing begins with the *shu*.
The *shu* (millet) is the millet used for food. Ten *shu* make one *lei* (Yan Shiguo says this is pronounced *lai* with the *ge* rhyme);

ten *lei* make one *zhu*; twenty-four *zhu* make one *liang*. Furthermore, the origin of measurement begins from the *su* (grain): ten *su* make one *chao*; ten *chao* make one *cuo*; ten *cuo* make one *shao*; ten *shao* make one *he*;
ten *he* make one *sheng*; continuing up to ten *hu*, which make one *zhong*. What is now called the balance (*heng*) [is based on these].
The arising of the *shu* (a unit of weight), the *lei*, and the divisions of the *dou*—the *gui*, *he*, and so forth—is such that the weights and measures do not lose their proper standard;

it is the same today. Regarding the Dharma encompassing both the agent (*neng*) and the object (*suo*): the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) belongs to the Dharma as the agent, and the proclamation of the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to confess) is also the Dharma;

it is not accomplished without the *karmavācanā*, thus it belongs to the object. As cited in the following proofs, they are mutually interpenetrating: for example, when the entire assembly commits an offense, the Vinaya provides a means of mutual exemption.

One holds the *śuddhaka-ekajñapti* (the single motion) and together performs the confession. Once the offenses have been brought forth, they are all extinguished; hence it is said that "all confessions consist of the *śuddhaka-ekajñapti*.

Regarding the Dharma, it is applied according to the specific matter. To say it is based on having a physical object is incorrect, because the names of the various Dharmas are universal; one invokes the Dharma according to the matter at hand.
The term "Dharma" is a general designation. Furthermore, how could it be that a location is not subsumed under the category of Dharma?

For example, when a site is formally consecrated through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation), that very place is designated as a *mahā-sīmā* (great boundary) or a *śīma-kaṇḍaka* (boundary enclosure). Regarding persons, this refers to those who perform the ritual.

As stated in the *Vinaya*, specifically in the section on the "Extinguishing of Disputes" (*adhikaraṇa-samatha*), he himself cites: "The three Dharmas being present," etc. As for what are called the "three Dharmas," the *Vinaya* states that there are three kinds of presence.
First, the presence of the Dharma and the Vinaya. What is the presence of the Dharma? It is the settling of disputes by means of the Dharma that is upheld.
What is the presence of the Vinaya? It is the settling of disputes by means of the Vinaya that is upheld. What is the presence of the persons? It is the exchange of speech and discussion.

Since it does not mention the *saṃgha*, it follows that the *saṃgha* is subsumed under the person (*pudgala*), which is the common locus. The five factors are: the Dharma, the Vinaya, the person, the *saṃgha*, and the boundary (*sīmā*).

What is meant by "the presence of the *saṃgha"*? It is when those who ought to come have come, those who ought to give their consent (*chanda*) have given their consent, and those entitled to censure do not censure.
What is meant by "the presence of the boundary"? It is the proclamation of the *karmavācanā*, whether performed individually, face-to-face, or through mental recollection (*manasikāra*).
If it is the *saṃgha* consisting of four or more persons, when performing a *karmavācanā*, five factors must be present before one.
This is because that which arises from a *karmavācanā* must necessarily be the *dharmadhātu*. Thus, one should know that these five factors must be present.
The distinction between laypeople and monastics lies in their respective capacities.

Regarding the possession of requisite virtues: for example, when appointing a person to pay respects to nuns, one must possess ten virtues; when appointing a person to receive the invitation to criticize (*pravāraṇā*), that person must possess two sets of five virtues, and so forth.

When receiving the [formal] day, one should first observe whether the candidate is a legitimate object for such an appointment before conferring it upon them. Regarding the relinquishing of robes: [the procedure follows].
One should observe that those who employ improper methods may be excluded, whereas those who manufacture [the object] improperly must not be excluded.

Furthermore, one must determine how many are required to constitute a *saṃgha* and how many monks are appropriate for performing this ritual act. Moreover, those who are pure and in accordance with the Dharma must clearly understand the Vinaya-piṭaka and be proficient in discerning the conditions for success or failure;
only then may they be included in the count of the *saṃgha* to perform the formal act (*karman*) of placing under the overturned bowl (*pātra-nyubja*).

One must wait until that person harbors faith before one may bestow [the precepts] upon them. Regarding the five and eight precepts (pañca-śīla and aṣṭāṅga-śīla), one must likewise observe their spiritual capacity (*bhājana*), such as whether they have previously received [the precepts] without violating them.
This refers, for example, to the fact that if one has violated even one of the grave offenses among the five precepts, one cannot receive the eight precepts.

When a matter presents itself—namely, those one hundred and eighty-four matters—or when a matter is such that it may be treated according to the rules, yet this [specific case] is not permissible, the text states:

"If it is not in accordance with the Dharma, it shall cease. There are eight types, ranging from a mere mental recollection (*cittānujñā*) up to a formal motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).
*Xiáng-cáng* (Practice and Concealment): "Practice" (*xíng*) refers to that which accords with the teachings; the opposite is termed "concealment" (*cáng*).

"Reaching the lower" refers to the seven grades of benefit and harm, meaning that each of the seven classes of offenses has its own hierarchical gradations. "Doubt" (*yí*) means hesitation and indecision. "Delusion" (*mí*) means having no prior training.

One who knows the Vinaya and relies on the teachings may not commit an offense due to a deluded mind; however, for one who lacks training, the offense must be formally adjudicated (*jié*) because they are deluded regarding the teachings. This is the principle.

One must distinguish between them; they cannot be treated as one and the same as the Dharma. "Matters are like morning and evening" means that distinguishing between clarity and darkness is like the difference between day and night.
When observing the nature of an offense, one should likewise act accordingly. One must not apply remedies where there is no offense, nor fail to treat what is diseased;

otherwise, the characteristics of upholding and violating precepts will become confused. Generally, those offenses within the same category are confessed together, while those that are distinct offenses are confessed individually; this is the rule. One must not [confuse these].
"委曲" (wěiqū) means to be exhaustive and thorough; "罔冒" (wǎngmào) means to be without concealment or deception.

"Humanity follows things": humanity follows as described above. Regarding "things," it refers to the six items provided for those who nurse the sick, by which one observes the presence or absence of virtue.

The gravity or lightness [of an offense] is determined by the specific circumstances, such as the value of the items involved. For example, if one commits the offense of possessing extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*) measuring six, eight, or ten *cun*, it is designated as "heavy" (*guru*);

if the measurement is less than that, it is designated as "light" (*laghu*), constituting a minor offense (*dukkaṭa*). Furthermore, the first day after receiving a robe is termed "prior" (*pubba*), while the subsequent nine days are termed "subsequent" (*pacchima*).

When clothing and other items are scattered about, they are abandoned individually; once they have been gathered into a bundle, their abandonment is termed "combined. For those belonging to the same category, a collective confession (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*) is performed;

for those of different groups, separate confessions are made. The preliminary effort is the cause, and the fundamental act is the result. Furthermore, the cause cannot be confessed in the same manner as the result.
Regarding such matters, one should not simply apply a remedy as soon as the situation arises; rather, one must first investigate and examine each case thoroughly until its true nature is established.
Only when this is the case may one apply the ritual procedure (*vidhi*); thus, there will be no error in the weighing [of the elements].

Regarding "possessing" (*samanvāgata*) below: if one possesses both, then person, dharma, and action arise together; if only one, they arise separately; if both are combined, they constitute a dual possession.
Therefore, the application of the ritual procedure varies accordingly.

"Tí-bài" (稊稗). According to the *Erya*, "tí" (蕛, pronounced tí) and "tì" (苵, cut with the initial *dú* and final *jié*) refer to weeds resembling *bài* (稗, pronounced bàng-guà), which grow spreading over the ground;
they are noxious grasses. It is also said that *bài* grass resembles grain. In the ritual procedures (*jīemó*), when there is a principle that allows for flexibility, it is open;
if one acts contrary to this, it becomes obstructed. How could this apply only to these matters?
Those who are not pure are not admitted. The Vinaya states that one who has committed an offense may not hear the precepts, nor may they inquire about offenses or explain them to others.

In this sense, it refers to the person. However, below, the methods for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) and the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*) are followed collectively by both the Saṃgha and the individual.
"Exclusively in" means that it is subsumed under the Dharma.

"However, 'below' refers to the ritual act (*śī*). 'Non-sentient' refers to the realm (*dhātu*). 'Human activity' refers to the person (*pudgala*) based on principle. 'The harmonious Sangha chanting the boundaries' originally belongs to the Dharma (*dharma*).
Now, these two conditions combined constitute the formal establishment of the boundary (*sīmābandha*); therefore, looking toward the primary [act], the peripheral elements belong to the ritual act."
Regarding the difficulty of establishing a fixed sequence between the preceding and the following: sometimes the matter precedes while the person and the dharma follow;

for example, as in the prior establishment of a boundary (*sīmābandha*), after which the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) and the reception of ordination (*upasampadā*) are performed. Or there may be only three parts, such as when the establishment of a boundary has endured for a long time before the reception and recitation are subsequently carried out.
Is this not because the initiation is indeterminate? Therefore, there are three parts.

There is an inferior [category]. This refers to a single item that inherently possesses three types of measurement. Regarding what constitutes "proper" clothing: for example, plain cotton cloth (*kārpāsa*) is proper;
furthermore, silk (*kauśeya*) that is free from killing is also called proper. Brocade, fine gauze, *sārī*, *ghuṭa*, and the like are improper.

Furthermore, the number of strips, length, and dyeing all pertain to the matter itself. "Mutual understanding" means having already explained it; for instance, as when people of the Middle Kingdom add [to their garments].

The dharma is not accomplished by being singular. For example, regarding the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*) and the confession of various offenses while seated, these objects of focus are not one.
When the mind gives rise to speech, it must be articulated verbally so that others may hear it; it is not accomplished merely through mental recollection.

This is the primary basis (*nidāna*), as in the case of the basis for receiving the precepts; it is not a basis consisting of the elements (*dhātu*). If there is any discrepancy, the rite is not accomplished.
How could one then mix these three types and present them together? That which is the element is precisely the matter (*vastu*).

This refers to the "heavy robe" (*guru-cīvara*) mentioned in the *cīvara-vippavāsa-kamma* (the formal act of being separated from one's robe). It must necessarily be complete; if incomplete, it is not accomplished. Therefore, they are combined. Such is the statement.
This is the method of the majority decision (*yadbhūyasikīya-vinaya*). It is like the aforementioned procedure for the distribution of voting sticks (*śalākā-śrāvaṇa*).

The entire tally refers to the person; the selection of the broken tally refers to the matter. This also combines two elements: seven conditions consist of three single factors, three pairs, and one combination.

The methods for distinct categories differ; one cannot simply place the *pāyattika* (提) and the *duṣkṛta* (吉) together under the same heading. Whether "same" (*tóng*) or "should be" (*dāng*) is used, they are indeed the same *pāyattika*.
Although their specific characteristics differ, those that share the same name of confession are "combined" (*hé*), while those with separate names of confession are "separated" (*lí*).
This is not contrary to principle; therefore, it is said that "all are permissible."
"Good and bad. "Good" (*zāng*) means accomplished; "bad" (*fǒu*) means not achieved.

[The commentary] merely takes the ultimate rules and principles to come and explain the text according to the *Shìwén*. Next, from "that which is like" up to "accomplished as a standard," it comes to explain the meaning.
Now, first, "monastic affairs" refers to the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual). "Difficult matters" refers to the obstructions caused by wicked bhikṣus.

To "abide in the school" (zong) means that the school is the fundamental basis. This *karmavācanā* is precisely the single dharma of boundary-establishment (*sīmābandha*), as illustrated by the examples cited below.
As mentioned above, this involves the mutual inclusion of both the general and the specific.

"Jiang" (to encourage) means to assist in completion; "wu" (diligence) refers to affairs. This means that one cannot assist in the affairs of the Dharma. Regarding the two substances, metal and stone:

the bell (*zhong*) and the chime-stone (*qing*) are originally musical instruments of this region. Metal is used to make the bell, and stone is used to make the chime-stone. As the *Li* (Book of Rites) says: "The shape [of the chime-stone] is like that of a *qing*."

Regarding "following that which makes sound": originally, this refers to copper and iron; anything capable of making a sound may be used for this purpose, with the sole exception of the *tendoku* (poison-adding) tree.
Striking a drum to warn the troops is a practice prescribed in the *Zhou Li*, which states: "Use the *fenggu* (drum with a raised rim) to signal the army. This is the correct method.

There are some texts that read the character *shi* (world/generation) instead, but this is incorrect. The *Zhou Yi* says, "It thunders with the thunderclaps," which is what the drum symbolizes. The *Li Ji* says: "I..."
The elder Qi’s use of a grass mat, a clump of bamboo as a drumstick, and an earthen drum represents its origin. The seven types of sounds are:

measuring shadows, splitting bamboo to produce sound, producing smoke, blowing the *bhaiṣajya* (chanting), beating the drum, striking the *ghanṭā*, and striking the ground. When chanting, "Venerable sirs, the time for the *poṣadha* has arrived," the current text’s categories of sound and color can subsume these seven kinds.
Furthermore, the specific chanting command is restricted to the last one.
The "lower rank" refers to śrāmaṇeras. The *Chao* states: "This means having a resident śrāmaṇera or a *karmadāna* beat [the offender].
The "fully ordained" refers to mahābhikṣus. There are two types: śrāmaṇeras and *karmadānas*.
"Slight density" (*weichou*) refers to striking ten times with a light touch. The *Guidu Tujing* states: "Measure the time and adjust for the assembly;
having roughly practiced the preliminary model, hold the mallet and settle the mind, then strike lightly ten times. For those who strike too thinly, begin from the eleventh stroke onward;
as the sound becomes gradually thinner and then thicker, continue until the thirty-seventh stroke. Wait for this sound to cease, then strike once more—this is called one [unit]."
"First strike: to assemble the assembly of Śrāvakas. Second strike: to assemble the assembly of Pratyekabuddhas.
Third strike: to assemble the assembly of Bodhisattvas; therefore it is said that three strikes are added. The *Tujing* states:

'There is none who does not use the three strikes as a rhythm to assemble the Three Vehicles. As for the establishment of the Vinaya regulations, the three strikes refer to striking three times. Thus it is said.
"Clouds and knots" refers to the meaning of the three types of karma.

Regarding "determinate or indeterminate": depending on the superior or inferior nature of a person's cultivation through meditation, one may be able to transform karma so that it is experienced in a future life, or in subsequent lives, or not experienced at all.
As for "determinate," both the karma and its retribution are fixed; even upon reaching the stage of a sage, [it cannot be altered].

It cannot be avoided; it ceases only when the conditions for its end arise. As recorded in the *Dharmatrāta-dharmapada-śāstra* (The Tradition of the Transmission of the Dharma), King Kaniṣka, due to his great slaughter and violence, died and entered the body of a thousand-headed fish.
A wheel of swords revolved around his body, cutting him as he was reborn again and again. However, upon hearing the sound of a bell, the wheel of swords suspended itself in the air.
Through such causes and conditions, he sent a messenger to inform the magistrate to strike the bell loudly, so that his suffering might cease.
Meeting with the virtuous is like the case of the monk Zhixing, who made a vow when the sound of a bell struck him.

Furthermore, the King’s previous repentance before Aśvaghoṣa served as the cause (*hetu*), while his current hearing of the bell and liberation from suffering serve as the condition (*pratyaya*). These are all instances of cause and condition mutually inducing one another.

The *Weiyijing* (Sūtra on Dignified Conduct) refers to the *Sanqian weiyi* (Three Thousand Dignified Conducts), translated in two fascicles by An Shigao of the Han dynasty. In its second fascicle, it says: "The *gāndī*..."
There are five matters for novices (*śrāmaṇera*): first, the regular assembly; second, the morning meal; third, the midday meal; fourth, clearing away the dishes; and fifth, impermanence.
Furthermore, there are seven rules: first, the local authorities; second, fire; third, water; fourth, bandits; fifth, the assembly of *śrāmaṇeras*; sixth, the assembly of *upāsakas*;

and seventh, calling one’s own children (these together comprise the twelve periods). Within these, there are varying degrees of striking. For instance, at the regular assembly, the gong is struck twice with great force.

Ten strokes for a minor offense; eight strokes for eating at dawn; down to three strokes for summoning a śrāmaṇera to an assembly, two strokes for summoning an upāsaka to an assembly, and one stroke for calling a private servant.
In the latter part of that same sutra, there are further rules involving thirty, twenty, ten, and five strokes;
to avoid prolixity, they are not cited here.
"Adultery" refers to the violation of ethical principles (*li*). It means to disorder the constant norms. "Stealing from the *saṃghika*" means stealing property belonging to the community.
"Creating division" means failing to achieve the characteristic of harmony and unity.

Regarding the "knower of the bell" (*zhīzhōng*): it refers to the person who rings the bell, who must act with the awareness and mindfulness that "this is being done. Originally, for all ritual actions involving pure speech (*jìngyǔ*), one was not permitted to perform them oneself;

therefore, pure speech was used as a substitute. Now, since one is permitted both to perform the action oneself and to instruct others to do so, [the role of the knower of the bell remains necessary].

What need is there for such words? Thus we know that those who employ [this interpretation] are mistaken. Regarding humans and animals: in terms of the emotional gravity of the offense, when discussing humans, it is as stated:

"Striking a bhikṣu constitutes a *thullaccaya* (grave offense); striking one of the lower assemblies constitutes a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing); striking a woman with lustful intent constitutes a *saṃghādisesa* (offense requiring suspension).

Regarding animals, it is as stated: "If a practitioner kills oxen or sheep, the sin is grave while the precept [violation] is light. One must not even raise a staff in threat against animals and the like.
Regarding "insentient things" (*asattva*): it is like picking up a worn-out garment after beating it, or following [the path] where the ground has been struck with a mallet or pierced by a blade.

Therefore, it was said above that such matters are extremely numerous and exist everywhere. Since the word "beat" (*ta*) appears in the precept text (*śikṣāpada*), might one instead change it to "knowing it is pure" (*jñāna-śuddha*) and act accordingly?
The following two lines both serve to explain the meaning of "knowing it is pure. This is for a distinct purpose.
Since there are those who grow and produce, their use is permissible. For example, one must employ people to strike grass, trees, flowers, fruits, and so forth;

this [text] likewise addresses the commoners and non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who cling to the notion that things possess the quality of growth and production. If one were to allow for self-destruction or production, one would be subject to ridicule and slander;
therefore, it specifically prohibits this. Thus, below, the meanings of striking, colliding, beating, and hitting are set forth, following the local terminology of this region. One.
The sequence is reversed. The phrasing appears out of order; it should be placed below "when striking the bells and drums.
The two following phrases should instead be positioned under "when the sound issues forth," and only then will the meaning be coherent. "Gigantic" means vast. "Dread" means fear.
This means that although the matter may be small, it constitutes a great object of dread for the student. The Confucians say: "Do not let there be careless speech. Now, if...
The phrase "that which is useful" refers to the act of discerning and discarding [false views].
As for the method of abandoning the self: if there were discord, each would cling to their own notion of "self" and "person. Now, we establish a common boundary so that they may assemble in harmony.
This is the way of losing and abandoning the self, persons, and dharmas.
Regarding the remaining realms (*dhātu*), they are subsumed under "food," which shall be explained in detail later.

Within the discussion of the binding and releasing of various realms, the term "person" refers to an evil bhikṣu, as will be shown later. This occurs within the section on establishing a small boundary (*sīmā*) below.
There are two locations: first, within the boundary (*sīmā*); second, outside the limit. One performs the *pratideśanīya* (confession) and the mental recitation (*manasikāra*).

Within the boundary, all dharmas may generally be performed, except for the dissolution of the boundary and the establishment of the boundary; these must not be undertaken arbitrarily, as they are all subject to specific regulations.

If one performs the *pravāraṇā* (invitation) or the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal act with a motion and three proclamations), both boundaries must gather together. If one performs other dharmas, then each of the two boundaries gathers separately.
There is no interior, because the Saṃgha sits in a dense cluster; there is no remaining space within. Thus, it can be said that there is no interior where they may assemble. [Objection:

If there is already natural ground outside the body, why is this not the same as the previous case of a large boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) without a designated field (*kṣetra*), which has an exterior where they may assemble? [Response: As stated below.

This means that the original establishment of the small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*) was precisely intended to exclude wicked bhikṣus. Although there may be those who do not assemble, it does not hinder the validity of the ritual procedure (*dharma*).
This is unlike the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*), for which it is said there is no designated site because it pertains to unrighteous and evil persons.

There are two types of assemblies. There are assemblies at four locations. For example, when performing the *pratimokṣa* (confession) rite outside the boundary (*sīmā*), one performs the *karmavācanā* for receiving the day’s grace within the boundary;

with the *pratimokṣa* rite held in between, the robes are maintained [within the boundary]. When performing the ordination rite within the body of the *śīmaṇḍala* (precept field), assemblies are held at each of the four locations, and each of the four rites is accomplished;
they do not obstruct one another. However, if one is to perform the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism), it is necessary that everyone assemble at the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*).
The *Prātimokṣa* is recited within the assembly because it is the foundation for communal harmony; logically, all members must gather at the four designated locations.

Should anyone privately abscond or flee to a distant place, they commit an offense. Upon seeing signs, one must immediately seek them out; even if only one person is seen, one must still seek to assemble them. There are many such cases.
The *Śīlaskandha-vastu* (Precept Section) of the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "At that time, in a certain residence, on the day of the *Poṣadha*, there was a visiting bhikṣu..."
[Someone] comes and sees a resident bhikṣu on the boundary of the precept-platform (*sīmā*). Seeing him, they do not seek him out, yet they proceed to perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*).
The bhikṣus inform the Buddha, and the Buddha says: "The ritual is established, but the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) is an offense" (first sentence).

If one sees [the resident] and immediately seeks him out, but having sought him, does not call him, the ritual is established and the recitation of the precepts is an offense (second sentence). If one sees him, seeks him out, and having sought him, calls him, the ritual is established.
Regarding the recitation of the precepts (three phrases). Hearing or suspecting [a transgression] is also like this (the same three phrases as above).

Furthermore, there is a residence where, on the day of the recitation of the precepts, resident bhikṣus see visiting bhikṣus on the boundary of the precept-arena (three phrases), as well as hearing or suspecting [them] (three phrases); all are identical to the above.

"Desolate" (*luòmò*) means having a vast and boundless appearance. If one must take the fundamental [non-dharma] as the basis, and if one thoroughly investigates the root, then since the formation of the dharma is not established, it will cause subsequent dharmas to fail to be accomplished.
Subsequent conditions—namely, receiving the precepts, repenting of offenses, and so forth—are they not instances of overstepping and confusion that prevent subsequent dharmas from being accomplished?
This is because the conditions for subsequent dharmas arise from the preceding boundary. The phrase "this statement below" means that this statement is very easy to understand.

Fearing that at the time of the ceremony, people’s minds might remain stubborn and it would be difficult to reform them, he therefore ordered a general collection [of monks] to verify whether the procedure was successful or not.

Regarding the question below: the intention is to ask whether, within the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), the four places from which the assembly gathers for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) and the invitation to admonish (*pravāraṇā*)—as already explained above—are still applicable here on the altar.
Even when there are two assemblies—that is, for both the *poṣadha* and the *pravāraṇā*—it is likewise necessary for the assembly to gather from the four places.

Two or four [boundaries] are difficult to open. As stated below: "The *zī* (invitation) is called 'clothing' (*yī*). These three were originally established as the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), which is difficult to open;
this refers to the *śikṣādattaka* (probationary) area.
In various Vinayas, such as those recited in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, they are listed as follows. As noted in the commentary, these are the items listed. Each is explained in the commentary.
The four types [of boundaries] distinguished therein are as follows:

regarding the Sangha, the individuals cannot be distinguished; regarding the location, the sites cannot be distinguished. Below the section on the *Saṃghāṭī*, it is proven that the location cannot be divided;
seven trees constitute the measure, and by calculating the total configuration of these seven trees, one obtains six intervals.
Seven *dhanus*. One *dhanu* consists of five *hastas*; one *hasta* is eighteen inches. Calculated at six intervals, this is sixty-three paces—assuming that six feet constitute a pace.
Each interval amounts to ten and a half paces; thus, six intervals equal sixty-three paces. Regarding the distance:
if there is a space of seven trees between the two groups situated to the east and west, then one does not incur the offense of being apart [from the community].

A Memorial for My Late Father, the Lay Disciple Chen, surnamed Yiniang, a Righteous Believer who took refuge in the Triple Gem:

I, your daughter, humbly submit this memorial for my deceased father, whose life has suddenly come to an end at Ren-shou Temple and who has already cast off his mundane existence. In bitter grief, I reflect upon the profound depth of his nurturing love and the great righteousness of his upbringing.

I am deeply grateful. Desiring to express my thanks, I must rely upon superior conditions; thus, with sincere resolve, I have contributed seventy thousand units of pure wealth to produce this one fascicle of commentary on the Vinaya-piṭaka.
May it aid in its widespread circulation, bringing glory to the Buddhas and Patriarchs, and may the wondrous secrets herein gathered serve as an offering for the journey ahead.
I, Chen Dalang, your humble son, prostrate myself before you, my late father. I pray that the mountains of transgression may collapse and the oceans of karma may dry up;

that you may instantly transcend the bodies of the nine realms and swiftly realize the fruit of the One Vehicle. Thereafter, may all beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—whether kinsmen or enemies within the Dharma-realm—rely upon these excellent causes and together ascend to the other shore.
Written on the first day of the first month of the first year of the Shaoxing era (the year Wuchen), respectfully titled:
*Zhengyuanji*, a Commentary on the *Suiji Jiemoshu* of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, Fascicle Three.

Since they were originally members of the Saṃgha, one must know that at the time of performing the ritual, one must thoroughly inquire among the laypeople within the boundary (*sīmā*) as to whether there is anyone who has previously received full ordination (*upasampadā*) and not relinquished it. Only if the answer is 'none' will there be no [obstacle]."

Regarding the "separate assembly" (biezòng): the five primary colors—blue, yellow, red, white, and black—are already permitted to be counted [as witnesses]. Conversely, this serves as a verification that [the formal act] is generally established.

As for a gravely ill person, because their mind is clouded and dull, they take no pleasure in the dharmas that lack sentient objects; thus, the two conditions for relinquishing [the precepts] are not met.

This means that the mutual face-to-face relinquishment of the precepts is not established, because the words spoken are not mutually understood. It is only when one later understands the speech that [the act] is completed; these two cases illustrate the general characteristics.
Sufficient. As for the dull-witted person who does not understand the meaning of the words:

"harmonious patience" (和忍) refers to that which is to be harmonized and accepted. To "understand the intent" (解意) means to grasp the underlying meaning of the text. "The present world" (即世) refers to the near world.
Vast as the Milky Way. The *Zhuangzi* states: "Great yet without a specific point of reference; once gone, it returns to me.

I was startled by these words, which were like the Milky Way, boundless and infinite. The commentary says: "It is expansive and grand, yet lacks a precise target; it moves forward once to present a general outline."

It has never been subject to reversal or contradiction that one might seek out; hearing this, one is struck with awe and fear. It is like the great celestial river, the Milky Way, which is vast, distant, pure, and lofty;

if one traces its source and flow, it is utterly without end. Now, when the ignorant are rebuked for failing to distinguish between the success or failure, and right or wrong, of the *karmavācanā*, it is also just like this.

To focus on an object without contradiction means that, as when reciting hurriedly, the subtle objects of focus are not distinguished; or, when the mind momentarily arises and focuses on another object, this is called "unlawful contradiction.
Regarding the "agent and the object": for instance, in the *karmavācanā* for receiving the precepts, phrases such as "Venerable Saṃgha, listen" and "The Saṃgha now bestows [the precepts] upon whom?
or "Do the elders consent? all belong to the Saṃgha acting as the agent. [The object is] the śrāmaṇera, so-and-so.
"First class" refers to that which belongs to the object of action. "That" and "I" are synonymous with "this" and "that. For example, when summoning a śrāmaṇera, one says "that";

at the time of formal reception [of precepts], one says "this. Furthermore, "that" pertains to both the object and the agent of action. If these are not now distinguished, they both belong to delusion.

Alternatively, the latter two phrases may be applied by reversing the former two; this is because the text is recited with strict adherence to its phrasing, yet it is not that the distinction is not made.
The textual forms consist of subject and object; because one has deeply practiced [the path] for oneself and others, it is not that one does not recognize "self" and "other.

Nevertheless, due to additions or omissions in the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual acts), they deviate from the primary purpose. When the written documents of the matters and the *dharma* are confused, erroneous, or redundant, those present who uphold the rite do not understand how to censure or suspend [the offender], which further constitutes delusion.
Or, when the text is placed below, it reverses the preceding sentence; although the words and phrases may be clear, [the meaning is lost].

The principles of the Dharma must not be confused; it is solely due to people having conditions of estrangement that they fail to distinguish between right and wrong, remaining silent and patient in all such matters—this, too, is delusion.

Regarding the boundaries of the realm: when performing the ritual for establishing a boundary (*sīmā-bandha*), one must clearly discern whether the previously established boundary is a non-boundary, a divided boundary, or whether its limits are distant or proximate.

"Contemplating the lower. "Contemplating" means observing. "The five delusions" refers to the four dharmas mentioned below. The first [delusion] generally clarifies the four dharmas of the dharma, the matter, the person, and the place.
The second [delusion] specifically clarifies that what is visible is limited.

If one can observe these five delusions and clarify these four dharmas, one may slightly participate in the propagation [of the Dharma] and be included within the quorum for *karmavācanā* (formal ritual acts). Therefore, it is said: "merely entering the ranks of the Sangha. "Merely" (*jin*).

It is near. Following the Dharma—if one follows the ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*) yet fails to clarify what is right and wrong, such instances of mistaken characteristics will proliferate like clouds and mist gathering together.
Unless one has extensively surveyed the various sections [of the Vinaya] and mastered the distinction between right and wrong, it is said: "What more can be discussed?
Regarding the following, as previously observed, the five delusions and the four dharmas pervade both mind and emotion; thus, this may also serve as a rough guide for propagating the Dharma.
[This refers to] a human being. The remainder is as extensively explained in the "Seven Non-[Valid] [Acts]" (*sapta-avasthā*). Regarding "under the hall":
it is like the *poṣadha* ceremony for three people, where the person who has sent their consent (*chanda*) is included in the count.

The *Daichao* states: "The person who gives consent is one in mind but separate in body. Regarding "two below": this refers to those who share the same covered space but have a partition between them; they do not constitute "the same" [space].

Regarding the characteristics: the third [category] is "half-covered and half-exposed," and so forth. Below this, according to the *Dàchāo* (Great Commentary), there is an additional interpretation that includes "separated by an open space," which is omitted in the present text.

Regarding the three [modes] for each of the four activities: taking "walking" as the first, one proceeds through standing, sitting, and lying down; continuing in this manner until taking "lying down" as the first, one proceeds through walking, standing, and sitting.
Thus, three times four makes twelve phrases. For now, however, we shall follow the four postures alone to form four phrases;
when combined with the previous five, such as "giving consent" (*chanda*), they total nine. "Walking and so forth" refers to standing, sitting, and lying down.

Regarding the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*): because many people do not hear it, the practice of reciting it was established as an allowance. When the instructor (*śikṣācārya*) enters the assembly, he calls the novices (*śrāmaṇera*) to enter;
they are established there because they are employed by the Saṃgha. For those who are ill, sitting or standing is inconvenient;

thus, lying down within the assembly is permitted, which also constitutes facing the Saṃgha—this is the meaning of conformity. Regarding "allowances and prohibitions" (*kai-zhi*): this means that even within the category of allowances, there are further prohibitions.
"I shall go. This refers to the group of six;
[the total is] twenty-eight. The ancients spoke only on the basis of the specific Vinaya rules. The above concludes the preceding meaning; it must necessarily lead down to what follows.

This is explained in detail in the *Shishi Yaoyong Chao*. There are further individuals who do not understand [the rules], and they are not to be included. This refers to what was mentioned above regarding "those who do not understand" and so forth.

The four categories refer to those who constitute a separate assembly (*biezong*) and are not counted as a quorum (*feizushu*). The general enumeration refers to the persons listed in the third position.

This is right and that is wrong: upholding the precepts is called "right," while violating the precepts is termed "wrong. However, it is as when a person is submerged; though they are not obstructed from being pure in essence, it is merely due to a discrepancy in conditions.
The phrase "the two persons" includes those who should have granted their consent (*chanda*) but did not do so; these are subsumed within the term "etc.

As for "disappearance," because being in a well or a cellar belongs to the same category as dry land, it constitutes a separate case. Furthermore, they do not count toward the quorum. The same applies to being out of sight and out of hearing.
There are seven persons: namely, those who have performed *parivāsa*, those undergoing *mūlaparivāsa*, those undergoing *mānatva*, and those about to be released from their offense;

these, together with the ten types of *parivāsa* completed, the *mūlaparivāsa* completed, and the six nights completed, constitute the seven persons. Regarding "general" and "specific": it is called "specific" because while it applies generally to the arising of wholesome qualities, it does not apply to the extinguishing of unwholesome ones.
The four distinctions refer to cases such as hearing [the confession] amidst partial concealment and partial disclosure, or being separated by a barrier.

"Two persons": this means that the feet are not distinct; the following explanation of "body" clarifies the number of feet, while the explanation of "mouth" clarifies the separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*).

"Four persons" refers to [the four types of] nuns down to the śrāmaṇerikā; this is the report on the distinctions. "Three persons among the nuns" refers to those with the thirteen *antarāyika* obstacles, excluding the eunuch (*paṇḍaka*) and the animal;

this is the discrepancy in the Dharma. "Two cases of staying as a thief" and "the two types of schism" (the broken assembly) constitute the violation of practice. "The two types of *pravāsanīya-karman*" and "the three types of *utkṣepanīya-karman*" constitute the disciplinary measures (*daṇḍa*).

"Serious" refers to the grave offenses (ānantarya) and the defiling of a nun; these constitute the substance [of the offense], while the subsequent explanations do not differ from this. "Various people" refers to the twelve types of individuals, such as those who are asleep;

although they are among the assembly, the subsequent explanations do not differ from this. That the formal act (kamma) is not accomplished means it is not sufficient. "Dhyāna" refers to meditative concentration (samādhi). Regarding the two conditions:
because the deaf cannot hear and the mute cannot speak, these two meanings—listening and speaking—are absent within the formal act.

The "two capabilities" refer to speaking and listening. "Entrusting it to the ground outside the realm" means entrusting and dropping it upon the ground. If one does not entrust it to the ground, it must be severed from its root;
therefore, it is said that "the internal and external are both distinct," neither subsumed by the two, neither the feet nor the distinct [limbs].
The essence is pervasive. The Path is like building a room to receive the sun; the mundane is like the signs of leaving home, shaving the head, or having the bowl turned upside down for a family.

These are identical in possessing the four modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*). "Not possessing" refers to cases such as the various disciplinary punishments where one may not sit. "Adding the rite before" means that the person performs the rite so that it applies to oneself.
"Performing the *jñapti* oneself" means that the Preceptor or the Confession Master makes the announcement together with the assembly. In all these cases, the body must be present.
Within the assembly, their deportment differs; they are not identical in their distinctions of right and wrong. If one is inferior, it explains the aforementioned worldly [status].
Because there is no fixed meaning, they may be subsumed as "sufficient" individuals.

The same as above; that is, identical to the third phrase previously mentioned. It is both a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*) and a quorum (*paripūrṇasaṃkhyā*). This refers to those who are subject to censure (*nigarhaṇīya*), such as the one who has been censured, and so forth.
The first phrase refers to a separate assembly that is neither a quorum nor a non-quorum. If one relies on the substance of the *parivāsa* (probation) and other such rules...

Because they are pure, they are counted among those who fulfill the quorum. Now, due to specific conditions, they do not belong to either of the two categories; that is, they are neither "sufficient" nor "separate.

This refers to the dharma of the "grave offense" (pārājika) and the dharma of "expulsion" (pravāsanīya), which differ in their retribution, such as the distinction between male and female. They are separated by dharma, such as the three types of formal accusations and the seven methods of disciplinary action.
They differ in mind, such as those who are asleep and so forth. Their characteristics shift, as in the case of the ritual for a bhikṣu climbing a tree.
"Transforms" means that it must necessarily descend; this reverses the preceding phrases. All of these constitute the pure and corresponding Dharma; they are complete and not separate.
"Reversing the preceding" can be understood as reversing the aforementioned state of being free from seeing and hearing.
Regarding the phrase "speaking to bystanders" (*pārśvavartī*), there are four interpretations. First, "speech" refers to the person who utters the censure;

"transgressing oneself" refers to the person being censured, who is subject to the judgment of the Saṃgha. "Other people" refers to those capable of abandoning the Saṃgha’s regulations, who stand outside the scope of the person being censured.

Furthermore, the second interpretation explains it in relation to outsiders (*bāhya-pudgala*); because they look toward the formal proceedings of the Saṃgha, they receive the name "bystanders. Third... [text fragment].
Thus, those sitting nearby are expected to act as witnesses. The fourth [point] supports the first interpretation, though it appears inverted;
for the commentary, citing the Vinaya, states that one speaks to those nearby and summons them to speak or remain silent, saying: "Which elders approve of this?
Those who do not approve, speak."

From the beginning down to the point where the sutra is annotated, the divisions and their correspondences can be seen. As listed in the table of contents, this refers to the "Intent of the Regulation," "Explanation of Names," and "Discernment of the Essence" within the first section.
Those whose physical forms dwell amidst worldly entanglements are burdened by the world. "Tongyun" (通允): according to the *Erya*, "yun" means "trustworthy.

Regarding the regulations for the monastic community: when one's body is present among the assembly, one may either speak out in reproach or remain silent. Now that there is a specific occasion, we therefore permit the sending of the mind [in its stead].
The *Dàocháo* states: "Even if there are conditions [for practice], if one does not open the mind for the assembly, then the capacity [of the practitioner] and the teaching will not coincide;

how then could they be rescued and delivered? 'Both self and others are raised together' means that, for them, the various dharmas are accomplished, and for me, the propagation of conditions is likewise fulfilled.
The *Chāo* says, "Both sides are accomplished," the meaning of which is the same as this: "raising" (jǔ) also carries the sense of "accomplishing" (chéngbàn).
Regarding "should desire" (*kṣiyati*): "desire" (*kṣi*) means to long for; "should" (*sū*) means that it ought to be so.

Because one has longed for the Saṃgha to act on one's behalf, yet now encounters an obstacle due to personal circumstances, one ought to send forth the intention to perform the task oneself, lest one contravene the pure assembly. As in the following, two of the five desires (*pañca-kāma-guṇa*) are cited;
these five are what worldly people desire. Now, upholding the Noble Dharma, they are merely what a bhikṣu desires. [This is] a detailed collection.
It was compiled after detailed deliberation, as follows. It is like having regained a boat or raft after being in the midst of crossing over.

"Matters were contrary" means that the circumstances of the matter involved mutual contradictions among the various factors. "To convey the intent" (chishin) means to send it forth so that it reaches [the assembly]. The *Daichō* states:

"If one wishes to clarify the formal procedures for the Saṃgha, the intention is to reach a decision through a collective assembly. However, due to discrepancies in conditions, the original wish was not fulfilled; therefore, we now send this intent to reach the Saṃgha."
Know that there is no contradiction.
"That which follows from the dharma" refers to the mental dharmas (*caitasika-dharma*). As for the *Abhidharmahṛdaya*, it asks: "What is the collection of the mind and its associated dharmas?"
The answer is: perception, desire, contact, wisdom, mindfulness, volition, liberation, concentration, and feeling—these are said to be the collection of mental factors (*citta-saṃprayukta-saṃskāra*).
That treatise itself explains them as follows: "Perception" is the grasping of the image and characteristics within an object; "desire" is the longing for and acceptance of an object-condition.

The remainder is explained as in the second fascicle of that treatise, in the chapter on Mental Formations (*citta-saṃskāra-varga*). Regarding bodily form, it is like the fivefold classification of diseases.

A person cannot convey this through speech alone; one must listen to the manifestation of their physical form and the granting of the pure desire (*śuddhaka-icchā*). Regarding the characteristics of the voice, as stated in the Vinaya:
"If one says, 'I give my desire'; or if one says, 'Give me your desire'; or if one says, 'For my sake, grant your desire'—these are correct. This concludes the section for a single monk.

Regarding the reception of precepts, the relinquishment of vows, and the performance of repentance (*pratideśanā*), the *saṃgha* must be present in harmony, whereas my presence is not strictly required. Because the Buddha did not establish a formal rule [to that effect], they require one another;

thus, the requirements for the *saṃgha* and for individuals are identical. If there is an offense, one may perform the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) as a separate group (*bhinna-saṃgha*). One may go far away, even outside the boundary (*sīmā*).
One must also establish the offenses, the prohibitions, and the allowances; these constitute the foundation for explaining prohibitions and allowances.

Regarding "not constituting a separate [assembly]": this means that because the conditions are not met, even if one speaks, it does not constitute [a formal act], and furthermore, one cannot avoid the offense of *pṛthag-varga* (separate assembly).

"Monastic affairs" (*saṃghakārya*) refers to the formal rituals performed by the community of monks. "Lacking sincerity" refers to the absence of a heart of genuine reverence in the one who conveys the *chanda*.

Regarding "false speech," the *Daichao* states: if one is not ill yet claims to be pure when impure, or claims to have the desire [to participate] when one does not, and causes another to transmit this false speech to the Saṃgha for them to speak, then for each individual monk present—regardless of how many there may be—one incurs three *pāyattika* offenses.
Those who receive this transmission should know it and report it accordingly. Each of these three offenses constitutes a grave karmic transgression; why then do you allow yourself to be negligent?

There are five [categories], beginning with Buddhist rites and extending to the care of the sick. According to the *Daocao*, this follows the precept regarding the non-transmission of the *chanda* (consent). Furthermore, including the matter of stūpas, there are six.

In the subsequent section on the circumstances regarding robes, it is stated that the group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*) communicated their consent while making robes; although this is not a formal regulation, it serves as a precedent.
At that time, the Saṃgha accepted and practiced it; therefore, it was also permitted. Regarding the term "Saṃgha," the following provides scriptural evidence.

Regarding the phrase "because of desire," etc., this explains the prohibition. It means that because the local terrain is weak, one cannot perform the formal legal acts (*karmavācanā*) of the assembly.

Since the formal legal acts of the assembly cannot be performed, the formal act of desire (*chanda-karman*) also cannot be transmitted. "Only excluding," etc., explains the exception; there is only the single case of establishing boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*).
Regarding the Dharma: naturally, it is opened and upheld upon the ground; however, with respect to the *kāmadhātu* (the realm of desire), it is not opened, as stated above.

Thus, in the *Fǎqǐ tuōchù zhōng* (Within the Basis for the Arising of the Dharma), it says: "The single dharma of boundary-binding (*sīmā-bandha*) is not a dharma of formal ritual action (*karmavācanā*).

For this reason, based on these initial foundations, this school establishes its doctrine. Furthermore, the text below states: "What is the manifestation of the boundary? It is that which performs the *karma* and proclaims the restrictions."
Furthermore, regarding "binding below": this refers to when one establishes a boundary (*sīmā*) or intends to open it, yet ultimately does not fully comprehend its limits.
Thus, looking downward from the two gates above, it receives the name "third."
The "four concise [versions]" refer to the first four types mentioned in the commentary. The "one extensive [version]" refers to the final type, the extensive exposition.

Furthermore, the concise versions correspond to serious illnesses, while the extensive version corresponds to minor illnesses. When the *Sū* (the sub-commentary) states that the extensive version applies to both minor and serious illnesses, this implies that there are cases where even minor illnesses are grave.
Thus, the *Dàchǎo* says: "The first four apply only to serious illnesses; the subsequent extensive exposition is used for both healthy and ill persons. One may obtain [this].

[The procedure] is accomplished. The Great Master said: "Although the Vinaya text states this, those who take the *karmavācanā* (consent) must understand the characteristics of being 'in agreement' (*samāna*) or 'not in agreement' (*visamāna*);

only then is it accomplished. If one acts as if there is agreement while the mind is actually in disagreement, although the taking of consent is not accomplished, it ultimately constitutes a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*)."

Regarding the phrase "the former being contrary to the Dharma," this refers specifically to a *bhikṣu* who conveys the consent (*chanda*). As for "the agent and the object," the agent is one capable of conveying the consent, while the object is the one to whom the consent is given.
If both parties act in violation of the legal rules (*vinaya*), they must likewise again provide the consent to another person capable of receiving it.

For example, if a person conveying consent, after having received the consent from another, declares, "I am one who has committed one of the thirteen grave offenses (*antarāyika-dharma*)," the text states that in all such cases, the transmission of the consent is not valid.

One must further grant the *chanda* (consent) to others; there are two ways to do so. At the time of the initial regulation, when the assembly was pure, one would grant the *chanda* during an untimely gathering.

Later, because the *poṣadha* was observed at an improper time, it became possible for the *chanda* to be transmitted. To prevent this from obstructing the monastic rites, the Buddha ordered that it be transmitted [together with the formal announcement].
The *Dachao* states: "Both must be recited together," as this is the authentic regulation; it differs from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, which still practices obsolete teachings.

Regarding "improperly issuing a formal motion" (*viniścaya-vyākaraṇa*): this refers to what is stated in the *Śikṣāpada-khaṇḍaka*: "If one intends to give a formal consent (*chanda*) by means of a detailed recitation, yet fails to utter the actual words;

or 'transferring the consent' (*chandasya parivartana*), which means that after having already received a consent, one suddenly encounters an obstacle and transfers that consent to another. The *Vinayamātṛkā* states: [as follows].

It may be recited up to seven times. The wording is as follows: "Venerable Sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, Bhikṣu [Name], receive the *chanda* (consent) and *pāriśuddhi* (purity) from Bhikṣu [Name].
Both he and I shall participate in the legal matters of the Saṃgha through this *chanda* and *pāriśuddhi*. Now, simply say this:"
"Such-and-such a bhikṣu grants his consent and purity for the formal act of the Saṃgha according to the Dharma.
This is an inference based on the meaning of the terms. Thus, the *Daijō Shō* states:

"The meaning is established as follows: 'mind' is the root; 'mind' encompasses the granting of consent (*chanda*), while 'root' encompasses purity (*śuddhi*). One is pure because one takes the precepts as the root."
Human speech. This is a record of the events compiled by Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty from the *Vyutpatti-vinaya-saṃvara*. Regarding "as when one forgets" and so forth:
as for those who transmit the *chanda* (consent), if they forget the names or categories of the individuals previously mentioned, they simply say, "I transmit the *chanda* with many bhikṣus."
One should exclude matters that are contrary to the Dharma. Because such matters are not legitimate *saṃgha* affairs, there is no need to grant one's consent (*chanda*).

This refers, for example, to acts such as acting as a matchmaker for marriages on behalf of the *saṃgha*. Regarding "one who is originally engaged in a matter," this refers to granting consent in accordance with the one hundred and thirty-four matters performed within the *saṃgha*.

Furthermore, if after initially being commissioned for one matter, another matter subsequently arises, one should not grant consent based on the former; if one were to go [to perform the latter], it would be improper.

If one were to take [the specific time], it would create obstacles for monastic affairs. Now, by using the phrase "monastic business conducted according to the Dharma," it can be applied universally to all *karmavācanā* (formal procedures).

When the assembly gathers, it refers specifically to the fortnightly *poṣadha*; thus, this is restricted by a fixed time limit. Since other occasions are not so limited, they are called "non-specific times" (*akāla*).

That which corresponds to the essence of the Saṃgha is precisely the "harmony of mind" (*cittasaṃvāda*) among the six kinds of harmony. As for provisional function (*upādāya-prajñapti*), it refers to what was previously stated: that a person is formed by gathering the aggregates (*skandha*).

The person is provisionally established as the essence, while the substantial dharmas (*dravyadharma*) have no such function. The four persons, through their provisional function, constitute the essence of the Saṃgha;

yet this function has no separate essence, for it ultimately takes the aggregates of those four persons as its basis. Now, since these fundamental aggregates are free from the fault of the sevenfold [classification], the [Saṃgha] is thereby established.
Regarding the meaning of "pure":
the phrase "three-one" refers to the statement of three recitations as one. As for "clarifying by oneself," the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:

"If it is accomplished through three recitations, one says 'the second and third [recitations] were likewise spoken. If it is accomplished by only one recitation, there are none [of these statements]."

The phrase "the abbreviated text of the *kṣepa*" refers to taking an example from the section on "the multitude. For instance, in the Vinaya, it is stated: "I grant my consent (*chanda*) to the multitude.

If the person who has received this consent falls asleep, enters meditative absorption (*samādhi*), forgets it, or does not act intentionally, [the act] is still accomplished. By analogy, how could a single declaration today not be accomplished? The phrase "it must necessarily" is concessive;
it means that one must certainly rely on the specific section [of the Vinaya], which is also a matter of the practitioner's intention. This is because of the four... [text ends].
"Below" means "to take away. This is because it is stipulated that there is no [separate] procedure for the four parts, as they are established by the three proclamations. The *Shisao* states:

"In accordance with the procedures for the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation), such as the rite of *śuddhi* (purification), these are directly accomplished according to the text; there is no need for further elaboration or to seek them from other external sections."

"Surname" refers to the four castes (*catur-varṇa*). "Appearance" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to physical characteristics. "Name" (*nāman*) refers to a personal appellation. "Category" (*jāti*) refers to a class or type;

this generally refers to a group of people and only rarely to a single individual. The *Daocao* (Great Commentary) quotes from the Vinaya: "If one does not record the surname and name, one should describe the appearance.
If it is still not recorded, one should say: 'I have spoken [of the *chanda*] with many bhikṣus,' and so forth. As stated below, since it says "many people," it also...

This is a general rule; the Vinaya, however, establishes specific exceptions. Regarding "one boundary with four locations," it means that within a single boundary, four persons may simultaneously receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), and they may grant their consent (*chanda*) to one another by moving through these four locations. This differs from the following case in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*:

where the number of those granting consent is few, but the number of those gathered for the assembly is many, one simply takes their mental intention. Since all those present there possess the requisite intention, now...
Although one does not recall it, it is verified as being accomplished because that person originally possessed the intention to send [the proposal]. It must be brought down [to the assembly].
If one were to wait for a person capable of clearly recording it, it could not be said that this applies to a large multitude. As the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

"Have him go to the Sangha acting in accordance with the Dharma, where he shall announce my name and cast the voting tally (*śalākā*) on my behalf. If it is not done in this manner, none of these acts will be accomplished.

Furthermore, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* clearly states that one should announce one's name in the presence of the elder; the underlying intent can likewise be discerned there. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* says:
"One should further inspect one another to ascertain who has arrived and who has not. These words make the meaning even more explicit.
"Receiving" refers to the case of one who has not yet recovered from illness. "The middle way" refers to one who has already recovered but has not yet reached the assembly of monks.
"Arriving at the assembly" refers to one who carries the *chanda* (consent) to the community.
