In the commentary on the section concerning the "non-existence of the object," it states: "The *dhātu* is that which is prohibited by the Noble Ones.
The phrase "separated from below" restricts the person's vision.

"Those who are not permitted to hear" refers to those who have committed an offense and are therefore not permitted to hear the precepts. Regarding "the agent and the object": the agent is the one who speaks, and the object is that which is heard.
In the section on the Vinaya, it is proven that what was heard is incorrect; that is, a formal censure (*pratikrośa*) is not established.

How could a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*) ever constitute a valid censure? Only when the quorum is complete can a censure be established. Regarding "dignity," this refers to the four modes of deportment being inconsistent. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

When performing *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical acts), sitting constitutes a separate assembly (*bhedaka*) and so forth; therefore, it is said that the characteristics of instruction should not be applied.

This is because the assembly is incomplete and thus not in accordance with the Dharma (*adharma-sāmagrī*). "Inverted" (*viparyāsa*) refers to being topsy-turvy, while "erroneous" (*vyatyasta*) refers to omission or transposition.

These occur within the three or four divisions. Regarding the three days for the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*: these are the fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth [of the lunar month] (the sixteenth is permitted as an exception).

There are circumstances. That is to say, when there are conditions other than those of the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*), one may perform an abbreviated recitation of the precepts. If few [monks] are present, it is a single section; if many, it may extend up to eight sections;

the intermediate cases can be understood by comparison. Regarding the degree of urgency: if the circumstances are relaxed, a detailed recitation is permissible; if the circumstances are urgent, an abbreviated recitation is permissible.

Therefore, the Vinaya contains fifteen types of abbreviations (*saṃkṣepa*) and seven types of abbreviations; these are precisely what is meant. As for the method of performing them together, one should harmonize the ritual with the degree of urgency to perform the abbreviated method. Now...
And the reverse is also true. There is no obstacle that constitutes a separate condition; that is to say, there is no evil bhikṣu who creates an obstacle as a separate condition.

Once a small boundary (sīmā) has been established for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) and so forth, it is immediately dissolved. However, if one becomes confused about the directions and has no means of reuniting with the assembly, one should not depart without first dissolving the boundary.

"Intertwined" (*cuòhù*) means crisscrossing and interlacing. Regarding the sequence "three above, four, five, six, and three below," it is said that these [categories] cannot manifest simultaneously and instantaneously;
therefore, they must be woven together through mutual interaction to form a framework and its details, thereby encompassing all errors without exception.

Regarding the phrase "due to the dissolution" (*yin jie xia*): because the preceding discussion stated that there are no obstacles or separate conditions for binding a small boundary (*kṣudra-sīmā*), and furthermore that one does not dissolve it immediately, this is a general evaluation.

As for "that which must be dissolved by *karmavācanā*": this refers to cases where, after the ritual procedure (*adhiṣṭhāna*) was previously performed, one must subsequently employ the formal act (*karman*) to dissolve it.

"Without mental acceptance" refers to the aforementioned lack of mental acceptance. For instance, regarding the seven types of *karmavācanā*, such as the act of censure (*tarjanīya-karman*), although they are performed in one's presence, because they contradict one's feelings, one ultimately does not accept them with a clear mind.

This can be understood by applying the same principle to the other six cases, such as the bowl being turned upside down for a family of practitioners (*śikṣādattaka*) and the refusal to pay homage to those who are no longer objects of veneration (*aprasādika*).

The seven disciplinary measures (*saptadaṇḍa*) are: censure (*tarjanīya*), banishment (*niḥsaraṇīya*), dependence (*nissaya*), prohibition from entering the homes of laypeople (*pratisedha-gṛhapraveśa*), suspension for not acknowledging an offense (*adarśana-utkṣepa*), suspension for not repenting an offense (*apratikarma-utkṣepa*), suspension for not relinquishing evil views (*adhyāpatti-utkṣepa*), and the formal act regarding offenses (*āpattisthāna*).
Once, when the elephant-force (*hastibalaka*) was debating with non-Buddhist teachers and was defeated, his previous and subsequent statements were contradictory.

The Buddha said: "The Saṃgha should apply the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) to discipline him. He shall be made to acknowledge his original offense and be deprived of his seniority for thirty days."

There are five matters. If one confesses the original offense (*mūlāpatti*), it should be resolved through a *jñapti-caturtha* (four-part) motion. Regarding insanity: this refers to a person of middling mental derangement;

having first been covered by the Dharma, when the madness subsequently ceases, it should be resolved by means of the Dharma. Regarding a family under restriction (*śikṣādattaka*): this refers to a family that has seen the Truths (*dṛṣṭasatya*).

Because their offerings were so numerous, their food and clothing became exhausted, leading householders to criticize them. The Buddha then commanded that a *jñapti-dvitīya* (two-part) motion be made to prohibit [the monks from visiting]. Hereafter, one should...

Furthermore, regarding the *pātra-nyāsa* (turning over the bowl): if a donor’s family refuses to accept an apology, the Sangha performs a formal act (*karmavācanā*) whereby the recipient is rendered unfit for use;
this is equivalent in meaning to *pātra-nyāsa*. Later, if they develop faith, one should resolve the matter through the Dharma. One does not prostrate [to such a person].

According to the Vinaya, because of Kālodayin’s speech, the Buddha ordered that a nun perform the *an-abhivādana-karman* (act of non-prostration). Later, if she becomes earnest and prudent, it is permitted to resolve the matter through the Dharma. [In the case of] expulsion (*pravāsanīya-karman*), [the same applies].
Regarding the śrāmaṇera: if he declares that his desire does not constitute an obstacle, yet does not comply after three admonitions, he should be expelled immediately.

If he later complies, he should also be reinstated for him. To divide this according to two principles: there are two reasons why the rules for establishing and releasing [the status] were formulated.
First, once released from the "salt" (corruption), he may again become functional and his person shall count within the number of the Saṃgha. Second, regarding the days of treatment...

It is infinite. Thus, throughout one's entire life, the principle of responding to sentient beings (*jī*) will never again be lost. Therefore, it must be explained as follows. Below, two matters are cited as examples.

Regarding the section on "merit" (*guòdé*), one should first raise an objection, saying: "If these six points are explained with reference to insentient things (*wúqíng*), then take, for instance, the 'emergence of merit'."
Regarding robes: robes are also insentient; why then are they not included in the count? To explain this by means of the text:

the time limit is from the sixteenth day of the seventh month to the fifteenth day of the twelfth month, during which one is permitted to receive the five benefits. This constitutes the limit. Fearing that people might transgress it recklessly, it is necessary to provide a legal interpretation.

Even if one does not understand [the rule], one will naturally forfeit [the benefits] upon reaching the limit; therefore, they are not included in the count. Thus, they are not the same as the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*).
These are the six [cases].

Regarding those that are not counted: this means that because one has not previously received [the precepts], one commits a grave offense; since both wealth and the Dharma are then lost, they must be relinquished.
This is discussed in terms of the forfeiture of the precepts.
If one is unable to prevent or control oneself due to external conditions that press upon them, they may relinquish the precepts to give rise to subsequent ones.

If this is not understood, one commits a grave offense while still bearing the precepts, thereby constituting a "limiting offense" (pārājika) that creates a permanent obstacle for the duration of one's life. Once the precepts have been relinquished, it is subsequently permitted to receive them again.

Both commit five kinds of improper acts. The *Vinaya* (Sifen lü), fascicle 43, states: "At that time, there was a monastic community residing at a certain location that performed an illegal and discordant *karmavācanā* for a bhikṣu.
At that time, many monks disputed among themselves; some said it was an 'illegal and discordant *karmavācanā*' (1)."
Some say it is an illegal concordant assembly (2); some say it is a legal separate assembly (3); some say it is a similar-to-the-law separate assembly (4);
some say it is a similar-to-the-law concordant assembly (5). Therefore, it is said that they collectively commit five types of non-dharma.

Furthermore, it is said that some claim the *karmavācanā* is accomplished, while others claim it is not accomplished (these two, together with the previous five who hold to the non-dharma, constitute seven people). Therefore, it is called "the seven."
People commonly dispute whether [a ritual] is valid or invalid. My current view is that even during the lifetime of the Tathāgata, there were bhikṣus who remained deluded and committed errors;
how much more so after his parinirvāṇa? It is essential to examine the principles with great care and precision. Thus, the *Jietan jing* (Sutra on the Ordination Platform) states:

"Even when the Dharma was upheld during the Buddha’s lifetime, people still committed five kinds of improper acts. How can this be due to a lack of learning or a failure to understand others? It is because at the critical moment, their mental state was contrary [to the rules] and they forgot them."
Because it is not inferior. Although there are differences according to the specific matter, if one subsumes them under the principle of "non-characteristic" (a-lakṣaṇa), then they are universal.
Why is this? There is no person who does not face [another] in person; it must be a qualified member of the assembly (*pūrṇasaṃkhyā*) who is pure. This indicates that the meaning is restrictive.

According to the lower [classification], if the method of face-to-face address (*saṃmukhī-vinaya*) is applied to higher matters such as the holding of robes or the declaration regarding medicines, it does not preclude the existence of differences based on their respective characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), just as in the case of holding [an object].
The robe is not the same as the discussion of medicines and so forth. Nevertheless, regarding those conditions of robes and medicines, they must accord with the teachings;

therefore, it is said "as such" (this indicates a difference in characteristics). Thus, one must understand this by applying analogous principles. Regarding "holding and speaking": "holding" refers to the robe and "speaking" refers to the medicine;
these are heavy conditions, and the offense is a *pārājika*. The three roots are: seeing, hearing, and suspecting.

Answer: Since the objects [of the precepts] are not identical, the precepts are also generated separately. Although one has now committed a grave offense, because the precepts were already previously generated regarding the wearing of robes and the explanation of medicines, how could one not practice the training for repentance (*śikṣādattaka*)? This refers to a *śikṣādattaka* śrāmaṇera;

due to the defilement of both self and others, and furthermore because of what is known and heard. "Suddenly" (*chà*) below means that one may suddenly form the mental resolve to wear the robe. "If" (*ruò*) below—this...
Because they are similar in type, it is permissible to perform the formal procedure (*karmavācanā*) by addressing each other face-to-face.
This refers to the words of testimony or the words of the formal declaration; if there is a deficiency in the declaration, one must reprimand the person to stop.
Regardless of whether the other person remains or not, all such cases constitute an offense against a person (*pudgala-dūṣaṇa*), because the person who was reprimanded has been successfully rebuked.

The *saṃgha* constitutes a distinct category, because a group of four or more monks performs the communal rites themselves. Furthermore, those of lower status are at the end of the seven classes of followers and are therefore not of the same kind [as the *saṃgha*].

Regarding the "two names": this refers to not reciting one's own name nor the name of the robe. As for the phrase "now, below," it refers to the *Mahāsāṃghika* practice of guarding [the robe] throughout the night.

Regarding robes: the *Caturvargika-vinaya* merely protects the "characteristic of light" (*prabhāsa-lakṣaṇa*). If one were to apply that method for formal acceptance (*parigraha*), it would follow that the substance of the robe itself could not be accepted.
Now, it is appropriate to employ the *Daśādhyāya-vinaya*, as its principle is comprehensive and its phrasing is consistent, since it likewise protects the characteristic of light.
The five colors are the primary colors of the five directions, namely blue, yellow, red, white, and black.
When these are mixed, they become the secondary colors of the five directions, namely green, vermilion, azure, purple, and bay-yellow.

Regarding "interlacing" (jiaoluo): The fourth is when there is a discrepancy between person and dharma, yet it does not obstruct the suchness of phenomena (shiruru). The fifth is when there is a discrepancy between person and phenomenon, yet it does not obstruct the suchness of dharmas (faruru).

The sixth is when there is a discrepancy between phenomenon and dharma, yet it does not obstruct the suchness of persons (renru). The seventh possesses all three discrepancies; these are all as described above.

Five *li*. This refers to a *araṇya* (forest hermitage) where there are no difficulties; [in such a case], one must assemble at five *li* [from the boundary]. As for the boundaries of other places, these are the five characteristics of the remaining four locations.

A person who can destroy the Dharma causes that Dharma to fall into ruin because of their censure. That is to say, they censure because their minds are discordant; once the censure is established, [the boundary is lost].
"Separate from the assembly" refers to that which is non-personal (*puggala-ajjhāpanna*). Because the rule is subject to censure, it is subsumed under the non-personal.

If, after [the formal act] has been performed, there are those who do not desist despite having been censured, this rule has already been censured; whether they are right or wrong, both cases belong to the non-personal. Regarding "one who goes because they have heard [the call] to desist":
this means that although one hears with one's own ears that the person before them has called for desisting, one intentionally persists in going away; even though one has gone, [the offense remains].

This is contrary to the Dharma. If one remains in accordance with the censure, that is in accord with the Dharma. To speak out of intolerance means that one’s inner mind cannot endure the person being confronted;
thus, although the meaning of the teaching is established, since it was not independently constructed, the Dharma is thereby defeated.

The three [categories] beginning with *śikṣāpada-pratyākhyāna* (renunciation of training) correspond to the three matters mentioned in the commentary. Regarding the harmony of person and dharma: the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states that harmony of body, speech, and mind constitutes the "person";
harmony of precepts, views, and livelihood constitutes the "dharma. As for the distinction between communal (*saṃghika*) and private (*pratyekaka*):

acts such as the renunciation of property or the returning of robes must take place within the *saṃgha*; however, even the renunciation of an offense may be performed before an individual, and is thus termed "private. Since their meanings are not uniform, [the distinctions are established].
One must distinguish between small and large.
A length of one chi and six cun and a width of eight cun; if the value of the object exceeds the ten-day limit, one performs a *pāyattika* (提) repentance.

If it is less than one chi and six cun or eight cun, one performs a *dukkaṭa* (吉) repentance. Thus, we know that both small and large items fall within the scope of repentance. Now, regarding the misconduct in the lower practice, there is a discussion on this.

Regarding "sincere speech," the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "One should not fail to speak when one has obtained [an item] by means of wealth that was not properly measured; nor should one speak beyond the limit. To do so constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Since it says "one should not [fail to speak]," whether the amount is large or small, how could one know not to speak? This is the same as for those who are defiled. The *Da-chao* states:

That which can cause defilement may be either of proper measure or improper measure. What is it that is defiled? The answer is: both the permissible and the impermissible. For example, regarding the offense of having finished eating (*pūrva-bhakta*), whether the meal was properly or improperly concluded, one incurs the offense of "having finished eating.

If that which can cause defilement is property of improper measure, does it defile that which is of proper measure? The answer is: although they differ in size, the meaning of relinquishment and confession is the same.

The Vinaya establishes this as a major offense (*sthūlātyaya*), while the Śāstra establishes it as a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*); therefore, in all cases, it is a single act of defilement, even when categorized as a minor offense.

[This is] the practice. Although the ancients performed repentance for what was permissible (*yìngliàng*), they did not perform it for what was impermissible (*bù yìng*); thus their offenses were not liberated. [The following] generally applies below, concluding and returning to the correct principle.
"Valuable items" refers to bedding, quilts, and the like. The Vinaya states: "If another gives them to you to make into bedding, there is no offense. The Great Master’s commentary says: "Because..."

Regarding these heavy objects, one should not regard wealth lightly; it is not permissible to perform the *śuddhi* (purification) rite for them. Since there is no fault of violating the rules regarding their description, they do not require the formal act of relinquishment (*pratyādeśana*) and confession.
As for small bowls, those that are not of the standard measure are not permitted to be kept or purified. Regarding primary colors, this refers to the five cardinal colors used for robes;
these also may not be added to or kept as personal property. There is no fault in being separated from them. "Improper seeking" refers to the five types of wrong livelihood (*pañca-kuhaka*).

The four types of improper seeking are likewise not permitted by the True Teaching; all such acts result in falling [into transgression]. However, they constitute only a *thullaccaya* (grave) offense.

It is not appropriate to perform the ritual of relinquishment (*paṭinissagga*) or confession (*pārisuddhi*), nor is it appropriate to receive the purification (*visuddhi*). This means that one should not receive the dharma of purification. Since this is so, how could there be any principle for performing the ritual of relinquishment and confession?
It is not that doubt is abandoned because it has been exhausted; rather, it is because [the offense] is considered excessive. In the Sūtras, ignorance is consistently concluded as a transgression.

Next, the Vinaya is cited: "One who knows [the offense] shall repent; one who doubts shall disclose it. Regarding those who have concealed [an offense] for days or months without treatment, this opens up the possibility that a doubtful offense does not incur the formal charge of concealment (*paryuṣita*).
The *Chao* states: "If one does not recall having a doubt or does not recognize [the offense], neither constitutes concealment."

Regarding "confession before others" (*pratideśanā*) and "confession not before others": for light offenses, it is sufficient to simply reproach one's own mind; for heavy offenses, confession must be made before others, as follows.

This refers to the offense of concealment (*praticchādana*) within the category of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offenses involving forfeiture). One must repent before a single pure person according to the proper ritual.

As for those offenses categorized differently that are not part of the same legal code (*vinaya*), this means that while those of the same category (*pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, etc. should be confessed together, those of different groups are distinct. Now, the offense of concealment cannot be combined with the actual offense of downfall (*pāyattika*).
This is the *chān* (confession). Furthermore, although the names of the two types—light and heavy—are identical, they must not be combined into a single confession.
The remaining two refer to the *pratimukha* (face-to-face) and the mental recitation (*manasikāra*) performed within the assembly. Some rely on the original text;

if there are people within the boundary (*sīmā*), one must follow the original procedure for the *pratimukha* method, and the same principle applies to the procedures for the assembly. The subsequent text below, including the annotations, must all be applied according to these examples.
The text for understanding matters according to their circumstances.
*Sifenlü suiji jiemoshu zhengyuanji*, Scroll Three.
At Da Hu Lake, west of Gaopingli Gaobuyan, Leimen, Huicheng County, Shaoxing Prefecture.
The disciple Ruji’s wife, Ding Sanjiu, who resides on the bank [of the river] and reverently serves the Triple Gem, became pregnant in her thirty-ninth year.

She reflected that while her age was now established and her husband and she lived in harmony and joy, she had not yet given birth after such a long time; thus, she constantly harbored a sense of anxiety regarding the continuation of the family lineage.
To fulfill the aspirations of husband and wife, one must rely upon the excellent causes of the Buddha-Dharma;

by reverently bestowing pure wealth, these engraved woodblocks have been produced to propagate this commentary on the Vinaya for the duration of the Buddha’s lifespan. In the future, at the end of the age, when wholesome fruits are difficult to obtain, there is now a basis for prayer and reliance.
May it be so hoped!

May the Buddha’s compassion fulfill these prayers, and may the will of Heaven grant silent repose. May the wife herself conceive a son endowed with fortune and wisdom, and may her station attain the prospect of great prosperity.
On the full moon of the third month in the Wuchen year of the Shaoxing era, Lu Ji respectfully offers this vow.
*Commentary on the Essential Source of the Sub-commentary on the *Sifenlü shanbu suiji jiemoshu*, Scroll Four.
Composed by the Tiantai śramaṇa Yunkan. Regarding the term "one’s own school" (*yijia*):
it means to cause one to compose and write as a distinct school of its own, setting it apart from the other schools such as those of former masters. Having already relied upon...

It arises from the realms (*dhātu*) and is not the ground of ritual action (*karmabhūmi*). Once one is no longer fit to perform monastic affairs, one’s conduct (*yòu*)—where *yòu* means the Way (*dào*)—must not exceed the precepts.

This is because the precepts are the foundation of all practices. The Preface to the *Chao* states: "The virtue of the precepts is difficult to fully describe; it stands supreme, surpassing all other phenomena.

Following the characteristics and following the basis, the essence of the vows gives rise to their formal characteristics; subsequently, through the objects of the phenomenal world, specific affairs arise. To elaborate on this essential point:

Since clothing and food are primary concerns, the subsequent [precepts] are received and elucidated accordingly. Regarding the vows and practices: "vows" refers to receiving them face-to-face, while "practices" refers to following them accordingly.

As for the categories of "assembly" and "individual": an assembly consists of four or more persons, whereas an individual consists of three or fewer. The various methods of reciting the precepts refer to the communal (*saṃgha-dharma*), the face-to-face (*pratimukha*), and the mental (*manasikāra*) recitations.
Furthermore, because the formal announcements (*jñapti*) and the timing—whether during the day or at an improper time—vary between extensive and abbreviated forms, they are referred to as "various."

Furthermore, the text below cites the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, stating that even laymen and laywomen (*upāsaka* and *upāsikā*), as well as those of the ninety-six types of renunciant practitioners, all undergo the *poṣadha* three times every half-month.
Thus, that text says: "The Buddha taught that purity is what is called *poṣadha*.

"Abiding in the Dharma" refers to the rules set forth in the section on the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*). "Lifting the Dharma" refers to the section on the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*) below, which clarifies the rules for the lifting [of restrictions]. All offerings...

The *Dharma* refers to the "Chapter on the Distribution of Robes," which clarifies the giving of robes at appropriate and inappropriate times; the "Upper Chapter" comprehensively encompasses the preceding chapters such as those on boundary-setting (*sīmā-bandha*).
The "Various Methods of Repentance" refers to the "Lower Chapter on the Repentance of the Six Classes of Offenses."
Regarding the section below [the title] "Master Guang": This refers to the arrangement he composed, which organizes the sequence of chapters based on the two categories of monks and nuns.
According to the Vinaya texts themselves, there is indeed a principle of placing the monks first and the nuns second; for example, the Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya follows after the Bhikṣu-vinaya.

Nevertheless, Master Guang’s intention is that regarding such matters as the ritual of boundary-determination (*sīmā-bandha*), where monks and nuns share common practices, these should simply be extracted from their respective sections as needed.
If each were established separately, it would merely serve to fill out the volumes in vain. Now, we shall simply present the intent of our own school (*jia*) below.

Within the eight chapters that follow, those where monks and nuns act together are termed "Common" (*tong*); those where they act individually are termed "Specific" (*se*). Within each chapter, matters are divided according to their respective categories.

This is based on the *Vinaya*, which, following the individual precepts, contains sections on offenses common to both monks and nuns, as well as those not common to them, and the rules for the three groups of followers regarding the formation of *duṣkṛta* (minor) offenses.
Since this format exists within the middle [section], it enables one to follow the general expositions according to the respective chapters.

If this is so, then within a single chapter, there is the capacity to address the faculties of all five groups of practitioners; through this, the intent behind the establishment of the title is made manifest.
Chapter Two: Explaining the Various Realms (*dhātu*) and the Ties of Bondage (*bandhana*).

"Various" (*zhu*) refers to the differences among people regarding food, clothing, and so forth. "Realms" (*jie*) refers to the boundaries demarcated according to specific matters. "Ties" (*jie*) refers to the formal ritual procedures (*karman*) established in accordance with these names.

The term "shā" (捨) means to relinquish; "yàoqī" (要期) refers to a formal agreement or vow; "hàojiě" (號解) means the title and its explanation. "Piān" (篇) is another name for chapters (*varga*) or sections (*parivarta*).

"Báqú" (跋渠) is a specific designation—Master Yìng states that *báqú* is correctly pronounced *vagga*, which here means a "division" (*nikāya*), referring to a class or category. "Rén" (人) refers to the boundary for the community of monks (*saṃgha-sīmā*); "yī" (衣) refers to the boundary for robes (*cīvara-sīmā*); and "shí" (食) refers to the boundary for food (*piṇḍapāta-sīmā*).

According to the Vinaya, when explaining the precepts, the establishment of boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*) comes first, while the regulations for robes and medicine follow later. This is likely because, at the initial stage, [the focus was on]...

The establishment of the *dharmas* based on dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) has already been clarified. Now, following this same principle, their sequence is arranged. Below this, the general meaning of the *saṃgha* as a substance is explained.
Because there are boundaries (*sīmā*), the six points of harmony (*ṣaḍ-sāmagrī*) are manifested. The outer robes give rise to the boundary for the collection of robes;
the inner medicines give rise to the boundary for the collection of food. As for those who require distinct forms, this refers to those who have dependencies.

Since their physical forms are distinct, they require clothing and medicine; furthermore, as the boundary (*sīmā*) is broad while the dyeing vat (*maṇḍala*) is narrow, one must perform the ritual for collecting robes (*cīvarasaṃkramaṇa*).

Because there are individuals of middling and inferior faculties, pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*) is required. Therefore, following this, the assembly is convened. These two conditions refer precisely to clothing and food.
Regarding the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual acts) below: these two dharmas constitute the foundation for the establishment and maintenance of the True Dharma (*saddharma*).

From the section below, those capable of propagating [the teachings] emerge; the monastic community (*saṃgha*) that universally observes the *karmavācanā* and the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) must universally and reverently uphold them.
In principle, there are no limitations, obstructions, or divisions. Thus, the realm of Jambudvīpa is universally a single assembly. Therefore, the *Dà cǎo* (Great Commentary) states:
Since the territory of Jambudvīpa is so vast and expansive, it is difficult to assemble the entire Saṃgha at every scheduled occasion;

this is precisely why the intention behind establishing separate assemblies for those born in the lower realms was to prevent the difficulties of travel from hindering the path and other such conditions.

Regarding the delimitation of boundaries (*sīmā*), if one speaks in terms of an assembly for the whole of Jambudvīpa, then the use of restrictions would serve to prevent the confusion inherent in such a universal gathering. Even though there are [separate assemblies] in the lower realms...
To share a heart of harmony and yet have one’s form and shadow rush toward [the object] is difficult to achieve. It merely diminishes one's primary practice because of such rushing;

it results in the loss of merit and the abandonment of one's vocation. "Prior conditions" refers to karmic conditions (*pratyaya*), which follow the environment—that is, they follow the environments of the four places and six aspects.

The gathering of the Saṃgha refers to the formal act of binding [the community]. "One opening" (ekāvakāśa) refers to the opening of the separate residence (pārivāsika). "Karma" (kamma) refers to the formal ritual procedure (jñapti-karman).

"Veneration of harmony" (saṃghasāmagrī-pūjā) means holding harmony in high esteem. "First opening" refers to the opening of the separate residence; "subsequent regulation" refers to the regulation that venerates harmony.

"Various texts" refers to various versions of the Vinaya texts; they are not the original Sanskrit sounds. This clarifies that the aforementioned four *mā* (measures) are the original Sanskrit pronunciation.
Now, the following explains the meaning of "present boundary" (*pratyutpanna-sīmā*). There are four types: village (*grāma*), forest (*araṇya*), road (*patha*), and water (*udaka*).

There are six types when the two categories of village and forest are expanded to form six, as explained above in the section on conditions, specifically within the fourth condition concerning boundaries among the ten conditions for performing formal acts (*karmavācanā*).

[This refers to] the three types of great boundaries (*mahā-sīmā*): those with a site for the precepts (*śīla-maṇḍala*), those without a site for the precepts, and the three small boundaries (*kṣudra-sīmā*).
Regarding the seven boundaries, within the great boundary there are further three kinds: namely, those where both persons and dharma coincide; those where dharma and food coincide;

and those where dharma coincides while food is separate. These six, together with the site for the precepts, constitute the seven. As for their mutual inclusion, they refer to the characteristics of the four aforementioned conditions.

Regarding the "Inclusion" section, the first three items refer to the statement in the Commentary that there are three types of *mahā-sīmā* (great boundaries). As for the "Great" boundary, it must be formally established;

otherwise, one cannot cross its measured limits. Regarding the phrase "separating by means of the light-signs," the *Dachao* states: "The *karmavācanā* for receiving the *chanda* occurs during the final watch of the night."

The phrase "because it is clear" indicates that one wishes to inform [the recipient]. Regarding the passage "according to this," it refers back to the statement above concerning going first on the fourteenth day;
this implies a distance of approximately one hundred *li*.
As for the forty *li*, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are three distinctions in a *yojana*: the large is eighty *li*, the medium is sixty *li*, and [the small is forty *li*].
The lower [calculation] is forty *li*. This refers to the fact that mountains and rivers differ between central and peripheral regions, resulting in unequal travel distances.
Within the rules for the distribution of robes (*caturbhāga-cīvara-dharma*), the statement that one *yojana* corresponds to eighty *li* is based on the superior grade.

For general application, according to the intent of the Vinaya text, it should be one hundred and twenty *li*, taking the inferior grade as the standard. "Below the Sangha" refers to the *Mahāsāṃghika*.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* and the *Samantapāsādikā* both state that the measurement is three *yojanas* combined; this is determined by measuring the corners, indicating that each side and dimension is three *yojanas*.
One *krośa* is calculated as two *li* according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*; ten *krośas* thus amount to twenty *li*. If [it is] below...
Regarding mountain temples: the upper and lower sections are mutually illuminated and expansive, yet they remain within ten *krośas*.
This is not because of a lack of space, but rather to ensure that the high and low areas do not excessively overlap; therefore, this is specifically clarified. As for rivers:

since the Vinaya permits the establishment of boundaries across confluence points, regarding the characteristics of the banks—if one chants the boundary markers from the opposite shore, the river waters will be included within this boundary. This requires the presence of a boat or a bridge.
This is because one must fear that [the boundary] will suddenly become obstructed and thus easily subject to violation; this is due to the weakness of women.
The Sarvāstivādins state: "The boundary for a bhikṣuṇī may only be one krośa square.
However, if there are unavoidable circumstances, one may establish it within three yojanas according to the *Mahāsāṃghika* school, as they are swift and capable."

[The section on] "Excluding" [the village]. If there is no difficulty in shallow water, it should logically be permissible. "Many" refers to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*. In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it states:
"If there is an island within a river, one should perform the *karmavācanā* at five locations," as detailed below. The *Erya* says: "That which is habitable within the water is called an island.
Regarding "gathering the robes," there is a textual authority; this refers to the establishment of the "robe-gathering boundary" (*cīvara-saṃvartana-sīmā*). Yuanzhao says: "Exclude the village."

Regarding the area outside the village boundary: conversely, this would subsume the *saṃgha*-boundary. Since there is no such textual authority, it is known that one may combine them and establish the boundary.

Within that [combined area], since the *poṣadha* is performed, and because the establishment of a boundary is mandatory when performing the *poṣadha*, it is permissible to establish the boundary by combining the village.
"Unable [to do so] within the Saṃgha" means, as it were, being unable to seek out and separately establish one dwelling within the same *sīmā* (monastic boundary).

"Not holding [the robe] below" is said for fear of the fault of being separated from one's robe (*cīvara-vinipāta*). "Also excluding [the case of] below" is explained by this: it is because the status of the Buddha and the Saṃgha are distinct.
"The Saṃgha represents" means it represents what is external.

The four sides have paths cleared; thus, the central partition is naturally formed. This central partition does not belong to either of the two boundaries, but belongs to the natural open space (ākāśa).
This is because *araṇya* is translated as "empty place" (*kongchu*). As the subsequent text states: "The two characteristics of inner and outer are separately designated as before and after."

Apart from what has been excluded, it is clear that this is empty space. Regarding the Cakravāḍa Mountains, Master Ying stated: "The Sanskrit term is *Cakravāḍa*; this is translated as 'Wheel Mountain' (*Lúnshān*).

The old translation was 'Iron Enclosure' (*Tiěwéi*); 'Enclosure' (*Wéi*) carries the meaning of 'Wheel' (*Lún*), whereas the name 'Iron' did not originally exist and was established by the translators based on their interpretation.
The current name 'Wheel-Enclosure Realm' (*Wéilúnjiè*) adopts this meaning. This is indeed the text from the *Abhidharmavibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle twenty.

"Exiting from the offense" refers specifically to exiting from the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. Regarding "including those for whom it was done": this explains that a single person may reside in a monastery, because a threshing floor is not a permanent dwelling place;

even if a king were to establish one there, if [the resident] possesses a sense of shame, they would dismantle it and transport the remaining timber and straw elsewhere. This applies to the bhikṣu residing in the monastery.
The boundary is established based on the seating arrangement. This is because it relies on the physical characteristics of the seated positions rather than fixed architectural features;

it takes the area where the Sangha is gathered and seated as the defining characteristic of the interior boundary, excluding anything outside the bodies of the individuals present. This implicitly refutes ancient interpretations. The *Shisao* states:

"In recent practice, when establishing a small boundary for the conferral of precepts, many have set up the limits of the monastery compound. This is not a thorough understanding. One should follow the Vinaya texts to prevent such improper practices."

For this reason, Qiu remains seated outside the boundary; ultimately, he cannot avoid being obstructed. Furthermore, "below" refers to the characteristics of the Great Boundary (mahā-sīmā) above, namely the Precept Platform (śīla-maṇḍala).

"At one time" means performing the ritual procedure at a single session. Once it is performed, it is immediately dissolved; otherwise, if one rises [without dissolving it], one will lose one's sense of direction.
This will be explained later in the section on resolving the Small Boundary (kṣudra-sīmā).

Naturally wearying, it would thus involve the toil of constant travel throughout the natural environment. Therefore, the *kṣetra* (boundary) was established in accordance with each location, delimiting the sphere of benefit according to the timing and circumstances.
Below this, there are four types of boundaries; because the occurrence of certain matters might obstruct one’s own practice, the *sīmāmaṇḍala* (ordination precinct) was established.
Regarding the two aforementioned great boundaries (*mahāsīmā*) and the *maṇḍala*, these are not the primary concern; rather, they are [established] to ward off wicked bhikṣus.
Because of those affairs, the three minor [rules] regarding binding and unbinding are opened up as in the text. Below, they are explained in sequence according to the text.

"The two are identical" refers to the identity of person and dharma. "The remaining two" refer to the identity of dharma and food, as well as the identity of dharma with food being distinct, according to their respective positions.

As for the reference to the text, within the division into three stages, the monastic grounds serve as the basis (*āśraya*), and the Sangha serves as that which depends upon it (*āśrita*). This is what was previously stated.

When first performing the formal act (*karmavācanā*), one must follow the precedent of the sacred words; if there is any deviation, then subsequent matters such as the *prātimokṣa-saṃvara* (or *jñapti-caturtha-karman*) cannot be successfully accomplished.
If one falls into error and overturns the procedure, how could any trace of the proper method remain? [There are] four gates.

Now, the Master [Yuanze] has criticized the ancient [commentary] for being too brief. I shall now expand and encompass [the meaning] through ten gates, thereby avoiding the fault of cluttered and overlapping confusion.
Regarding "floating and diffuse": this refers to being superficial and vast, such that there is no practical application when facing the immediate situation.

Therefore, below, I generate the intent for establishing these ten gates so that one may obtain the essential matters by examining the text; that is, by reading the main text, one encounters the various categories of phenomena, which serve as the basis for the ten gates.

Based on the substance of the sign (*nimitta*), one subsequently cognizes the substance of the element (*dhātu*) based on the characteristics of the sign. How could this directly point to the mountain?

To say it cannot directly point to the mountain is because there is a fear that the boundaries (*sīmā*) will not be recognized. Among the four parts [of the boundary], there is a mountain in the east called "Mountain" and a moat called "Moat," and so forth.
The Great Master said: "To establish the dharma according to this is truly unacceptable; it must be based on the requirement below to be at the edge of the mountain."
At the edge of the peak, a distinct marker is established; thus it is said that the specific location is pointed out for clarity. Therein are seventeen kinds of distinct dwellings, namely:
long, circular, square, wavy, mountain-like, rocky, crescent-shaped, and ring-shaped, all of which have clearly defined boundaries.

There must be no vagueness or confusion. Regarding the phrase "in accordance with this": it refers to the text by Da’an Shi. If a separate marker is established on the mountain, it is logically permissible to distinguish between the general and the specific.
Regarding the phrase "grass and bamboo": grass is not firm, and the substance of bamboo is hollow;

one must rely on the edge, lean against a tree, and pass through the heart of the tree before one may proceed, for it cannot be traversed at will. The "marker" (biao) refers to a tree or grove; even the smallest is like a needle.
This refers to the large needle. Because it ultimately possesses the significance of "joining together" (he-bao), it is called the "exhausted path" (qiong-tu);

this means that communication does not extend to other places, representing the ultimate limit of the Way. "Short and low," reaching as far as three or four villages, is a brief description that certainly will not be discarded.
"Ant-hills" (yǐ-fēng) refers to the appearance formed when ant larvae transport soil to build up mounds. "Good kings" and below refers to enlightened monarchs.

Regarding governance and transformation: if rain does not fail its appointed time, this river cannot serve as [a sign]. If, however, there is no rain for a year and yet the flow of the water is not exhausted, this may be taken as a sign.
Because it has endured for a long time, it is a natural pool; one should likewise take a spring source that is inexhaustible.

If, because it will not last long, one establishes a temporary boundary—such as within the space of a single mat—and performs the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) to demarcate the limits, then upon its completion, that boundary may be dissolved;
this is appropriate for using materials such as grass or straw. Regarding the Vinaya treatises, this refers to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, and the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*.
The *Daichao* states: "In accordance with the *Śāstra*, the characteristics established by conditions such as city walls and moats can be understood;
the meaning of the text is the same. Regarding the seventeenth [category], the *Shu* (Commentary) lists only ten; here they are cited in full. It says: first, long and circular distinct dwellings;

second, four-cornered; third, water-wave shaped; fourth, mountain-shaped; fifth, rock-shaped; sixth, half-moon shaped; seventh, natural shape (*svabhāva*); eighth, circular enclosure (*parimaṇḍala*); ninth, single-gated.
1. The soil of the ten directions; 2. the four sides; 3. the two boundary lines;
4. bhikṣus; 5. upāsakas; 6. fences and walls; 7. the complete [boundary]; 8. one who is insane or living apart.
It is said that "attainment lies in subtlety" because it requires the fulfillment of ten conditions. [Such attainment] is rare;
it must lie outside the substance, for the marks serve as the method by which the substance is encompassed.

Depending on whether one refers to the internal or external boundaries, it is acceptable to chant either the internal or the external; both are permitted. This ultimately defines the precise measurements, thereby implicitly showing that vague pointing is not permissible.

There are three types of boundary markers (*lakṣaṇa*): first, the marker for the *śīmaṇḍala* (precept site); second, the internal marker for the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*); and third, the external marker for the great boundary.
If there is no [inner] boundary, there is one layer. Regarding "no *śīmaṇḍala* (ordination site)": it means simply establishing one outer marker.

As for distance, proximity, width, or narrowness: one *hasta* is eight *cun*. Below this, the ancients cite evidence; since it says "one mountain, one stone," we know that a large marker is permissible.
Furthermore, below this, it cites the forty-seventh fascicle of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, which states that all are to be bound together. This refers to the mutual [connection].

This is also a case of simultaneous binding. The Buddha’s answer below speaks of the two aspects of internal and external, each describing their arising and ceasing in a complete cycle. Furthermore, they are separated by a great distance;
based on this, the ancients established [the measurement], so it must not be made too narrow.

Now, the following clarifies the correct meaning. Regarding the two cords: the forest hermitage (*araṇya*) and the village settlement constitute the two cords. One employs the cord to delineate the Dharma;

since the cord itself constitutes the substance [of the boundary], why wait for it to reach a length of one cubit or more? Furthermore, if one takes mountains and rocks as examples, even if their breadth and width cannot be distinguished, this [boundary] would still not be established.
One should know that although the markers may be broad or narrow, if one understands the distinction between the two aspects, what [need is there for further measurement]?
"Going to the stone is permissible; it is by descending that one explains the intent of the former resident.

Although it is descending, the Great Master makes a definitive judgment based on the meaning, taking only the understanding [of the matter]. It is not fixed as either host or guest; the meaning applies to both [the departing and the staying].
As for the statement that 'there may be one who understands,' based on the meaning, this refers to the one who is the former resident."
In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, Part II, it states: "Since it says 'to dispatch one bhikṣu,' that person is not necessarily a resident monk.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "then he proclaims," this refers to first proclaiming the internal boundaries (*sīmā*) of the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) in order to exclude the interior area. Now, the following section sets forth the current practice:

having first proclaimed the boundaries of the *śīmaṇḍala* (precept platform), one next proclaims the internal boundaries of the great boundary, and finally proclaims the external boundaries; thus, there is no need to first exclude the interior.
This refers to the "Ground" (Bhūmi). That which is excluded is naturally separated by the intervening text; this is indicated in the section on the "Resolution of Bonds" (*kṣema*) below.
Furthermore, in the subsequent resolution, it also points to this, stating: "This is the fourth gate of the first meaning."
"Binding below" refers to granting permission. "Fearing below" refers to taking away [the robe]. "Establishing a person's expectation" refers to one who has not yet received the precepts.

"Eight persons" refers to the bhikṣus. "It should first be placed below" follows the method for donning the robes. As for "not being counted," what harm is there? Those who have broken the precepts and do not understand the Vinaya were never fit to be counted in the first place;
even if they are set aside, what harm is done? "This is sufficient to exclude them" means those who uphold the precepts clearly.
[The Buddha] explained: "This may be counted as sufficient. If people do not assemble, it obstructs the Dharma-activity.
The boundary of mutual accommodation is wider than the marked boundary (*saṃketa*). If the marked boundary is wider, and if the erected markers are wider than the natural boundary (*prakṛti-sīmā*)."
One must gather at the designated boundary; otherwise, one should naturally assemble within the *prakṛtisthā* (natural) boundary at the time of the proclamation and the time of the formal binding.
The ancients maintained that even if the designated boundary is wide, one must still rely on the natural boundary for the assembly. The following explains the reason for this;
thus, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* cites analogous texts to support it.
Three *yojanas*. This prohibits [those who are] difficult to summon; it establishes a boundary of one hundred and twenty *li*, yet even those beyond that are still called forth.

Thus, we know that everyone within the designated area must assemble. If one goes outside the boundary, then although the three-*yojana* boundary for the *bhikṣuṇīs* does not obstruct [the *bhikṣus*], because monks and nuns are naturally within sight of one another, they do not count as being present.
Furthermore, there is no need to call them, because the natural ground [of their presence] is weak, and thus there is no assembly.

The ritual for establishing the *dharmadhātu* and the principle regarding the arrival of the Saṃgha are the reverse of this; until the boundary has been formally established, it is necessary to assemble all members. One must not depart immediately.
This is in accordance with the second of the four reliances: relying on the Dharma and not on the person, and relying on the meaning and not on the letter.
The *Jìnzìnrán* (Natural Realm) is inherently weak. The *Dàchão* states: "If the natural realm is weak, monastic affairs cannot be carried out;

that is, one cannot perform formal acts (*karmavācanā*) such as those involving consent. One should first raise this objection: "If that is so, why is it permitted to perform the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for establishing a boundary? This is resolved by the text itself:

because the act is performed by the Saṃgha without [individual] conditions having been met, the transmission of consent (*chanda*) is only then permitted. Furthermore, the establishment of a boundary is...

Because it is the root of all dharmas, it cannot be treated by analogy. The *dhātu* (realm) is inferior; if, after being bound, the realm and stage (*bhūmi*) to which it belongs are strong, it may include dharmas of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Conversely, if it has not yet been bound, it is weak and therefore cannot do so.

Regarding the two types of retribution—the environmental (*āśraya*) and the personal (*sambhoga*): the "environmental" refers to the realm and stage (*dhātu-bhūmi*), while the "personal" refers to the bhikṣu.

If one were to permit the transmission of the *kāmacchanda* (the formal expression of consent) and thereby conclude the rite, one would fail to exercise discernment regarding the breadth or narrowness of the environmental retribution. Furthermore, how could one then justify the regulations concerning the summer retreat (*varṣā*), the separate assemblies (*pṛthaggaṇa*), and the protection of food (*bhojana-rakṣā*)?
Regarding the first case, which relies on what is natural: this refers to the general assembly hall (*saṃgha-śālā*) and its designation.

Because the boundary (*sīmā*) arises wherever the monks happen to be, they gather based on this. It is chaotic, as there is no fixed marker to definitively indicate the location; therefore, the place is not fixed.
The *Daichō* states: "In each instance of assembling the saṃgha, it is essential that this [time] be difficult to secure. Regarding the establishment of the boundary and its binding (*sīmābandha*):

because of the aforementioned rushing about, a separate binding is permitted. Since a separate binding is allowed, there are four benefits, such as the thorough knowledge of the place of proclamation and so forth.

As for *kōgi* (extensive meaning), *kō* means "great" (*mahat*), and furthermore, it means "to propagate" (*pravartana*). Fearing that [the assembly] might become identical with the *dharmadhātu*, although there was previously a warning and restriction, it still...

Fearing that those who are indolent might not come, [the procedure] is made identical to the *dharmadhātu* ritual; thus, one grants the *chanda* (consent) as at ordinary times and thereby restricts it once more.
Regarding the "first text" and the "subsequent meaning," this is pointed out in the commentary from the passage beginning with "from among these" up to "according to what exists."

This is the scriptural text (*vinaya*). "Should be established through meaning" (*yìshè*) below refers to indicating the subsequent meanings. From the beginning up to the section on "practical application" (*xíngshì*), the emphasis is placed on indicating the meaning of the text.
This first point clarifies the underlying intent: it states that this single dharma is the fundamental source (*mūla*) of all dharmas.

If the subsequent dharmas are not first established, there will be no basis from which they can arise; therefore, it is called the "source of the multitude. Thus, [the text] says "should be established" below.
This expresses the intention of establishing the meaning.

"Commentary" (*shū*) means to expand upon [the text]. It explains the reasons for its elaboration. Generally, the primary purpose of composing a commentary is to facilitate understanding; secondly, it is to select and clarify the obstructions and stagnations within the literary text.
Since these have not yet been fully elucidated, it is also a matter of resolving them. "Without laboring" means that one does not wish to exhaust future generations with toil.

It would trouble their reflections to search for and investigate [the boundaries], resulting in a vain waste of many generations—where "generations" implies many years. It depends solely on what is natural;

furthermore, because subsequent re-establishment is not permitted, it is governed by the markers. If the markers are wide, one must assemble according to the markers; if the boundary is wide, one must assemble according to the boundary.
"Four persons" means that four persons may perform the establishment of the boundary, distinguishing them from five persons, who serve as the chant-leader for the boundary markers.

Because it is included within the numerical categories, the supernormal power (ṛddhipāda) that is non-numerical abides in emptiness. Although the four—madness, agitation, sleep, and intoxication—are not established [as such], the cited text issues a proclamation;
that is, it first points to the four as markers, having already announced them in the four intermediate directions, and proclaims the ritual procedures internally and externally.

I fear it would be confused with the "separate" (individual) category. This is because I fear that by citing the name and including it within the formal procedure (*dharma*), it would be confused as being subsumed under a specific individual rather than being included in the number of the Saṃgha.
If this were the case, would those who are called by name still be able to attain [the status]? This is explained below: although their names are cited, it is not for private purposes;
therefore, they are included within the Saṃgha. As stated later: "Because in the context of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), it says: 'One establishes the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*).'"
This is manifested for the sake of the Saṃgha; thus, "name" refers to the formal cause (pratyaya). This is why the boundaries are proclaimed, rather than using [the individual's] title.

"Characteristics" (lakṣaṇa) are not like this, because within the formal ritual procedure (karmavācanā), the characteristics of the four directions are recorded, as in the following passage that distinguishes it from other texts.

Regarding the general rule for mountains and rivers: this refers to the method of announcing [a boundary] at a *āraṇya* (hermitage). For example, if there is a mountain to the east, one announces it as "mountain";

if there is a moat, one announces it as "moat," and so forth. This is not a detailed demarcation of limits. To pass directly through from the gate—this refers to the method of announcing [a boundary] for a village settlement (*grāma*).
Regarding the two types of chanting, internal and external: one does not understand the intricate chanting of "entering," "leaving," and so forth. As explained extensively below, it says:
"For example, from outside the courtyard, one chants: 'From the southeast corner straight to the southwest corner,' continuing until one full circuit to the main southern gate of the temple."

Otherwise, there would be the fault of performing the ritual apart from the assembly (*pṛthag-jana-doṣa*). If the boundary were to extend straight from the wall outside through the threshold of the gate, it would constitute being "within the boundary" (*sīmāntara*).
Thus, when various *karmans* (formal acts) are performed within the monastery, if monks standing outside the wall limit do not assemble, would this not be a case of acting apart from the assembly?

Therefore, one should know that the proclamation of the boundary marks must be made in a winding manner so as not to cause later regret; furthermore, it must not be proclaimed in a way that is too general or inclusive.
The term "following the curves" refers to the winding paths; these curves may also be deep or shallow, distant or near, ultimately making it impossible to determine their exact boundaries.

If one were to define the boundary by singing the markers from within, such that the path goes straight from the gate, then everything inside the threshold would be outside the boundary. This would result in faults such as being part of a separate assembly (*bhedasaṃgha*), violating the summer retreat (*varṣā*), or being separated from one's robes (*cīvara*).
This is like the ritual performed in a monastery where, once someone has finished announcing their consent (*chanda*) and reaches the inside of the threshold, they must return [to the assembly].

Upon arriving, does this not constitute leaving the boundary? To enter the boundary constitutes being apart from the assembly (*bhedasaṃgha*). If one breaks the summer retreat (*varṣābhedana*): suppose someone relies on a boundary for the rains retreat;

when the dawn light appears and reaches the gate, if he clearly perceives it and returns, does this not constitute breaking the retreat? As for "losing the robe": suppose one relies on a boundary to establish a robe-holding zone (*cīvarasīmā*);
before the dawn light has appeared, if one goes outside the boundary without carrying the robe and the dawn light appears there, does this not constitute losing the robe?
[Regarding] the robe: [the text] thus provides a detailed exposition of the faults before proceeding to the formal proclamation (as the *Chao* states).
Following the proclamation, the commentary explains the sequence of the three proclamations. The first two refer to the senior monk (*upādhyāya*) and the next-ranking seat;
the latter two refer to the one who recites the Vinaya and the one capable of performing the *karmavācanā*.
"Having no one above" means that when there is no one superior to oneself, one is called an *upādhyāya* (senior elder).

According to the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, it says: "From those with zero summer retreats (*varṣa*) up to nine summer retreats are junior elders (*navaka*); from ten summer retreats up to nineteen summer retreats are middle elders (*madhyama*); and from twenty summer retreats up to forty-nine summer retreats are senior elders (*sthavira*).
This is according to the sequence of summer retreats. If one is to restrict [the designation] based on manifest virtue, one must follow the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*."
The Elder’s recitation of the precepts is precisely the place where the Tathāgata resides; is this not, then, an interpretation based on the possession of merit?

That which is destroyed is the decayed and rotten framework of consciousness and cognition. Śāriputra was named "Pearl" (Muktika) because his mother possessed a beautiful physical form and the marks of intelligence resided in her eyes;
he was also called "Son of Śārī" (Śāriputra), as he was the son of that body.
Regarding the "Great General of the Dharma-Wheel": this refers to Śāriputra, who was foremost in wisdom. Because he was able to uphold the True Dharma and crush the heterodox, he was given this name.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: Among the five thousand bhikṣus, there were more than a thousand elders, such as Uruvilvākāśyapa and others.
Why, then, does the text specifically mention these four individuals? It answers: Śāriputra was the elder brother on the right side [of the Buddha].
"Disciple. Maudgalyāyana is the foremost disciple on the left. Subhūti is foremost in cultivating the dharma of non-contention (*araṇā*) and emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Mahākāśyapa is foremost in practicing the twelve *dhūta* ascetic virtues. ... These are called the 'knowledgeable bhikṣus. To recite the text means to recite the Vinaya three times.
To know the meaning means that the fourth [type] is one capable of performing *karmavācanā*. Below, this explains the four types of those capable of performing [the ritual]."
This means that although one may not be able to recite the text by stringing together sentences or filling pages, one is nonetheless able to understand its meaning; this is considered superior.

As for the remaining Vinaya, namely the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, those who should participate must already possess such capability and have necessarily mastered the principles of success and failure regarding participation.

Xuānbing stated: "If one has not yet become proficient in the methods of *karmavācanā*, even for a person who has just been permitted to undergo training and repentance (*xuéhuǐ*), it is also permissible to perform the rite.

The *Dàcǎo* says: 'As for those undergoing training and repentance, there is no fixed limit; provided they certainly do not know the ritual procedures, it is also permitted to perform the rite for them. There is no fault in doing so separately.
Such a person is therefore one of intermediate capacity."

Regarding the ninefold gradations of disparity: these begin with mere mental intention and culminate in the *jñapti-caturtha* (the formal motion followed by three proclamations); such is the distinction of the nine grades. Regarding "conditions" (*pratyaya*) and "non-conditions" (*apratyaya*):

this refers to the ten conditions and seven non-conditions previously discussed. Regarding "sacred teaching" (*āgama*): this refers to the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedure), specifically the verbal expressions that serve as the means of communication.
Regarding the principles to be expounded: it is only the general framework that serves as a means of access; the specific conditions are not intended as obstructions.

"The subsequent texts" refers to the various *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedures) that follow. Because this meaning has been clarified, there is no need to provide further explanation in the subsequent texts. "Unable to... [and so forth].
These have been explained extensively according to their respective sections; for now, they have not yet served their intended purpose. Students should reflect upon this meaning. [Commentary:

Ying Shao of the *Hanshu* says it refers to weights and measures (*quanheng*). Wei Zhao says it refers to the counterweight of a scale. Today, it is used to mean a balanced measurement or a systematic narrative.

Regarding the admonition for the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*): it means to cause the moving consciousness of the ear to be gathered and listen to the Dharma being performed. Regarding the two sounds being called separately, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states:
"This listening is the function of the mind employing a listening characterized by harmony and patience; it differs from what was obtained by the ear-consciousness in the first phrase above.

If one does not understand these two types of listening, then when the words are heard together as a single sound, the expression will not be communicated, and the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) will not be accomplished. This refers to the preceding listening.
This refers to the departing tone (*qùshēng*); what follows is heard as the level tone (*píngshēng*). Fearing that you may not understand this and thus cause much harm, I say:

while one’s transgressions and merits can still be relinquished at the time of reciting the precepts oneself, the affliction and injury are even more profound when actually receiving the precepts; therefore, one must exercise extreme caution.

The second and fourth [phrases] refer to two instances of the causal conditions (*pratyaya*). However, while the preceding phrase presents both the basis (*mūla*) and the conditions together, the subsequent phrase briefly cites the conditions by restating the basis.
Regarding the section on "binding the boundary" (*sīmā-bandha*), it states that binding the boundary is the action to be performed;

if the two are identical, it is not so. This is because it originally arises from the recitation of the *Poṣadha* (*śīla-uddeśa*); thus, the eight [phrases] are cited in succession. This is generally the case in the Vinaya texts; it is said that all the Vinayas are like this.

Because the *dhātu* (boundary) is the fundamental basis. Regarding the objective entity (*vastu*), if one considers it in relation to the original establishment of the boundary, it belongs to the non-sentient;
however, since it is now established through the concordant assembly of the bhikṣu-saṃgha, it belongs to the sentient.
Regarding speech and silence: the Vinaya states that "to endure" means to remain silent, while "not to endure" means to speak. If one cannot remain silent for long, one must speak.

As for the matter at hand, it refers to the act of establishing a boundary (*sīmābandha*). This is now restated here; this pertains to the formal ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*). There are two types of announcements:

first, the announcement within the *jñapti* (the motion), and second, the announcement during the *karmavācanā* itself. In both cases, once the assembly has signaled their consent by remaining silent, subsequent speech constitutes silence [of dissent]. Below...
When reaching the character "chi" (持), the two [preceding characters] are cited as the basis for the object of cognition (*ālambana*). Regarding the *jñapti-caturtha* (four-part) legal procedure:

it consists of one *jñapti* (motion) and three *karmavācanā* (formal acts); hence it is called "four-part. Furthermore, when it comes to the formal act (*karman*), the principle that "one must necessarily establish three" can serve as a high precedent.

The "three above" refers to the present master and the two ancients. As for the *sinan* (司南), it is the south-pointing chariot. Cui Bao’s *Gujin Zhu* (Ancient and Modern Notes) states: "The Great Chariot..."
The Southern Car originated with the Yellow Emperor. When the Emperor was at war with Chiyou on the plains of Zhuolu, Chiyou raised a great mist, causing everyone to lose their sense of direction.
Thereupon, he fashioned the South-pointing Car to indicate the four quarters. He subsequently captured Chiyou and ascended the imperial throne.
Later generations have traditionally maintained that it was created by the Duke of Zhou; however, it is now said that each [version] has its own specific indications.

Regarding the meaning: whether it is explicit or implicit—when explicit, the second phrase is retained; when implicit, it is omitted. As for "having [the requisite]": as in the case of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and so forth, five phrases are required to constitute the formal motion (*jñapti*);
if they are absent, it is constituted by only four phrases. The second point concerns the basis of the conditions. Regarding the appointment of a person, it is as prescribed in the Vinaya.
Appointing people to distribute rooms and bedding; appointing people to make the *guṇakīva* (merit-cloth); and appointing a nun to request instruction—these are as previously stated.
That is to say, if [the preceding] is absent, it is omitted. Regarding "without" (*mūla*), it means that the four or five phrases cannot be discussed.
First: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen. Third: "If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen. Fifth: That is...
The announcement is as follows. Second, one cites the original double clauses. Fourth, one briefly cites the original clauses.

Regarding the single matter—such as the delimitation of boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*) or the reception of the precepts (*upasampadā*)—the meaning applies universally; in all such cases, the former is detailed while the latter is abbreviated, and it is announced to the entire Saṃgha.
This refers to the section on the descent [of the Buddha] into the world.

Regarding "poṣadha" (布薩) and "preaching the precepts" (說戒), both the Chinese and Sanskrit terms are presented together. To now say "the assembly of monks preaches the precepts" (*zhòngsēng shuōjiè*)—changing the character *bùsà* (poṣadha) to *zhòngsēng* (assembly of monks)—is incorrect.
Nanshan [Daoxuan] recorded this according to the Vinaya; it was not a mistake made by later generations. How could one dare to alter it arbitrarily?
"Revised. This means that both [the original and the revision] belong to the category of being non-pure due to their conditions.
Regarding "the compilation was translated as non-pure": this refers to the process of compiling and translating; because there were redundancies and intermixture, the text was rendered impure.
Therefore, the subsequent text states: "Because the scriptural passage is impure, one loses the ear by cutting.
What follows below says that within this *karmavācanā* context, it likewise merely restates the essential summary of the text.

Regarding "both the text and the meaning are comprehensive": since these belong to the structural framework, they encompass all ninety-five dharmas. Regarding "the meaning is comprehensive while the text is restricted":

this refers to the dual or single nature of the conditions (pratyaya), as well as the verbal proclamation versus silent consent; such are the comprehensive meanings. To cite the specific conditions according to each particular case is what is meant by the restricted text.
"Furthermore, to cite one or two instances" refers to the method where the phrasing is restricted while the meaning is universal.
In the section below that raises the inquiry, one or two matters and dharmas are cited again for further clarification. "Nā" (pronounced *nu jiā*) means to lead or draw forth.

"Head and heels"—"heels" refers to the feet—means to place what follows before what precedes, or to place what precedes after what follows. This refers to cases where words and phrases are inverted, confused, misplaced, or omitted. Or...
Seeking to become a *śramaṇa* for others’ sake is truly due to a failure to distinguish between right and wrong; how could one claim that such a person can achieve [enlightenment]?

This is likely because they have not yet seen this text which exposes such fallacious reasoning. These words are precisely the aforementioned refutation: a "semblance bhikṣu" is merely an outsider who resembles a bhikṣu because he lacks the precepts.
As it says in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, "The land of Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra is devoid of precepts"—these words are indeed trustworthy.
Regarding "What is below?": The meaning of the preceding statement is comprehensive, while the text is restricted; this should be understood. What is meant by "the meaning is comprehensive"?

It refers to "governing the text," which means governing the text to eliminate impurities and errors through cutting and clipping. The *Preface to the Book of Documents* (*Shangshu xu*) states: "Cut away redundant words.

To follow the *Karmavācanā* (Karma) as the sole standard means that the causal conditions and the structural framework are identical, and neither increase nor decrease is permitted. The *Great Commentary* (*Dàchǎo*) says: "However, one must know..."
The locations must not be identical. Regarding the "framework" (綱骨) of the text's meaning, it will be explained below.
As for what is called "not reaching the point" (無詣), it means that if there is even one missing character within the framework, it causes the words placed therein to have no place to arrive.

The "text" (文) explains the "conditions and fallacies" (緣非), which generally covers both addition and omission. How could these two be distinct? The intent is to say that they may also be cited [together].

The two cases are identical. Why are they not listed here? It is simply because they are omitted. As it says below: "Dwelling together, performing the *poṣadha* together, and receiving offerings together, as in the various *dharmas*.

This refers to the *sīmā-bandha* (boundary-establishment) grounds prescribed in the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, as well as the minor boundaries (*kṣudrasīmā*) and so forth. The great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) is distinguished from the small by its magnitude;
furthermore, it is precisely the fundamental basis for ritual acts (*karman*).

There are cases where the phrasing is abbreviated yet the meaning is comprehensive, such as the term "network-bone" (*jālaka*). There are cases where the phrasing is restricted and abbreviated yet the meaning is comprehensive, involving both single and compound terms.
When the phrasing is abbreviated it is called "single," and when the words are repeated it is called "compound.

Provided that the essential intent is not lost, even if there are variations in addition or subtraction—as in the examples cited below, such as translating the "three robes" (*tricīvara*) as "bedding and requisites" (*śayanāsana*)—it is acceptable so long as one obtains the underlying meaning of the robes.
The appearance [of the robe] has been completely lost, yet the substance of the *kāṣāya* is still used for one's own purposes. This is as stated in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*:
"When making a new bedding, one should maintain it for a full six years," and so forth.

As stated below, regarding the "net" (jāla) and the "bones" (asthi), there is no difference in their increase or decrease. However, while the wording is restricted to the statement of the conditions (*pratyaya*), the increase or decrease does differ.

For instance, in the text on the *pañcavargika* boundary-establishment (*sīmābandhana*), even the single-announcement (*jñapti*) lacks the fourth phrase, and within the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), the second phrase is likewise absent;

yet, it is still validly established because the conditions permit both increase and decrease. These are merely the specific assertions of different schools (*nikāya*), and [the ritual] must not be increased or decreased [beyond those limits].
Therefore, there are no differing terms; thus it is said that "the meaning can be seen.

Regarding the provisional application, this refers to the aforementioned discussion on the capacity to uphold [the Dharma]. Within the context of the Saṃgha, it is said: "The Buddha-Dharma manifests the Saṃgha, which necessarily consists of four persons;

there are none who do not grasp at the provisional to constitute its function. Furthermore, within the determination of the essence of the Saṃgha, it says: "One grasps the aggregates (skandhas) to form a person; the person is the provisional body, while the real dharmas [are the basis]."

It is useless. Four people must provisionally employ [the precepts] to constitute the body of the Saṃgha. Although they now collectively uphold them, the provisional application of the six harmonies has not yet been fully manifested.
This requires at least one person and above who expresses harmony through both speech and silence. If even one person lacks harmony, the Dharma will not be accomplished;
therefore, it is necessary to inquire about their individual status.
