If one refers to the specific matter [of the *karmavācanā*], it is not established; one merely says "a legal matter for the Saṃgha. Regarding other matters that are not established:
if one says "for the purpose of a single *poṣadha*," does this mean that after the boundary has been established, one performs the *poṣadha* collectively, while other matters remain unestablished?

As for the previous point regarding the general statement being restricted: for example, if one says "I grant my consent (*chanda*) for the purpose of the *poṣadha* ceremony," one should not separately distribute robes or request the day.
Regarding such matters: here, the phrase "matters of the *saṃgha* according to the Dharma" refers to all wholesome *karmans* appropriate for the *saṃgha*.
When a separate matter arises, one need not remain stationary; one may go elsewhere to receive the consent (*chanda*). This is not the case for the formal delimitation of boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*).

Because this delimitation is performed subsequently for the sake of various distinct activities, its conditions do not apply in the interim. Once the Great Boundary (*mahāsīmā*) has been established, it is only then that [the members] are said to be "of one accord."

Regarding the *poṣadha* (recitation of the precepts): it is not like the case below, because within the formula for granting consent (*chanda*), the formal monastic matter (*dharmika saṃghakārya*) is set forth first, and the phrase "granting consent" is stated subsequently;

therefore, they do not coincide. Thus, the citation of evidence below can be understood accordingly. The answer below states that it is precisely because of the *poṣadha* that the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedure) is established.
Therefore, it is said that the precepts are the foundation. They comprise the equipment of livelihood, conduct, and view.
"Livelihood" refers to right livelihood, which is the departure from the four and five wrong modes of making a living; this is harmony through material benefit (*lābha-sāmaggī*).

"Conduct" is harmony through precepts (*śīla-sāmaggī*), and "view" is harmony through view (*dṛṣṭi-sāmaggī*). Above, the three types of action (*karmapatha*) were raised; next, the three harmonies were raised; below, it is said that the six harmonies are fully possessed.
This clarifies the original boundary. As for the "original boundary," it is because the original boundary was established specifically for the purpose of reciting the precepts.

Regarding the term *kamma* (formal act), this teacher’s intention is that a *kamma* may be performed either for the sake of the Saṃgha as a whole or for an individual; however, the recitation of the precepts is not like that, as it applies universally to both the Saṃgha and individuals.
Therefore, one recites the *Poṣadha* (precept recitation), but does not mention the *Karma* (formal ritual).

When the assembly gathers from different boundaries—such as when the *Śīma-kuṇḍa* (boundary enclosure) and the *Mahā-śīma* (great boundary) are being traversed for the recitation of the precepts—one must ensure that the monks are fully assembled at all four locations, including those within the circular perimeter (*parimaṇḍala*). This is why the recitation of the precepts is restricted solely to those within the same [boundary].

Regarding "the same boundary" (*sīmā*): it is said that for *karmavācanā* (formal ritual acts), one must proceed only when the boundaries are identical; otherwise, they do not apply to different boundaries.
The following section explains the reason for this, which conversely clarifies that for the *poṣadha* (confession of precepts), monks from various boundaries must gather together.
There is one who says: "The intention of this master is that the boundary is established even if the two commonalities are not recited.

The reason they are recited now is because the boundary was originally established for the purpose of reciting the precepts; therefore, it follows that they must be recited. However, as stated below, if these were not recited, [the boundary] would still be established. [Commentary:

If the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) were not established when not recited, then other small boundaries (*kṣudra-sīmā*) and the *sīma-maṇḍala* (precept-platform) would likewise not be established when not recited.
Within [the area], there are various *dhātus* (territories), such as those that exist separately like the encircling wheels.

Since there are many *dhātus*, when the boundary is subsequently demarcated, one must necessarily cite each *dhātu* according to its respective territory; one must not rely on the literal text and recite: "In these internal and external boundaries, shall a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) be established internally?
The answer below prevents prolixity, stating that it is not necessary to cite each of the minor *dhātus* individually, as they are excluded.
Regarding an empty space: it is also permissible to establish a great boundary (mahā-sīmā) by defining the internal and external limits of these four directions.
This is because, when this boundary is compared with that boundary, both are situated outside of one's own boundary. "By means of the marks" means that one compares these marks with those marks.

However, when the boundary is first proclaimed as being "inside," it is called internal; when later proclaimed as being "outside," it is called external. Furthermore, regarding the internal markers of a Great Boundary (mahā-sīmā), they may also be considered in relation to the external markers;
thus, the markers themselves possess both internal and external aspects. As for the substance (*tattva*) below, this refers to the intermediate phenomena;
in relation to the internal and external markers, the marker must necessarily lie outside the substance.

"Non-existence" means that no dharma arises. However, the following explains the reason why it is "concomitant with the practitioner's mind. "Practitioner" refers to the one who is the object of the rite;
that is, the one who performs the rite and the one who is its object. If both share the same intention, then there is non-informative action (*avijñapti*); if they lack such intention, there is none.

Just as when a preceptor administers the precepts, one receives them by means of a formal ritual and a mental resolve; because there is a dharma that can be attained through such a rite, this preceptor is now formally designated.
That which is the object of the boundary-establishment (*sīmā-bandha*) is the ground (*bhūmi*). Since the ground belongs to the category of non-sentient things (*asattva*), no dharma arises therein.
As the Vinaya cites scriptural evidence below: "What is it to perform a *karmavācanā* in the presence of the boundary and proclaim its limits? Therefore, we know that [no dharma arises].

There are dharmas; this extends even to the lower categories of examples. For instance, regarding robes, bowls, and medicine, if one applies the ritual formula (*dhāraṇī*) and undergoes the purification (*pariśuddhi*), one is exempt from the offense.
What "arising of a dharma" (*dharmotpatti*) could there be? The *Dàxiào* (Great Commentary) refutes the ancients' citation of scriptural evidence, stating:
"This refers to the fact that the application of the formula does not depend on whether or not the dharma arises. If it were otherwise, it would mean our own patriarchs adopted the lower category."

Regarding the *Sūtra on the Arising of Lower Goodness*, it says: "In the worldly dharmas, where there is a cause, there is a fruit; just as when there is water or a mirror, there is the reflection of a face.
Therefore, we know that the *kṛta* (the actual act) exists in the prior life, while the *avijñapti* (non-informative action) arises subsequently. Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* states:

"Because they arise from the mind, demerit, merit, and so forth are called the aggregate of non-informative wholesome conduct (*avijñapti-kuśala-karma-skandha*). This is because within the mind of wholesome conduct, there is a continuous flow of creative activity.

Because it is accomplished, it is likewise subsumed within the aggregate of wholesome conduct (*śīla-skandha*). It is also thus accomplished within the mind of unwholesome conduct. As for the power of karma:
through the power of mental karma, phenomena arise as their result.
The Water Wheel: Beneath the Golden Wheel is the Water Wheel; beneath the Water Wheel is the Wind Wheel. The *Dàocháo* (Great Digest) treats "water-limit" (*shuǐjì*) as having the same meaning.
This is because the realm (*dhātu*) is form (*rūpa*). [The phrase] ends here.

This is a separate case and not counted [in the quorum]. Because they reside within the boundary (*sīmā*), they constitute a separate group; according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, because the bhikṣus are on a tree, they do not count toward the full number.
If they are beneath the branches—meaning the bhikṣus are also outside the boundary—it is permitted for those on the branches not to commit an offense.

Regarding "outside the boundary" and "beneath," this refers to the root. Even if the branches extend over the interior of the boundary from the outside, it is considered severed from the root; thus, it is provisionally stated that there is no offense. (End of section ten)

Citing scriptural evidence: This point is also not fully clarified in the Vinaya text itself. According to the Master’s [Daoxuan’s] definitive interpretation below, both the root and the branches must be situated outside [the boundary].

A bhikṣu who is positioned on the branch may [legitimately] obtain [the status of being within the boundary]. The rest is as stated in the *Shanbu suiji jiemo* (Excerpts from the Vinaya). Within the section on the ritual for delimiting the boundary by means of branches, it cites the *Xiaofa miejin jing* (Sūtra on the Extinction of the Lesser Dharma), which says:
"When the kalpa-ending fire arises, places that were formerly monasteries will not be consumed by the flames, even unto the vajra [mountain]."
The *dhātu* (boundary) serves as the foundation for the territory.
An *upāsaka*, having received the five or eight precepts and mentally taking refuge in the Three Jewels, is included among the seven classes of followers;
therefore, he is able to maintain the boundary without losing it. If a village falls under the control of bandits, the *bhikṣus* must, in all cases...

"Realm" (*dhātu*). "All outside" means that they are all external to it; "external" (*bāhya*) signifies the act of abandoning or relinquishing. If one subsequently performs a ritual action, one must again bind [the boundary].
Therefore, the following text says: "Because of the abandonment, [it is] entirely outside the realm. The subsequent text says: "The boundary is abandoned;
facing away from the signs, it is entirely outside the realm. The meaning is identical to the above.

The pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*) is not lost. Since the pure ground belongs to that which depends upon it (*āśrayin*), and the *saṃgha*-boundary is its support (*āśraya*), one knows that [the boundary] exists because the dependent does not lose its support.
Regarding the remaining lower cases, he further states: "If there is doubt, one should dissolve [the boundary] and then re-establish it; therefore, one knows the boundary exists.
Impurity refers to things such as food cooked overnight (*sāyantanapāka*).

The monks and nuns must mutually dissolve [the boundary]. For example, when the two assemblies perform the *upasampadā* together, they must necessarily mutually dissolve and mutually establish [the boundary] so that neither side loses it.
Although the establishment is now clearly explained, one must first dissolve [the previous boundary]; thus this may be understood by analogy. They must not overlap.

This is because it is said that since the two assemblies are performing the ritual together, their boundary markers (*sīmā*) must not overlap. Therefore, the treatise states that "they may jointly establish" refers to the two...
When the community performs communal acts together, a *bhikṣuṇī* must establish a boundary (*sīmā*). It must not overlap with the boundary of the *saṃgha*.

Furthermore, it is feared that if she were outside the *saṃgha* boundary, the act would not constitute a shared legal procedure (*dharmasamānatā*), as it would result in a discordant view (*vibhinna-dṛṣṭi*)—for within the six types of concordance, a discordant view is not considered concordant.

Thus, both [the *bhikṣuṇī* and the *saṃgha*] would be insufficient for the counting required for resolving disputes. As the text below states: "As in the case of Kauśāmbī, they are likewise not in concordance. This refers to the allowance for separate proclamations (*pravāraṇā*) within the same boundary. *Saṃgha*.

"Broken. This refers to the division between the two factions of the heterodox and the orthodox. Just as with the Dharma and the Saṃgha, when the previously established boundaries are reopened and re-bound such that there is no longer mutual interference, they are said to be "already broken," meaning they have been destroyed.
Regarding "speech according to the Dharma": for one who speaks according to the Dharma, the relinquishment is accomplished; this constitutes the accomplishment of the relinquishment of the boundary.

Conversely, for one who speaks contrary to the Dharma, even if they attempt to dissolve it, it is not accomplished. This is because the languages of the central and peripheral regions do not mutually intelligible.
Therefore, if the subsequent [category] is pervasive, it is not opened;

this is the reverse of the above. This "reverse of the above" refers to the nine gates. For example, if the characteristics [of the elements] are present, then [the formation] is established; if they are absent, it is not established.

The mutual connection of two realms occurs naturally without any intervening space. "Interpenetration" means the characteristics of the two realms are intermingled. "Lack of rescue" means there is no bridge.
"Boat" refers to crossing over by means of a vessel. "Conditions are neither singular nor plural" means to encompass the seven non-principles.

"Repeatedly spoken of" is like saying it with a sense of entrustment. "The four means of integration" (*saṃgrahavastu*) refers to the four categories of person, dharma, place, and matter. "Presiding over" means to govern.
"Presiding over and wielding [authority]" refers to the Great Design (*mahā-vyūha*). "Design" (*vyūha*) means the Dharma and the Way.

When many people form a single *saṃgha* and have already completed the ordination procedure for sixty thousand years, they include future monks within that superior ritual act. This is not a precedent; it does not accord with the traces of the teachings.

As for "self and other," if one's own formation is not accomplished, yet one further causes others to perform the ritual act above, the matter will fail for them as well; this is equally a fall into error.
It means "to obstruct.

The two [terms] are identical; that is, they share the same dwelling place and the same recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*). Now, it is explained that they cannot be the same. Below this, one should ask:

"At the time of the formal boundary-determination (*sīmā-bandhana*), did you declare the boundaries of the four directions for this dwelling place, and did you state 'this [area] is bounded on all four sides'?"
Regarding "within the boundary" and so forth: why, when explaining the time [of the ritual], do you not state, "one who resolves the boundary within these four directional marks"?
This will be addressed later in the section on the formal establishment of the boundary (*sīmā-bandha*).
"Below the text" means that the scriptural passage from the Vinaya is cited within the commentary itself. "Both are outside" refers to their nature: both characteristics exist outside the substance.

Furthermore, in relation to this boundary, the *sīmā-maṇḍala* (precept field) is outside the characteristics; and in relation to this [field], the *sīmā-maṇḍala* is again outside the characteristics. This is what follows below.

All these return to the preceding general section. Since the general section titled "The Distinction Between Binding and Liberation" belongs to the fourth [part], and the current explanation of binding and liberation has now concluded, they are thus subsumed under their respective category.
This refers to the requisites for the Path; that is to say, they are the instruments and equipment for cultivating the Path. Regarding the phrase "when the capacity arrives" (*jī zhì xià*):

it means that when this capacity reaches the teaching, how could one not penetrate it according to that capacity? It refers back to the human factors and the Dharma: that is, returning to the same dwelling place and the same recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*).
The reason for specifically mentioning "the same recitation of the precepts and the same offerings" here is to follow the original conditions. Furthermore, although [this] is restated...
"Sharing benefits. Does this not mean dwelling together? Thus we know that both [meanings] are contained therein.
"Benefits abound for both parties" explains the original meaning of separate benefits. "Dwelling in one place without dharma" explains the present desire to share the same dharma;
for both the Way and its causes refer to the Dharma. "Each clarifying through the True Dharma" explains the separate recitation of the precepts. Material gains...

The following commentary concerns "equal distribution of offerings" (*sādhāraṇa-lābha*). "Monastic offerings" (*saṃghika-dāna*) distinguishes these from "offerings for those present" (*pratyutpanna-dāna*).

Regarding "the permanent property of the four quarters": the term "four quarters" signifies that its utility extends to the entire community; "permanent" (*sthāvara*) means the items remain within the specific boundary (*sīmā*);

"property" refers to physical objects such as beds, mats, and so forth. "Utility extends to the community" means they are for the common use of the assembly. For the remainder, refer to the second fascicle of the *Śīla-viniścaya-śāstra*.
"Monastic concord in performing acts": this means that if the Saṃgha is in harmony, the performance of *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical acts) will only then achieve fulfillment.
"The opportune moment" refers to the convergence of conditions for receiving confession and so forth; if one does not grant [the opportunity], there is no way to attain salvation.

"Comprehensively encompassing correct practice" means that all virtuous deeds are entirely included therein, precisely because it distinguishes them from improper conduct. This is stated in contrast to the *Abhidharma*.
Thus, with the exception of the rules regarding the *pravāraṇā* (the ceremony of mutual invitation) and the *pātra* (alms bowl), all [other practices] may be implemented.

"Refined" (*jing*) refers to the deer; it is like a field for selecting livestock: the refined are selected and retained, while the coarse are chosen out and discarded. "Different categories" (*yipin*): "category" (*pin*) here means class or type.

"Victory" means supreme benefit. Just as a country gains prosperity and its people find peace when it obtains worthy sages, so too does the Saṃgha find relief through the support of the teachings when it obtains worthy sages;
all are gathered together at this site. Is this not indeed beneficial? Some texts read "category" (lei) instead.

Because it overlaps with the preceding section, it is placed at the bottom of the various sections. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "In foreign lands, the *sīmāmaṇḍala* (precept field) is mostly located in the open air, such as at sites for sacrificial altars or suburban sacrifices.

In the Vinaya, 'precept' (*śīla*) is termed a 'precept altar' (*śīlamaṇḍala*). Regarding the many ritual procedures, one may perform them except for the *poṣadha* (confession of precepts) and the *pravāraṇā* (invitation)."
Furthermore, since the present *mahā-sīmā* (great boundary) also commonly encompasses multiple [sites], it should likewise be called a "site" (*sthāna*).
As stated above, it is not merely a gathering of various distinct items; rather, the establishment of the boundary constitutes the communal residence of the bhikṣus.

This is not a case of indirect implication (*paryudāsa*). A *sīmā-kṣetra* (precept-field) is designated as such because it is specifically for the purpose of repenting offenses, which is exclusively for the eradication of evil, or for the purpose of receiving the precepts, which is exclusively for the generation of good.

Since the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) lacks this specific restriction, it cannot be called a "field. If that is so, why do the three small boundaries (*kṣudrasīmā*), which are precisely for the purposes of receiving the precepts and repenting offenses, not receive the name "field"?
This is explained below by means of a general principle. This general principle applies universally to all phenomena (*dharma*). It provides a comprehensive analysis of all dharmas.

[This is] also [the case]. Regarding "harmonizing" (和) as the latter term: because there are many monks, harmonizing is difficult; because harmonizing is difficult, performing the ritual procedure (作法) is difficult. "Divergence and difficulty" (乖難) refers to the obstacles of discord and delay.

Furthermore, there is no obstacle of discordant separation regarding the assembly. Both the level (平) and departing (去) tones are applicable to the pronunciation of "receiving" (受) and "renouncing" (捨).

The *guṇa-cīvara* (merit robe): receiving the *guṇa-cīvara*, relinquishing the *guṇa-cīvara*, and so forth, all take place within the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), because the receiving and relinquishing of benefits are based upon the original place of retreat (*anvāsa*).
As for the boundaries of robes and food, they both rely upon the great boundary.

Regarding the "four dharmas," the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: First, receiving the confession for the primary offense through a *jñapti* (a formal motion); second, taking the lowest-ranking person and granting [the bowl] to them through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation);
third, granting the bowl through a *jñapti* and bestowing it in succession; fourth, using a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* to have the lowest-ranking person hold the bowl, or else to set it down.

Alternatively, according to another interpretation, these serve to encompass the Saṃgha and thus receive the name of a "great boundary" (*mahā-sīmā*); while the reception of confessions and so forth receives the name of a "site" (*kṣetra*). Thus, they mutually manifest their excellence.
The meaning of the second gate is precisely this "inner and outer" or "prior and subsequent" gate; it corresponds to the second [gate]. "Pǒ" means "not possible.
If [the boundary] were below, or if it were originally established as being outside, there would be the fault of countless congregations becoming agitated and restless.

Thus, one knows that because it is difficult to assemble [the community] within a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), the separate designation is made inside; the underlying intention can also be seen from this.

The following citation provides the proof. Although the *Vinaya-vibhaṅga* (the Code of Origins) prescribes the Great Boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) first and the Ritual Ground (*sīmā-maṇḍala*) later, when performing the ritual procedure, one need not follow the sequence of the origins. The principle is as follows:

it states that one should first establish the Ritual Ground and subsequently establish the Great Boundary. If one were to establish the Great Boundary first, one must relinquish it and then proceed again.

Having performed the formal act of binding [the boundary], one then proclaims the establishment of the Great Boundary (*mahā-sīmā*). The *Vinayamātṛkā* and the *Samantapāsādikā* also state this in the same way.

Based on this textual evidence, it appears that Master Guṇabhadra had not read the sacred teachings, but relied solely on his own mental fabrications and followed human authority. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Rely on the Dharma, do not rely on the person."

In the lower volume of the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, it is stated in its first fascicle: "Externally there is no great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*). This serves as proof that the great boundary is established by surrounding [the area] from the outside.

Regarding the phrase "if one forgets," the eighth fascicle of that same work states: "Appoint persons to first demarcate the pure ground (*śuddha-bhūmi*), next demarcate the monastic dwellings (*saṃgha-vihāra*), and finally demarcate the great boundary" (this is the main text).
This is because that text describes the process of demarcating from the inside outward; it is not the same as the current practice of demarcating the pure ground.
The character "di" (地) refers to the *saṃgha-kṣetra* (monastic boundary). This is fully explained in the following section. "Master Bei" (卑公) refers to Vimalākṣa.
The phrase "ji kě" (即可) below explains the meaning of "jiǎoxìng" (僥倖). As for "jiǎoxìng," it is a term used for blessings that exceed one's proper lot.

Now, as for the Master’s [Vasubandhu’s] interpretation: if one wishes to rely on that treatise, one should first demarcate a small boundary (sīmā) below, and then further demarcate a pure ground (śuddhasthāna) above it;
otherwise, there would be confusion, as the method for dividing [the space] also pertains to the natural ground (prakṛtistha-bhūmi), which constitutes a single entity.
Second, regarding the unity of the ritual substance (*dharmakāya*) and its natural substance:

it must necessarily descend. That is to say, if one relies upon conditions and must establish various realms (*dhātu*), they should also be arranged according to their respective forms and circumstances.

One should know that since the surrounding circles (*parimaṇḍala*) and separate dwellings are numerous, their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are also established according to the realms—whether as three, four, or more layers of signs and so forth, all the way to the end.

The lower [boundary]. Although the preceding section concerned the formal proclamation for establishing the boundary, even so, when discussing the initial gathering, it must necessarily extend to the natural boundary (*prakṛti-sīmā*).

This is because the *śīla-maṇḍala* (precept circle) is generally smaller than the natural boundary. As for the subsequent method, it receives its later name in contrast to the previously established [boundary], owing to its greater width.

This constitutes a difficulty. Because it is difficult, it becomes distinct; this results in an obstruction. For this reason, the characteristics of a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*) are not opened. According to the *Dà cǎo* (Great Commentary), it adds:

"The characteristics of the small boundary field in the four directions are also good dwelling places; these are subsumed within the monastic boundary (*saṃghasīmā*). One should possess both types of 'sameness' (*sāmānya*).

Although there is no mention of "sameness of speech" (*sabhāṣa-sāmānya*), there must be "sameness of dwelling" (*sahavāsa-sāmānya*). Why, then, is it excluded by analogy? The answer is as stated in the text.

Question: Regarding the section below, the intent is this: why must the entire assembly of monks gather upon the *sīmā* (precept field) for the two procedures of the *Poṣadha* (recitation of the precepts) and the *Pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults)?

Furthermore, since the two boundaries have already been established. Answer: Regarding the section below: the two procedures of the *Poṣadha* and *Pravāraṇā* equally encompass both those who have committed offenses and those who are pure.

For those with offenses, one must repent their transgressions to become pure; this was originally ordained so that both the monastic community (*saṃgha*) and individuals (*pudgala*) would follow it together. Therefore, the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*), the *sīmā*, and the surrounding circle...
In the *dhātu* (boundary), the Saṃgha assembles together; other dharmas are not like this, for they are not established by a common rule.

[The phrase] "some people" below refers to the practice of another school (*nikāya*), which the Great Master did not adopt. Since the text contains no partial restriction and simply says "to dissolve the boundary," why would it not apply to both?
There was originally no duality of agreement. As a defense, it is said: at the time of binding the *śīlākṣetra* (precept platform), the two agreements were not recorded.

Furthermore, at the time of subsequent release, it is precisely the two types of "sameness" (sāmagrī) that constitute release; since this corresponds to the manner of binding, it can likewise be established.

As for the dissimilar case: how could it be that there is no "two-fold sameness" during binding, yet there is "two-fold sameness" during release? This would indeed be dissimilar. Since both lack their respective characteristics, [the analogy fails].

Because the boundaries were established according to the seating arrangement of the *śramaṇeras*, no external markers (*liṅga*) were set up; furthermore, this was merely a provisional opening of a single seat.

Once the ritual was completed, it was immediately dissolved. Upon rising, one would inevitably lose one's sense of direction. However, the current site is long-established and firm, and because markers have been set up there, how could that method possibly apply?
It is not analogous.

Inference (*anumāna*) means that which can be known through comparative reasoning. Thus, the *Daichao* states: "Now, according to the boundary of the difficult matter, we simply reverse 'binding' (*bandhana*) into 'release' (*mokṣa*).
This is logically consistent and the phrasing is smooth; the monks shall dwell [there] by way of release. The text says: "The Saṃgha now assembles at this dwelling place.
Since this has already been refuted above, why is it mentioned again here?

Answer: The previous rejection of [the term] "dwelling" (sthiti) referred to a dwelling that remains fixed for a long duration; this refers to a dwelling in which four postures are maintained simultaneously.

Therefore, they are not the same. Hence, it is said to be of "many kinds. If one were to uniformly reject the use of the word "dwelling," then in the previously mentioned ritual for establishing a *sīmā* (boundary), it would also be improper to refer to "monks dwelling in this residence. Thus, one must understand [the distinction] well.
Regarding the meaning of "releasing" (解):

"throughout the boundary" refers to the Great Boundary (*mahā-sīmā*). As it says below, "throughout the enclosure of the Great Boundary. To make this easier to understand, the explanation of releasing is given later.

When it comes to the actual performance of the rite, it is not necessarily the case that one releases immediately after the formal act of binding (*bandhana*) has been completed; rather, it remains at the discretion of the one versed in the Vinaya to apply, conceal, or relinquish [the boundary].
[The term] "ear" [is used]. "Ultimately increasing" refers to the fact that water may overflow. "Obstructing the assembly" refers to the difficulty of the monastic community arriving.

"Rescuing those drowning" means using the Sangha Jewel to rescue and pull out those submerged in the human and celestial realms. If, at this time, the karmic conditions do not converge and the Sangha does not arrive, the meaning of the Sangha is not fulfilled.

Thus, emptiness manifests this designation. Because it is difficult to assemble [the community] when relying on expedient means (*upāya*), one cannot respond with the vehicle of expedient means to save sentient beings;
this is to lose its actual practice. Where there is no ferry or crossing, it is sufficient to simply provide a boat or bridge.
Regarding the "five locations," the eighth [chapter] states: "If there is an island within a river, the *karmavācanā* should be performed at five locations: first, Māthura..."
1. A monastery; 2. amidst two bodies of water; 3. atop an island; 4. amidst four bodies of water; 5. a settlement of seers—on both sides, below. He further said:
"A bhikṣu came carrying a formal consent (*chanda*), but was swept away by water.

Having escaped the boundary and nearly died, he was able to reach safety. He informed the bhikṣus: 'I previously came carrying a formal consent, but was swept away by water. I nearly died before escaping. It may now [be accepted]..."

Regarding the extensive establishment of the boundary (*sīmābandha*): the bhikṣus said, "It is permitted for you to go three *yojana*s upstream and downstream along the river and establish a marker, such as a tree or a stone.
One who performs the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) should speak as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, please listen.
From the Maṭhura Vihāra to the Ṛṣipatana Vihāra, including the river’s boundaries upstream and downstream—up to this limit, we perform the ritual."
Perform a single *poṣadha*. Thus it is announced (*jñapti*). (This proves that water and land may be combined to form a boundary. Three times [the gong] is struck. He further says:

"On land, on both sides of the path, twenty-five *hasta* each (this is the small [boundary]). Or, for those seeking refuge, one may establish a boundary of three *yojanas* (this is the large [boundary]).

Having finished explaining as above, he then states: "If we discuss the natural [boundaries], there are four different types regarding the boundaries; when defined by fixed measurements, they are divided into six characteristics."

Because there is a distinction, water and land are not included [within the same boundary]. Regarding the section on the Saṃgha: by performing a general binding, it constitutes a single boundary; logically, this is unimpeded.
This is as in the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, where the river itself is directly included in the boundary-binding, as mentioned above; this refers to the ancient interpretation cited previously.
Now, our Master, following the *Vinayavibhaṅga*, states that since it mentions "two cords," how could it refer to being within eight feet?

The three stages are chanted together. That is to say, having first chanted the characteristics of the site on the ground, one then chants from a distance the internal and external boundaries of the Great Boundary (mahā-sīmā).
Alternatively, at the lower stage, one chants from a distance the characteristics of the site within the Great Boundary and adds the formal ritual of binding (*bandhana*).

However, if only the external boundary is chanted, and the internal boundary of the Great Boundary is absent therein, the two boundaries will overlap. Furthermore, if only the internal boundary is chanted...

If one does not proclaim the external boundaries, at what point is the limit of the boundary established? Furthermore, even if both types of boundaries are proclaimed, if they do not encompass the entire area, all such cases are termed illegal.
Furthermore, it is "arising naturally. This means arising within the natural boundaries (*jātisīmā*). One should assemble according to the marked boundaries (*sīmālakṣaṇa*):
if the marked boundaries are wide, one should assemble according to the marked boundaries; if the natural boundaries are wide, one should assemble according to the natural boundaries.

There is no [mention of] "lower" in the Vinaya, because the Vinaya contains no method for binding a great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) by universal enclosure. However, regarding the procedure for assembly, at the time of performing the ritual, one must certainly recite it accordingly. Therefore...
This is merely a specific instance of that one method. The commentary states: "It is no different from the procedure for first establishing the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*).
According to the *Daochao*, it says: "Only the single character 'nei' (inner) is added. It reads: "The Saṃgha now establishes a great boundary within and without these four sides.
However, according to the Vinaya text itself, this character is not added; it simply says: "Within these four sides, establish [the boundary]."
Regarding the Great Boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), it is also logically permissible to establish it according to one’s own inclination;

generally speaking, there is no hindrance. As for "medicine and disease": medicine corresponds to the superior teaching, while disease corresponds to the superior capacity [of the practitioner]. Since the teaching arises from the capacity, medicine is prescribed as a remedy for disease.

Because the emotional views of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) involve the conglomeration of diverse categories, the Sage specifically opened this allowance. Thus, those who are like-minded in accordance with the Dharma may perform the formal act of demarcation (*sīmā-bandha*) in a single location.
The *dhātu*. These three dharmas were enacted at Kauśāmbī.
They had been engaged in strife for a long time, for twenty years, and did not perform the *poṣadha* together. "Matter" (*vastu*) refers to the matter of dispute;

Seeing that this is merely a temporary obstruction of the Dharma— whereby one may either come but not sit, or sit and then leave because of a reprimand— and fearing that it might result in a schism within the Saṃgha,
the tying [of the robe] is permitted.
"Without having left the boundary" means that one has departed from that *dharmakṣetra* (Dharma-realm). Regarding "the lower path":

this refers to cases where there is no common teacher (*sārdhavihārin*) or where those on the lower path each gather in one place to establish a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*) for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), etc., at separate locations. As for "different locations," the Vinaya states:

"If it is not possible to assemble together, one may move to a different location according to one's own teachers or close associates and establish a small boundary there for the invitation (*pravāraṇā*). Although this is a "lower" case, it is because within one's own school...
It merely mentions the wilderness outside the boundary (*sīmā*), but does not say it is within the natural boundary (*prakṛtistha-sīmā*).

Now, according to the text, since it speaks of "moving to another place" and "below the path," one should know that this refers precisely to the natural boundary. This is indeed an authentic passage. It says "below the path."

The text speaks of traveling on a road; this refers to the single boundary of the "Road-Traveling" (mārga-gamana) [monastery]. It is also said that the "lower road" (adhva-mārga) refers to an araṇya (wilderness).

Since the text states it is a desolate wilderness without a village, if one is traveling on a road, one may follow the standard of six hundred paces (*krośa*) as prescribed in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya).
Alternatively, if one is in an araṇya, one may follow the standard of seven *paṭa* (bow-lengths) as prescribed in the *Samantapāsādikā*; there is no need for the five-li (*li*) measurement.

There are those who claim that this rule concerns the place where people are gathered for sitting; this reasoning is incorrect. This is because the Vinaya text specifies "having completed the formal act (karmavācanā) regarding the boundary," and does not refer to the time when people are being gathered.
If that were the case, there would be difficulties regarding forest hermitages (*araṇya*) where there is no sufficient number of monks to convene a formal assembly.

Furthermore, since the Vinaya below states "not yet having exited the boundary," it clearly indicates that one has not yet entered one's own natural boundary (*prakṛti-sīmā*). As for the common practice...
Five *li* equal seven *paṇḍa*. One *paṇḍa* is twenty-eight *zhǔ*. Calculated, this totals one hundred and ninety-six *zhǔ*.

Since each *zhǔ* is eighteen *chǐ*, the total is fifty-eight paces and four feet eight inches. Regarding the phrase "outside of that" (*bǐ xià bǐ yún*), it means that if there is disagreement, one may perform ritual acts outside [the boundary];
this is the meaning of "crossing the boundary" as set forth in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. The intent is the same as above.
Furthermore, there are no two assemblies; there is no second gathering, because this reveals that it is a single session of the Dharma.

They do not mingle and do not arrive together, for that which is not in harmony cannot be fashioned into the assembly. From "it clarifies" below, the seated body of the bhikṣu is used as the standard.

The boundary markers constitute the *lakṣaṇa* (characteristics). That which is situated within the boundary is the *śarīra* (substance); this is the fourth section of the General Gate (*sāmānya-mukha*). Therefore, it is specifically distinguished as "the fourth within the General Gate.
Regarding the statement that the method of dissolution (*vimocana*) is not analogous to that of the formal act of binding (*bandhana*):

at the time of binding, it is said, "The bhikṣus of this residence proclaim the characteristics of the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) in the four directions," and further, "Within the boundaries of the four directions, one binds the great boundary," and so forth. However, at the time of dissolution, [such statements] do not exist.
This text merely cites two similarities to provide an explanation. Furthermore, the former person ties the vertical aspects together, while the latter person unties the horizontal aspects;
these do not resemble the three cases where the person who ties is the same as the person who unties, such that the person and the position correspond, and the person is seated in the same place.

The location is within the body. The person who performs the binding [of the boundary] is the one who releases it. As for "other people," this refers to those who are not later-arriving bhikṣus; this is the fifth gate.
The meaning is that it specifically belongs to this gate, though the literal phrasing may differ. Regarding the presence or absence of obstacles:

because the Great Boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) is free from obstacles, it is broad, and its markers (*lakṣaṇa*) are established so as to remain firm for a long time. The Small Boundary (*khuḍḍaka-sīmā*) has obstacles; conversely, it is not established in the manner described above. Thus, we know it is established.

This is not for nothing. Regarding the contradiction between the Dharma and the ritual procedure: since the ritual procedure involves difficult conditions, if one were now to establish a formal characteristic that makes it lax and leisurely, then the procedure would not accord with the Dharma;
therefore, it is said that [the rite] is not accomplished.

To monopolize authority and establish small boundaries (*kṣudrasīmā*) for the sake of having no formal conditions (*anālambana*), while exclusively practicing the opening of permissions (*anujñā*), is a direct violation of the teachings. As illustrated by the following examples:

if there is a difficulty and one wishes to go outside the boundary, permission should be granted according to the monastic rules (*saṃghadharma*); conversely, if there is no difficulty, it is not granted. Regarding "frugality" (*durbhikṣa*):

this refers to the eight practices such as "storing within" (*antarvasati*) and "cooking within" (*antarpāka*), which are permitted only during times of scarcity; conversely, when it is not a time of scarcity, they are likewise not permitted.

It is not permitted [to be separated from one's robes]. Regarding "being separated from one's robes": if one is separated from one's robes because the road is cut off and cannot return to the assembly, only then is it permitted.

There are nine [cases], etc.: the superior, middling, and inferior faculties each have three categories, thus forming nine. Although they are inferior, they establish the conditions for the superior permission.
Both are "crooked coverings. *Jin* (矜) means "to boast of one's own excellence. This refers to ordinary people who, failing to conform to the words of the Sages, arbitrarily open up their own paths.

The section on the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* below serves as proof for the preceding established doctrine, as it applies to all four modes of conduct. The section on "ironing" (*niwen*) below states that this is the point where questions are raised as prohibitions.

"Pointing toward the directions" indicates that one points outward from the body to designate the boundaries as the characteristic marks. "Reciting the binding" means reciting the eight *karmavācanās* to complete the formation [of the boundary].
Regarding the meaning below: "Now one should quickly dismiss them," because one fears that evil bhikṣus might arrive.
"Reversing the above" refers to reversing the four aforementioned [correct actions] to constitute the four non-correct [actions].
Below the text [of the *Vinaya-mātṛkā*], the *Vinaya* states that questioning and challenging outside the boundary (*sīmā*) is not valid; this makes it clear that one must be within the boundary.

Now, since there are no external signs, how can there be questioning and challenging? "Yinjian" (殷鑒) means profound and thorough examination; it has the same meaning as "broad observation. "Bingzhi" (冰執) refers to emotional views.

"Kaijian naqu" (開間納取) means to admit and receive; here, it refers to admitting a śrāmaṇera. The *Dàcǎo* (Great Commentary) says: "Ten people sit together in a cluster and first perform the formal act of binding [the boundary]. It is sufficient.

To establish the portion for one person, half of the body must extend beyond the boundary; this is also based on the texts of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Samantapāsādikā*, which suffice to complete the number of the Saṃgha.

Regarding the initial binding and the formal binding, these last for three hours. If someone comes to criticize [the boundary] during that time, this binding is not established, as it is identical to a naturally existing boundary. (Ancient Record)

That is to say: if the boundary has not yet been formally declared, all share one and the same natural field (*prakṛti-sīmā*). If one touches [food] with an evil mind, it is as if one were touching pure food with an evil mind;
thus, the act of touching is not established. Now, if one relies upon my own bodily field with an evil mind, it does not constitute a separate censure.

Now, regarding the "lowering" (*adhaḥ*): at the time of the formal binding (*bandhana*), as well as during the three subsequent actions performed after the binding, those who lean against [the boundary] all become established [within it].
Regarding the "lowering," because it reveals the absence of external characteristics, the prior "closing" (*pūrva-nirodha*) refutes the initial binding as being unestablished;

the subsequent "opening" (*paścāt-vivaraṇa*) refutes the ancient view that even if one rebukes [the violators] after the boundary has been bound, it remains unestablished. This is because there are no such words regarding "prior closing and subsequent opening" in the Vinaya. As for the "lowering," it is as previously stated.

Commentary: Regarding the one allowance and one prohibition, there is no need for further elaboration on the subsequent binding. Concerning the initial binding of the body, it is identical to the natural boundary (*dharmatā-sīmā*).

This is simply to ensure that both the beginning and the end serve the purpose of preventing those who would criticize [the community]. Furthermore, at the time of the initial binding, because no external markers are established outside the body, there is no room for those who would criticize;
thus, the text below cites the Vinaya precepts as proof. It speaks of "virtuous bhikṣus" and also makes manifest the "evil bhikṣus."
Although one may lean against a boundary marker, this does not constitute a formal objection (*khaṇḍana*). Question:

If it does not constitute an objection when referring to the time of the preliminary assembly, why does the Vinaya text state that one should not perform the formal binding while those who do not consent have not yet left the boundary, but rather do so "quickly"? Answer: This refers to the intent of strict prevention during the time of the assembly.
As for the actual moment of the formal binding, even if one leans against a boundary marker, because the person is an evil bhikṣu, the two parties do not [interfere with] each other.
[Included] in the *Daichao* (Great Commentary): "The single category of 'separate assembly' (*biezong*) only involves twisting [the cord] into one color of purity.

Furthermore, because there are no external signs at the time of the formal binding, the Great Boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) is used. This means: why use the Great Boundary? It refers to the single teaching that permits [this practice] on specific occasions.
This teaching is not intended to facilitate a collective assembly.

Because prior conditions constitute an obstacle, one opens the reception of precepts by relying on the conditions of the *prasāra* (the invitation for confession). Regarding the site and boundaries (*sīmā*), if there is no obstacle, it is logically necessary to establish the site and boundaries according to the original [rules].
As for the statement that "many people are of no benefit," this means that if the performance of the rite does not accord with the teaching, it will cause many [problems].

A person will not obtain the benefit of the precepts; since the precepts are not complete, there is no basis for practice. Practice exists by following the essence of the precepts. "The four 'is'" refers to the aforementioned four:
knowing that there is no difference from the external, and so forth. "The four 'is-not'" refers to these four: this is not [the case] regarding the opening of conditions, and so forth.

This is a conjecture. It is said that the *karmavācanā* (ritual formulas) were produced in antiquity; their measure was not understood. What is practiced today is intended to reveal that what is improper to perform should be kept hidden.
To write them all down in one sequence is unsatisfactory; it is merely to suit the capacities of those living in this age. This refers to the following section.
The meaning is this: nowadays, those who are negligent regarding the Dharma are many.

Even when a *sīmā* (precept field) or *mahāsīmā* (great boundary) has been established, those wishing to perform formal rituals must still issue invitations and extend formal requests before [the monks] will deign to attend. How could there be anyone coming to create obstacles? Therefore, it is useless to go out [to invite them].
If this is so, one understands the concise intent of our current school. [Question: But what if there should happen to be such people? One must certainly...

This is extended [to other cases] below. It should be recited according to the precedent; following the Vinaya, this extension is self-evident. Fearing that later students may not have seen it, I shall now provide a detailed citation.

The Vinaya says: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen! Now there are so many bhikṣus assembled. If the time has come for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, I announce that we shall establish a small boundary (kṣudrasīmā).
Thus is the motion (jñapti). (The formal ritual procedure, *karmavācanā*, may be inferred accordingly.)
Regarding the monastery compound (*ārāma*) and its surroundings:

if the boundary established for the gathering of the Saṃgha is coextensive with the compound, or if the boundary is narrow while the compound walls are wide, these two cases do not require the establishment of a separate "robe-holding boundary" (*cīvarasaṃvartana*). Below this refers to the natural robe-holding boundary.

It arises based on the walls of the monastery compound (*ārāma*). However, outside the four surrounding boundaries, there remains an additional area of thirteen paces as a zone of influence (*pradeśa*).

If one were to establish a robe-boundary (*cīvarasīmā*) [without accounting for this], it would conversely make the boundary too narrow and, moreover, devoid of its zone of influence; that is to say, because a formal rule exists, [the boundary] does not [otherwise] exist.
Or, [if the boundary were established] below the compound wall, this would demonstrate that the boundary lies within the zone of influence, which conversely makes the robe-boundary even smaller.

Regarding "losing one's robes for the entire summer": this refers to those who have fully observed the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) by means of dwelling within a defined boundary (*sīmā*), yet still lose their robes.

This is because the natural robe-boundary (*prakṛtisīmā*) extends only as far as the monastery grounds (*ārāma*). Thus, if one goes outside the grounds, even if one is said to be "within the boundary," one cannot avoid losing one's robes.

Now, if one establishes the robe-boundary so that it encompasses the monastic community boundary (*saṃghasīmā*), then both the protection of the *varṣā* and the protection of the robes will be complete.
Therefore it is said: "In summer, one may be separated from one's robes for two assemblies.

As explained below in the context of the *dhūta* bhikṣu who, weary of worldly pleasures, dwells in forest hermitages or caves—the Buddha permitted such a person to establish a boundary for not losing one's robes (*akṣaya-cīvara-sīmā*).

Regarding the phrase "from beyond walls, fences, or hedges" in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, this clarifies that the person comes from outside the hedge and reaches the very edge of the boundary. The rule concerning the five robes is stated with reference to nuns.

There is a lower [view]. This master [argues] that since there currently exists a village, it may be mentioned and excluded; however, if there were none, there would be no need to mention and exclude it.

As stated below, he cites the Vinaya as proof for this: it is a case where the substance (the object) is absent but the rule (the dharma) remains—just like having medicine when there is no illness, which is merely a false application.
"Presently removed" (*pratyutpanna-niṣkāsana*): when a village currently exists within the boundary, one may not maintain the robe within that village.

Once it has been suspended and the village is no longer bound, one may no longer maintain the robe at this location; therefore, it is said that "if the village is subsequently moved out, it is improper to retain the robe.

"Below, there is no village" (*nirgrāma*) means that currently there is no village. "Presently bound" (*pratyutpanna-bandhana*) refers to the formal establishment of the robe-boundary in the present state. "Suspended removal of the village" (*niṣkāsita-grāma*).

If one arrives later, one must not maintain the protection of the robes within the robe-boundary (cīvara-sīmā). However, once the village has departed from this place, it is again possible to maintain the protection of the robes;
therefore, it is said: "When the village departs, [the boundary] returns."

The robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*) is thereby dissolved. This specifically refutes the previous [view] that it does not encompass the village from which one has come; thus, the robe-boundary naturally dissolves.

If the robe-boundary were not all-pervasive, this would refute the previous [view] that it excludes what is suspended and is not formally established. If, after leaving the village, one were not permitted to carry the robe with oneself, then it would be established as being within the boundary markers (*cihna*).

Thus, the robe-boundary would not be all-pervasive; how much less so when the robe-boundary is coextensive with the monastic boundary (*saṃgha-sīmā*), whereas the previous [view] held that it pervades the boundary markers?
Because it arises internally, this merely clarifies the current meaning regarding that which is situated below the village;

it does not say "excluding the village," thereby indicating that this pertains to the entire garment-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*). This is because the Vinaya first establishes the garment-boundary such that the village is included within the boundary for the purpose of keeping garments.

Later, due to obstructing conditions—specifically, because a bhikṣu had deposited his garment in the village and encountered obstacles when going to retrieve it—it was subsequently prohibited that one may not [do so] within the village.
One puts on one's robes; therefore, it is said that "only then does one leave the village. This indicates the removal of obstacles, not the removal of the village itself.
Later, when descending [from a height], this same principle is applied. If the village is present and one cannot [leave], this refers to the removal of obstacles.

Once the village has departed and the robes have been gathered, there is no longer any hindrance to protecting the robes, because at the time of the formal binding (*saṃvara*), the boundary was established within the designated markers.
They share the same ground, as they arise together with the boundary of the Saṃgha. This differs from the ancients who excluded the empty space within;

what is meant here by "excluding" refers only to excluding obstacles within the boundary. How could it mean that, since there was originally no village within the current monastery, one need not formally record its exclusion?

If a village were to arrive later, one would have to perform the ritual procedure again—would this not be cumbersome and redundant? Furthermore, below... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)

At present, the exclusion of villages (*gāma-pariccheda*) is not formally recited; however, when a village subsequently enters the boundary, one might then claim that the protection of the robe (*cīvara-rakṣā*) applies within the village.

For this reason, it is necessary to recite the exclusion of villages in advance. As illustrated by the following example: if the boundary is established on the first day of the month, and two [villages] are formally recited at that time, can it be said that the *Poṣadha* ceremony is likewise being performed?
It must also await a later occasion; therefore, it is recited beforehand. This is the case for the robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*).
It is the same here as well. Since the initial formulation of the rule already specifies the exclusion of villages, the subsequent formulations follow suit.

Question: Both [formulations] contain two meanings and both inquire about the presence of a formal act (*saṃghāṭi-bandhana*). Regarding the method for taking up robes (*cīvara-parigraha*) and the method for the absence of a formal act, they are identical in that the village comes to obstruct the robe.

Why is it necessary, within the rules for formal demarcation (*sīmā-bandha*), to include the phrase "excluding villages" as an example, whether a village is present or not? Thus, the intent of both questions is: why must the exclusion be included?
In the response, the terms "internal" and "external" are inverted; they should properly read "the area outside the courtyard and inside the boundary.

As for the unavoidable loss of robes, this is because the defining characteristics (*nimitta*) of inclusion for the *saṃgha-sīmā* located outside the monastery grounds are weak, whereas the defining characteristics of inclusion for boundaries such as those of carts and trees are strong. [The formal] demarcation...

Once the robes have been gathered, the various boundaries naturally cease; however, it is said that "only the village boundary does not cease. This is stated because there is concern that the village boundary might also cease, and thus it is clarified that they are both worn and removed.
As for the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* (the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā*), it is not fixed: sometimes [the boundary] exists and sometimes it does not, or it may be more or less scattered.
Regarding "slander," it arises because taking the robe from where it was deposited in the village invites censure. Regarding "contention," it is caused by going to the village.
There may be disputes between husband and wife, as well as disputes over the seeking of clothing; therefore, the holy life (*brahmacarya*) is pure conduct.

Because of suspicion and doubt—suspicion leads to disrespect and doubt to the fear that it is contrary to the Dharma—one remains dispassionate. This is not for the sake of guarding the men and women of the village.

The last two lines of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* refer to the village and its surrounding territory (*sīmā*). Regarding the demarcation of open space and dwellings, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* permits their preliminary demarcation.

As for the clothing boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*), it is not established below [the village]. Although it is said that there is "preliminary demarcation," because the village is present, one cannot include the robes within the boundary;

the principle is the same as "not being established," which means there is no pervasion. The passage from the *Sammohavinodanī* below serves as proof for the surrounding territory. "Person" here refers to the finger-measure (*vitasti*).
Regarding "ancient masters": "present exclusion" refers to existing villages; "exclusion" refers to robes that cannot be protected.

"Hanging and binding" means tying off the area of open space and the dwelling site. Once the village has moved out later, it is no longer necessary to bind [the area], because it was already bound by the hanging method.

In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya), the lower section states that the ancient masters say the *Dharmaguptaka* simply says "excluding the village," and outside the village there is no need to bind.

Therefore, the following section refutes this as not being the correct interpretation, for how could the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* ever have failed to state that when one has left the village to fold up one's robes (*cīvara*), one is immediately considered to be within the village boundary and its surrounding area?

It clarifies that there is a formal notice (*sūcaka*) posted; this refers to the removal by means of such a hanging notice. Once the village has moved away, one may place robes there as soon as they are obtained; however, while the village remains, it constitutes an obstruction which must be removed.

Some versions omit the character "notice" (*sūcaka*) under the phrase "it clarifies that there is something. Regarding "the area outside the monastery grounds" (*saṃghārāma-bahirdhā*): this refers to the area outside the *ārāma*.

[The text] says: "The Sangha descends. This proves that the boundary of the monastery (vihāra) is narrow while the boundary of the settlement (sīmā) is wide; one must therefore demarcate the "Eye-Opening Forest" (*Kāṇabhañjana-vana*), so that one may cast one's gaze about freely.
[The text] states "residing together," which refers to a shared dwelling place. Since there is already a village, one cannot maintain the "robe-protection" (*cīvara-rakṣaṇa*) within the village;

it should not be considered "residing together. How then can it be recorded as such? [The answer] says: This means the robe-boundary arises from above the monastic boundary. Since the monastic boundary...

rather, it is said that they do not necessarily agree with one another, not that they are never permitted to stay. Why are these two cited separately? Or, as stated below:

since the original robe-boundary (*cīvarasīmā*) universally encompasses the monastic community boundary (*saṃghasīmā*), "dwelling together" is cited; however, because the village acts as an obstacle creating a temporary separation, "excluding the village" is cited. There are two [points] regarding this.
This means that previously it was non-pervasive with respect to the substance (*vastu*), whereas now it is non-pervasive with respect to the conditions (*pratyaya*).

For a person who obstructs [the ceremony] by remaining outside after the formal act of binding (*bandhana*) is completed, there is the offense of staying overnight together [with the Sangha]. this is the boundary for gathering the Sangha and gathering the robes (*cīvara*). The subsequent section below distinguishes the abolition of both types of pervasiveness; [it concerns] the village...
The phrase "in a forest hermitage" (araṇya) generally establishes the boundary for the robe-holding zone (*cīvarasaṃvāsa-sīmā*).

Since it specifies the exclusion of villages, it is clear that within a settlement (*grāma*), the monastic boundary (*sīmā*) is also permitted to be established as a robe-holding zone. Because this is permitted, it is not invalidated.
A small village refers to the boundary of a hamlet (*grāma*). Although it was initially small, if the number of men and women later increases, the village becomes progressively larger;

Conversely, if it was initially large and later becomes small, the area previously excluded from the boundary may again serve as a place for protecting one's robes.
This is established according to the principle that the lower [case] determines the meaning of the upper [case]. In terms of the specific conditions, this refers to the village itself.
The text states "there is no bridge. This means that for those who remove the swift current, there is simply no bridge. Furthermore, if there were a bridge, the principle would still permit it;

this is analogous to the *saṃgha-sīmā* (monastic boundary), which allows for exceptions when there are bridges or boats. Regarding the "lower ground," this refers to the area where men and women reside on the lower ground, which is within the village.
Alternatively, "lower" may refer to the interior fields and villages; once one has departed from them, one may then carry one's robes with oneself. Thus...
Because it was previously suspended by means of a formal act (*karmavācanā*).

Regarding "the boundary of the settlement and the open space": that which currently exists as a village is called the "settlement" (*grāma*); the area surrounding the village is called the "open space" (*śūnya*).

Ancient masters claimed that since the Vinaya only mentions the exclusion of the village and does not state that the *cīvara-sīmā* (robe-boundary) remains after the village has departed, [this section] below serves to refute that view.

As stated above, it is as previously mentioned: when one returns from one's own village, the robes remain within the robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*) and are thus still encompassed. This serves as proof that the name is the same for the section on "Improper Time" (*akāla*).

For among the ninety rules, there is the precept against entering a village at an improper time; in the *Śarīpura-vinaya-śikṣā-samuccaya*, the enumeration of the conditions states: "going toward the house of a layperson."

He further provides his own commentary, stating: "This refers to the courtyards of the pure households within the monastery. This proves that 'excluding villages' here means excluding those places where men and women reside within the monastery grounds;

Furthermore, regarding "families that eat together" (*śālā-bhojana*) and so forth, as for the specific mention of "families that eat together," the Vinaya itself explains: "There are men and women.

Is this not the same as "staying overnight," "sitting in a secluded place," or "sitting in the open"? All of these refer to the dwelling places of men and women; one should know that these are also what constitute a "village" (*grāma*).
This applies whether there are only men and women, or only women without men, and so on.
In the *Shanjian* (Sudarsana), it states: "Since it says 'the monks have not lost the robe-boundary,' this indicates that there are monks outside the robe-boundary;
one cannot therefore claim that [the robe] has a specific owner. The defining characteristics (*nimitta*) are limited solely by the presence of a village and the words of the donor;
