and thus both the ignorant and the wise will understand simultaneously. Regarding the changing of names: for example, if one asks, "Are you a person of the Great Way? there is no formal adjudication (*vinīta*).

There is no textual authority stating that one does not obtain the precepts if this is not asked; thus, there is no harm. This is like the case of a debtor; this principle exists naturally within our own tradition.

Regarding the meaning of "returning": how could it be said that this obstructs the precepts? From this point downward, excluding what has already been explained in response to specific difficulties, the term "the rest" (*śeṣa*) is used. However, this refers to the essential points;
one must be skilled in questioning and answering. Otherwise, it does not constitute a question.

Regarding the conditions for the precepts: these are the primary conditions for the arising of the precepts. As for the names of the teacher and the disciple—namely, the name of the *upādhyāya* together with one’s own name—and the fact that one is a man (*puruṣa*):
these three factors must not be lacking. This is because the teacher is that upon whom one relies for the remainder of one’s life;

"self" refers to the recipient of the formal reception; and being a "man" means possessing the moral integrity required to receive them. To act contrary to this is improper. Any addition to or subtraction from these is [unacceptable].
As the *Gāthā-śāstra* states: "One who is deaf yet hears the sound of the *karmavācanā* may receive the fivefold [ordination].
Or, if one previously harbored mutual resentment and creates obstacles by means of some minor pretext, it is a *duṣkṛta*."

As stated in the *Jikishō* (Commentary on the Essentials), this refers specifically to the section within the "Chapter on Receiving Precepts" titled "The Single Gate of Teaching the Conditions for Generating the Precepts. There was a master [cited here] whose origins remain unknown.
The *Daishō* (Great Commentary) also states: "Each is discussed according to its respective object. The *Bekishō* (Separate Commentary) should consist of more than thirty sheets of paper;

to summarize, it does not go beyond the categories of sentient and non-sentient beings, the two truths of emptiness and existence, the principle of cessation (*nirodha*), and the Nirvana taught by the Buddha as the holy.

The teachings, written scrolls, physical images, stupas, and temples, as well as earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness—all that is measured by the *dharmadhātu*—are collectively the substance of the precepts (*śīlaskandha*).
This is the same as stated below, where it says: "A single elder monk serves as a substitute for the Tathāgata.
If one can thus provide guidance so that people may obtain the precepts and advance toward liberation, how could there be any difference [between such a teacher and the Buddha]?

"Great resolve" refers to the superior grade of mind. This means: "I now generate the aspiration and receive the precepts in order to fulfill the three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*), to enter the three gates of liberation, and to rightly seek the fruit of *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, by means of this Dharma, I shall guide sentient beings, leading them to *nirvāṇa* and ensuring that the True Dharma endures for a long time.
Even such a generation of the mind is still a false conception; how much more so for one who does not generate it at all? It is certain.
Because there is no one to be honored [as a superior], it is said that concentration is difficult to accommodate. As stated in the *Sukṣiṇa-śīla-sūtra* (The Sūtra on Good Precepts), it says:
"What is called precept? It refers to the precepts of the seven assemblies: bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to receive and uphold the bodhisattva precepts must first purify [themselves]."
The mind receives the precepts of the seven classes of followers. These precepts of the seven classes are precisely the purification of the mind that leads toward the bodhisattva precepts.
It is like a person of the world who wishes to invite a great king: they must first thoroughly clean and prepare their residence and so forth.

Later, when the time arrives for receiving the Dharma—specifically at this moment—the instruction and the formal reception are brief and cannot be expanded upon; it is essential that one first [prepare].
The instructions and commands open the treasury of the mind. Thus, the *Daichao* states: "One must receive [the transmission] beforehand;

the wise teacher provides instruction so that the mind continues in succession, seeing the objective realm as clear and pure. One must not wait until the last moment to speak of generating the resolve (*bodhicitta*). If it were granted by a teacher at the last moment," [it would be ineffective].

Since the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are themselves inherently empty and insubstantial, how could they cause the recipient to attain a superior grade of mind? One should simply rely fully upon the text;
that is, rely upon this very commentary. "Other paths" refers to the sentient beings of the six realms of existence;

for the most part, these constitute obstacles to the precepts, leading one to loathe the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*) and seek transcendence. "Retribution" refers to one's own body and mind.

Regarding the four inquiries: the motion (*jñapti*) and the three formal acts (*karmavācanā*) each involve a question and an answer. As for the citations from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* mentioned in the commentary:
one should first ask, "For what reason does this motion state, 'Do not be distracted by other thoughts, other reflections, or other matters'?
If it is not so stated, one should reconcile the text accordingly. This concludes the formal act; it is now summarized within the [following] section.
The character *jing* (concluded) is precisely this. It signifies the completion of the foundation of the precepts. Thus, the *Dacào* states: "Having finished the third proclamation, one says:
'The Sangha has consented; the matter for [Name] is concluded. At this moment, the *karmavācanā* is finished. Following the section below, this is explained by citing the notes:
because it is necessary to distinguish the time and the seating order within the *ṣaḍ-anusmṛti* (six recollections), one must clearly record this.
"Someone descends": this refers to the completion of the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*. "Kṣaṇa" (moment): this refers to the first moment. "The Vinaya Master descends":
this refers to reaching the point where it is said, "Whoever does not approve," at which point it is finished. "Now": the Great Master’s logical adjudication. "Two times":
namely, the first and second *karmavācanā* (formal acts). "Next, the third": in comparison with what precedes, this appears to be the conclusion. "Citing what follows": namely, the third...

Regarding the three *karmas*: when the words are being recited, the preceding matter may be accomplished. This is like saying, "How could the dharma not be established beforehand? Therefore, below [the section on] the assembly:

if the assembly does not speak, it constitutes acceptance through silence; if one can state that it is not accepted, then it constitutes a protest (*pratikṣepa*). This principle can be universally applied.
Only upon reaching the final conclusion (*nigamana*) is the definitive meaning established. If this is so, it likewise does not contradict the wisdom [of the Vinaya].

Commentary: "The *karmavācanā* is completed; I have finished conferring the precepts upon you. This is the text from the upper scroll, specifically within the section on establishing the boundary (*sīmābandha*).
Thus, up to the character "completed" (*jing*), it serves as a concluding mark for what precedes it; this meaning is certain.

All of this occurs simultaneously within the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). Upon hearing the *jñapti* (announcement) for the absolution of offenses, one understands that the transgression occurred when [the speaker] was awake;
subsequently, because one fell asleep and did not perceive it, one understands that the state is pure when [the speaker] was unaware.

According to the following case, since he was already asleep after hearing the *jñapti* and yet still attained absolution from the offense, it is evident that in the present case, having heard the *jñapti* and then fallen asleep, one should likewise attain the precept. In the present instance, neither of these occurs; rather, it refers to the three *karmavācanās* (formal proclamations).

If both do not perform [the formal act], they should still be subject to the transgression regarding the precepts. This is because it is already known that the *jñapti* (motion) has been made during the announcement. The answer below refers to the śrāmaṇera;

although he has entered into a state of moral neutrality (*avyākṛta*), this does not prevent him from performing the *jñapti*, which is the foundation for the harmony of the Saṃgha, as it is understood by the entire assembly.
When the subsequent *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is performed, the intent of the instruction becomes complete; thus, the conditions are not discordant.

If it is not performed, it is not accomplished—this is illustrated by the example of a person descending [into a pit]. As for the prior matter, there is no offense; that is, one does not commit the fundamental offense of killing.

Since the determination of the offense within the precept against killing is thus, the "receiving" [of the precept] is likewise not a result [in itself]; it is established through conditions, being accomplished by means of various contributing factors. The preceding mind is distinct [from the subsequent].

When one performs [an action], the mind that was previously clear and lucid differs from the deluded and confused mind at the time of the subsequent performance; thus, it does not constitute the fundamental basis [of the karma]. Therefore, it is said that there is no [inherent] karma.

It is only through the conjunction of conditions that a response is evoked. Although one has entered a state of non-defined (avyākṛta) consciousness, because one relies on the conditions of another's defined (vyākṛta) consciousness, one is able to give rise to the precepts.
If one does not sit [to commit the act] as instructed, then the person so instructed is not guilty of the offense of killing or stealing.

"Below" refers to the case where the person instructed gives rise to a deranged mind. "If below" means that at the time of instruction, the mind was clear and conscious, and when the person instructed reached the location and committed the killing or stealing...
This [act] can cause the instructor to go mad. Among the three natures, the instructor incurs the sin of killing; therefore it is said:

"Provided that the original intent is fulfilled, the instructor incurs non-informative karma (*avijñapti*). Now, the following provides examples. "Requesting from the Sangha" exemplifies the clarity of mind at the initial moment.

"The Sangha acceding to his request" exemplifies the instructed act. Although the requester enters a state of neutral (*avyākṛta*) consciousness, what is received is nonetheless not [neutral]. Therefore...
Based on the clarity of the mind regarding what has been received, one generates the precepts within the recipient's neutral (*avyākṛta*) state of mind.

If it were according to the previous example, then the recipient would become insane upon the arising of the instruction. Even if the prior conditions are incomplete—such as the number of monks being insufficient or the boundaries (*sīmā*) being indistinct—one should still be considered to have received the precepts;
this is simply because the recipient possesses a conscious mind. Thus, in the latter case, one merely takes up the capacity [to receive].

The instruction regarding the arising of insanity applies equally to those who lack half [of their faculties], as does the textual passage concerning the induction of the precepts. The first half of that passage specifically concerns the instruction for one whose insanity arises;

this refers to the text of the first half. Now, as for the category of those instructed who are capable of receiving [the precepts]: although it is said that they receive them with a conscious mind, [it is so].

If one is without the intent (*citta*), one does not obtain the precept. In the first half [of the teaching], although the recipient lacks intent, the teacher also incurs a grave offense because the conditions for receiving [the precept] are complete.
If the conditions are lacking, the subsequent precept is not generated. Killing and stealing are defined by the impairment of the object;
since the object is impaired, an offense is necessarily incurred. Therefore, it is said that this is not the same as the first half of the teaching.

This extends even to the arousal of karma—that is, from the initial moment of generating the aspiration, prostrating to the Sangha, joining the palms and requesting the precepts, up until the conclusion of the *karmavācanā*.
If, during this interval, unwholesome thoughts suddenly arise, they take advantage of the preceding wholesome states to be accomplished within an unwholesome mind.

"Teaching the performance" refers to instructing them in their petitions and so forth; it does not mean that the attainment [of the precepts] occurs while one is exclusively in an unwholesome state of mind.
It is attained because, in all cases, it is preceded by the arousal of a wholesome mind. The same applies to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and mindless (*acittaka*) states.
Together with the preceding [wholesome] state, there are thus four types of mind in total.

Answer: Even if the formal boundary (sīmā) is not formally established, the summer retreat (varṣa) is still accomplished. This is like the cases where forgetting [the rules] results in accomplishment, or where one attains the boundary and accomplishes prior seating, and so forth.

Furthermore, the undertaking (*samādāna*) is directed toward the infinite dharmas that are like grains of sand; because the vow is to be universally applied, it is thus. Moreover, the time limit is for the duration of one’s life;

therefore, the vow arises immediately upon the conclusion of the three *karmavācanās*. Regarding the summer retreat (*anujñā*), since there are both earlier and later periods of seating, the days must be reckoned until the period is fulfilled.

When [the period] is complete, it constitutes the summer retreat (*varṣā*). It is extremely numerous; because the objects are many, the characteristics of the precepts (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*) are also numerous. Regarding the mind:

those associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are common to both tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) minds, whereas those associated with the Path (*mārga*) are exclusively untainted minds.
"From conditions" refers to the myriad objects as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Since these conditioned objects are all-pervasive, the precepts are likewise equal;
they are immeasurable and equal, encompassing the boundless great earth, and thus the precepts are also boundless. Grasses and trees are immeasurable, and the precepts are likewise immeasurable.

Just as the void and the great ocean are vast, so too are the height and depth of the virtue of the precepts. Using this text as proof, the principle extends throughout the entire Dharma-realm. Now, [the text] proceeds to... *nirvāṇa*.
Baoyun said: "There are two kinds of precepts: first, the precept of action (*karmapatha*); second, the precept of non-action (*avijñapti*). This follows the meaning of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
As for the threefold [classification], why not further establish 'action' and 'non-action' as separate categories to constitute the three? [The opponent asks: "What is the characteristic [of these]?"
The provisional (vijñapti) arises from the provisional; it is called provisional because it prolongs one form.

Regarding a single moment, the Sarvāstivādins say that in the first moment of matter there is bodily and vocal intimation (*vijñapti*), while in the second moment there is only non-intimation (*avijñapti*), which is attained as something never before obtained.
This means that since beginningless time, one has never before attained this pure and white dharma (*śukla-dharma*); because it can now be attained in every moment of thought, it is "short.

[The following passage is missing from the text. It should read: "Because it acts as a defense against wrongdoing, it is 'short'; because it is non-action (*avijñapti*) which defends against wrongdoing, it is 'long.

As for the arising of non-action, there is no point from which it originates; I have grave doubts about this one sentence, as it is erroneous. The text is identical to what precedes it, as the previous section states: 'If it were merely non-..."

It is produced; it cannot arise spontaneously. These two dharmas—action (*kriyā*) and non-action (*akriyā*)—are accomplished through the power of the Path. Just as when the path that destroys the fetters [is attained], the essence of the precepts (*śīla-tattva*) arises instantaneously.

"Three combined. [The opponent asks: "If they constitute both 'action' (*vijñapti*) and 'non-action' (*avijñapti*), why are they not combined into a third category? This is a question regarding number; this is a question regarding combination. Their meanings are different.

The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) consists of only two types: because the substance of the precept as action consists of matter and mind, whereas the substance of the precept as non-action is neither matter nor mind.
Furthermore, there is a distinction between the names "action" and "non-action. Regarding the five phrases on loving-kindness and hatred, there is no third.
The *Ekottarika-āgama* of the Vinaya states: There are five types of speech that lack a third alternative. Regarding "timely" and "untimely," this phrase lacks a third.
Regarding "truth" and "untruth," this phrase lacks a third. Regarding "diminishing benefit" and "increasing benefit," this phrase lacks a third.
Regarding "harshness" and "gentleness," this phrase lacks a third. Regarding "anger" and "a mind of loving-kindness," this phrase lacks a third. These are the five.

"There is no third [alternative] among the categories" (as stated in the main text). This is because, as mentioned above, the two natures are distinct; thus, it does not apply universally to all objects and so forth. "As with a person," and so on:

extreme fragrance is a metaphor for virtuous precepts (*śīla*), while extreme stench is a metaphor for unvirtuous precepts. "At the moment of grasping" is a metaphor for the act of commissioning (*kṛta*). "Having let go."

The metaphor of having fragrance or a foul odor on one's hand illustrates non-informative action (*avijñapti*). Furthermore, receiving [an object] without a sincere mind is like a person holding an object that is neither fragrant nor foul-smelling.
The *Abhidharma-hṛdaya* states: "It is like a hand grasping a fragrant flower; even after it is discarded, the residual scent continues to arise."
This is not like grasping wood or stone; at that very moment of a single kṣaṇa, the active precept (*vijñapti*) has not yet fallen away, and the non-active precept (*avijñapti*) arises as well.
This is called the accomplishment of the fundamental wholesome karma for the realization of the Way. If it is the second kṣaṇa, there is only the non-active precept.

It is as follows. There is no conjunction of the three [factors]. Consider a potter’s wheel, a clay mold, or an object rotating on a cart. The body of the cart is a metaphor for the resultant form (*vipākavarṇa*);

its movement and turning are metaphors for the form of application (*prayogavarṇa*). Therefore, it is said: "the movement of the body and the application of the body. Regarding the movement of the body, the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* states:

"That which possesses informative intimation (*vijñapti*) is the movement of the body; the remaining consciousnesses are of the nature of the four or three minds. The *Hṛdaya-śāstra* further states: "As with feeling..."

Regarding the person of virtuous precepts (*śīlavat*), even when within states of mind that are unwholesome (*akuśala*) or neutral (*avyākṛta*), those [unmanifest actions] still persist in accordance with them;

this is what is meant. In the lower volume of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, he asks: "What dharma is called the cause of non-manifestation (*avijñapti-hetu*)? The passage beginning with "In the mind" is his response. He himself cites a sutra, saying:
"If one plants trees, gardens, or groves, or constructs wells, bridges, and the like, the merit produced by such a person increases day and night. There are two dharmas [involved].
It refers to the manifest and the unmanifest.
"Good and evil" refers to the precepts of the good restraint and the precepts of the evil restraint. First, the latter refers to the prohibition and severance of all unwholesome dharmas.
*Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*. In the third fascicle, the *Karmavarga*, the verse states: "One should know that bodily action (*kāyakarman*) is twofold:
namely, manifest (*vijñapti*) and non-manifest (*avijñapti*). Verbal action (*vākkarman*) is likewise. One should know that mental action (*manaskarman*) is volition (*cetanā*)" (end of verse).

The author himself explains this: "Bodily action is of two kinds: the nature of manifestation and the nature of non-manifestation. Manifestation is the movement of the body and the bodily expedient; non-manifestation is the cessation of the movement of the body."

It arises together with other consciousnesses; its nature follows accordingly. That is to say: when a wholesome mind—such as the undertaking of precepts—or a defiled (i.e., unwholesome) or neutral mind manifests, the wholesome precepts arise accordingly.
For one who possesses evil precepts (unwholesome discipline), when a wholesome or neutral mind manifests, the evil precepts arise accordingly.
It is the same for vocal karma. Vocal karma is of two kinds: its nature as manifest action (*vijñapti*) and non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) is as previously explained. Regarding mental karma...

Regarding "the knower of volition": mental action (*manas-karman*) is volition (*cetanā*). It possesses desire as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Now, it is not the case that mental action has non-manifestation (*avijñapti*) as its intrinsic nature;
for the mind is not of the nature of manifestation, nor is it material (*rūpa*), and because there are three types [of action].

Non-manifestation is also called "non-delight," also called "detachment," also called "equanimity," and also called "non-doing" (end of the prose section). Now, it is said that the non-manifestation of the first moment has seven names. The first name is...

Discipline (*saṃvara*). Second, it is called the *prātimokṣa* discipline (*prātimokṣa-saṃvara*). Third, it is called excellent conduct (*sucarita*). Fourth, it is called the path of action (*karmapatha*).
Fifth, it is called *prātimokṣa*. Sixth, it is called action (*karman*). Seventh, it is called morality (*śīla*). Regarding the five names:
by excluding the fifth, *prātimokṣa*, and excluding the fourth, *karmapatha*, there are thus five names. This is explained in detail in that treatise.
This is what is explained in the tenth fascicle.

As for "alerting" (*jing*), it means to admonish and spur the three types of action (*trikarma*). Regarding the passage beginning with "The ancients," Han Kangbo said: "To prevent calamity is called *śīla* (precept).

As for "essential nature and characteristics," this refers to the essential nature and formal characteristics of the two types of precepts. "Knowing the reception" means knowing that one receives [the precepts] with reverence in every movement—whether turning, advancing, bowing, or looking up. And...
It is not yet known what the essential nature (*dharmatā*) of that which is received is. The answer is as stated in the text. Regarding "Discourse on Precepts" (*Śīla-śāstra*):

it is a treatise explaining the Vinaya precepts. Regarding "The Path of Practice" (*Caryā-mārga*): it clarifies only the path and way of practicing the precepts. Regarding "The Principle of Karma" (*Karma-naya*): it is the principle and way of the essential nature of karma.
The title refers to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

Regarding the provisional and the real: the provisional refers to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, while the real refers to the various schools (*bahu-mata*). The *Tattvasiddhi* discourses on emptiness, whereas the various schools speak of existence.

Since the *Dharmaguptaka* school, as one particular tradition, partially accords with the Mahāyāna, it follows the gate of emptiness. As for the sense organ being able to see, it is as stated in the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*.
The verse says: "One's own eye sees forms; it is not that eye-consciousness sees. His own commentary explains:

"Therefore, when other consciousnesses are simultaneous, one does not see, because they are empty while coexisting with other consciousnesses. Furthermore, [the rule] is established only when there is a mind; there is no offense when there is no mind.
The phrase "all are forms" clarifies that this is not contingent upon the mind. The seven branches of body and speech are all discussed in terms of form. Not...

In this school, an offense is determined by questioning the state of mind; if there is no intention, there is no offense. Regarding good and evil karma, it does not depart from the actions performed through body and speech;
these actions are what is termed "karma. Furthermore, when investigating the substance of karma, it consists of both "active" (*vijñapti*) and "non-active" (*avijñapti*) karma.
The first is what is called "the unmanifest" (*avijñapti*). As for their difference: wholesome and unwholesome karma are distinct. This is a brief designation;

the names "wholesome" and "unwholesome" briefly express the essence [of the action], as they refer simply to the manifest (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*). Regarding movement and stillness: the manifest is movement, while the unmanifest is stillness.

Furthermore, once bodily movement has ceased, it continues to coexist with other consciousnesses; because its substance may be either robust or emaciated, it is categorized as belonging to movement. It does not follow the four minds.
The transformation of the three natures (trisvabhāva) pertains to the realm of quiescence. "As with various objects" refers to derived form-objects (rūpārtha);

they are subtle and difficult to perceive, not within the range of ordinary vision. This serves as an analogy for the unconditioned (anabhisaṃskṛta), whose characteristics are difficult to describe. As stated in the treatise, this constitutes the second of the many arguments.
Our own school [the Satyasiddhi] takes the fourfold emptiness and pervasiveness as its basis; it establishes reality through non-attachment and does not stagnate in substantial existence.

Because its principles and contexts are interrelated, it is able to rely upon those [categories] to define its essential nature; thus it is called the School of Provisional Designation (*prajñapti-nāma*). That which is "constructed by conditions" means that it is formed by the collective construction of various conditions;
this is precisely the meaning of "conditioned" (*kṛtaka*). There are many interpretations, as will be set forth below.

Regarding "form and mind" (*rūpa-citta*), this is discussed in terms of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). One aggregate is form; four aggregates are mind. For example, when one kneels in devotion and begs for something, the physical and verbal actions constitute form.

The universal mental engagement with the three periods of time, giving rise to the abandonment of evil and the cultivation of good, constitutes mind. It is through these together that the substance of the *karmapatha* (the precept-body) is accomplished.

As for "the equipment of action" (*karma-pariṣkāra*), this refers to the "equipment" in the sense of tools or implements; these are all merely mind—that is, the mind-king (*citta-rāja*). Apart from [mind]...
The mind has no volition. If one is separated from the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), there is no mental volition. This is because mental volition arises from the mind-king.
If the mind exists but lacks its volition, then karma is not established, for the body and speech are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
The fourteen kinds of matter consist of the five faculties, such as the eye; the five objects, such as visible form; and the four great elements, such as earth.
The present matter of body and speech is included within these, and therefore belongs to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Since it is not of a nature to produce evil or create good, it does not constitute karma of either good or evil.
Regarding form and sound: "form" subsumes bodily action (*kāyakarman*), while "sound" includes vocal action (*vākkarman*).

This master takes conventional form as the essence [of these actions], because it possesses the nature of demerit and merit. Vocal action is likewise; he does not take the actual physical sound as such.
Rather, he takes that which exists upon sound—its inflections and its indicative power—and names this vocal action.

Questioning the lower [position]: This school refers specifically to the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra). They ask: "If non-manifestation (*avijñapti*) were of the nature of form (*rūpa*), what fault would there be?
The answer is: "The five dharmas—form, sound, odor, taste, and touch—are not by nature merit or demerit; therefore, one does not take the nature of form to be non-manifestation.

Furthermore, the Buddha taught that form has the characteristic of being afflicted and disintegrating (*bādhanā-lakṣaṇa*); non-manifestation does not have the characteristic of being afflicted and disintegrating, as it cannot be apprehended."
"Not of the nature of form" (the above is from the treatise).
"What follows" is the formal objection. The answer [to this] means: "That which I previously established as having form and sound as its essence does not take actual, substantial form and sound;
it merely takes conventional, provisional form and sound. "A single thought-moment" refers to the very first instant.

Because one merely apprehends the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of form and sound, they do not possess the nature of sin or merit. From the second moment onward, one discriminates between good and evil;

this is the nature of sin and merit. Therefore, it is said that form and sound continue in succession. When the preceding moment has passed away, only the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) takes them as its object and knows them.

The mind is capable of accomplishing karma; therefore, it is said that [the mind] is the nature of both demerit and merit. Thus, the treatise below refers to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, specifically the "Chapter on Formations Dissociated from Mind" (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra-pāda*).
That text states in full: "Some say that names, phrases, and syllables are formations dissociated from the mind. This is not so."

That which is called "dharma" is the nature of sound; it is subsumed under the sphere of dharma (dharmāyatana), for the nature of sound constitutes the essence of sound. That which "assists in forming names and phrases" refers to that which assists in the modulation and inflection of phonemes.

Question: [The text] below should state that volition (*cetanā*) arises from the mind. Since it takes the mind as its substance (*tattva*), the actions of body and speech also arise from matter and mind;
should they not likewise take the mind as their substance? Answer: [The text] below states that volition and the mind arise simultaneously;

it is merely that their substances are distinct. Therefore, what is called "mind" there is precisely volition. However, [the text] below now establishes that the mental sovereign (*citta-rāja*) is also... [uncompleted].
This must refer to what is thought by the mind (*citta*). Regarding the phrase "below" (*xià*):

because there is nothing existing separately outside of the mind, the meaning is that while citing the mind-king (*cittarāja*) does not encompass the mental factors (*caitta*), since it is said that mental factors necessarily belong to the mind-king, one may say that apart from the mind there is no thinking. Furthermore, regarding the passage below:
Establishing the external position: This refers to the claim of non-Buddhists that the two types of karma—bodily and vocal—are accomplished independently of the mind.

For instance, they assert that desire arises from its object and does not originate from the mind. To refute this, [the author] states: "Desire originates from the mind," and so forth. Apart from the mind, there is no volition (*cetanā*).
There is no bodily or vocal karma.

Regarding the continuity of bodily karma: previously, it was established that the substance consists of the continuity of form and sound. The beginning and end of the continuity of bodily form can be seen;
however, the karma of names and phrases is severed and does not continue, nor is it visible to the eye. Since the mind has no object of perception, it is said [to be] "should."
It has non-verbal action as its essence. "Blue and so forth" includes yellow, red, white, black, and other colors. It is neutral (*avyākṛta*);

that is, the sound itself belongs to the neutral category, as it is merely a means for generating the precept. This is spoken in reference to the initial time of ascending the altar to request [the precepts], arising from a remote commitment (*samaya*).

Furthermore, it is said that the following section discusses this in terms of worldly phenomena (*saṃvṛti*). In reality, there is continuity and interruption; however, based on its beginning and end, it constitutes a single act of receiving.
Here, the person’s request for alms is the beginning, and the Saṃgha’s conferral of the ritual formula is the end.

Because these mutually depend upon one another to achieve their completion, they cannot be analyzed as a single, unitary entity. Furthermore, "the following" means that although the speech has ceased, the body expresses the verbal intention.
The four minds are consciousness, sensation, perception, and formations. Regarding the three aggregates: that treatise establishes four aggregates—first, form;
second, mind; third, neither-form-nor-mind; and fourth, the unconditioned—which together comprise eighty-four dharmas. This present case concerns the third [aggregate].
Furthermore, within this third aggregate there are seventeen dharmas; the present "non-informative" (avijñapti) dharma constitutes the seventeenth. This is the non-concomitant [formation].
It should be included in the category of "to be practiced. Regarding the second [point], it says: "That which is non-associated with practice" refers to the absence of manifest action (*vijñapti*).

As for "objects" (*viṣaya*), these refer to the five objects such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) such as earth and so forth; because these are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), they do not constitute the essence of manifest action here.
As for "shape" (*saṃsthāna*), there are fourteen types as previously mentioned, such as square, round, long, short, and so on. As for the "twenty," these refer to the varieties of color (*varṇa*).
Twelve [types of color]: namely, blue, yellow, red, white; light, shadow, brightness, and darkness; smoke, clouds, dust, and mist (these are exclusively indeterminate).

There are eight types of shape: namely, long, short, high, low, square, round, slanted, and straight (these pertain to all three natures). Now, the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) is neither of these two kinds of form.

It is "afflictive" (*nirvedana*) and "destructible. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "If this form is destroyed, it gives rise to sorrow and affliction. It further states: "Sentient beings possess affliction; non-sentient things possess destruction.

It is "substantial and obstructive," like walls and so forth, because it possesses substantiality and acts as a barrier to images. It is that which is apprehended by the five consciousnesses and the mind.
That is to say, the five objects such as form are what the five consciousnesses apprehend; for example, visual consciousness apprehends visible, resistant form and so forth.
[The text] concludes by returning to the point that these are not form.

"Conditioned cognition" (*yuanzhi*): "conditioned deliberation" (*yuanlü*) is itself cognition. "Deliberative cognition" (*lüzhi*) refers to the awareness resulting from reflection and deliberation. Regarding clarity and obscurity:

if the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) apprehends objective forms and so forth, it is clear and distinct; if the mind alone conditions objects that have already passed away—the five sensory realms—it is obscure and dim. Regarding the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

Because they are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate, there are extensive and abbreviated [explanations]. To focus specifically on the three periods of time is called "extensive"; to focus on only one period of time is called "abbreviated. Regarding the retributive dharma:

this refers to the physical heart, which is like a lotus bud measuring one inch square; it opens during the day and closes at night, serving as the locus upon which the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) relies.
This is a dharma obtained through retribution, following one's past karma; thus, faculties may be sharp or dull. A person of superior faculties has seven apertures.
Those of inferior faculties may have three, two, or one [moment of merit], or perhaps none at all.
As stated in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, quoting from a sūtra:

"Because a person of diligence gains much merit according to their lifespan, they enjoy celestial pleasures for a long time. If it were merely a virtuous mind, how could there be so much merit? This person..."
Because one cannot always maintain a virtuous mind, [it is proven that] merit resides in the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*) and does not depend on the mind.
Furthermore, regarding the planting of trees and so forth, it is said that merit constantly increases day and night. Moreover, it is said that the observance of precepts is firm;
if there were no unconditioned [merit], how could it be said that merit constantly increases and that the precepts are firmly maintained? (The above is from the treatise).

Furthermore, it is also stated in the seventh fascicle of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, in the section on "Non-manifest Action" (*avijñapti*): "Because only the seven branches of body and speech are prescribed, there is no restraint of the precepts regarding the mind.
Regarding the three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*), it says: "If a person is in a state of unwholesome or neutral mind, or even when without mind, they are still said to be 'maintaining the precepts.
Therefore, one knows that at such times, non-manifest action exists. (The above is the main text. The meaning of this is that [it applies to] the three natures.
Within this [context], for what reason is it called "maintaining the precepts" (*śīla*)? It is truly because there is non-action (*avijñapti*) within that which was previously received.
Below, the reason is investigated by first establishing an objection: "For what reason do the three natures possess non-action?

Furthermore, since non-action arises from action, and yet within these three natures there is originally no action, how can there be non-action? From this point downward is the explanation, namely: this...

The substance of non-informative action (avijñapti) is neither form nor mind; therefore, even if one currently performs actions of the three natures such as evil, the non-informative action acquired from the original performance of the precepts is not termed a "leakage" (loss).
One should know that this non-informative action arises based on the prior informative action.
Furthermore, it should be understood that if this non-informative action were of the nature of mind, it would undergo transformation according to the three natures. Indeed...
Because it is not of the nature of mind and does not undergo transformation accordingly. That [passage] also refers to the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra).

"Form and so forth" includes the five sense objects—sound, odor, taste, and touch. It is not of the nature of transgression or merit; conversely, this reveals that non-action (*avijñapti*) is indeed of the nature of transgression and merit.
Therefore, form and the other [objects] cannot be taken as non-action. Furthermore, the following passage is also cited from that same treatise itself.

The Buddha taught that it is not of a nature subject to affliction or destruction. That treatise correctly states: "Because within non-action (avijñapti), the characteristics of affliction and destruction cannot be found, it is not of the nature of form (rūpa).
Regarding the question below:
that treatise asks, "Is non-action of the nature of bodily and vocal karma? Since bodily and vocal karma are themselves form, [how can non-action not be form? The answer follows.

"Below. The intent is that although this non-informative [action] (*avijñapti*) arises solely from the actions of body, speech, and mind, it is therefore described as having the nature of bodily and vocal action;

in reality, however, it does not have the nature of bodily and vocal action. This is because the nature of bodily and vocal action is form (*rūpa*), whereas this non-informative action is currently not form.
Furthermore, below, that treatise explicitly states: "Moreover, there may be non-informative action that arises solely from the mind. This is non-informative action..."

What is the nature of form (*rūpa*)? (Because it arises from the mind. As follows: if one were to say that non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) is form, then consider, for instance, the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), where there is also non-manifest action;
would that then be form? (The above [passages] are all the Master of the Commentary’s implicit citation of the *Tattvasiddhi*.)
Therefore, the following passage from the eighteenth fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is cited to conclude and verify that it is not material (*rūpa*).

As for "contact and resistance," the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) is able to perceive touch, while the other faculties are able to encounter resistance; this is because they possess form. Now, since the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) lacks these characteristics, we know it is not material.
Although it is said to be non-material, if one skillfully cultivates the means, the essence of the dharma is spontaneously present. Question:
"Reaching the point where it takes non-action as its essence" refers to the preceding argument.
"It acts below" constitutes the formal objection. The intended meaning is that because non-action is the nature of good and evil, it does not take form-and-color (*rūpa*) as its essence.
If the present *kṛta-śīla* (the morality of action) is also of the nature of good or evil, should it not have non-form (*arūpa*) as its essence? The *kṛta-śīla* relies upon form;

specifically, it is the form of the primary retribution (*vipāka-rūpa*). Its "function" (*vṛtti*) is the provisional form of the preparatory means (*upāya-rūpa*). Since the present *kṛta-śīla* arises simultaneously with these two types of form, it takes the form of the function as its essence.
The "School of Real Dharmas" (dravya-dharma-vāda) refers to many schools. Regarding the calculation below:

because the School of Real Dharmas and the School of the Four Divisions (caturvarga-vāda) are calculated to be different, one cannot define the essential substance (*svabhāva*) based on the latter. The reason for clarifying this now is as follows:

regarding the phrase "the five aggregates have five characteristics," it means that each of the five aggregates possesses its own distinct essence and characteristic. For example, matter (*rūpa*) has distinctions such as distant, near, internal matter, and so forth.
External forms and so forth also intersect with the tenets of the Realist school (Sarvāstivāda), and thus their essential nature may be cited again.
Furthermore, since both are Buddhist, they differ only in the views and conceptual attachments of those with varying capacities. Regarding the fifth point below, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"For example, five hundred bhikṣus asked Śāriputra: 'The Buddha spoke of the causes of the body; which of these are false? Śāriputra replied: 'All..."
"Venerable sirs, each of you has attained right liberation; you should know this for yourselves. For what reason do you ask? A bhikṣu said:
'Venerable sir, when I had not yet attained right liberation, I thought that ignorance (*avidyā*) was the cause of the body. When I practiced such contemplation, I attained arhatship.
Furthermore, I [realized] that ignorance, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and so forth, up to the five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*), are the causes of the body.'"
At that time, after each of the five hundred bhikṣus had individually explained their own understanding, they went together to where the Buddha was to present them.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying, "Among these people, who has spoken correctly and who has not? The Buddha told Śāriputra, "Excellent!
There is not a single one among these bhikṣus whose explanation is not correct."

The three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are, as stated in the *Abhidharmakośa*: the unconditioned of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), the unconditioned of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and empty space (*ākāśa*).

This is explained in detail in the first fascicle [of this work]. The four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are arising (*jāti*), duration (*sthiti*), change (*anyathātva*), and cessation (*nirodha*). The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* states: "All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) consist of arising, duration, change, and cessation.

These all involve the benefit or harm of form (*rūpa*). For example, by means of bodily form, one may kill another in four locations (the brain, throat, heart, and waist), thereby obtaining [the result].

"Death. This is called "using form to damage form. The opposite of this is called "holding [the precept] with benefit. Once one branch is thus established, all other branches follow the same principle.
Regarding the passage below, "this teaching does not stem from binding the mind": in reality, it is not that one commits an offense by failing to bind that mental intention. Why is this?
Because for those of inferior capacity, the precepts for binding the mind are not prescribed. Therefore, in the passage below, he himself cites scriptural evidence. Since the sutra...

It is called "unmanifest form" (*avijñapti-rūpa*). Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* refers to it as "nominal form. One should know with certainty that both types of precepts are indeed form.
The eleven forms consist of the five faculties—eye and so forth—the five objects—form and so forth—and the unmanifest form within the sphere of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).

Although the five faculties and four objects are invisible, they possess resistance because the faculty of hearing can encounter them; therefore, they are said to be "invisible and resistant" (*anidarśana-sapratigha*). As for the remaining [objects], such as fragrance...

The same applies to the others. As for the *dharmāyatana* (the sphere of phenomena), it consists of the unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) which is non-substantial (*asattva*). This is precisely the unmanifest within the *dharmāyatana*.

It is not something confronted by the eye, nor is it composed of atoms (*paramāṇu*). Furthermore, it is not an object known by the mental faculty (*manas*). Therefore, it is said to be "invisible and non-obstructive" (*anidarśanam apratigham*).
The three colors are the aforementioned three [primary] colors. The eight colors are fragrance, flavor, tangibility, and those of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body.
These eight are not the substance of the unmanifest precept (*avijñapti-śīla*); they are non-obstructive and consist of conventional color. This is the substance of the unmanifest precept.

Physical action (*kāya-karman*) begins from the moment one ascends the altar and continues until the conclusion of the *karmavācanā*; this is visible and obstructive color. Verbal action (*vāk-karman*) refers to the time of making the formal request.
It is invisible and possesses resistance (*sapratigha*). When it manifests as a continuous succession following a single impulse, this is invisible and non-resistant matter (*apratigha-rūpa*).

Regarding the five sense faculties and the five objects, these refer to substantial matter; because each has its own distinct demarcation, they are called "resistance through obstruction" (*āvaraṇa-pratigha*). (7)

"Mind" refers to the six consciousnesses together with the fundamental mind-faculty (*manas*). It is like the sphere of visual consciousness, not the sphere of auditory consciousness and so forth, because each has its own respective object.

The "mind that acts as the perceiver" is, for example, when it perceives the five sense-objects that have already passed away. Now, since non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) is neither of these three types of objects, it belongs to the category of the "objectless" (*anālambana*).
"Retribution" refers to the colors obtained through retribution that have qualities such as being beautiful or ugly, and the sounds obtained that have qualities such as being clear or turbid.

"Skillful means" refers to the arising of movements, postures, and melodic rhythms upon those retributive colors and sounds; this is skillful means. Regarding sound, one does not grasp at the actual colors and sounds obtained through retribution.
"Physical movement" is physical skillful means, meaning that the locus of the body obtained through retribution is the color of the skillful means of the body.

Therefore, this is taken as the substance of the precept (*śīla-skandha*). Regarding the phrase "stirring below," the differentiation is likewise one, because the entirety of the retributive form (*vipāka-rūpa*) serves as the provisional form (*upāya-rūpa*).
Furthermore, "lower" refers to the fact that the explanation is also different. "Arbitrarily lower" means that the uprightness of the present world is a recompense for causes from the past.

"Extended lower" refers to bending and stretching, or making things long and short, high and low; these are the colors of *upāya* (expedient means). Because they follow what is currently established and are not a result of retribution, they are so called.

"Retribution lower" means that the body obtained through retribution is substantial color (*dravya-rūpa*), as it is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). The provisional color of *upāya* is common to both [the determinate and the indeterminate].

Regarding the three natures, such as the wholesome and so forth—just as acts like kneeling and prostrating today—are they not of a wholesome nature? Since there is both a general and a specific application, this constitutes their difference.
Regarding retribution, it arises from the lower [realm]. Furthermore, when past karma manifests in the present, it is discussed in terms of two time periods, as follows:
the moisture of water is a metaphor for the matter of retribution (*vipākavarṇa*), while the movement of waves is a metaphor for the matter of skillful means (*upāyavarṇa*).

Question below: The intention is this: If the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) takes retributive matter (*vipākaja-rūpa*) as its essence, then since retributive matter is neutral (*avyākṛta*), the preparatory effort should also be neutral.
How can it be said that preparatory effort pervades the three natures (*tri-vidha-svabhāva*) and constitutes informative action (*vijñapti-karman*)? Answer below:
It is said that matter itself possesses no nature of good or evil; rather, it becomes good or evil through the agitation [of the mind] that brings it about.
"If that is so," and so forth, rebukes the preceding response by stating that there is no good or evil in physical form (*rūpa*). Regarding the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, its Karma Chapter states:

"The wholesome is the pure movement of body, speech, and mind, such as giving, morality, and so forth. The unwholesome is the unwholesome movement of body, speech, and mind, such as killing and so forth.
The indeterminate is the indeterminate movement of mind, speech, and body. Now, referring specifically to wholesome precepts, it is therefore called "pure."

The movement of the mind manifests as both body and speech; thus, two [aspects] appear externally. There are two external conditions, good and evil, which give rise to two internal forms, good and evil.

From "by means of" (*yī xià*) below, the text further explains the passages of the preceding sutra and treatise. The image changing according to conditions serves as a metaphor for the skillful means (*upāya*) that arise, encompassing both good and evil.

That the original face does not change serves as a metaphor for the retributive form (*vipākavarṇa*), which is fixed and exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). It is solely these [changing images] that constitute the skillful means.
This excludes the two types that are not of the nature of retribution (vipāka-dharma): namely, the unmanifest (avijñapti) of body and speech. These are neither retribution nor matter of retribution;
they are matter produced by application (prayoga) and matter produced by resolve (adhiṣṭhāna).
"Distinct colors have distinct causes" refers to the color of skillful means (*upāya-rūpa*). "Causes" refers to the color of retribution (*vipāka-rūpa*). The following is the explanation:

regarding "the fruit of the color of retribution," the color of retribution serves as the cause and skillful means serves as the fruit (viewed from the subsequent arising, the former is called the fruit). This is explained below.
The two types of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) are neither resultant form (*vipākaja-rūpa*) nor form produced through effort (*prāyogika-rūpa*).

The remaining two natures are the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). "Not different from the causes of form," etc., includes by implication those that are not different from the effects of form.
The original undertaking is not lost; it is precisely because of this non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) that it remains undestroyed within these two states of mind.
[The text] below states that this non-informative matter is established through its differentiation from the form of the preparatory application (*prayoga*).

The informative action (*vijñapti*) lasts but a single thought-moment—specifically, at the first moment when the three *karmavācanās* are completed—because the informative precept (*vijñapti-śīla*) has already fallen away. Now, since the non-informative matter persists for the duration of one's entire life...

Therefore, it is not an "unmanifest" (*avijñapti*) among the [three types of] "undertakings" (*vijñapti*). If this is so, then this "distinctive matter-result" (*rūpa-phala*) refers to unmanifest derivative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*), while the "cause" refers to the manifest precept (*vijñapti-śīla*).
Because the manifest precept gives rise to the unmanifest, the manifest is the cause of this unmanifest derivative matter.
Regarding the phrase "not making," the full text says: "not making a distinct matter-cause for a distinct matter-result," which means that in accordance with...

In the intermediate state, there is the cause of this distinct matter, namely, the intermediate *vijñapti* (informative action). Following that, there is the fruit of this distinct matter, namely, the intermediate *avijñapti* (non-informative action). Furthermore, it is not the case that it is inferior;

that is to say, both the intermediate *vijñapti* and *avijñapti* arise from the materiality and mind associated with the preparatory effort (*prayoga*). When the activity ceases, they no longer exist, as both are causes of the precept.

The text states: "Because both are short. This makes it clear that the essence of *prāpti* (possession) is non-manifest (*avijñapti*). It is called "non-manifest" because it is conventionally established based on prior conditions through the application of skillful means.
"Corrupt" refers to the present state of an evil nature. The previous statement that there is no non-manifest within *prāpti* was not understood [by you].
"Following birth" refers to its continuous and progressive growth.
It is not others; rather, it is among other unwholesome and neutral states, as stated in the treatise. "Etc. refers to *kaukṛtya* (remorse).
As for "both being neutral," this is because they are visible forms (*varṇa*). "High" and "low" belong to shape-forms (*saṃsthāna*), and thus they pertain to all three natures.
They include the wholesome nature because they constitute wholesome precepts.
Regarding the three types of sound, the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* states: "The sense-base of sound (*śabdāyatana*) is of three kinds:

namely, sound produced by the four great elements that are appropriated (*upātta*), sound produced by the four great elements that are not appropriated (*anupātta*), and sound produced by both. Sound produced by the four great elements that are appropriated refers to sound generated through the conditions of the throat, lips, and tongue.

Sound produced by the four great elements that are not appropriated refers to sound generated through the conditions of wind, bells, trees, and the like. Sound produced by both refers to [sound] such as striking..."
The sound of the drum and the chanting has causes and conditions. Each of those sounds is of two kinds: namely, agreeable and disagreeable.
This commentary now selects the second type of sound. "Now" below refers to the second cause for receiving sound;

furthermore, it is of a wholesome nature, encompassing both wholesome and unwholesome natures, because even unwholesome precepts give rise to non-informative action (*avijñapti*). Regarding "the indeterminate is not karma," the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* says:

Because the indeterminate mind is weak and inferior, it is restricted to the wholesome. This is stated with reference to the wholesome [mind] being able to restrain evil. If one receives an evil precept (*duṣkṛta-śīla*), it likewise restrains the wholesome.

Regarding its beginning and end: the beginning is from the time of requesting a teacher; the end is designated as the conclusion of the three rituals. It is wholesome but not a formal precept (*śīla*). That is to say:

It belongs only to what is wholesome, yet it is not itself the precept (*śīla*). The answer below states: If one receives [the vow] through a formal commitment (*samādāna*), it is called a "precept," because the ritual of the precept is restricted in scope.
All other wholesome factors are also called "restraint" (*saṃvara*), because restraint applies universally and without limit.
Other general ten courses of action that lack such a formal commitment are wholesome, but they are not precepts.

If it were only a single thought, the meaning would be this: if it were only at the moment the third *karmavācanā* concludes that the first thought receives the name "created precept" (*kṛta-śīla*), then prior to ascending the platform to invite the preceptor, even if there were unfavorable conditions, one should still have induced the precept;

however, this is not the case. Because it must be entirely in accordance with the Dharma from beginning to end, it is necessary to encompass the entire process as the substance of the created precept. [The phrase] "verbal cessation below" refers to that.
The verbal expression of the request has already been completed, yet the mental conditions remain unfathomable; therefore, it is not merely what is heard by the ear.
Although the intention is proximate to its object, one must understand that the three types of action (trikarma) are taken together to explain the beginning and end [of the rite].

If this is so, does it not contradict the statement in the *Vinayavibhaṅga* that the first moment of the *karmavācanā* is called "vow-action" (*kriyā-śīla*)? Answer: The treatise speaks from the perspective of the time of completion; it does not refer to the preceding moments.

It is called the "precept of name. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "obstructing what follows": this master’s intention is that although the mouth may have ceased [the action], the body can still manifest it.

Regarding the phrase "sāngyú (桑榆) below": this explains the substance of the aforementioned "solitary joy" (*dúlè*); it is made from *sāngyú* wood. The "musk-wheel" (*xiělún*) can be understood by analogy.
Fearing that beginners may not yet know, he provides an example, saying: "For instance, the musk deer possesses a 'retributive form' (*bǎosè*); when a killer takes its navel-gland..."
This refers to the color of the expedient means. Taking the substance of musk and rice as a metaphor for the performance of precepts:

when the substance of the fragrance disperses and perishes, only the scent remains; this is a metaphor for non-manifest action (*avijñapti*). If that were so, how could one discard the musk deer and other such creatures while taking only the scent?
The performance of precepts is likewise thus.

The "seven kinds" refers to the seven virtuous restraints (*śīla-saṃvara*). Regarding "formless," this school maintains that non-manifest form (*avijñapti*) is indeed form. The following citation provides proof;
it is the same as the ten kinds of precepts, namely the ten kinds of virtuous precepts. These are: "possessing adornment," which explains the aforementioned manifest form (*vijñapti-rūpa*);

and "having been accomplished," which explains the aforementioned non-manifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*). This means there is no further preparatory effort (*prayoga*), but rather only the actual resultant manifest form.

Because there is no physical form (*rūpa*) produced through deliberate effort (*abhisamskāra*) due to a lack of skillful means (*upāya*), there is only the form of action (*kriyā-rūpa*), but no form of non-action (*avijñapti-rūpa*).

Regarding its derivation from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), the *Vibhāṣā* states that "derivation" (*nirmita*) carries the sense of "cause. Since the productive [action] belongs to the *kriyā-śīla*, and non-action arises from that action, it is therefore derived from the four great elements.
The *Abhidharmakośa* states that it is derived from the four great elements—namely, earth, water, fire, and wind—or is otherwise called...

The subsequent explanation refers to the arising [of the unmanifest] before and after [the manifest]. "Before" refers to simultaneous arising; that is, when performing the manifest action, the unmanifest arises concurrently with it.
This can be described as being like the two horns of an ox growing simultaneously; thus, there is no impediment to their coexistence in form.

Non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) still arises subsequently. Regarding "volitional karma" (*cetanā-karman*): "volition" refers to that which experiences [the object]. "Mental karma" (*citta-karman*) is the very essence of karma.
"Possessing" explains the aforementioned possession of both manifest and non-manifest action.
Now, the following is explained. Although this is discussed in terms of simultaneity (*sahabhū*), it does not adopt the position of the first master.

This is because, while the first master speaks of simultaneity, he is unable to distinguish between "concomitance" (*saha*) and "concomitance with form" (*rūpasaha*). In the present master’s system, within the category of "concomitance" and "unmanifest action" (*avijñapti*), the cause for "concomitance with form" has already begun to sprout;
thus, the principle is not severed. From the phrase "due to the original," the cause results in the fruit, and once the fruit is attained, it is never interrupted.
This refers to the limit of verbal expression. Upon reaching the subsequent moment—that is, at the very instant when the three factors are completed—both types of restraint are fully perfected:
namely, the restraint of action (*kriyā-śīla*) and the non-manifesting restraint concomitant with action (*kriyā-sahabhū-avijñapti*).
It is not that they are non-concordant with their co-existent substance; this speaks of their identity. "Co-existent with form" means being co-existent with form without activity.
Its cause has already arisen, but it has not yet reached its fruit (this first point correctly clarifies the aforementioned "simultaneity"). It still co-exists with activity;

once the three dharmas are complete, at the very moment the first thought-moment has not yet fallen away, it remains as before—namely, it is non-concordant with the aforementioned activity in terms of substance, yet it does not obstruct the formation of the cause co-existent with form while it remains unmanifest.

[The first] "also" [indicates this]. Second, "below" refers to the actual explanation of the non-manifest (*avijñapti*) at the time of fruition. "Manifestation" means that the aforementioned cause co-arising with form becomes manifest upon reaching fruition.
Third, "below" refers to the second moment: both forms have ceased, and the non-manifest arises at the moment the precept-essence (*śīla-tattva*) is produced, persisting until the end of one's life.
This is divided into two: the actual reception and the period after reception. "Pervasive through three" refers to the non-manifest at the time of the cause.

Regarding its duration: because it persists for the entirety of one's life, it falls into the category of being continuous.
That is to say, once initiated, it continues to manifest as a stream throughout the course of existence, persisting spontaneously within the four types of mind and the three moral natures.
