Strong conditions mean that the sacred realm is before one's eyes, because the Buddha-body pervades all places. Furthermore, the *Jingxin jieguan* (Pure Mind Precept Contemplation) states:
"How could the Buddha’s pores allow for concealment or omission? However, the subsequent passage says that it is simply because the practitioner cannot yet be wholehearted.

If [the practice] is not effective for those being influenced, then one should employ the mind and mouth to encourage and admonish; when the mind contemplates while the mouth recites, the merit is indeed great.
As stated below, during the time of confession, one should personally state one's own name as well as the names of those who have committed evil.
The beginning of merit: from now on, I shall begin my repentance. The end of transgression: I vow that it shall be forever severed. Binding the mind:
binding a covenant that is not firm. "Or below": or seeing dusty objects within dreams, or seeing them while awake—is this not a transformation produced by the deluded mind?
"If it is below": this distinguishes it from demonic realms, for it is fundamentally delusion; it arises because you have not yet emerged from the realm of demons.

Because it is an object, it is revealed to be a false arising; now one further falsely clings to it, and thus it is said that "inversion arises again. Regarding the phrase "the original is not the original":
if one does not know that the external falsity which originally arose was fundamentally the original mind, how could one bring stillness to the cause of delusion?
Furthermore, once consciousness has cognized this and then dispatched it, the cognizing mind itself cannot be apprehended. If one were to cling to it again, that would likewise become a delusion.
If it were not so, to pursue delusion with joy would itself be a sickness. Therefore, I urge you to clarify and master this as soon as possible.
This is a vulgar remark. It was said by Confucius. The *Appended Phrases* of the *Book of Changes* states: "The number of the Great Proliferation is fifty;
forty-nine are employed. Wang Bi remarked: "Forty-nine is the ultimate of numbers. When a person reaches this end, how could they fail to be aware of it?"

Regarding those of lower rank, add four elements: namely, when facing a junior seat-holder, one should bare the right shoulder, remove leather sandals, kneel with the right knee on the ground, and join the palms.
If it is a senior seat-holder, one should further add prostrating at their feet as previously described; this is detailed in the second fascicle on the full ritual protocol.
"Same assembly" means a harmonious community that is identical in its observance of the precepts and in their reception and practice. "Same view" means being identical in right view.

Regarding "life-threatening danger," fearing death while still bearing transgressions, one is permitted to confess together with those who have committed the same offense—excluding the *pārājika* (defeats) from the four categories of offenses, as these are like severing the head.

Although confession is permitted, such a person remains ultimately a *śrāmaṇera* undergoing training and repentance. "Mutual reach" refers to the open space where monks must extend their hands so that they can reach one another. This must be fully prepared.

It is sufficient whether performed before an individual, in the presence of others, or through formal ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*); the verbal instructions must be complete according to the gravity of the offense.

Regarding the section on "reproach" and below, the second sentence speaks of many bodies cultivating the practice, demonstrating that one cannot accomplish the Mahāyāna repentance in a single lifetime.

If one speaks from a remote perspective, it can be said that even the principle-contemplation of non-arising and consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*) may lead to extinction; how much more so for those in the three stages of worthiness prior to the [Bodhisattva] grounds.
There still remains birth-and-death in segments (*paricchinna-jarāmarana*); therefore, it is not mentioned as "karma.

As for "superior patience" (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), this refers to the stage of superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti-avasthā*). It is "similar" because upon entering the Path, one gives rise to true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava*), does not fall into the evil destinies, and likewise does not receive the retribution of a female body.
As the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Patience does not lead to falling into the evil realms. This is established.
The section "In Reality" below cites evidence that one does not receive the total retribution [of all past karma]. This is because worldly right view is similar to outflow-free (anāsrava) wisdom.

Therefore, as stated below, according to the *Ekottarika Āgama*, Mahāmaudgalyāyana was struck by a Brahmin while begging for alms, such that his bones were shattered and his flesh destroyed by shards and stones.
Furthermore, Aṅgulimāla, though he had already realized the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), still suffered his body being consumed by the fires of hell. Thus, it is due to karma.
It can follow one along; even upon reaching the state of a sage, one cannot escape it. One merely severs the general retribution of evil karma, yet the individual retributions do not perish.
To perform good deeds refers to the meritorious goodness of the three realms. The golden ball: although this is precious, it carries the danger of burning the hand.
The blessings of humans and devas are likewise thus. "Indeterminate" means neither unwholesome nor evil. "Habitual arrogance" refers to the absence of the aspect of respect. To act...
As for what "remains," it refers to the fact that among the six realms of existence, one does not yet know in which place one will receive retribution; hence it is said below:
"At the end of a hundred years, there is fear of being the same as birds and beasts."

Those who do not delight in committing sins and are single-mindedly diligent in refraining from transgressing against others are rarely encountered in these degenerate times; hence it is said, "How can they be met?
However, those who, having already committed an offense, are able to repent—whether out of fear of transgression or with the intent to perform confession—are likewise a blessing in this final age.

Regarding the mutual relationship between the act and the offense: this refers to a case where the committed act does not correspond to the specific rule (dharma) that was violated. Furthermore, this is clearly evident.
When there is an offense committed intentionally, it is a transgression; when one is deluded or forgetful, there is no transgression. Now, [the text] does not distinguish between these two cases.

"Excessive praise" (làn bāo) refers to an overestimation of one's merits. "Praise" (bāo) is a term for amassing [rewards]. As for saying that "all offenses," whether light or heavy, are equally "everything committed," this means they are all to be repented of.

To say "or facing [another]" below [in the text] is incorrect, as it refers to the person who receives the repentance. "Deluded teaching" (chī jiào) means being ignorant of the teachings. "Granting and withholding" refers to recognizing the nature of the offense.

Receiving the confession is called "granting"; the opposite is called "withdrawing. This does not refer to numerical status; it refers to those who possess grave transgressions and thus do not enter the ranks of the Saṃgha.
To sit peacefully and receive the confession, yet fail to distinguish the characteristics of the individual portions, is collectively termed "neither subject nor object."
"Now, below": previously one falsely created, now one falsely destroys; "covering, below": previously covered, now exposed—both are due to the mind.
"Busily engaged" and "confused turmoil" are both signs of the restlessness of false karma. "These," below: this refers to speech.
It is essential that the mind’s practice reaches full realization; this is truly not easy, and thus it is said to be "difficult. It is not inferior;

this means that although one is not yet a sage, one should study what the sages have cultivated. As the saying goes: "Upon seeing the worthy, think of emulating them. Regarding the two types of repentance: they concern the phenomena and principles of both the Great and Small Vehicles.
"Suppressed karma. This "suppression" refers to a temporary subduing, like using a stone to press down grass so that it does not sprout;

it is not the same as the principle of repentance mentioned previously, which results in permanent extinction. "The family is large" means that even after being driven away, they return. "When strength prevails, they arise alternately."

When the wholesome mind prevails, evil does not arise; when evil karma prevails, the wholesome does not manifest. Therefore, one must constantly distance oneself from and constantly illuminate evil karma so that it finds no opportunity.
Thus, the following passage from the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* cites a sūtra:

"When a person who has planted the roots of merit conducive to liberation hears it said that there is virtue in Nirvāṇa and faults in saṃsāra, tears flow and their hair stands on end. This refers to those whose minds are scorched [by the heat of their afflictions].
Karma is like a parched seed; it will never grow. Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states below:
"In the practice of the Śrāvaka, those of sharp faculties [attain the goal] in three lifetimes.

In the first, they cultivate the Śrāvaka-provisions, the wholesome roots conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*), performing the five stabilizing meditations (*pañca-vastu-sthiti-dhyāna*), the meditation on specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇasmṛtyupasthāna*), and the meditation on general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇasmṛtyupasthāna*). In the second..."

Second, one cultivates the Śrāvaka preparatory practices (*prayoga*) that accord with the levels of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), such as the four truths and sixteen mental moments, the casting off of objects, and the reduction of aspects.
Third, by giving rise to knowledge, one abandons the afflictions and enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). Regarding the sixty kalpas: the first twenty kalpas [are as follows].
One cultivates the provisions (*sambhāra*). Next, one cultivates the application (*prayoga*) for twenty *kalpas*. Finally, after twenty *kalpas*, one enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* provides an analogy to explain this: "The first stage is like sowing the seed; the next stage is like the growth of the sprout; the final stage is like the actual ripening of the fruit."
There is no moisture; it does not moisten the practitioner’s rebirth within the three realms. From here below, this is explained according to the Mahāyāna.

The "three levels of worthiness" (sankhya) refers to the stages of the *marga* (path) and *prayoga* (preparation). "Segmented" means that one still possesses a body subject to segmented birth-and-death (*paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa*), and therefore it is said that [this state] has not yet perished.

The stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and Summits (*mūrdhan*) are the first two among the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). Because the roots of goodness cultivated during these two stages are all subject to regression and fluctuation—

as, for example, when Devadatta, though at the stage of Heat, later committed a heinous offense— it is only upon reaching the subsequent stage of Patience (*kṣānti*) that the mind is free from regression and fluctuation.

Regarding the necessity of relying on principle: one should constantly cultivate the three types of Mahāyāna contemplation. As for following after phenomena (*dharma*), this refers to practicing the path during the six periods of the day and night and upholding the precepts;
these are all matters of phenomena (*vastu*). One should practice the simultaneous integration of phenomena and principle until the end of one's life, constantly urging and goading the mind.
"Throughout the ten directions," and so forth, refers to the five repentances (*pañca-pratikramaṇa*). The text omits the section on making vows.

"The grave transgressions" refers to the four grave offenses and the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*). "Neither obstinacy nor self-assertion" is quoted from the *Analects*. The full passage there states: "The Master renounced the four [biases]:

no arbitrary will (because one takes the Way as the measure, one does not act according to personal whim); no compulsion (if employed, one acts; if abandoned, one hides; thus there is no fixed insistence); no obstinacy (there is neither 'yes' nor 'no'...)."

This is acceptable. "Non-self" (wú wǒ) means following only the Way and not possessing a self-centered body. Even in Confucianism, one restrains the self and follows the Way, for it values the absence of self-attachment;
how much more so for those who have left the household life? One must not speak of non-self in empty words while lacking its actual practice.
The karma of consciousness does not truly exist; it is merely that the eye has a disease, and thus flowers appear in empty space. These flowers are, in fact, unreal.

"To divide" (fenxia) means to partially perceive the True Principle while partially remaining within deluded karma. It is like one who polishes a mirror: failing to realize that actual karma is not real, they remain deluded regarding the Principle and perform repentance.
This is like polishing a worldly mirror; it does not equal the immediate clarity [of sudden enlightenment].

"I do not know its boundaries. "Boundaries" refers to the limits of a field; here it means that one does not know the limits for performing a ritual confession (*liǎochàn*). If one prefers the lower [vehicle], one may perform the ritual confession according to the Vinaya;
however, this only removes offenses against the regulations (*zhìzuì*), while the karmic paths (*yèdào*) are not removed. Furthermore, one may perform the ritual confession of the Mahāyāna.

If the seeds of karma have not yet been eliminated, the fruit remains within the tainted (*sāsrava*). If one practices cultivation and repentance, this is the merit of the supramundane and untainted (*anāsrava*).

Regarding the "two contemplations," these refer to the two contemplations of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). The two subsequent lines beginning with "In relation to the self" explain the emptiness of persons:

that is to say, by means of the analytical wisdom of the contemplating subject, one breaks down form to reveal emptiness; seeing only what is illusory and false, where could the nature of a "self" possibly exist?

One contemplates down to the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*). At the point where analysis can no longer proceed, one leaves behind a single *paramāṇu*; thus it is said, "one sees only this dust. Reaching this state is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

The two lines following the section on the aggregates (*skandha*) explain the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*): that is, when contemplating the phenomena of the five aggregates, they are fundamentally empty and quiescent.
Because one seeks each phenomenon individually and finds no inherent existence, it is said, "there is only name and form" (*nāma-rūpa*). This refers to seeking the person (*pudgala*).

The following section provides a summary. Being able to analyze form (*rūpa*) and perceive the two emptinesses of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*) constitutes the practice of the emptiness of nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) in the Hīnayāna;
it is the contemplation of the arising and ceasing of phenomena.

"Taking the emptiness of consciousness as fundamental" refers to the two contemplations of the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) and representation-only (*vijñapti-mātra*). This involves contemplating that the verbal designations of objects do not exist outside of the mind.

Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) still belongs to the coarse and superficial; realizing that objects are consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) is what is profound. This means that the great Bodhisattvas realize that objects are not [external] objects, and that their essence is solely consciousness.
Thus they know that the three realms are mind-only and all phenomena are consciousness-only, as explained in detail within the section on the practices of ordinary beings and sages.

"Correcting the classification" refers to cases such as the *yiran* (remaining offenses) and so forth; these should be gathered into their respective categories. Within each of the six classes of offenses (*ṣaḍ-varga*), there are specific types.

For example, the offense of physical contact belongs to the category of sexual misconduct, and so on. "Deep censure" refers to the class of censure (*pācittiya*). This means that offenses from different sections or classes are confessed together.

This is intended to remove doubts, for one might fear that by not studying [the rules], one would remain ignorant and thus fail to commit an offense—namely, the notion that "one does not offend through ignorance."

Therefore, one attains liberation. Regarding the passage "and below": if one constantly maintains [the precepts] in mind and commits an offense through forgetfulness, this is the occasion for an exception.

"Violating the vow" refers to the aspirational mind at the time of initial reception. Regarding "not below": this is due to delusion caused by a lack of study; it is not a delusion of the mind itself.

"The mind does not take the object as its condition" means that the mind does not fixate upon the correct object, such as when a person perceives a tree stump and so forth. "In the countryside," as in taking [an object] as a condition...
"Initial consciousness" refers to the realm of non-humans; it is not recognized because it is not something studied, yet this is not called a deluded mind.

According to the *Yuanyia* (Source of the Lower), although these are people who have not studied, because they are fundamentally deluded, their perceptions of the realm also arise. The *Chichan* (Holding and Violating) states: "It is simply that [the realm] is deluded, as it is not understood through study."

The Buddha has opened everything for all. Furthermore, how could it be limited only to those still in training (*śaikṣa*)? Therefore, it is said: "This one is also exempt. This exemption refers only to the six categories of offenses (*ṣaṭ-saṃghāvaśeṣa*);

it merely exempts one from the offense of transgressing the regulations (*prajñapti-āpatti*). Ultimately, one must rely on wise observation (*prajñā-vipaśyanā*), which pertains to the path of karma (*karmapatha*); let one reflect upon this quietly for oneself.

As stated above, this corresponds to what was previously mentioned regarding the stage of "superior patience" (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), where there is a semblance of outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava*), and the retribution of female form in the evil realms is finally [eliminated].
One does not receive [the fruit]. The Path is still attainable;
it is said that while one may not realize the Holy Path in this life, there is still hope for it.

Furthermore, the retribution of future lives is most formidable; therefore, it is said, "What can be done about the retribution of birth? *Abhijiti* is also called *Hebizhi*; in Sanskrit, it is *Abhijit*.
This refers to a shift in terminology.
There is no concealment whatsoever. According to our current Master, if at the time of the formal confession there is not a single thought of concealment, it is immediately opened;

this differs from the ancients, who held that it was only opened after the offense had occurred provided there was not a single thought of concealment thereafter, such that the conditions for concealment were not fulfilled—for instance, cases involving confusion or forgetfulness. Or...
There is a lower [interpretation] that presents an ancient view. If this lower view is now refuted, it may not necessarily accord with the conditions [of the rule].

For example, in the case of Sūdanaputra, the rule was established because of his offense involving a former wife (*pūrvapatnī*). How could a later offense also be judged by reference to a former wife? Therefore, it is said: "What need is there to inquire whether it is new or old?"
Regarding the following two sections: it is said that these must be exhausted. Once they have been exposed, one may bring forth a single request;

this is also permitted for those whose remaining offenses have not yet been fully confessed. "If born" means as if a person were born again. "Precept-body" refers to the integration or separation of the precept-substance (*śīla-skandha*).

One may perform the concealment (*praticchādana*) for each individually, or if there is a long robe used for concealment, one may perform them collectively; both methods are permissible. "Byways" (*khi*): *khi* is a small path; *shu* (術) is also a road.
"Following the night" means following the night to conceal [the offense] as it passes;

whether for one day and night, up to a hundred nights, or for one or two years from the time of purification, this serves to compensate for the concealment of previous days. "To subdue" (伏) means to suppress or to admonish.
By looking at what follows, one understands the intention of the monk Sengxi: that "it is easy" refers to the ease with which one commits an offense. "Root" (根)... [text fragment].
Root. If viewed in relation to the prior acts of concealment and so forth, this *śeṣa* (residual offense) is precisely the root and the primary obstacle, obstructing pure cultivation.

It is paired with the "deprivation of practice," which consists of thirty-five matters; these are the methods for depriving one of their practice. [The term] "extracted below" means that if one extracts and arranges them:
This would result in an excessive proliferation of scrolls; therefore, I have been brief. The names are as in the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts). It states:

"The term *sthūlātyaya* means 'great obstruction,' referring to that which hinders the path to goodness," and so forth. For detailed instructions, refer to the text; this is as explained in detail in the *Dacǎo* (Great Commentary).
It must be contrasted with what follows below. This clarifies that for a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense, there must be five or more persons. Regarding greed and pride:

for example, keeping extra robes is an offense of greed, while being separated from one’s robes is an offense of pride. Furthermore, the thirty [offenses] concern the improper method of acquisition and use, while the ninety [offenses] concern the improper method of manufacture and action.

"Confession before another" (pratideśanā): this refers specifically to confessing before a single person; by this simple acknowledgment, the offense is extinguished. "Giving to another": giving as an act of almsgiving to others.
"Purification through relinquishment" (niḥsargika-pāyattika): one must first bring the object into the midst of the Saṃgha and relinquish it before it may be given away.
"Relinquishing and sending away": relinquishing wealth and sending it away. "Not defiled": referring to wealth that is defiled by illegality; such items cannot be used to make the three robes.

Each time one descends [into the water], one incurs an offense for every instance of wearing [the robe]. This is intended to cause the practitioner to remain free from the conditions that lead to transgression. There are five types [of such descent]:
pouring [water] onto someone, dispatching it to another, and so forth, up to the ritual of *śuddhi* (purification/declaring purity).

Regarding the three objects [of confession]: as noted in the commentary, whether the Sangha is numerous or consists of a single person—[the text] asks below: "If one wishes to perform a ritual washing and confession, it cannot be accomplished separately;
the Sangha is established as the object [of confession]. By facing them, one gives rise to shame, which enables the severance of future transgressions.

Now, if one faces only an individual, how can this be called 'earnest shame'? Regarding the rule for returning [an item] to the Sangha: if there are monks within the boundary, one must return it by facing them.
The ritual for the Saṃgha is only to be performed when no one else is present; this is the sole restriction.

If it were restricted solely to performing the confession before the Saṃgha without allowing for individual confession, then while those capable of confessing would be very numerous, the monks required to receive the confession would be difficult to find, and there would be no way to achieve purification through reflection on the offense.

Therefore, "according to the place" means that wherever there is a Saṃgha, one confesses before the Saṃgha; where there is no Saṃgha, one confesses individually. "As currently" explains the same principle regarding shared offenses.
Regarding the meaning: each has its own assembly. They assemble according to the natural dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), as explained above.

This refers to what was previously distinguished within the section on the nature of the *saṃgha*: concerning those who assemble individually for the purpose of relinquishing property, although it is permitted to relinquish property before an individual, they likewise assemble before the entire community (*pariṣad*) to complete the result.

As for those who repent their offenses before an individual group, this means that while the relinquishment of property is restricted to being performed before the *saṃgha*, the repentance of offenses may be done before an individual group. However—
This also applies to a single person.

There are those who hold that, for this master, both the relinquishing of wealth and the repentance of the offense must take place before the Saṃgha. This is because the offense arose on account of wealth;

therefore, the relinquishment and the confession must correspond. How could it be possible for the relinquishing of wealth to be before the Saṃgha while the relinquishing of the offense is before an individual? That person...

This refers to the first master. Because he renounced [the property], he immediately performed repentance. This means that because the property renounced remained with the Sangha, he repented his offense on the spot.
Since he was already among the assembly, the presiding repentance master did not dare to accept it unilaterally; therefore, he made a formal announcement (*jñapti*) to harmonize the Sangha.

However, this did not prevent the offense itself from being individually confessed before the repentance master alone; hence it is said, "the original offense is separately removed. If the material object has been completely consumed, then since the substance of the property has already been used...
[The opponent asks: "If [the offense] is exhausted by merely confessing the primary downfall (mūlāpatti), why is it necessary to further assemble the Saṃgha?
[The respondent replies: "The former person refers to the next teacher.

He means that regarding those offenses listed at the beginning of the *Prātimokṣasūtra*, although they are grave offenses due to greed for material things, hoarding, and the fault of arrogance, they must still be confessed before the Saṃgha. As will be cited below:"

This is an example used to refute [the opponent's view]. If it is argued that when the materials for robes are exhausted, one cannot face the Saṃgha—just as, for instance, when a cotton robe is torn apart or a precious item is surrendered to a layperson, these are relinquished without being before the Saṃgha—then for what reason must the confession of an offense also be made before the Saṃgha?
If that is so, [the text below asks: why are the two treasures of silk and cotton not separately mentioned in the Vinaya as requiring confession before the Saṃgha?

The answer [below] states: because in the previous case of clothing, one relinquished it before the Saṃgha and consequently confessed the offense before the Saṃgha; now, this silk treasure is being relinquished.

This is not because [the confession] is directed toward the Saṃgha; rather, the Vinaya has omitted the passage concerning the relinquishing of offenses before the Saṃgha. How could one simply omit the text and then claim that an offense may be confessed without being before the Saṃgha?

Since the root Vinaya is thus abbreviated, I have cited the texts from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Mahāsaṃghika-vinaya-mātṛkā*, both of which clearly establish that such a rule is mandated within the Saṃgha.

"If that is so," [the questioner asks], "regarding the offense of *niḥsargika-pāyattika*, the formal regulation (*prajñapti*) must necessarily take place before the Saṃgha. I do not yet know whether a simple *pāyattika* offense may also be confessed collectively.

The answer is as follows: While the ninety offenses (*navati-śikṣāpada*) involve committing an offense due to material things, they differ from these thirty [offenses] which stem from a mind of greed or arrogance.
In terms of the mental state, they are divided into two categories—light and heavy—but in terms of the offense itself, they are equally one *pāyattika*. Therefore, collective confession is permitted.

Question: Since the offenses are identical, how can they be distinguished as light or heavy? Answer: Regarding the thirty [offenses], because the karma produced by greed and pride is heavy, the rule prescribes the relinquishing of the object, the relinquishing of the offense, and the relinquishing of the mind.
If the mind is not relinquished, the two relinquishments will not be accomplished;

therefore, one must repent before the Sangha, which is a superior field of merit. Whether considered in terms of the offense itself or its karmic retribution, how could there be any difference? In all cases, one employs the threefold declaration for repentance.

...as well. Second, the formal acceptance of robes (*cīvara*). This follows the sequential explanation of the text; it should properly be placed third, as the current textual arrangement is inverted. Second, regarding separation:

namely, separation from a village for one night, and separation from a forest hermitage (*āraṇya*) for six nights. Having made a new bedding and furniture (*śayanāsana*), if less than six years have passed, one must hold [it].

One does not fold the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*). Both [the mat and the robe] are lowered. Generally speaking, for those who maintain these items as personal requisites, there is no need to perform the ritual of "purification" (*śuddhi*) or "renunciation" (*utsarga*).
Regarding the *yinnang* (hidden-recliner): it refers to a bag made by sewing together silks and brocades, filled with soft material inside, which one uses to lean against.

The *Qingzhong yi* (Rituals of Light and Heavy Matters) states: "The *yinnang* and the *ruyi* (wish-fulfilling gem) are correctly written as 'yin'. As for the sandals (*jue*), the upper character is pronounced "jiao" (meaning straw sandals) and the lower character is pronounced "mo" (meaning thick socks). This also applies to the robes of the *bhikṣuṇīs*, etc.
This refers to taking robes that have been sold; in all such cases, there is an offense, as it does not accord with the rules of purification (*śuddhi-dharma*).

If the owner is absent—that is, if the person to whom the item was entrusted has passed away—it is designated as "at the border" (*prānta*), meaning it is a frontier region where no one is available to serve as a witness.
It is permitted to take possession for ten days before committing the offense of "excess" (*atireka*). One may also share [the robe] with two or three others.

There is an object that has not yet been divided; since it is unknown which portion belongs to oneself, and because the original property was impure, even if one were to accept it, the acceptance would be invalid. Since the acceptance is invalid, there is no fault in relinquishing it.

Therefore, there is no need to relinquish [the robes]. This is for the purpose of establishing the boundary below. The four obstacles are removed; the three stages of the higher meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are: first, the determination of surplus wealth; second, the determination of what is to be relinquished;
and third, the determination of receiving the robe. One relinquishes them according to their respective locations, because both parties are the Saṃgha.
Furthermore, because there is the principle of returning [the items] again, it is not necessary to assemble [the monks].

The purification through relinquishment (*cetanā-śuddhi*): by forming the resolve to relinquish, this becomes purified. Regarding the "returning of robes before they have been declared pure" (*anukta-pariśuddha-cīvara*):

this refers to when the Sangha has finished returning robes, but has not yet performed the formal declaration of purity (*pariśuddhi-vyavahāra*). If one subsequently sees that a long robe (*atireka-cīvara*) was forgotten, it is all subject to being stained [by the fault of non-relinquishment]. One relies entirely upon the subsequent relinquishment;
however, only the subsequently forgotten item is brought into the act of relinquishment, while the property already relinquished is not stained.
There are two offenses. First, upon seeing the forgotten property, one immediately claims it as one's own; this constitutes greed and defilement, which is the first offense.

Second, one points out the person to whom it was given and fails to return it to the place of relinquishment; this is the second offense. Regarding the question below: although there is indeed forgotten property, one intends in one's mind that there is none.

The Vinaya permits the completion of the act of relinquishment (*pratyākhyāna*). Within a boundary (*sīmā*), if one considers that there are no monks present, one should likewise complete the formal act.

Answer: This is not the same case. Clothing and wealth are non-sentient objects; they do not obstruct the completion of the relinquishment. However, if there are monks within the boundary and one personally believes there are none, this constitutes a failure in the exercise of careful inspection (*saṃvara*).

Therefore, it cannot be treated as a single uniform rule. Regarding the requirement for "purification through overnight stay" (*rātri-pariśuddhi*), it necessitates returning after the night has passed. [Otherwise,] one incurs an offense, violating the rules concerning deficient clothing and impaired decorum.

This is auspicious. One must gauge the timing; if the Sangha is difficult to assemble, one may return the [robe] at the very seat. In the *Śāstra*, this refers to the confession of the six classes of offenses (*ṣaḍ-varga*);

thus, the treatise points to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, as cited in the commentary. Regarding the three conditions: the abandonment of the robe, the confession of the offense, and the severance of the intention [to keep it].

"Going far away" means that if the bhikṣu confessing the offense suddenly encounters circumstances necessitating a long journey, he is also permitted to return it at the seat. "Not expecting a sender" means...
The mind was not what was expected; he suddenly sent it himself.

Once the document was completed, he relinquished his intent. Had there been no intention of relinquishment, the Saṃgha would not have returned it to him, and [the monk] would have incurred a grave offense (pārājika).

Because he relinquished it, the Saṃgha incurs only a *duṣkṛta* offense. Therefore, it is as stated below: "Relinquishing wealth and goods does not constitute a grave offense. This is the classification according to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, which applies universally.
This is one of the five meanings of the Mahāyāna.
"The host" refers to the master of the repentance ceremony. "To establish a vow and set a term": "term" (*yào*) here means a fixed period. "To exhaust" means either to destroy or to bring to an end.

Although one may lack robes or wealth to offer as gifts, seeking the Sangha for the sake of repenting one's transgressions is the same [in principle]; therefore, it is called the "fundamental offense."

It is also recorded accordingly (the first master asserts that when clothing and resources are exhausted, one performs a mental confession for the primary offense; this is equivalent to the ninety [minor] offenses and requires no further assembly of the Sangha to request formal confession. Judging by this text, the meaning of "lacking the Sangha" is correct).
*Shangcan* (upper remainder): This explains the meaning of having an upper remainder segment that is not relinquished.

[The text] frequently mentions "lower" [robes]. Although there may be robes such as those chewed by oxen that must be discarded because they have reached the required dimensions, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* cited above state that robes damaged by fire and the like do not need to be discarded;
this must refer to cases where the fabric is so fragmented and ruined that it no longer counts toward the required dimensions. Regarding the violation concerning the use of robes:

This refers to the forfeiture incurred through the use [of prohibited items]. For each type of robe, there is a *duṣkṛta* offense; now, this *duṣkṛta* is to be confessed together with the *pāyattika*.

According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it is permitted to confess these combined when they belong to different categories. Because some rely on the recitation of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, they claim that [the confession] is not valid. Below follows...
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* specifically states that those belonging to different groups (*visabhāga*) are not permitted to perform confession together;

this is extensively listed and detailed in the commentaries with careful citation of the Vinaya texts. Regarding the common saying among people today that confession is permitted even when the offenses are not identical—provided only that the persons involved are not the same—this is an ancient interpretation.
Although there is a distinction between being guilty of the same offense and a different offense, neither constitutes a state of purity.
One must not confess and purify oneself before such a person; it is only when there is a threat to one’s life that an exception is permitted. This is the present meaning.
The passage beginning with "By means of the sutra" clarifies that during times of leisure and composure, one must not confess before someone who has committed an offense.
One must instead seek out a person of pure knowledge who can give rise to one's superior resolve; only then may it be done.

"How could it be only the external object? This means that it is not merely the external object that is pure; rather, it is because the practitioner encounters it that their superior resolve is aroused.
For instance, even in the case of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, one still requires many people as a "superior object" before the practitioner's superior resolve can be aroused.

If one intends to go down to that place to confess, yet suddenly encounters a corpse lying across the path, although the confession has not yet been performed, it is permitted that [the state of] purity is established.
"Purification. This refers to relying upon that superior object; it is also because the mind exerts pressure [upon the transgression].

According to this [principle], when the internal [mind] relates to the external object, if the object is superior and the mind is earnest, then the offense can be extinguished. Since offenses cannot be purified through the mere performance of ritual methods of repentance (*pratideśanā*), one must not fail to select [a superior object].
"Those who possess both [the offenses] including *sthūlātyaya*": this refers to performing the confession for *sthūlātyaya* and also inviting a presiding confessor (*karmavācanācārya*).

"To claim existence where there is none": this describes the delusion of one capable of confessing. Regarding the two faults mentioned as "concealment" (*chādana*) and "speaking" (*bhāṣaṇa*): "concealment" means hiding [the offense]; "speaking" refers to the offenses of lying by remaining silent during the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* and so forth.
As for the transgressor's lack of knowledge, it is not that they fail to understand when told; for who possesses the principle of innate knowledge (*jāti-jñāna*)? These constitute the three grades.
The "Root" refers to the aforementioned root offenses of concealing [a fault], remaining silent during the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, speaking falsely, and wearing [improper robes].

The "Nine Grades" means that for each of the three aforementioned grades, there is one grade of concealment during the first watch of the night, along with two grades that increase sequentially with each subsequent watch.

First, one should repent of the preliminary acts (*prayoga*), which consist of six grades of *dukkaṭa*. Second, regarding concealment, there are two: first, the root concealment; second, remaining silent [during the recitation].

Concealment (*paticchādana*) and wearing [the robe] constitute three categories together, as stated in the *Shanbu xuemo chao* (Excerpts from the Vinaya-mātṛkā), specifically in the section on Repentance (*Sānti-piàn*).

If one examines the lower [sections], whenever receiving the repentance of another’s offense, one must first inquire whether there are any offenses of concealment that have not yet been repented; if there are none, one simply repents the original *pārājika* or *saṃghāvaśeṣa* downfall.

Therefore, the Great Master said: "Do not recite conventional phrases, causing others to become confused and distressed. When asked, he replied: "It is well to establish a vow"; this is what is meant by "name and reality" (*ming-shi*).

"Reality" refers to the essence itself; that is, to recite the text with meticulous care. By doing so, one loses sight of both the name of the transgression committed and the essential nature of the offense. Regarding "the reckoning of evil": this refers to the evil of breaking the precepts.
Fearing that it might not be counted, one now fails to dread the offense. Because one does not fear the sin, one is held accountable for the fault of being beyond reckoning;
thus, one is said to be shameless. Therefore, it is said: "Before long, one will fall and be reborn in the lower realms."
"According to the text": (1) self-reproach is the sixth; (2) answering "yes" is the seventh; (3) making a vow is a distinct fault;

(4) a private fault refers to a personal transgression; (5) "the next day" means the following morning; (6) "disregarding others" refers to summoning the Saṃgha; (7) "distinct activities" means that each has their own specific conditions.
There are four cases: first, many and easy to collect; second, many and difficult to collect; third, few and easy to collect; fourth, few and difficult to collect.
"Knowledge" refers to one's relatives and friends. As stated in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, this refers to the case where one acquires wealth on the very day the intention to possess it is severed.
"Without entanglement or obstruction" refers to the severance of the intention to relinquish. "Two fingers" refers to the two fingers mentioned in the commentary above.

It is so. Although there are matters concerning material wealth, among the ninety [offenses] there are also those committed due to such matters; however, they do not involve the forfeiture (*naiḥsargika*) prescribed by the rules.
○ Chapter Ten: Explanation of the Section on Miscellaneous Rules for Maintaining the Community.
"Propagation" (liú-tōng) means the circulation and widespread dissemination of the True Dharma for twelve thousand years, ensuring it does not fall to the ground.
There are five kinds of propagation, as detailed in the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts). "Descendants" (*yì*) refers to the ends of garments; "leaves" (*yè*) refers to branches and foliage.

These terms collectively designate the bhikṣus of the Final Age. "Fortunate Destiny" (*jiāyùn*) refers to the period of Śākyamuni’s single transformation; within the three divisions [of the Dharma], this corresponds to the Final Division.

Finally, one should contemplate the Dharma as one contemplates the sun and moon. This is how one knows the distance for the *poṣadha*. Seeking it by way of the body, one collects [the requisites] at the place where food is taken, including the five [conditions] such as illness and weakness.
Next, the Śākyas all share the meaning of "mindfulness" (*smṛti*). As for "removing hindrances" (*āvaraṇa-vinodana*), "hindrance" (*āvaraṇa*) encompasses them all.

Regarding the five hindrances and so forth, there are "before" and "after. "Before" refers to before the meal; "after" refers to the improper time (*akāla*). These indicate the characteristics of what is not the Dharma (*adharma-lakṣaṇa*), indicating the departure from what is non-conforming to the rules (*asamaya*).

Regarding "the path is plain" (*dao su*): "plain" (*su*) means pure and simple. Alternatively, it may be understood as indicating the subsequent condition, namely, the permission to leave and seek out another preceptor.

"Friendship and accomplishment. One polishes and refines oneself through friends to complete one's vessel; there is none who does not require friends to achieve completion. "Transcribing the practice" (xìngxíng):
this refers to transcribing the laws and regulations for correct conduct. Furthermore, it causes the bhikṣus to initiate their practice in accordance with these words.
"Senility" (mào): the *Lǐjì* says, "At eighty years of age, one enters senility. Kǎngchéng says, "Senility is a state of mental confusion and forgetfulness."
"Bì" refers to Bì Prefecture. "Bù" (section) means a subordinate division. It is the name of Mianshang County and Luanchao Village.
"Light before and heavy after" means that while the former consisted of only two fascicles, the latter was increased twofold. "Heavy before and light after":

the former is called "heavy" because its topical categories (*yìmén*) were extensive, whereas the latter is "light" because it contains much abbreviation. According to the principle below, this is the Master’s modesty; he says "the former... [and so on].

Although it is said that this was a later re-translation, from the standpoint of its principles and meaning, such has never been heard of. As for its literary composition, it is brilliant and clear from beginning to end.
There is no need for hesitation; I hope that future readers will not hesitate to regard it as anything other than a complete and thorough exposition.
The Dharma-work is now fully prepared.

It began in the third year of the Huangyou era of the Song dynasty, the year of Xingmao (1051 CE), and concluded on the thirteenth day of the first month of the year of Kuisi (1053 CE) at the Qingsi Hall of Jingzhu Monastery.
At that time, his age was forty-nine. The ten records were thus completed. May he dedicate these roots of goodness to adorn the Pure Land;

may he pass away from this world to be born through transformation within a lotus flower, where he shall behold the Buddha, realize the truth, and extensively deliver all sentient beings. Hereafter...
Those who read this will come to know my aspirations.
*Zhengyuanji*, a Commentary on the *Sifenlü Suiji Jiemoshu*, Scroll Eight (End).

This is a preliminary compilation of the *Śīla-karman-śāstra* (Commentary on the Ritual of Ordination). [Compiled by] Miao Tong.

During the Xuanhe era, the Vinaya Master Wuxiang Zhenjiao traveled to Qiantang for study. He generally did not use existing commentaries, stating that the "Correct Source" lacked woodblocks and that the manuscripts were full of errors;
therefore, he did not use them. Subsequently, due to the fires of war, he followed Vinaya Master Shenshui Xiyan.
I have expounded upon the records transmitted by the Master of the Records (the Master of the Records entrusted them to Yuan, and Yuan entrusted them to Yin). These records are quite detailed.
Alas for these writings! Having circulated for a long time, they have never been carved onto printing blocks.

Like the "three sheep" crossing the river or the "four monkeys" following their whims, later generations have focused on scrutinizing their shortcomings rather than appreciating their virtues. How futile this is! Such is the conduct of their hearts.
He was one who bore the instructions and guidance of his predecessors. Moreover, the mind and wisdom of Master Píng were unfathomable, and his bodily realization remained beyond human knowledge.
Possessing views that transcended the common and manifesting a talent for independent judgment, he drafted the *Jièjì* and *Yèjì*, as well as various other records that have circulated in the world.
By reviving the Nanshan school, how does he differ from Jīngxī, who brought glory to the teachings of Fólǒng?

(Miaotong) Having the honor of being included among the later descendants, I intend to propagate the Way of Nanshan by carving this into woodblocks for circulation in the world, so that the Great Commentary and its three sub-commentaries may be complete in their entirety.
This will spare those of later generations from seeking them elsewhere. Now that the work of opening these commentaries is accomplished, I shall briefly record the date and year.
On the day of the latter *anvaya-vāsa* (winter retreat) in the eighteenth year of the Shaoxing era of the Sagely Song (the Wuchen year),
written by Xiao Shan Bochu (Miaotong) at the Zisheng Lecture Hall in Kuaiji.
